title: NGA: Flood - 08-2026 - Flood – Ondo State, Nigeria (2026-08-18)
content:
Description

Sustained and heavy rainfall across Ondo State beginning in early August 2026 has triggered widespread riverine and urban flooding across at least seven Local Government Areas in the state, inundating homes, submerging roads and bridges, destroying property and displacing large numbers of residents. The flooding is ongoing and worsening, with multiple communities in the riverine south of the state particularly severely affected as water levels continue to rise.

The situation in Ilaje Local Government Area is the most critical. Igbokoda community in Ilaje LGA, including the Naval Base in Igbokoda and the council headquarters, has been submerged. Displaced residents have been observed sleeping under improvised shelters by the roadside, while others have sought refuge with friends and relatives in other LGAs. The Nigerian Red Cross Society Ondo State Branch has formally recommended to the Ondo State Government that an urgent IDP camp be established in a safe LGA to accommodate the displaced population. In Okitipupa LGA, communities including Ayeka, Ikoya, Igbodigo, Igbotako, Erinje, Kuneyin and Apata have been severely affected, with homes and commercial premises submerged, bridges destroyed and movement restricted. Properties worth millions of naira have been lost.

The NRCS Ondo State Branch conducted a rapid assessment of three of the seven affected LGAs; Ondo West, Ilaje and Okitipupa through the branch volunteers. Assessment of the remaining four LGAs (Irele, Ese-odo, Ile-oluji/Okeigbo and Odigbo) is ongoing in coordination with the Ondo State Emergency Management Agency (ODSEMA) and NEMA. From the three assessed LGAs alone, 2,527 households have been confirmed as affected. The true scale of impact across all seven LGAs is significantly higher and will be confirmed upon completion of the full assessment.

The Ondo State Government has deployed amphibious machines to clear waterways and drainage channels in Ilaje LGA under the direction of Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa, targeting the removal of obstructions from canals and river channels to reduce the risk of further flooding. NEMA has also conducted an assessment in the affected LGAs, attributing the severity of the flooding to blocked waterways, indiscriminate refuse disposal and illegal structures erected along river channels. Ondo State is explicitly listed among 21 states identified by the Federal Government on critical flood alert for 2 to 15 August 2026, which covers 944 communities at highest risk nationally.

title: Indonesian Humanitarian Coordination Platform: Situation Report No. 1 - Earthquake and Tsunami in Flores and Surrounding Areas (17 August 2026)
content:
Situation Report

• Telecommunications services have been restored to 86.02 per cent. According to monitoring by the Ministry of Communications and Digital Affairs as of 16 August at 18:00 WIB, 683 of 794 base transceiver station (BTS) sites across 11 regencies/cities were operational; 111 sites remained out of service. Disruptions included power outages affecting 701 sites and transmission problems affecting 93 sites. Services in Alor, Lembata, and North Central Timor have been fully restored.

• Manggarai Regional Hospital sustained damage that affected clinical and administrative services. Patients are being treated temporarily in the hospital grounds. BNPB and the Ministry of Health will establish a field hospital at Golo Dukal Stadium in Ruteng. The facility is still being prepared and has not yet been declared operational.

• MDMC reported that many residents have chosen to remain outside their homes or in open areas because of trauma and concern about continuing aftershocks. Some displaced people are staying in public facilities, including sports halls and open fields, while others have erected emergency tents in the yards around their homes.

• The Larantuka–Maumere road is open and passable by logistics vehicles. The Ende– Nagekeo road remains completely cut off by landslide debris, and work to clear alternative routes is ongoing. Sections of the Ruteng–Km 210 and Aegela–Ende City roads have been affected by severe landslides. The Government is prioritising the deployment of heavy equipment to these areas.

title: Myanmar Flood 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRMM024)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
05-08-2026

What happened, where and when?

Heavy and continuous monsoon rainfall caused rising water levels and flooding across low-lying and flood-prone areas of Ayeyarwady Region. The situation escalated on 30 July 2026, when an embankment near Myit Kyo Village in Laymyatna Township breached, and floodwaters rapidly entered Laymyatna town and surrounding communities. The flooding has affected residential areas, agricultural land, roads, and public infrastructure, with communities along the Ngawun River being particularly affected. Water levels in the Ngawun River have exceeded the danger level and remain elevated, with further rainfall potentially worsening the situation.

The Myanmar Red Cross Society (MRCS) Regional Branch started the response with its own resources on 1 August 2026, and the information indicates impacts across 5 wards, 23 village tracts, and 122 villages in Laymyatna Township; 2 wards, 16 village tracts, and 14 villages in Yegyi Township; and 10 village tracts and 33 villages in Hinthada Township. The most significant impacts are in Laymyethna, Yegyi, and Hinthada Townships, among other townships in Ayeyarwady, particularly communities located along the Ngawun River and other low-lying areas. In August 2026, the request was submitted to IFRC by MRCS Headquarters, following six days after the trigger date, as the situation had escalated and required more support from the Headquarters level.

The same preliminary information estimated that approximately 8,907 households, representing 28,455 people, had been affected and displaced to 28 evacuation camps, including community centres, schools, temporary shelters, and monasteries. The situation remains ongoing, with water levels continuing to pose a risk to additional communities. Rescue and evacuation operations are underway, but access to affected areas is severely constrained by inundated roads, making motorboats the primary means of rescue and emergency transportation. The number of affected people and the overall extent of damage remain provisional and subject to further assessment, particularly as additional rainfall during the monsoon may further expand the impact.

title: Attacks on Health Care Bi-Monthly News Brief, 22 July - 04 August 2026
content:
Attacks on health care were relentless in 2025. Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) recorded 2,546 incidents in 33 countries in which damage to or the destruction of health care facilities was reported on at least 790 occasions, 455 health workers were killed, 218 kidnapped and 263 arrested.

In 2025, violence by state actors was reported in 26 countries and territories, an increase of nine compared to 2024. Over 80% of these incidents involved state actors attacking health care outside their own territory, including through cross-border operations or attacks in contested areas. The vast majority of such incidents were attributed to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) in Iran, Lebanon, the oPt, Syria, and Yemen and to Russian forces in Ukraine. Other state actors linked to attacks on health care outside their own territories included the Bolivarian National Intelligence Service (in Venezuela), the Burundi National Defence Force (in the DRC), the Indian Armed Forces (in Pakistan), Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (in Israel), the Turkish Armed Forces (in Syria), the US Armed Forces (in Yemen), and the Ukrainian Armed Forces (in Russia).

The report includes detailed profiles of 21 countries and territories where many acts of violence against health care by state parties and non-state armed groups, including organized criminal groups, took place. These include:

  • Africa: Burkina Faso, Cameroon, the CAR, the DRC, Ethiopia, Mali, Nigeria, Somalia, South Sudan and Sudan
  • Asia: Myanmar and Pakistan
  • Middle East and Europe: Lebanon, Iran, the occupied Palestinian territory; Syria, Ukraine and Yemen
  • The Americas: Colombia, Haiti and Mexico
  • Year in Review: 2025; 2024; 2023

title: UNHCR Romania Ukraine Refugee Situation Weekly Update #209 - 17 August 2026
content:
Key figures

215,532 refugees obtained temporary protection and refugee status in Romania (as of end June 2026).

1,949 refugees supported with community-based protection activities in 2026.

5,775 refugees provided with protection counselling services and legal support in 2026.

1,872 refugees supported with livelihood and employment services in 2026.

Highlight

The UNHCR Inter-Agency Coordination Unit finalised its assessment of the funding situation of the 2026 Refugee Response Plan (RRP). Of the $48.6 million appealed for by the 43 RRP partners, only $6.4 million (13 per cent) had been received, leaving a funding gap of $42.2 million. Funding remained particularly limited for Basic Needs, which had received no funding against the appeal, Child Protection (1 per cent funded), Education (4 per cent), Gender-Based Violence (5 per cent), and Health (11 per cent). 32 partners reported receiving no new funding. The funding shortfall is constraining operational capacity: 13 partners reported no ongoing activities, while another 10 maintained only limited or occasional activities, often through voluntary efforts or alternative funding sources. These constraints come at a time when needs persist among refugees from Ukraine and progress towards inclusion remains uneven. The 2025 SocioEconomic Insights Survey (SEIS) found that 34 per cent of surveyed refugee households experienced severe material and social deprivation, twice Romania's national rate of 17 per cent, while 40 per cent reported a decrease in household income over the previous 12 months. Financial pressure is translating into difficult trade-offs: among households resorting to crisis coping mechanisms, 33 per cent reported reducing essential health expenditure and 13 per cent reducing education expenditure. At the same time, limited RRP funding is constraining partners' capacity to respond. By June 2026, partners had reached only 650 people with Basic Needs assistance against a target of over 23,000, 1,524 children with Child Protection services against a target of 4,957, and 4,442 people with support to access health services against a target of nearly 24,000. These gaps illustrate the growing mismatch between persistent refugee needs and resources available to address them, risking further constraints on refugees' access to essential services and longer-term socio-economic inclusion in Romania. Detailed findings are illustrated in the Inter-Agency accompanying infographic. The results will help inform fundraising efforts to ensure continued provision of essential support to refugees.

title: Afghanistan WASH Cluster Bulletin, Issue 1, January –June 2026
content:
Performance Overview

During the first half of 2026, Afghanistan’s WASH response continued to operate in a complex humanitarian environment characterized by prolonged drought and water scarcity, localized flooding, earthquakes, Acute Watery Diarrhoea (AWD), displacement, and increasing return movements from Iran and Pakistan. These overlapping shocks placed additional pressure on already limited water resources and essential WASH infrastructure, particularly in underserved and high-risk communities. Against an estimated 15.9M PiN and an annual WASH Cluster target of 7.84M people, 25 operational partners reached 908,176 beneficiaries between January and June 2026, without double counting across WASH interventions. Partners delivered an integrated package of lifesaving and resilience-building assistance, including safe drinking water, gender and disability sensitive sanitation, hygiene promotion, critical WASH supplies, and basic WASH services in schools, health facilities and nutrition centers. At intervention level, partners reported reaching over 1.01 million people with safe water, 1.48 million through hygiene promotion, 987,447 with critical WASH supplies, and 118,633 with sanitation services. In addition, 608,954 people benefited from WASH services in institutions. These intervention level achievements may overlap and should therefore be distinguished from the Cluster’s unduplicated overall reach of 908,176 people. Emergency WASH assistance remained particularly important at key border reception and transit locations in response to continued return movements from Iran and Pakistan. Partners sustained water supply, sanitation, hygiene promotion and essential WASH supplies while the Cluster supported preparedness, operational coordination and continuity of services. AWD preparedness and response also remained a priority as rising temperatures, deteriorating water availability and water-quality risks increased the threat of waterborne diseases. Partners strengthened water-quality monitoring, chlorination, hygiene promotion and coordination with health actors, complemented by continued engagement through AWD coordination mechanisms. Alongside emergency interventions, partners continued rehabilitating and constructing climate-resilient water systems to improve sustainable access to safe water and strengthen the resilience of communities exposed to recurrent drought and climate-related shocks. However, response coverage remained geographically uneven, with substantial differences in achievement and operational partner presence across provinces. The Cluster continued using response monitoring and partner-presence analysis to identify underserved areas, support geographic prioritization and promote more effective use of available operational capacity. The WASH Cluster maintained national and sub-national coordination throughout the reporting period, bringing together partners, government counterparts and inter-sector actors to review response progress, identify gaps and address implementation bottlenecks. Engagement focused on preparedness for population movements and AWD, border response coordination, administrative and MoU-related challenges, continuity of essential services, and strengthening partner capacity in priority locations. The Cluster also maintained donor engagement and advocacy while contributing to efforts to strengthen localization and the participation of national organizations in humanitarian coordination. Despite these efforts, the response remained critically underfunded. By mid-year, only US$43.06M of the US$163.3M required had been received approximately 26% of requirements, leaving a funding gap of around US$120.2M. Funding shortfalls, rising operational costs, administrative delays, limited emergency supplies and uneven partner capacity continued to restrict response scale and coverage. With return movements, drought and water scarcity, seasonal AWD risks and potential climate-related shocks expected to continue during the second half of 2026, additional donor support and strengthened operational partnerships will be critical to sustain life-saving WASH services, close geographic and sectoral gaps, and strengthen preparedness and resilience.

title: Colombia Earthquake: Situation Report #3 (August 13, 2026)
content:
Project HOPE's Emergency Response Team is on the ground in the Valle del Cauca and Risaralda departments of Colombia, distributing hygiene supplies and rapidly assessing needs after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck 150 miles west of Bogotá causing widespread damage, landslides, and impacted critical infrastructure across a large geographic area.

Situational Context

The full scale of the impact continues to be assessed since a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck near San Jose del Palmar, Colombia, on Monday August 10, continued to be assessed. Damage extends across a wide geographic area, including urban and rural areas across a range of socio-economic levels. More than 395 municipalities across western Colombia were affected and connectivity and access issues continue to limit a full assessment.

As of this morning, August 13, Colombia’s national disaster management agency (UNGRD) reports 273 dead, 3,824 injured, and 377 missing nationwide. Other sources state the number of missing at nearly 500. Approximately 75% of fatalities are concentrated in Quibdó, Pereira, and Valle del Cauca.

Over 12,500 homes have been destroyed and nearly 75,000 homes have been damaged, and 172 structures collapsed. Search and rescue operations, led by the National Risk and Disaster Management System, are transitioning from active rescue to recovery in the hardest hit areas. Chocó’s SAR phase was formally closed yesterday after a family of four was located alive. In Pereira and Cali, teams report shifting to recovery of bodies as the window for finding and rescuing survivors narrows, though efforts continue.

With 216 health centers sustaining damage, the need for hygiene, water, and medical support is significant. Access to more rural areas, especially Chocó, continues to be difficult. Chocó also sustained a 4.2 magnitude aftershock this morning, and officials stated the aftershock hindered utility restoration efforts.

title: Yemen: A Sharp Escalation in Houthi Strike Lethality, and a Widening Cross-Border Campaign (3–9 August 2026)
content:
119 incidents and 102 confirmed fatalities. Two Houthi mass-casualty strikes on 6 August, against Nation's Shield camps in Hadramawt and against Marib, killed some 45 and drove the week's toll, as ballistic missiles and drones concentrated on the Marib and Hadramawt fronts.

Data Analysis

119 operational incidents and 102 fatalities were recorded across Yemen from 3 to 9 August 2026, in a week marked by a sharp escalation in the lethality of the conflict. Ansar Allah, the Houthi movement, initiated 36 incidents causing 61 fatalities, and Yemeni Government forces of the Presidential Leadership Council initiated 32 incidents. The single deadliest event was a Houthi strike on camps of the Nation's Shield Forces in Hadramawt on 6 August, which killed approximately 30, while a Houthi ballistic missile and drone strike on Marib the same day killed a further 15, making 6 August the deadliest day of the week with 49 fatalities. 8 August recorded the highest incident volume at 24. Ballistic missiles, drones and artillery were the dominant conflict modalities, concentrated on the Marib and Hadramawt fronts, and Houthi forces also conducted cross-border attacks against Saudi and maritime targets. Hazards, principally flooding and a declared public health emergency in Marib, caused a further 20 fatalities.

title: Syria: The Assad Death Sentence, Israeli Entrenchment in the South, and Consolidation Rather Than Stabilisation (3–9 August 2026)
content:
178 incidents and 20 confirmed fatalities, a low toll for the volume. An in-absentia death sentence against Bashar al-Assad drove a nationwide wave of at least 17 peaceful demonstrations, as Israeli forces sustained 17 operations in the south and rejected any withdrawal.

Data Analysis

178 operational incidents and 20 fatalities were recorded across Syria from 7 to 13 August 2026, a low toll relative to the incident volume that reflects a week dominated by political mobilisation, policing and localised violence rather than large-scale armed conflict. The defining development was the issuance of an in-absentia death sentence against former President Bashar al-Assad and other senior former officials, which triggered a nationwide wave of at least 17 public demonstrations marking a major milestone in the postAssad transitional justice process. Israeli military activity in the south continued at a steady tempo, with 17 recorded incidents concentrated in Quneitra and Dar'a and comprising incursions, checkpoints and searches with zero Syrian fatalities, coinciding with an Israeli statement rejecting withdrawal from Syrian territory. Syrian security forces sustained a high tempo of law-enforcement and counter-narcotics operations and dismantled an ISIS-linked cell in Khan Arnabeh, Quneitra. Dar'a recorded the highest incident volume at 25, and 11 August was the peak day with 40 incidents.

title: Situation report #1 - Nagekeo earthquake, East Nusa Tenggara (NTT) - Update: Saturday, 15 August 2026
content:

Magnitude: M 7.7 (BMKG / USGS). The earthquake was triggered by an upthrust fault mechanism (Flores Back Arc Thrust) at a shallow depth of 10–15 km. USGS estimates that up to 1.5 million people experienced strong shaking at intensity IV–V MMI across Flores Island to Sumbawa.

Earthquake Epicentre: Offshore at coordinates 8.41° S – 121.39° E, approximately 30 km northeast of Mbay, Nagekeo Regency, East Nusa Tenggara.

title: Comoros | Volcanic Ash: Simplified Early Action Protocol - Final Report (EAP №: sEAP2023KM01, Operation N°: MDRKM012 / PKM514), June 2026
content:
SUMMARY OF THE SIMPLIFIED EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL

The IFRC Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) allocated CHF 210,958 for the implementation of anticipatory actions to reduce and mitigate the impact of volcanic ash in Comoros. This simplified Early Action Protocol (sEAP) includes an allocation of CHF 136,906 to preposition stock and undertake annual readiness activities in order to implement early actions, if and when the trigger is reached. The early actions to be conducted have been pre-agreed with the National Society and are described in the simplified Early Action Protocol [Link to the EAP summary on IFRC’s appeals website].

This Final report summarizes the achievements, results, challenges, and lessons learned from the implementation of the sEAP for Volcanic Ash in Comoros, implemented from April 2024 to April 2026. The operation aimed to strengthen anticipatory action capacities and preparedness for volcanic ash hazards associated with Mount Karthala through institutional capacity building, community engagement, institutional coordination, and the prepositioning of critical response supplies. During the reporting period, the activation trigger threshold for the volcanic ash sEAP was not reached and, therefore, no early actions were activated.

Nevertheless, the operation achieved its primary preparedness objectives by establishing the systems, capacities, partnerships, and prepositioned resources required for rapid activation should volcanic activity escalate in the future. Through the implementation of readiness activities, the Comoros Red Crescent (CoRC) directly reached 4,121 community members with preparedness and risk awareness interventions, trained 160 volunteers across Health, WASH, PGI and DRR/CCA sectors, strengthened community feedback and engagement mechanisms, and prepositioned essential protective, WASH, and dignity supplies in Ngazidja. The operating context continued to be shaped by the persistent threat posed by Mount Karthala, while implementation built on lessons learned from previous disruptions caused by the cholera outbreak and Tropical Cyclone Chido. CoRC further strengthened its institutional preparedness and operational capacity through enhanced coordination with key government partners, particularly the Directorate General for Civil Security (DGSC) and the Karthala Volcanological Observatory (OVK), ensuring alignment with the latest risk assessments and preparedness planning.

Collaboration with IFRC, the French Red Cross PIROI, and other technical and Movement partners also contributed to timely progress against planned objectives, strengthening logistics, stock management, anticipatory action systems, and overall readiness for a potential volcanic emergency.

title: Colombia | Earthquake - DREF Operation (MDRCO036)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
10-08-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 10 August 2026, at 07:34 a.m. local time, a magnitude 7.4 (Mw) earthquake struck western Colombia. According to the Colombian Geological Service (SGC), the epicentre was located in the municipality of San José del Palmar, department of Chocó, at a depth of 103 km.

The SGC identified it as the highest-magnitude earthquake recorded in Colombia during the twenty-first century. The main event was followed by at least 103 aftershocks, including a magnitude 4.8 event recorded near San José del Palmar 44 minutes later. Further aftershocks may continue to occur.

The earthquake was felt across much of Colombia and was also reported in parts of Panama and Venezuela. Initial reports indicated possible impacts in as many as 16 departments. As information was subsequently verified and consolidated, the latest available humanitarian update, issued on 12 August 2026, reported impacts across 14 departments and 395 municipalities. The most severe impacts are concentrated in Chocó and Valle del Cauca, in western Colombia, and in Risaralda, Caldas and Quindío, which comprise the Coffee Region (Eje Cafetero). Major affected urban areas include the departmental capitals of Quibdó, Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Armenia.

Preliminary information indicates significant loss of life and injuries, as well as damage to housing, public buildings and essential infrastructure. Access and communications constraints, particularly in remote and rural areas of Chocó, continue to complicate the consolidation of information and the identification of affected communities and priority humanitarian needs.

Following the earthquake, the coordination mechanisms of the National Disaster Risk Management System (SNGRD) were activated at national and territorial levels. The National Government convened the National Committee for Disaster Management and established a Unified Command Post at the headquarters of the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) to coordinate search and rescue
operations, emergency assistance, initial damage and needs assessments, and the deployment of response capacities.

Given the magnitude of the earthquake, its geographical reach and the severity of the reported impacts, the National Government declared a national disaster situation on the same day. This declaration enables the administrative, budgetary and coordination mechanisms required to mobilise resources, support affected territorial authorities and facilitate the immediate response and subsequent recovery.

The situation remains fluid. Assessments by the Colombian Red Cross Society and the competent government authorities are ongoing, including in remote and hard-to-reach areas. Consequently, the situation overview, geographical scope, identified needs and reported figures are expected to evolve as further information is verified and consolidated.

title: NGA: Flood - 08-2026 - Nigeria: Flood – Lafia, Nasarawa State (2026-08-15)
content:
Description

In the early hours of Wednesday, 13 August 2026, between approximately 4:42am and 8:39am, a heavy downpour struck Lafia, the capital of Nasarawa State, triggering severe urban flooding across four communities in Lafia Local Government Area: Bukansidi, Millionaires Quarters, Sadaji Junction/Police B Division and the Makurdi Road/Local Government Secretariat area. The intense and sustained rainfall overwhelmed the area’s inadequate drainage infrastructure, causing floodwaters to inundate residential buildings, damage essential public facilities and disrupt livelihoods.

In total, 37 houses were destroyed across the four affected communities, with further damage reported to household property, non-food items and furniture workshops in the affected areas. Many furniture workshops and businesses along the flooded streets sustained significant losses. Floodwaters also caused heavy traffic disruption across Lafia metropolis. A total of 307 persons were displaced by the flooding and are currently sheltering in host communities within Lafia LGA.

No deaths or injuries were recorded. The displaced population now faces pressing needs for shelter support, food, non-food items and psychosocial assistance, with particular attention required for the most vulnerable among them including women, children and older persons. The Nigerian Red Cross Society Nasarawa Branch conducted a rapid assessment of the affected communities, and the figures in this report reflect confirmed assessment findings.

Nasarawa State and Lafia LGA sit within a wider flood-risk context: the NiMet 2026 Seasonal Climate Prediction specifically identifies Lafia and Doma LGAs among the areas in Nasarawa most likely to experience severe flooding, and the NIHSA 2026 Annual Flood Outlook lists Nasarawa among 23 high-risk states, with the state’s vulnerability closely linked to proximity to the River Benue, rapid urban expansion and inadequate drainage infrastructure. The flooding on 13 August 2026 is consistent with this forecast pattern, and further flooding is anticipated as the rainy season peaks through September.

title: IDN: Earthquake - 08-2026 - Impact Assessment Report: East Nusa Tenggara Earthquake (2026-08-15)
content:
Description

An earthquake with a magnitude of 7.7 struck the Nagekeo Regency, East Nusa Tenggara (NTT) Province, on Saturday (15/08) at 04:58 WIB. The earthquake occurred at a depth of 15 km, with coordinates located at 8.41 S – 121.39 E, approximately 30 km Northeast of Mbay, Nagekeo Regency.

The earthquake triggered a tsunami warning. According to BMKG (Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency) monitoring, tsunami waves were detected in several areas with sea level heights reaching 0.94 meters in Maurole–Ende, 0.36 meters in Labuan Bajo, 0.38 meters at Kewapante Port–Sikka, and 0.25 meters in East Flores. The tsunami warning was officially lifted at 07:30 WIB.

Casualties and Damages by Region:

  • East Manggarai Regency: 14 fatalities and 2 people seriously injured. Data on building and public facility damage is currently being processed.
  • Manggarai Regency: 14 fatalities, 7 people seriously injured, 5 slightly injured, and 15 people displaced. Recorded damage includes 28 heavily damaged houses, 9 moderately damaged houses, and 9 slightly damaged houses.
  • Ende Regency: 2 fatalities and 1 person seriously injured. Impacted infrastructure includes 15 slightly damaged houses, 1 community health center (Puskesmas), and 1 house of worship.
  • Sikka Regency: 3 fatalities, 1 person seriously injured, 3 slightly injured, and 4 people reported missing.
  • Nagekeo, West Manggarai, and Ngada Regencies: These areas were affected; however, casualty and damage assessments are still ongoing.
  • Bima City: 1 person slightly injured, 2 moderately damaged houses, and 1 house of worship affected.

Total Impact Summary:
A total of 33 people have died, 11 are seriously injured, 11 have minor injuries, and 4 people remain missing. Furthermore, 15 individuals have been displaced. Infrastructure damage consists of 28 heavily damaged houses, 11 moderately damaged, 24 slightly damaged, 12 community health center, and 2 houses of worship.

Based on preliminary information from BNPB (National Disaster Management Authority), reports of casualties and damage to homes, government facilities, and infrastructure continue to come in from several affected areas. In Nagekeo Regency, approximately 2,000 residents conducted self-evacuations as a precaution following the quake and tsunami warning. Field verification and data collection are ongoing.

As of Saturday, August 15, 2026, at 02:55 pm, 172 aftershocks have been recorded with magnitudes ranging from 2.5 to 6.2. BMKG urges the public to remain vigilant regarding potential aftershocks. According to current reports, community activities in the affected areas have returned to normal. Meanwhile, rescue teams are still searching for 4 victims who reportedly fell from a boat during the event.

title: IDN: Earthquake - 08-2026 - Field Report Update 1: M7.7 East Nusa Tenggara Earthquake #2 (2026-08-16)
