title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 14 August 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Humanitarian response efforts continue across the Occupied Palestinian Territory despite persistent restrictions and funding shortfalls.
  • In Gaza, most people remain internally displaced, in harsh living conditions, and exposed to ongoing military strikes; in early July, 90 per cent was experiencing moderate-to-high water insecurity, an increase from 84 per cent in June, a survey finds.
  • Every fourth Palestinian injured in Gaza since October 2023 is estimated to live with spinal cord or brain injuries among other potentially life-changing conditions, while the entry of rehabilitation supplies and assistive products remains restricted.
  • In the West Bank, a large-scale operation by Israeli forces in Qalandiya Camp injured 51 Palestinians and disrupted health services. Nine structures were also demolished in nearby Kafr Aqab and near Qalandiya checkpoint, affecting 71 people.
  • In just one week, 38 settler attacks were reported, resulting in casualties, property damage or both. In Tuba, Masafer Yatta, settlers injured five Palestinians and destroyed three homes, displacing 23 people, including 14 children.
  • Israeli authorities demolished 25 Palestinian-owned structures in eight incidents, displacing 29 people, including 17 children. The demolitions included part of a school in Masafer Yatta, affecting 54 students.

Overview

In a statement issued on 12 August for International Youth Day, Deputy Special Coordinator, Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov said that for Palestinian youth, hopes for dignity, opportunity and a peaceful future remain constrained “by occupation, conflict, displacement, violence and profound uncertainty.”

In Gaza, young people have borne “the devastating consequences of the ongoing conflict, including persistent violence, the loss of loved ones, repeated displacement and the widespread destruction of homes, schools and universities.” Dr. Alakbarov warned that the future of an entire generation in Gaza is threatened by “the collapse of essential services, disruption of education and loss of livelihoods.” In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, “youth continue to face escalating violence, expanding settler presence, severe restrictions on movement and access, and shrinking economic opportunities.”

Dr. Alakbarov, who is also the Acting United Nations Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, reaffirmed UN’s commitment to work alongside young people in Palestine, advocating for their rights and supporting access to education, health, decent work, meaningful participation and pathways to economic and social recovery.

Gaza Strip

The reporting period for this section is 3-9 August unless otherwise specified.

The humanitarian situation in Gaza remained critical, with military activities continuing across the Strip, causing more casualties and displacement.

According to the Ministry of Health (MoH) in Gaza, which operates under the de facto authorities, seven Palestinians were reported killed, including those who died of wounds and had their bodies retrieved from under the rubble, and 28 people were injured between 5 and 12 August. This brings the overall reported casualty toll since the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 to a total of 1,259 fatalities and 4,148 injuries, according to MoH.

So far in 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) has recorded 45 attacks affecting health care in the Gaza Strip, nearly half of them in Rafah. In most cases, health transport was affected and the delivery of health care obstructed. The majority of reported incidents occurred during medical evacuation operations in the vicinity of Rafah crossing, convoys were obstructed, delayed or searched, and, in some cases, patients or their companions were detained.

Access to safe drinking water remains a challenge for the people of Gaza. The Light Touch Monitoring Survey completed by the Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) Cluster in early July shows that 90 per cent of the population are experiencing frequent, unpredictable disruptions in access to safe, clean, and reliable water for daily drinking, cooking, and hygiene, an increase from 84 per cent in the previous month. At the governorate level, Gaza city scored the lowest, with 92 per cent of surveyed households moderately-to-highly water insecure, followed by Khan Younis at 90 per cent and Deir al Balah at 87 per cent.

Despite ongoing efforts to increase water trucking operations to address the overwhelming needs (see cluster section below), challenges persist. Since early July, for instance, WASH partners have been unable to access approximately 5,000 people sheltering in six displacement sites in northern Rafah due to ongoing insecurity and stray bullets.

When it comes to hygiene and sanitation conditions, the proportion of households reporting sewage or sludge within 10 metres of their shelter decreased to 43 per cent, from 52 per cent in June, while those reporting nearby solid waste piles declined from 43 to 26 per cent. Regular domestic waste collection at household level also improved slightly, increasing from 65 to 68 per cent. Consistent funding, more approvals to bring in spare parts, and renewed access to Gaza’s landfills, which are in the access-restricted areas, remain essential.

According to the Health Cluster’s Rehabilitation Task Force, a quarter of those injured in Gaza since the escalation of hostilities in October 2023, are estimated to live with potentially life-changing injuries such as amputations, spinal cord injuries and traumatic brain injuries. According to the task force’s latest report, MoH data suggests that children account for 18 per cent of amputations and 31 per cent of spinal cord and traumatic brain injuries. The report notes that there are no specialized paediatric rehabilitation services available in Gaza.

Overall, the task force estimates that approximately 2 per cent of Gaza’s population – as it was before the October 2023 escalation – is now living with severe conflict-related injuries.

The importation of rehabilitation equipment, supplies and assistive products continues to face significant constraints, including engine oil and spares for generators. No rehabilitation equipment for rehabilitation facilities entered Gaza between May 2024 and 14 April 2026, the task force notes, adding that the average waiting time for pending shipments containing assistive products is 136 days (as of 14 April 2026). According to the report, overstretched rehabilitation services, combined with shortages of essential equipment, assistive products and consumables, are contributing to preventable secondary complications and further increasing pressure on already limited rehabilitation capacity; presently, about 30 per cent of inpatient beds in remaining specialist rehabilitation services are reportedly occupied by patients with advanced pressure sores. Limited beds are also driving early discharge, increasing risks of deterioration, loss of function and avoidable readmission, the report says.

On 4 August, in North Gaza, a 13-year-old child was injured by the detonation of an abandoned explosive ordnance at his displacement site, as reported by Mine Action partners. Since October 2023, partners have reported a total of 589 explosive ordnance incidents across Gaza, resulting in the killing of 274 people and the injury of 1,142. For background, see last week’s report. For mine action response during the reporting period, see below.

Incoming Supplies

According to data collected by the Logistics Cluster, the UN and partners’ aid offloading rate, representing the proportion of truckloads that were successfully offloaded at Kerem Shalom against those authorized to be manifested each day, increased from 77 per cent in the previous reporting period to 87 per cent in the current one. The Egyptian corridor continues to face the highest levels of truck returns and rejections with a 72 per cent offloading rate. The Jordanian route was the most utilized route for UN and partners’ humanitarian cargo entering Gaza during the week, with 170 truckloads offloaded. Kerem Shalom remained the only operational crossing point for cargo.

On the commercial front, data from the Gaza Chamber of Commerce, shared with the Cash Working Group, indicates that the private sector collected 878 truckloads into Gaza between 3 and 9 August. Overall, the number of commercial truckloads reported as entering Gaza has remained stable in recent weeks, with only minor variations. This remains insufficient to sustain the demand. Moreover, of all private sector trucks, 264 (30 per cent) still carried non-essential items, at the expense of more critical supplies as shelter and WASH materials. Only eight trucks reportedly carried animal feed and two medical equipment.

According to the Chamber of Commerce, prices of basic commodities on the local market remained relatively stable, with only minor variations compared to the previous week. According to the Gaza Consumer Index, the inflation rate has increased to 209 per cent more than the time before October 2023. Cash-out fees equally remain stable at 7-8 per cent, according to Cash Working Group, but they are again closely monitored in light of the announced development of the banking system.

The UN is only able to confirm the entry of supplies tracked by UN 2720. For breakdowns of those, see the online UN 2720 Mechanism Dashboard.

For a detailed account of the latest humanitarian operations in Gaza, see Annex 1 below.

West Bank

The reporting period for this section is 4 to 10 August unless otherwise specified.

Humanitarian needs across the West Bank continued to be driven by operations by Israeli forces, settler violence, demolitions and movement restrictions, which disrupted access to essential services and constrained humanitarian operations. In Qalandiya Camp, a large-scale two-day operation by Israeli forces resulted in dozens of injuries, temporary displacement, damage to residential property and disruption of health services.

Despite these constraints, Health Cluster partners continued to support life-saving and essential health services through a network of 870 service points, including 59 hospitals, 477 primary health-care centres, 230 mobile clinic locations and 16 emergency centres. Mobile clinics remain particularly critical for communities in Area C, the “Seam Zone” and H2 area of Hebron, where they are often the main or only source of essential primary health care. Many facilities run by the Ministry of Health have reduced operating hours and service days amid the ongoing fiscal crisis. In addition, shortages of medicines, medical supplies and consumables, which the Ministry has attributed to the prolonged withholding of Palestinian clearance revenues, have persisted since at least early June and continue to affect the availability and continuity of care. Checkpoints, road closures and operations by Israeli forces also continued to delay or prevent the movement of ambulances, mobile health teams, patients and health workers.

Against this backdrop, according to the latest WHO data, which cover incidents through the end of July, 37 attacks on health care were recorded in July, compared with eight in June and a monthly average of about 10 incidents during the first six months of 2026, bringing the total recorded between January and July to 98. Overall, these attacks affected 83 health transport vehicles and 11 health facilities and resulted in 33 injuries and four fatalities. Obstruction of health-care delivery was documented in 92 incidents, while 66 involved the use of force against health care, 25 involved the arrest or detention of health personnel or patients, and 13 involved militarized searches of health personnel, facilities or transport. WHO identifies obstruction and detention at checkpoints, full closures during operations and requirements for “prior coordination” of ambulance movements among the factors impeding access to health care across the West Bank.

In July, WASH partners delivered more than 9,000 cubic metres of water across the West Bank (66 per cent of which supported internally displaced people) and distributed more than 400 household water tanks. Partners rehabilitated nearly 15 kilometres of water networks benefiting more than 65,000 people, installed or rehabilitated 127 household latrines, provided sewage desludging services to displaced populations in the northern West Bank and collected 200 metric tonnes of solid waste from displacement sites. Nearly 1,200 household hygiene kits were distributed, about half to internally displaced people.

In the northern West Bank, where the humanitarian situation remains particularly severe following prolonged operations by Israeli forces and large-scale displacement, child protection partners have provided psychosocial support, awareness-raising, in-kind assistance, services for children with disabilities and case management to more than 29,600 children and 14,300 adults since the beginning of 2026. In July, mine action partners conducted 761 sessions to educate people on explosive ordnance risks, awareness and conflict preparedness and protection, reaching over 11,600 people across Tulkarm, Hebron, Tubas, Jenin, Nablus and Bethlehem governorates. According to the Palestinian Mine Action Centre and Palestinian Explosive Ordnance Disposal Police, nine explosive ordnance-related casualties were recorded across the West Bank between January and July 2026.

Operations by Israeli Forces

During the reporting period, no Palestinian fatalities were reported in the West Bank. At least 89 Palestinians were injured by Israeli forces or Israeli settlers, most during a large-scale operation in Qalandiya refugee camp, in northern East Jerusalem, and six during two separate raids in Burqa, in Nablus governorate.

The operation in Qalandiya Camp, with an estimated 16,900 residents, took place on 5 and 6 August, involving extensive deployments of Israeli forces, military bulldozers and other heavy vehicles. Israeli forces sealed the camp’s entrances for about 48 hours and restricted movement within the camp. The majority of residential buildings in the camp were searched, with some residents reporting that family members were confined to single rooms for prolonged hours. Israeli forces took over three houses, as well as the offices of the camp’s Popular Committee and the Jerusalem Governorate, for use as temporary interrogation centres. At least six households were temporarily displaced from their homes and sought shelter with relatives and neighbours; all have since returned. Local sources reported that approximately 150 Palestinians were detained and interrogated inside the camp, most of whom were subsequently released. On 6 August, Israeli forces entered the UNRWA Kalandia Training Centre and inspected the premises before leaving after approximately an hour.

According to the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS), 51 Palestinians were injured during the operation: 44 (including a 9-year-old) were physically assaulted; one was hit by a rubber-coated metal bullet; and six were treated for tear gas inhalation. According to the Health Cluster, the operation and associated movement restrictions prevented the UNRWA Health Centre in Qalandiya Camp from operating on 5 and 6 August. Medical teams also faced restrictions entering the camp, but were able to evacuate at least 11 patients following coordination with the Israeli authorities through the Palestinian District Coordination Liaison Office. Following the end of the operation, Israeli forces eased access constraints, and UNRWA extended the operating hours of its health centre and waste collection services through 8 August to address health and sanitation needs following the two-day disruption. On 7 August, humanitarian partners conducted a joint assessment and documented damage to doors, windows, furniture and other household property in approximately 30 homes. Affected families reported significant financial losses associated with damage to their homes and belongings. No significant structural damage to residential properties or displacement resulting from the damage was identified.

During the same two-day operation, Israeli forces also carried out demolitions in Kafr Aqab and the vicinity of Qalandiya checkpoint, citing the lack of Israeli-issued building permits. A post-operation humanitarian assessment documented the demolition of nine structures, affecting 13 Palestinian households comprising 71 people, including 31 children. These included four livelihood structures hosting six commercial facilities as well as five agricultural and storage structures attached to residential buildings near the Barrier. Israeli forces also dug a trench alongside the Barrier, destroying the backyards of private properties and leaving some residential buildings immediately adjacent to the excavation. Humanitarian partners are mobilizing assistance to address needs identified through the assessment.

Late on 10 August, during a raid in Burqa (Nablus), five Palestinians, including two children, were physically assaulted while their homes were searched and subsequently taken to hospital. Earlier, on 4 August, an elderly Palestinian woman was treated for tear gas inhalation during another raid in the village. Elsewhere, Israeli forces injured two Palestinians with live ammunition or shrapnel during raids in Balata Camp (Nablus) and Jenin city, including a 14-year-old child in Jenin.

Settler Attacks

During the reporting period, a total of 38 incidents involving Israeli settlers resulted in Palestinian casualties, property damage or both. Attacks affected Palestinians and their property across the West Bank, including homes, vehicles, agricultural land, water and electricity infrastructure and other livelihood assets.

On 5 August, about 30 Israeli settlers attacked the Tuba community in Masafer Yatta (Hebron), throwing stones and flammable materials at homes and physically assaulting residents. Five Palestinians, including two girls, were injured. Three residential structures were destroyed by fire, displacing three families comprising 23 people, including 14 children, who subsequently sheltered with relatives and neighbours. A kitchen, storage tent, about 10 tonnes of animal fodder, a mobile latrine and the community's solar power system were also destroyed, leaving about 100 residents without electricity. Elsewhere in Masafer Yatta, on 9 August, settlers threw flammable material into a Palestinian home in Shi'b al Butum while its residents were sleeping, destroying furniture before the family and neighbours extinguished the fire.

Palestinian access to agricultural land and livelihoods was also affected, particularly in Nablus and Ramallah governorates. Between 6 and 8 August, four attacks in Beit Furik and neighbouring Beit Dajan (Nablus) resulted in seven Palestinian injuries, primarily while Palestinians were accessing agricultural land or working in the area. In three incidents, settlers were reportedly wearing military or military-style uniforms. On 7 August, more than 200 olive trees were found vandalized in Deir Sharaf (Nablus), after landowners had reportedly been threatened by settlers and told not to return to their land two days earlier. In Beitillu (Ramallah), settlers expelled Palestinian farmers from agricultural land in Area B and set fire to a vehicle.

Access to essential services, including health care, was also impeded. On 7 August, Israeli settlers attacked a PRCS team responding to reports of injuries near Abu Njeim (Bethlehem), injuring four Palestinians, including two paramedics who were sprayed with pepper spray, and damaging three PRCS vehicles and a mobile water tanker. In Qusra (Nablus), settlers installed a road gate on 9 August that isolated at least three Palestinian households comprising about 13 people and restricted their access to food, water and other essential supplies. Late on 10 August, settlers reportedly stopped an ambulance that had coordinated access to evacuate a sick child; it was subsequently able to leave after Israeli forces arrived.

Demolitions

During the reporting period, eight demolition incidents were documented (including in Kufr Aqab as reported above) in which 25 Palestinian-owned structures were demolished across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. The demolitions displaced six households comprising 29 people, including 17 children, and otherwise affected more than 160 people, including nearly 100 children. Of the 25 structures demolished, 24 were demolished for lacking Israeli-issued building permits and one on punitive grounds.

On 10 August, the owners of two apartments in Jabal al Mukabbir, East Jerusalem, were forced to demolish their properties that lacked Israeli-issued building permits. As a result, two households comprising 10 people, including six children, were displaced. According to the family, attempts to obtain building permits had been rejected and they had accumulated more than NIS 800,000 (US$270,000) in fines for unlicensed construction. In July, the family received a final demolition order giving them 21 days to carry out the demolition themselves or face additional costs if the demolition was carried out by the Israeli authorities.

Lack-of-permit demolitions in Area C also displaced three families comprising 13 people in Nahhalin and Al Maniya (Bethlehem) and Khallet al Farah (Hebron). The demolitions included residential, commercial and agricultural structures.

Demolitions also affected education and agricultural livelihoods. On 4 August, Israeli authorities demolished two administrative rooms and a storage room at a mixed basic school in Shi'b al Butum in Masafer Yatta (Hebron), citing the lack of an Israeli-issued building permit. The main school building remains intact but is also subject to a demolition order. The demolition affected 54 school and kindergarten students and 14 educational personnel, including 11 teachers. According to the Education Cluster, the resulting rubble has created safety and access concerns ahead of the new academic year. Reconstruction remains on hold due to the risk of further demolition and ongoing legal proceedings, while efforts are under way to clear the rubble and mobilize mental health and psychosocial support for affected students. On 9 August, Israeli authorities also demolished three agricultural structures in Mirka (Jenin), following a seizure order affecting about 3.5 dunums of land for stated military purposes, affecting the livelihood of a family of five.

Separately, late on 10 August, Israeli forces used explosives to demolish, on punitive grounds, the family home of a Palestinian accused by the Israeli authorities of killing a member of Israeli forces in Tell (Nablus) on 24 July. The demolition displaced a woman and her five daughters. Residents of about 25 neighbouring homes were evacuated during the operation and could subsequently return; several homes sustained damage to doors, windows and water tanks.

For key figures and additional breakdowns of casualties, displacement, and settler violence between January 2005 and June 2026, please refer to the OCHA West Bank June 2026 Snapshot. For key figures on the impact of settler attacks, please refer to the West Bank – The Impact of Settler Attacks, January 2023 – April 2026.

title: DRC: Ebola BVD Outbreak: LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #9 (Reporting period: 01 - 14 August 2026)
content:
Summary Points

• LTC Telecoms is scaling up telecommunications support for the Ebola response in Bunia, Mongbwalu and Kisangani, providing coordination, connectivity, security communications, power solutions and Information Management (IM) services to enable humanitarian operation.

• Security communications capacity is being strengthened across Ituri Province through upgrades to the Security Communications System (SCS), including the arrival of VHF repeater equipment in Bunia that will enhance radio coverage for UN and NGO responders in Bunia and Mongbwalu.

• Connectivity capabilities continue to expand, with 20 Starlink Mini units acquired and additional Starlink kits positioned in Kinshasa for deployment to Ebolaaffected areas, supporting reliable communications for response teams.

title: Indonesian Humanitarian Coordination Platform: Flash Update #2 - Earthquake and Tsunami – Flores and surrounding areas
content:
• The NTT Provincial Government has set an emergency response status for 14 days, effective August 15-28, 2026 based on the Decree of the Governor of NTT Number 305/KEP/HK/2026. This status is the basis for resource mobilization and APBD financing for search, health services, IDPs, basic needs, and access and infrastructure recovery. Three districts have also imposed an emergency response period, namely in Manggara, Ngada, and East Manggarai.
  • The number of IDPs increased to 9,290 people, based on the BNPB update at 00.00 WIB. The details include 3,356 Sikka people—1,356 in the Samador GOR and 2,000 spread independently in 10 points—Manggarai 2,078 people, and Nagekeo 500 people. The rest are in other regions including Bima City and the Selayar Islands, but details have not been made public
  • The earthquake shock was followed by 341 aftershock activities. The number of fatalities recorded to date is 47 people, with the highest death toll in Manggarai Regency with 23 people and East Manggarai with 17 people. Meanwhile, other fatalities were spread across Sikka Regency with 4 people, West Manggarai with 1 person, Ende with 1 person, and Nagekeo with 1 person. At least 101 residents were reported injured with varying degrees of severity.
  • Damage increased significantly compared to previous reports: BNPB now records 914 houses severely damaged, 126 moderately damaged, and 317 lightly damaged—a total of 1,357 houses. The affected facilities include 93 educational facilities, 36 health facilities, and 38 government offices. This data is a temporary update at 00.00 WIB
  • Harian Antara reported that national road access was disrupted by landslides on the Malwatar – Ruteng City border, Ruteng-Km 210, Ruteng-Reo-Kedindi, Km 210 – Manggarai Regency boundary, Gako-Aigela – Ende City border, Danga-Maropokot, Ende-Wolowaru City, and Wolowaru-Maumere. In addition, five of the 15 airports in NTT were reported to be affected, but the entire runway was still usable; The damage is said to be limited to the terminal. Two ports were severely damaged and two crossing facilities were also affected. The location of each facility has not been detailed.
  • The IHCP network reported that several roads were cut off in Watungene, Komba City district, Maumere.
  • Land access to Reo, which was previously covered by landslides, has been able to be passed by SAR officers since 06.00 WITA. The second day of search operations was prioritized in Manggarai and East Manggarai, using land and sea routes.

title: UNHCR Tanzania Operational Update - July 2026
content:
As of 31 July 2026, Tanzania hosts 130,924 refugees and asylum seekers, mainly from the DRC and Burundi. Of these, 89,574 live in Nyarugusu Camp, while 41,350 (mostly Burundian) refugees live in urban areas, villages, and old settlements in Dar es Salaam, Kigoma, Katavi, and Tabora regions.

In collaboration with the Government, UNHCR, and partners, have been receiving asylum seekers fleeing violent clashes in the DRC. In July 2026, a total of 175 new arrivals were received in Tanzania, bringing the total number of arrivals to 4,566 since renewed violence in eastern DRC in January 2025.

UNHCR continues to provide protection and assistance to the people we serve. Some services, including primary health care and education, are also extended to the host community. In addition, UNHCR seeks durable solutions for refugees.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 307: Week 2 – August 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Market Overview

Market conditions remained generally stable at the national level during the second week of August, with moderate price movements across most monitored commodities. Several food prices eased during the week, although key staples remained elevated compared to last year and the three-year average. Persistent trade disruptions, regional supply constraints, and high transportation costs continued to influence market prices. Diesel prices increased during the week and remained significantly above historical levels, adding to supply-chain and delivery costs. However, the pass-through of elevated fuel costs to retail food prices remained moderate.

Food Items:

• National average food prices showed a modest easing during the second week of August, with several commodities recording week-on-week declines. Despite this moderation, prices for several key staples remained elevated compared to historical levels, while market availability remained generally adequate.

• Wheat and Wheat Flour: Wheat grain and wheat flour prices remained broadly stable week-on-week, with only marginal increases recorded across the three commodities. However, prices remained significantly higher than last year, particularly wheat grain and low-price wheat flour, which were 14% and 13% higher, respectively.

• Rice: Rice prices declined during the week, with high-price Palawi and low-price Sholae rice falling by 1.5% and 0.7%, respectively. Nevertheless, rice prices remained substantially above last year and the three-year average.

• Other Staples: Prices of cooking oil, pulses, sugar, and salt showed negligible movements during the week. Meanwhile, compared to last year, cooking oil and sugar remained elevated, while pulse prices were 14% lower, reflecting relatively favourable availability and domestic production.

• Vegetables: Vegetable prices eased during the second week of August, led by a 7.1% decline in tomato prices. Potato and onion prices also decreased by 2.1% and 2.0%, respectively. Compared to last year, tomato and potato prices remained significantly higher, while onion prices continued to remain below last year's level.

Non-Food Items:

• Exchange Rate: The Afghani remained broadly stable at AFN 65.6/USD, appreciating by 0.6% week-on-week. The currency remained 4% stronger than last year and 12% stronger than the three-year average, helping to partially offset imported inflationary pressures.

• Fuel: Diesel prices increased by 1.2% during the second week of August and remained significantly elevated, at 15% above last year and 17% above the three-year average. Continued regional supply constraints and elevated international fuel prices are sustaining pressure on transportation and supply-chain costs.

• Fertilizers: Fertilizer prices declined during the week, with DAP falling by 1.4% and urea by 4.7%. Despite the weekly declines, prices remained substantially above last year's levels, with DAP 15% and urea 35% higher.

• Livestock: The price of a 1-year-old live female sheep remained broadly stable, with negligible week-on-week fluctuations. However, it remained 5% below last year and 2% below the three-year average, indicating a slight decline in pastoralists' terms of trade.

• Labour Market: Labour market conditions remained subdued, with labour availability unchanged at an average of 2.1 days per week. Availability remained 14% below both last year and the three-year average, while unskilled and skilled daily wages remained unchanged during the week.

title: UNICEF Guinea-Bissau Flash Update No. 2 (Mpox Outbreak Response), 21 July – 13 August 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Six laboratory-confirmed mpox cases have been reported since the outbreak was declared, including two new cases during Epidemiological Week 32. Five cases are in the Autonomous Sector of Bissau and one in Biombo Region, with no deaths reported to date.
  • While all confirmed cases are adults, children under 15 account for 50% of suspected cases (23 of 46), including 16 children aged 0–4 years, reinforcing the need for particular attention to children as the response evolves.
  • UNICEF GB continues to support the Government-led response, including participation in COES coordination mechanisms, strengthening RCCE/SBC materials, supporting IPC/WASH measures in priority health facilities. A multisectoral UNICEF Mpox Response Plan aligned with the national 42-day response plan has been developed.
  • UNICEF GB currently requires approximately USD 152,000 in flexible emergency funding to support priority response interventions.

title: UNICEF Nigeria Situation Report (Cholera Response), July - August 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Cholera transmission remains widespread, with 57,030 suspected cases and 357 deaths across 35 states.
  • Borno remains the epicentre, with Maiduguri, Monguno and Jere among the highest-burden LGAs.
  • UNICEF has scaled up an integrated response, 2,744 case-households were reached through CATI. The 78 CATI teams comprise teams from all partners in the WASH Sector, not only those funded by UNICEF, chlorination of 411 water points, 85,809 individuals among at-risk neighbours received Hygiene promotion, expanded treatment capacity and oral cholera vaccination reaching 2.8 million people.
  • Priority actions remain expanded CATI, safe water access, decentralized treatment, stronger surveillance and laboratory confirmation, intensified RCCE and targeted vaccination.
  • Funding gaps remain critical. Additional flexible funding is urgently needed to sustain CATI teams, replenish essential supplies and extend lifesaving WASH, Health and SBC interventions to affected and at-risk areas.

title: Lebanon Cash Working Group: Situation Report #4 (Reporting period: 1 to 31 July 2026)
content:
Situation Overview

During July, humanitarian needs in Lebanon remained substantial despite continued population returns and a gradual decline in overall displacement. As of 29 July, an estimated 821,077 people had returned to their areas of origin, while 360,132 people remained displaced across the country, including approximately 27,200 individuals residing in collective shelters. Although displacement continued to decrease, returns remained uneven and often fragile, constrained by damaged housing, insecurity, unexploded ordnance, movement restrictions, disrupted livelihoods and limited access to basic services in conflict-aected areas. Many households continued to face dicult choices between remaining displaced and returning to locations where recovery conditions remained inadequate. Humanitarian actors increasingly adapted their response to a changing context characterized by returns, residual displacement and localized secondary displacement. Communities in aected areas consistently identified cash assistance, restoration of basic services, health care, livelihoods support and shelter rehabilitation among their highest priorities. At the same time, rising living costs, economic hardship and funding constraints continued to erode household coping capacities and increase reliance on humanitarian assistance. Humanitarian partners also reported growing protection concerns, particularly among women, children, older persons and persons with disabilities, as prolonged displacement, limited livelihood opportunities and inadequate housing conditions continued to heighten vulnerabilities.

Against this backdrop, the Cash Working Group (LCWG) continued to support the transition from blanket emergency assistance towards more targeted interventions under the Shock Responsive Safety Net (SRSN), while advancing planning for the post-Flash Appeal period through the 2026 LRP Addendum. Eorts during July focused on strengthening targeting methodologies, refining analysis of displacement-related costs, improving reporting and information management, and promoting complementarity between MPCA, sectoral cash assistance, social protection and livelihoods programming to ensure limited resources are directed towards households with the greatest needs.

title: Afghanistan: Humanitarian Update, July 2026
content:
NATURAL DISASTERS DEEPEN HUMANITARIAN NEEDS IN AFGHANISTAN

Natural disasters continued to drive humanitarian needs across Afghanistan, creating another layer of vulnerability. Across the country, floods, flash floods, landslides and other weather-related hazards have continued to damage homes, disrupt livelihoods and claim lives throughout 2026. While these shocks are a recurring reality in Afghanistan, the scale and frequency of impact recorded this year highlight how environmental stresses are increasingly compounding existing humanitarian needs.

The latest wave of disasters during late July and early August offers a stark reminder of this reality. Between 20 July and 3 August, nearly 5,000 people were affected across 10 provinces. The affected provinces were Ghazni, Kabul, Kapisa, Laghman, Logar, Nuristan, Paktya, Paktika, Panjsher and Parwan, highlighting the wide geographic reach of recent disasters.

The eastern region bore the brunt of the impact, with Nuristan emerging as the most severely affected province. Deadly floods and landslides claimed dozens of lives, including of a humanitarian worker, impacting thousands of people. Hundreds of homes were either damaged or destroyed, leaving many families in urgent need of assistance and shelter support. Yet these incidents represent only a fraction of a much larger picture unfolding across the country.

Since the beginning of the year, natural disasters have affected more than 92,000 people across all 34 provinces and 202 districts of Afghanistan. The cumulative impact has been substantial. Between January and early August, 97 people were killed and 331 injured, while nearly 10,000 houses were damaged and more than 2,100 houses were destroyed, leaving thousands of families facing longer-term recovery challenges. Overall, nearly 13,000 families have been affected by natural disasters nationwide.

What stands out in this year's data is both the scale and geographic spread of the impacts. Although eastern Afghanistan has experienced the highest number of affected people, disasters have reached communities in every region of the country.

More than 51,000 people were affected in the eastern region alone, while significant impacts were also recorded in the southern and western regions.

Behind these figures are families who have lost shelter, farmers whose agricultural land has been flooded, and communities struggling with damaged roads, irrigation systems, water networks and local markets. For households already facing limited livelihood opportunities, the loss of a home or productive assets can push them deeper into vulnerability and increase their reliance on humanitarian assistance.

Flooding continues to be the defining hazard of 2026. Nearly 88,000 people affected by natural disasters this year were impacted by floods and flash floods, making them by far the largest driver of disaster related humanitarian needs. Seasonal rainfall, rapid snowmelt, environmental degradation and inadequate infrastructure continue to amplify risks, particularly in rural and mountainous areas where communities often have limited capacity to recover.

The consequences are especially severe in provinces where communities have limited coping capacity and where access limitations can complicate assessments and response efforts. In places such as Nuristan, recurring disasters often strike communities that are already isolated and face challenges obtaining services and assistance.

The growing impact of natural hazards also highlights the close relationship between climate shocks and humanitarian vulnerability. Decades of conflict, environmental degradation and underinvestment in infrastructure have weakened resilience in many areas. At the same time, changing weather patterns may be contributing to more intense and less predictable hazard events, increasing both exposure and risk.

As humanitarian actors respond to immediate needs, there is growing understanding that emergency assistance alone cannot address the challenge. Investments in early warning systems, community preparedness, disaster risk reduction and climate adaptation measures remain essential to reduce future losses and strengthen resilience.

For Afghanistan, natural disasters are no longer isolated events. They have become a recurring driver of humanitarian need, affecting communities across the country and reinforcing existing vulnerabilities. As the year progresses, strengthening preparedness alongside response efforts will remain critical to protecting lives, livelihoods and community resilience.

"Before the flood, I had a very beautiful home. We lived happily and had everything," recalled one woman in Nuristan. "When the flood came, it swept away our entire house and all of our belongings."

Her story was one of many shared during a recent OCHA mission to flood-affected communities in Nuristan Province, where families are struggling to rebuild after devastating flash floods destroyed homes, livelihoods and critical infrastructure.

Many survivors described how the floods forced entire communities to flee. Although emergency assistance has reached affected areas, the reality remains challenging for many families now living in temporary shelters.

"We are living in a tent under very difficult conditions," a survivor said. "We have nothing to light the tent, and we do not have the money to refill the gas cylinder." The floods also destroyed crops and agricultural land, threatening livelihoods at a time when many families were already struggling. One resident explained that years of hard work were washed away along with the floodwater.

"The floods destroyed all our crops. I had 2.5 jeribs of farmland, and that land was also washed away by the floods." Women and children have been among those most affected. Families reported injuries sustained during the floods and described the difficulties of caring for loved ones while displaced. "Our children were injured, and women were also injured," a survivor said. "Our request to the international community is to help and support the affected women and children."

During the mission, OCHA spokesperson Olga Cherevko highlighted the particular challenges facing women in the aftermath of the disaster. "Women have been disproportionately affected here," she said. "They now have to navigate taking care of their families in temporary shelters, without proper access to sanitation, hygiene or safe drinking water."

Humanitarian partners continue to scale up the response through Education, Food Security, Health, Protection, Shelter and WASH interventions, despite access challenges caused by damaged roads and floodwaters.

For many families, the immediate response has provided temporary relief, but the longer-term challenge of rebuilding homes and livelihoods remains.

"The assistance provided by the organizations that have supported us will not be enough to meet our needs beyond one month," a survivor said. Cherevko emphasized the importance of continued support for flood-affected communities.

"What matters most now is that these communities continue to be supported," she said. "Not only so they can rebuild their lives, but so they can also be prepared when the next disaster strikes."

As the immediate impact of the floods passes, families are beginning the long process of recovery. Yet the stories shared during the mission serve as a reminder that behind every disaster are people rebuilding their homes, livelihoods and hopes for the future.

title: Colombia: Flash Update 006 - Update on the Impact of the Earthquake in Colombia - August 14, 2026
content:
This Flash Update is produced by OCHA Colombia in collaboration with humanitarian partners, based on official reports (as of 14 August, 18:30 local time). The next update to this document will be issued on Monday, 17 August 2026.

Humanitarian impact and multisectoral effects. Five days after the magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck San José del Palmar in Chocó Department, 183 aftershocks have been reported, along with impacts across 15 departments and 437 municipalities. At least 135,179 people have been affected, including Afro-Colombian and Indigenous communities, while significant damage to housing, critical infrastructure and essential services persists.

Priority needs and scaling up of the response. The most pressing needs remain in health, temporary shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), food security, energy and communications, particularly in Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó and Caldas departments. Rapid and intersectoral assessments are ongoing to identify gaps, prioritize interventions and complement the Government's response in the most affected areas.

International support mobilization and humanitarian coordination. The international response continues to scale up, with an initial allocation of US$5 million from the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), additional donor contributions and the operational deployment of national and international humanitarian partners. Efforts are focused on strengthening immediate response capacity, restoring essential services and supporting early recovery in coordination with the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) and territorial authorities.

title: Indonesian Humanitarian Coordination Platform: Flash Update #1 - Earthquake and Tsunami – Flores and surrounding areas
content:
Date: 15 August 2026

Information cut-off: 07:35 WIB / 08:35 WITA

Status: Tsunami warning ended; impact verification ongoing

This report consolidates official information and preliminary reports received by IHCP. It is not a substitute for instructions issued by BMKG, BNPB, BPBD or affected local governments.

1. Key updates

• A strong and shallow earthquake occurred in the Flores Sea at 04:58:24 WIB/05:58:24 WITA. BMKG’s initial M7.0/10 km parameters were subsequently updated to M7.7 at a depth of 15 km, approximately 30 km northeast of Mbay, Nagekeo.

• The earthquake generated a tsunami. BMKG detected sea-level changes at ten monitoring locations, with the highest reported measurements of 0.94 metres at Maurole–Ende and 0.54 metres at Bulukumba.

• At 07:31:30 WIB/08:31:30 WITA, BMKG issued Tsunami Warning Update PD-4, formally ending the tsunami warning for all Indonesian territory.

• The end of the tsunami warning does not remove risks from aftershocks, damaged buildings, rockfalls, landslides, electrical hazards or disrupted infrastructure. Movement from evacuation areas should follow local government and BPBD instructions.

• Strong shaking was estimated at up to VII MMI in parts of Nagekeo and Ngada. Shaking was reportedly felt throughout Flores and in parts of Sumba, Adonara and Solor.

• Preliminary reports indicate damage to houses and public buildings, including reported damage at the Pelni passenger terminal in Maumere. Community-generated media also show evacuation and possible earthquake-induced rockfalls. Verification remains ongoing.

• As of the reporting cut-off, no consolidated official figures were available for casualties, injuries, displaced people or damaged buildings.

• IHCP members should shift their immediate focus from tsunami evacuation support to impact verification, safe return, structural safety, protection monitoring and assessment of humanitarian needs.

title: IOM Nigeria Flash Report #295: Population Displacement - North-west Nigeria - Katsina State - Conflict/Attacks (14 Auguest 2026)
content: On 6 and 8 August 2026, armed bandits attacked the communities of Na’alma in Na’alma ward of Malumfashi Local Government Area (LGA), Turare in Makera ward of Dutsin-Ma LGA and Tsiga in Tsiga ward of Bakori LGA, all in Katsina State. According to key informants, the attacks a ected 6,023 individuals across 862 households and displaced 3,509 individuals from 524 households, including 1,458 children, 1,224 women, and 827 men.

title: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 13 (3-9 August 2026)
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Central African Republic
content:
According to the World Health Organization, as of 10 August, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 4,449 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus (BVD), including 2,061 deaths.

With the recent increase in reported cases, the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak has become the largest and fastest-growing outbreak ever reported in DRC. The rapidly escalating outbreak is unfolding against the backdrop of an ongoing triple crisis in eastern DRC, where health risks, large-scale displacement and persistent conflict intersect. Displaced populations living in camps face complex and multidimensional needs requiring coordinated, multisectoral interventions. Across affected areas, most deaths continue to occur within communities, underscoring the urgent need to strengthen contact tracing and community event-based surveillance to support earlier detection, referral and response.

The spread of the outbreak into Tshopo and Haut-Uélé Provinces underscores continued need to comprehensively address the mobility dimensions of the ongoing public health response. While no positive Ebola case has been reported on vessels arriving via riverine routes in Kinshasa, heightened transmission risks require strengthened coordination and vigilance at points of control (PoCs) along the river to prevent further geographic spread. In parallel, the rising number of cases in Haut-Uélé requires enhanced disease surveillance and cross-border coordination to prevent disease transmission into neighbouring South Sudan and the Central African Republic (CAR).

During the reporting period, key highlights include :

  • 4,449 confirmed Ebola cases and 2,061 deaths in the DRC as of 10 August 2026, making this the largest and fastest-growing Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the country.
  • Over 16.5 million health screenings supported at 225 points of entry and points of control across affected and at-risk countries.
  • During the reporting period, IOM supported 2.57 million health screenings in the DRC alone
  • More than 13.1 million individuals reached through risk communication and community engagement activities.
  • Trained 575 health workers in Rwanda on Ebola detection, infection prevention and control, surveillance, and response measures.
  • Continued to strengthen surveillance and preparedness capacities along critical mobility corridors, including riverine routes into Kinshasa and border areas near South Sudan and the Central African Republic.

The outbreak continues to unfold in a complex operational environment marked by insecurity, displacement, and population mobility. As transmission persists in eastern DRC, sustained investment in surveillance, border health measures, community engagement, and support to displaced and mobile populations remains critical to containing the outbreak and preventing cross-border spread. Learn more HERE

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #22 (11 to 13 August 2026)
content:
Situation Report No. 22 provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 11 to 13 August 2026.

Highlights

  • IOM coordinated the distribution of approximately 1,700 non-food item (NFI) kits in Mare Abajo and surrounding communities, expanding assistance to households affected by the earthquakes.
  • IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) assessed 110 community settlements, identifying 4,733 households and 12,127 individuals in La Guaira, Capital District, Carabobo and Miranda to inform the response beyond temporary camps.
  • IOM completed the operational closure of Playa Grande, supporting the relocation of families and finalizing the removal of humanitarian infrastructure from the temporary camp.

IOM Activities

IOM continued the co-management of the temporary camps at José María Vargas Sports Complex, Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo and César Nieves, three of them jointly with the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC), ensuring service coordination, population registration and needs monitoring. In Mare Abajo, IOM coordinated the distribution of approximately 1,700 non-food item kits, following registration activities, household verification and community mobilization efforts to facilitate access to assistance.

IOM strengthened information management mechanisms through updated camp records and the rapid assessment of 110 community settlements, identifying 4,733 households and 12,127 individuals across four affected states. IOM also advanced preparations for a household survey to strengthen needs analysis and assistance planning.

In the health sector, IOM and its partner Ven Da Tu Mano continued providing mobile health and mental health services in temporary camps. During the reporting period, teams conducted 445 consultations at José María Vargas Sports Complex and 230 consultations in César Nieves, maintaining follow-up for chronic diseases and reinforcing surveillance of diarrhoeal syndromes, particularly among children.

Protection activities included coordination to facilitate access to specialized services, strengthen referral mechanisms and improve coordination among humanitarian actors. In César Nieves, IOM promoted the establishment of a technical protection coordination space to strengthen service coordination and the follow-up of individuals with specific protection needs.

IOM also facilitated inter-agency coordination spaces to strengthen distribution planning, update available services and improve referral mechanisms and needs monitoring in temporary camps. In addition, IOM completed the operational closure of Playa Grande, supporting family relocations and the progressive withdrawal of humanitarian infrastructure.

IOM Planned Response

IOM plans to:

  • Continue coordinating planned non-food item distributions in Mare Abajo and surrounding communities, preventing duplication and ensuring appropriate targeting of assistance.
  • Follow up on infrastructure gaps identified in Mare Abajo, particularly shower drainage and tent anchoring systems.
  • Maintain surveillance and medical follow-up of diarrhoeal syndromes, particularly among children and adolescents, and support continuity of treatment for hypertension, diabetes and other chronic diseases.
  • Strengthen referral pathways for mental health, protection and other specialized services.
  • Implement the household survey in IOM-managed temporary camps and expand needs monitoring and population movement tracking in community settlements and affected areas.
  • Maintain updated information on available services, operating hours and referral mechanisms in temporary camps.
  • Consolidate sector coordination mechanisms and strengthen systems for reporting and tracking security incidents and protection risks.

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Flash Floods and Landslides in Bangladesh (8 July - 10 August 2026)
content:
Heavy rains since 5 July, including renewed heavy rainfall in early August, have triggered widespread flooding and landslides across Bangladesh, affecting approximately 1.3 million people in seven districts of the Chattogram Division. Among those affected are an estimated 364,000 women of reproductive age, including 17,490 pregnant women.

Damaged roads, flooded pathways and landslides have isolated remote communities from hospitals, clinics and other essential services, further increasing sexual and reproductive health needs. Despite damage, a UNFPA-supported maternity facility remains operational through temporary arrangements and emergency referral mechanisms, helping ensure continuity of essential maternal health services.

Protection risks for women and girls increased as economic shocks drove reliance on negative coping strategies, including child labour and child marriage. For people displaced by the floods and landslides, overcrowded shelters, inadequate privacy and lighting, insufficient sex-segregated sanitation facilities, and shortages of menstrual hygiene supplies further compromise the safety, dignity and well-being of women and adolescent girls.

UNFPA continues to deploy essential supplies, midwives, community volunteers and mobile health services to affected areas. To date, 1,018 women and girls have accessed essential health services through four health camps and 15 deployed midwives at health facilities, while 6,326 people have been reached with gender-based violence risk mitigation support. UNFPA has also maintained seven safe spaces and distributed 4,500 dignity kits, 1,951 menstrual health management kits and 1,000 baby kits to affected women and adolescent girls.

UNFPA requires US$966,930 to ensure the continued delivery of life-saving reproductive health and protection services for affected women, girls and young people. To date, US$130,330 has been mobilized, leaving a funding gap of US$836,600. Urgent additional funding is needed to sustain and scale up critical interventions and ensure that reach those most in need.

title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #33 (14 August 2026, Time: 02:00 pm)
content:
Situation Report No. 33
Earthquakes in Venezuela
14 August 2026
Time: 2:00 pm

Highlights

  • Over 304,000 people affected by the earthquakes have accessed humanitarian assistance and essential services through a coordinated multi-sector response involving humanitarian organizations, United Nations agencies, communities, and national and local authorities.
  • As of 10 August, authorities reported 6,301 deaths and 73,356 people that received care at hospitals.
  • The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency to address the needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.

Situation overview

Venezuela continues to face the consequences of the two major earthquakes (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5) that struck the north-central region of the country on 24 June at 18:00 local time, causing significant humanitarian impacts and damage to infrastructure. The first earthquake, measuring 7.2, was centered along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). According to a recent update from the United States Geological Survey (USGS), the second earthquake, measuring 7.5, had its epicenter 17 kilometers west of Catia La Mar, off the coast of La Guaira State.

As of 10 August, authorities reported 6,301 deaths from the earthquakes. They also reported that 73,356 people received care at hospitals and 53,314 homes were evaluated, out of which 9,567 are at high risk. According to national authorities, 23,26% of the total rubble has been cleared. A preliminary assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) estimates direct damage to housing and infrastructure at approximately US$37 billion, while preliminary estimates from UNDP place direct physical damages at US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.

More than one month after the earthquakes, the humanitarian response continues to expand across the affected states. As of 14 August, over 304,000 people (57% women and girls) had access to essential services and humanitarian assistance through the joint efforts of communities, humanitarian organizations, United Nations entities, donor partners, and national and local authorities.

title: Dengue in the Pacific: Multicountry Situation (As of 14 August 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Since 1 January 2025, twelve dengue outbreaks have been reported across Pacific Island Countries and Areas (PICs).

• During 2025, dengue outbreaks were reported in American Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Naoero, Samoa, Tonga, and Tuvalu. A total of 21,258 confirmed cases and 21 deaths were recorded across the Pacific. Fatalities were reported in Fiji (n=8), Samoa (n=7), Tonga (n=3), Naoero (n=2), and Kiribati (n=1).

• Between 1 January 2026 and 2 July 2026, a total of 4 545 dengue confirmed cases, 175 hospitalisations and 3 deaths have been reported across the Pacific.

• The Pacific Syndromic Surveillance System (PSSS) has reported a total of 9 050 Dengue-like Illness (DLI) cases to date, a lower trend compared to the same period last year.

• In 2026 dengue outbreaks were officially declared in New Caledonia, Tonga and Shefa province Vanuatu.

• The most affected countries and areas in 2026 include: American Samoa, Cook Islands, Samoa, and New Caledonia. These account for 94% of confirmed cases.

• Dengue serotype-1 (DENV-1) and serotype-2 (DENV-2) are currently in circulation.

• The Cook Islands officially declared the end of its dengue outbreak on 25 May 2026.

• Tonga has officially declared the end of its dengue outbreak on 31 July 2026.

• As of 14 August 2026:

o The dengue outbreak remains ongoing in Shefa Province, Vanuatu, with dengue virus serotype 1 (DENV-1) continuing to circulate.

o Low levels of transmission are observed in American Samoa, Kiribati, New Caledonia, Samoa, Vanuatu and Wallis and Futuna.

This Flash Update is produced by OCHA Colombia in collaboration with humanitarian partners, based on official reports (as of 13 August, 18:30 local time)

  • The scale of the emergency continues to grow. The most affected departments are Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó and Caldas. However, the emergency continues to expand and figures may increase due to access constraints and possible underreporting.
  • Humanitarian needs remain critical, particularly in rural areas. Challenges persist in reaching affected rural communities, limiting the full assessment of damage and needs. Humanitarian partners continue to conduct rapid assessments to identify priority needs and guide the response.

While the Government continues to deploy its immediate response, humanitarian partners from the Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) and Local Coordination Teams (LCTs) are complementing efforts in the most affected areas. At the same time, implementation of the US$5 million allocation from the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) is advancing, prioritizing life-saving interventions in hard-to-reach rural areas with limited institutional presence and where assistance can provide immediate added value.

Coordination among national and local authorities and humanitarian partners remains essential to ensure a timely and effective response. We will continue to monitor the evolution of the emergency and support efforts to protect and assist the most affected populations.

title: NGA: Landslide - 08-2026 - Floods (2026-08-14)
content:
Description

Weeks of continuous, unprecedented torrential rainfall across Calabar, the capital of Cross River State, have triggered devastating landslides and severe flooding across multiple communities in Calabar Municipality, resulting in loss of life, widespread destruction of homes and property, and the collapse of critical infrastructure. The rainfall, described by observers as unprecedented in scale and intensity for the city, has caused the terrain to collapse in several locations, destroying buildings, roads, utility lines and agricultural investments, and threatening federal agencies and public infrastructure including a naval base and an inland waterways authority office.

The first major landslide struck Ikot Anwatim in the northern part of Calabar, where buildings caved into a gully, killing five persons including four siblings, Bright (18), Godswill (12), Daniel (11) and Richard (10) from one family. A fifth victim, Mr Udo, was also killed. A second devastating landslide occurred in the Anansa area of Obutong Community, Calabar Municipality, cutting off a key waterfront road, snapping high-tension electricity poles and damaging underground public water pipes. The collapse of the road has isolated residents, severed access to vehicles and disrupted power and municipal water supply across the affected axis. At least ten deaths have been reported across the full extent of the Calabar flooding and landslide disasters, with property worth hundreds of millions of naira destroyed.

The disaster has affected homes, shops, businesses, farmlands and major infrastructure. Community and traditional leaders in Obutong have appealed for urgent government intervention to save homes and livelihoods. The Member representing Akpabuyo, Bakassi and Calabar South Federal Constituency who also chairs the House of Representatives Committee on Disaster Management and Preparedness has called for a coordinated national and international response, warning that the scale of the crisis is beyond the capacity of the state government alone. Cross River State Governor Bassey Otu visited victims, extended financial assistance and pledged to strengthen flood mitigation and emergency response systems. The governor, upon visiting the site, described the scale of destruction and the loss of life as deeply heartbreaking.

On 4 August 2026, the Federal Government, acting through the South South Development Commission (SSDC) in collaboration with NEMA, the Nigerian Red Cross Society and the Cross River State Emergency Management Agency (CR-SEMA), conducted a comprehensive assessment of the flood and landslide-affected communities in Calabar. The assessment, led by the SSDC Managing Director, aimed to coordinate humanitarian interventions and formulate longer-term environmental resilience strategies. The NRCS was actively part of this coordinated assessment, and the figures in this report reflect findings from that exercise alongside verified media and official reporting.

title: South Sudan - Operation Overview, April - June 2026
content:
Background

South Sudan continues to face a complex humanitarian crisis driven by conflict, climate-related shocks, disease outbreaks, displacement, food insecurity and economic deterioration. Access to affected communities remains constrained by poor road conditions, seasonal flooding, and limited transport infrastructure. In this context, the WFP-led Logistics Cluster continues to enable humanitarian operations through logistics coordination, information management, capacity strengthening and common transport services, including air, river and road transport to hard-to-reach and priority locations.

Operational Highlights

• During the reporting period, the Logistics Cluster facilitated the transportation of 3,077 MT of humanitarian cargo, supporting 43 organizations and reaching 37 destinations across South Sudan.
• Road transport accounted for 46 percent of the cargo moved, followed by river transport at 39 percent and air transport at 15 percent.
• The Cluster coordinated eight humanitarian road convoys delivered approximately 1,417 MT of multisectoral supplies.
• The Logistics cluster completed 31 service requests, enabling partners to deliver critical assistance to priority and hard-to-reach locations.
• The Logistics Cluster supported the Unity State cholera response in Leer, Mayendit and Mayom by facilitating the transport of 30.2 MT of emergency relief cargo.

title: UNFPA Colombia Earthquake Flash Update (10 - 12 August 2026)
content:
On 10 August, Colombia was struck by a 7.4-magnitude earthquake, affecting 380 municipalities, with the most significant impacts reported in Chocó, the Eje Cafetero and Valle del Cauca. Preliminary reports indicate that 181 people have died and 2,754 have been injured, while search and rescue operations remain ongoing.

The earthquake’s epicentre was located in San José del Palmar, in Chocó Department. Characterized by remote and rural areas, Chocó relies heavily on river and air transport as the primary means of access, creating significant challenges for the delivery of essential services and supplies. Existing structural vulnerabilities in the department further exacerbate the impact of the disaster and the difficulties faced by affected communities.

The healthcare network has been significantly affected, with 1,172 health facilities reportedly impacted. At the same time, the surge in demand for medical care resulting from the large number of people injured has placed considerable pressure on already strained health services. Disruptions to essential healthcare services pose heightened risks to pregnant women and newborns.

Preliminary assessments indicate that more than 19,000 homes have been damaged and 3,971 destroyed, displacing thousands of people. Displacement, overcrowding in temporary shelters, disruption of community support systems and economic hardship are increasing protection risks, including gender-based violence, exploitation and abuse, particularly for women and girls.

UNFPA is on the ground, working with partners to mobilize resources and rapidly assess and respond to the most urgent sexual and reproductive health and protection needs of women, girls, adolescents and other people in vulnerable situations. Priority areas include maternal healthcare, emergency obstetric care, family planning, prevention of and response to gender-based violence, and the clinical management of rape.

title: Pakistan Rain Monitor - Issue Number 8 (11- 17 August 2026)
content:

The satellite data for a period of thirty years from 1993-2023 is extracted from CHIRPS (Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station data) and analyzed to estimate deviation from normal rainfall. For the forecast of total precipitation for next seven days, the data is sourced from global model of ECMWF (European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts).

The satellite-based national rainfall forecast analysis for 11-18 August indicates below rainfall across most parts of the country with the exception of northern parts of GB, northern and central KP and northeastern districts of Punjab, Given the ongoing flood conditions in parts of north and central areas, additional rainfall may exacerbate the risk of flooding, GLOF and landslides, particularly in vulnerable locations across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gilgit-Baltistan, Azad Jammu & Kashmir, and northeastern Punjab.

title: Colombia Earthquake: Situation Report #2 (August 12, 2026)
content:
Project HOPE's Emergency Response Team is on the ground in the Valle del Cauca and Risaralda departments of Colombia, rapidly assessing needs after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck 150 miles west of Bogotá and caused widespread damage, landslides, and impacted critical infrastructure across a large geographic area.

Situational Context

There have been over 29 aftershocks since a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck near San Jose del Palmar, Colombia, and caused extensive damage across a wide geographic area that includes rural, urban, hard-to-reach, and low-income communities hundreds of miles from the epicenter. More than 357 municipalities across western Colombia have been impacted, with the full extent of the damage unknown due to internet connectivity issues.

The earthquake has damaged or destroyed more than 9,400 homes, killed at least 254 people, and injured at least 2,595 more — thousands of people are likely missing, and these numbers are expected to increase in the coming days and weeks.

Across the impacted region, 84 health facilities sustained damage and many have been forced to reduce or suspend services. In El Águila, San Rafael Hospital suffered near-complete destruction and, in Cali, Hospital Universitario del Valle Evaristo García suffered damage that forced it to move patients outside and reduce services, despite being one of the department's primary tertiary hospitals. Public officials have declared a “red alert” for hospitals in Cali as facilities are fully at capacity due to both the damage caused by the disaster and the subsequent surge of patient needs. Departments have established shelters across the region as impacted individuals attempt to avoid residing in damaged buildings. Shelters have noted the need for increased support for hygiene supplies and larger provisions of potable water. Damage to municipal water systems has left some communities without running water until assessments and repairs can be completed. Information remains limited on health, water, and medical needs in more rural areas — especially in Chocó Department — due to limited road access and connectivity issues.

title: Preliminary situation report: Earthquake in Colombia – August 10, 2026
content:
Executive Summary

On August 10, 2026, Colombia was affected by a major earthquake with a magnitude of 7.4, occurring at approximately 7:34 a.m., with its epicenter in the department of Chocó, near San José del Palmar. The earthquake was widely felt across the country and caused significant damage, particularly in Chocó and several areas of the Coffee Region.

The department of Chocó is facing a particularly complex situation due to the combination of earthquake-related damage, existing infrastructure limitations, historical access challenges, and limited local capacity to respond to an emergency of this magnitude.

According to reports available as of August 11, approximately 500 homes had been affected and around 20 structures had collapsed in San José del Palmar. In Quibdó, at least 40 homes were reported destroyed, with 13 people killed and 131 injured. Authorities and emergency response organizations continue to conduct search and rescue operations, damage assessments, and assistance to affected populations.

The situation remains dynamic, and figures will need to be updated as access is gained to rural and hard-toreach communities.

In response, Fundación ABBACOL is coordinating a humanitarian response with the support of local communities and stakeholders, initially prioritizing psychosocial support and needs assessments while seeking national and international cooperation to expand the response and mobilize humanitarian assistance to affected communities.

title: Attacks on Health Care in Myanmar: 22 July - 04 August 2026
content:
Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) identified 259 incidents of violence against or obstruction of health care in Myanmar in 2025. Health facilities, including clinics, hospitals, pharmacies, and rural health centers, were reportedly damaged or destroyed on at least 110 occasions. Most damage or destruction involved MAF military jets using rockets and cannons that hit facilities and killed and injured health workers and patients. MAF air strikes frequently damaged or destroyed health facilities, including makeshift clinics operated by CDM-affiliated health workers, particularly in Sagaing.

Five health facilities in Kachin, Kayah, Magway, Mandalay and Ta’ang were reportedly used by opposition groups as bunkers during confrontations with MAF soldiers. These are five of the rarely reported cases where damaged health care buildings were not functioning facilities at the time and therefore had lost their special protection guaranteed under the rules of war. Combatants’ use of former health care buildings as bunkers reduces access to health care for the civilian population and as such is a further example of how violence affects health care during conflict.

Documented incidents

The publicly reported incidents below are not a complete nor a representative list of all incidents that affected the provision of health care in Myanmar between 22 July-04 August 2026. The incidents have not been verified through ground investigations. There is a delay in reporting incidents due to our open-source verification protocol.

20 July 2026: In Sin Pu Hnit village, Myo Haung village tract, Launglon township, Dawei district, Tanintharyi region, a male health assistant was arrested by the Myanmar military. Source: Dawei Watch

27 July 2026: In Aye Ka Ni village, Aye Ka Ni village tract, Yebyu township, Dawei district, Tanintharyi region, a sub-rural health centre and two houses were torched by the Myanmar military. Source: Dawei Watch

Our work in the media

A recent Guardian feature on Myanmar's health system drew on Insecurity Insight's data to document the scale of attacks on health since the 2021 military coup. The article highlights how violence against health workers and facilities has contributed to the country's deepening health crisis, underscoring the importance of systematic monitoring to inform public understanding and humanitarian advocacy.
