title: UNHCR-IOM Flash update #106 Arrest and detention by years - Key findings and limitations 15 Sep 2023 to 8 Aug 2026
content:
Introduction

Prior to 2023, there was no data collected on the arrest and detention of ACC holders or undocumented Afghan nationals. Since January 2023, IOM has started to collect this data. The figures, particularly of undocumented Afghan nationals, should be considered underreported.

• During the reporting period (2 – 8 August) a total of 1,407 Afghan nationals were arrested and detained, representing a 40% decrease compared to the previous week (26 July – 1 August).

• Out of all arrests and detentions during the reporting period (2 – 8 August), ACC holders and undocumented Afghans represented 96% of the total rate of arrest and detentions, and PoR holders represented 4%.

• During the reporting period (2 – 8 August), 43% of the total reported arrests and detentions took place in KP, 34% in Balochistan, 17% in Punjab, and 5% in ICT.

• Across Pakistan, the top three districts for arrest and detention between 1 January and 8 August 2026 were Chaghi (Balochistan), Peshawar (KP), and Karachi (Sindh).

title: Eswatini Drought - DREF Final Report (MDRSZ004)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met
30-11-2023
What happened, where and when?

The Kingdom of Eswatini persistently experienced dry spells that further exacerbated the country’s existing food insecurity challenges.

For successive years, Eswatini battled prolonged drought, whose effects on agriculture were further compounded by cumulative socio‑economic challenges the country had not overcome. As of 30 November 2023, ACAPS classified food insecurity in Eswatini as high, with 24% of the population (282,800 people) affected by food‑insecurity vulnerabilities, facing challenges in accessing food and water, with many households still reliant on welfare and social safety nets.

During the operational update in June 2024, food security had declined further, as indicated by the IPC report of 2024/25 (current period: June 2024-September 2024), where 270 000 people were in Crisis (IPC 3+), and while the projected period (October 2024-March 2025) indicated an increase to 304 000 people to be food insecure. Prolonged dry spells and other climatic conditions remained one of the main drivers of food insecurity in the country. The regions with the highest prevalence of food insecurity were the Lubombo and Shiselweni, which are the same areas mostly affected by droughts.

Despite efforts engaged by government and humanitarian actors in the country, the assessment conducted in June 2024 gathered community insights on drought impacts and food security needs, identifying a 33% gap, approximately 4,675 people, within the targeted constituencies. Consequently, the Government of Eswatini, through the National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA), relaunched a call for support from humanitarian actors and National Food Security Consortium partners, citing insufficient funds to address the needs.

However, new developments showed that in the 2024 IPC report, 243,000 people (20% of the population) were estimated to be in IPC Phase 3 (Crisis) or worse during the period June to September 2024, and for the projected period (October 2024 to March 2025), an estimated 270,000 people were classified in IPC Phase 3 (Crisis), while 34,000 people were in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency). This indicated an increase in the number of people who needed assistance to 304 000 people.

In addition, an assessment was conducted in June 2024 to gather community insights on the impacts of the drought and to understand food‑security needs among the targeted population. The assessment revealed a 33% gap (about 4,675 people) in the already targeted constituencies. Therefore, the Government of Eswatini, through the National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA), requested once again that Eswatini humanitarian actors and the Eswatini National Food Security Consortium partners intervene, as the Government did not have sufficient funds to respond to the humanitarian and food‑insecurity needs. Targeted constituencies were Hosea, Sigwe, Matsanjeni, Somntongo, Lubuli and Nkilongo. The project informed its target based on its complementarity with the ECHO PPP based in the same areas.

Between June and September 2025, 193,000 people (16 percent of the population) in Eswatini experienced high levels of acute food insecurity and loss of livelihood, classified in IPC Phase 3 or above (Crisis or worse). Although food security had improved significantly compared to the same period last year, the situation was expected to deteriorate during the projection period (October 2025 to March 2026).

title: Wildfire, Republic of Tunisia July 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRTN013)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
25-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

Since 1 June 2026, Tunisia has been affected by a severe wildfire season, with the situation escalating significantly from 25 July 2026 as multiple simultaneous wildfires spread across several governorates. High temperatures, dry vegetation and strong winds contributed to the ignition and rapid spread of fires, particularly in forested and agricultural areas.

The wildfires primarily affected the governorates of Bizerte, Béja, Jendouba, Le Kef, Siliana, Zaghouan, Nabeul, Manouba, Tunis, Kasserine, Sidi Bouzid, Sfax, Gafsa, Kébili, Tozeur and Mahdia. Among the most significant incidents were the Sakiet Sidi Youssef wildfire in Le Kef Governorate, which affected approximately 2,000 hectares, the Jebel Chahma fire in Zaghouan Governorate, which damaged around 1,300 hectares of forest and agricultural land, the Ghar El Melh and Rafraf fires in Bizerte Governorate, and the Cap Negro fire in Béja Governorate. Additional fires were reported across several other affected governorates.

According to official information, approximately 12,000 hectares of forest and agricultural land have been damaged since the beginning of the fire season, compared with 4,400 hectares reported by 23 July 2026 and 2,705 hectares during the same period in 2025. Historical records indicate that around 70,000 hectares of forest have burned in Tunisia over the last ten years, representing an annual average of approximately 7,000 hectares and highlighting the exceptional severity of the current wildfire season. The Director General of Forests confirmed that the fires have mainly affected cork-oak and Aleppo pine forests, which are environmentally and economically important for local communities.

The scale of the emergency has been unprecedented. Civil Protection reported approximately 900 fires within a 72-hour period between 20 and 22 July 2026, while nearly 2,800 interventions were conducted within 48 hours, covering around 600 separate fire incidents. Since the beginning of the season, the Directorate General of Forests has participated in 917 firefighting operations, compared with 620 during the same period in 2025. In response to the deterioration of the situation, the Government of Tunisia requested international assistance, resulting in the deployment of aerial firefighting assets from Italy and Algeria.

The wildfires have caused significant humanitarian, environmental and economic impacts. Evacuations were carried out in several locations, particularly in Bizerte and Jendouba, while livestock were moved from affected areas in Siliana and Ain Draham. Damage has been reported to homes, commercial premises, wooden cabins, restaurants and tourism facilities, particularly in Ghar El Melh and Rafraf. Large areas of agricultural land, fruit trees and natural resources have been destroyed, significantly affecting the livelihoods of rural and forest-dependent communities.

Firefighting operations continue to face challenges due to rugged terrain, difficult access conditions and highly flammable vegetation. As of 31 July 2026, firefighting and cooling operations remained ongoing in several governorates. While no fatalities had been officially reported at the time of writing, cases of smoke inhalation, minor burns and respiratory distress were recorded, and three Civil Protection personnel were injured. According to assessments conducted by the Tunisian Red Crescent, an estimated 27,117 people were directly affected by the wildfires. In addition, 14,362 people were affected by electricity and water supply disruptions associated with the emergency, resulting in a total affected population of 41,479 people.

title: Burkina Faso Floods Anticipatory Actions - Imminent DREF Final Report (MDRBF022)
content:
Event development

Update regarding the event’s development

The preparedness activities planned under this operation were primarily implemented in the provinces of Balé and Ioba, areas particularly exposed to flooding risks during the months of August, September, and October. This period traditionally corresponds to the season when overflow of the Mouhoun River causes recurrent flooding, especially in the provinces of Mouhoun, Balé, Ioba, Houet, and Tuy.

In August 2024, riverine flooding effectively affected the villages of Hèrèdougou and Goro in the municipality of Pâ (Balé Province), following a critical rise in the water level of the Mouhoun River. These floods affected at least 800 people, causing damage to housing, loss of household assets, and disruptions in access to essential services such as safe drinking water, healthcare, and food.

In this context, activities implemented under the DREF Imminent operation mainly focused on early disaster risk reduction actions. These included, in particular:

training 40 volunteers on flood risks and the early warning system;

training 50 volunteers (local teams) in first aid;

mobilizing 112 volunteers to conduct community awareness sessions on appropriate behaviors before, during, and after floods;

producing and broadcasting radio spots in local languages to reach a wide audience;

supporting the organization of three coordination platforms (COPROSUR) bringing together local authorities, technical services, community structures, and the Burkina Faso Red Cross (CRBF) to harmonize actions and strengthen information-sharing;

ensuring the continuous dissemination of reliable information through community radios and social media;

supporting the monitoring of early flood warning signs through the follow-up of 10 hydrological stations and the timely transmission of data to the relevant authorities.

These actions contributed to strengthening preparedness, awareness, and vigilance among exposed communities.

However, despite the mobilization and preparedness of local actors, no major flooding occurred during the implementation period of the operation. Trigger thresholds were not reached, as recorded rainfall levels were slightly below initial forecasts. Although a rise in water levels was observed in Hèrèdougou, which temporarily submerged National Road RN1, the impacts remained limited. Nevertheless, the CRBF deployed volunteers to raise awareness among road users and reinforce safety at the site.

This situation can also be explained by ongoing works in the municipality of Pâ, notably the construction of new water retention and crossing infrastructures, which helped mitigate the potential effects of heavy rainfall.

As a result, rapid response activities were not activated before the planned date of 30 September 2025, as no major flooding occurred that would have justified their implementation.

title: Venezuela | Earthquake - Operation Update #2 (MDRVE015)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS
Description of the crisis

On 24 June 2026, two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela in rapid succession; with the first one reaching a 7.2 magnitude, and a second one of 7.5 magnitude taking place approximately 39 seconds later. The epicentres were located near Morón and Yumare, in the states of Carabobo and Yaracuy, west of Caracas. USGS analysis confirmed the epicentre of the second earthquake to be approximately 17 km west of Catia La Mar, off the coast of La Guaira State1. Authorities have reported 1,463 aftershocks since the event, creating a high risk of further structural collapse2. The impact was severe and widespread, with tremors felt across much of the country, including the Capital District, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo, Miranda, Falcón, and neighbouring states. The earthquakes were also felt beyond Venezuela, including parts of Colombia, the Caribbean and northern Brazil, highlighting the exceptional geographic extent of the seismic event3.

The Government of Venezuela declared a National State of Emergency the same day and designated La Guaira, where the greatest concentration of damaged infrastructure and rescue operations was concentrated, as a disaster zone.

According to the Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS) approximately 530,000 were exposed to extreme earthquake intensity. The scale of the disaster led to a significant expansion of international humanitarian presence in the country. On 15 July, the United Nations announced an addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP), increasing financial requirements and expanding the number of people targeted for assistance for their overall humanitarian response to Venezuela (which extends beyond those affected by the earthquakes).

The event occurred during the San Juan festivities, a national celebration that attracts large numbers of people to coastal areas; and as many workplaces were closed, this also led to families having many or all members present inside their home when the earthquakes happened. In La Guaira State, a popular beachside destination to spend this festivity, this resulted in higher population concentrations in public spaces and along the coastline at the time of the event, increasing the number of people potentially exposed to the impacts of the earthquakes. La Guaira also serves multiple critical functions for the country given very close proximity to the Capital, Caracas. It hosts the country’s main international airport (Maiquetía) and one of its major ports, making it a strategic transportation, logistics, trade, tourism, fishing and service hub. Consequently, the incident impacted not only local communities and visitors present, but also essential infrastructure and activities that facilitate connectivity and the supply of goods to the capital and other regions of the country. This increases the number of people with secondary affectations and the extent of logistical capacity impacted.

As of 3 August, 6,125 people were reported dead, 16,740 injured, 6,462 rescued and approximately 17,907 had lost their homes due to severe damage to housing.4 The United Nations interagency indicated that tens of thousands of people remained unaccounted for during the response period; while many families including from those having opened tracing requests with the RCRC system have reported having been able to reunite with their loved ones in the days and weeks following the disaster. Efforts to identify and notify direct family members of persons hospitalized and persons deceased also continue. It is expected for the death toll to continue to rise as the Search and Rescue phase focused on extraction of survivors has moved towards a focus on recovery, identification and dignified return of bodies retrieved from collapsed structures to their family members.5 Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams operating under the coordination of the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) have now concluded their assignment. Response teams from over 29 countries deployed to Venezuela, including the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination (UNDAC) team and multiple RCRC Movement specialized teams such as the USAR teams of the Mexican RC, Colombian RC, Costa Rican RC who deployed in support of Venezuelan RC search & rescue efforts. The initial response focused on search, recovery, debris-removal, and initial shelter provision has now shifted towards bridging emergency relief to rehabilitation and reconstruction efforts under national leadership, with a broad range of bilateral and multilateral support focused on humanitarian assistance, restoration of essential services and recovery.

According to OCHA, 2,501 infrastructure assets had sustained some degree of damage, with 856 affected buildings, including 190 that have collapsed.6

On 21 July, the Venezuelan President of the Presidential Commission for the Assessment of Infrastructure Habitability reported that 6,907 buildings had been inspected in La Guaira using the traffic light assessment methodology to determine the condition of structures. Of the total inspected, 3,237 received a green tag indicating that the infrastructure poses no risk; 1,785 structures received a yellow tag indicating restricted use; and 1,885 were classified with a red tag indicating high risk. Structures assigned yellow or red classifications are now undergoing a secondary more thorough assessment7.

Disruptions of electricity, water-supply, telecommunications and transport systems caused by the earthquakes are undergoing repair to continue restoring functionality across the affected areas. Damaged roads and bridges have also affected movement to and within some affected areas; prompting authorities to relocate mobile bridges to facilitate access while repairs are finalized. Public transportation and airport operations are also under repair, with Maiquetia International Airport (which was severely damaged) expected to resume use for commercial cargo flights in the coming weeks. Commercial international passenger flights remain operating mostly in and out of Valencia airport, located approximately 2 hours out of the capital. Humanitarian cargo donated by Governments bilaterally to the Venezuelan Authorities, and through humanitarian actors, continues to flow in country through air, sea and land shipments.

In terms of essential services, healthcare capacity has been particularly including given the mass scale needs following the rapid onset emergency (trauma injuries), as well as given rates of chronic illness among displaced communities and affectations to water supply and sanitation services. More than 400 schools were also reported as affected, while some have been assigned as temporary shelters while authorities assign free permanent housing units and/or transitional single-family homes until the academic cycle resumes after the summer. To this end, Venezuelan authorities have already provided 240 permanent housing units to affected families; and while land & public housing infrastructure is evaluated and attributed for the assignment of additional seismic resistant units entirely free of charge, they have also enabled a parallel option for affected families who prefer to buy existing homes from the private market (whereby 80% of the price is subsidized by the government and the 20% remaining be granted on 25-year-loans extended by the local banking system.)

The physical impacts on affected people remain significant, with many requiring continued medical care, rehabilitation or referral services, as well as mental health and psychosocial support. Many families have experienced loss and grief, injury, displacement, separation from relatives and loss of homes, livelihoods and community support networks. The magnitude of the tragedy on human terms, continued aftershocks, displacement from damaged homes, and exposure to destroyed environments and recovery operations contributed to heightened levels of stress, anxiety and sadness among the affected population.

The earthquakes have resulted in grave humanitarian needs while exacerbating existing vulnerabilities, which increases the severity and complexity of the situation for the affected communities. This context reinforces the need for a response that addresses immediate lifesaving needs while supporting early recovery and strengthening community resilience.

title: Agrometeorological 10 days Bulletin for 11–20 August 2026 Across the Northern Tonle Sap Basin of the PEARL Project
content:
Flood Early Warning
No flood risk for the next 10 days. Keep a clean watering basin around each tree with a low earthen ring about half a palm high to slow splash; during heavy showers cut a small notch so water drains. Mulch under the canopy 10-15 cm {about a palm to a palm-and-a-half thick} using dry rice straw, chopped prunings, dried grass/leaves, leaving a hand-width gap at the trunk. Maintain diversion furrows one hand wide and one palm deep to guide rainwater away from trunks. Keep tools and bags on shelves about one palm above the floor.

title: UNICEF Afghanistan Humanitarian Flash Update No. 3 (Central and Eastern Region Flash Floods), 11 August 2026
content:
Highlights

  • On 20 July, heavy rainfall triggered flash floods across several provinces in central, northern and eastern Afghanistan, resulting in casualties, damage to homes and critical infrastructure, and disruption to essential services and livelihoods.
  • In the Eastern Region (ER), Parun district of Nuristan Province was among the most severely affected areas. Preliminary reports indicate 24 fatalities (26 per cent women, 74 per cent men), and 125 injuries (7 per cent women, 93 per cent men), with additional individuals reported missing. The floods destroyed or damaged 120 houses and affected health facilities, local markets, bridges, roads, flood protection walls, agricultural land and water supply networks, disrupting livelihoods and access to safe drinking water.
  • On 3 August, a second flash flood struck Barg-e-Matal district in eastern Nuristan, affecting 191 families through destruction or damage to their houses. This flood similarly disrupted livelihoods and damaged critical infrastructure, including bridges, roads, flood protection walls, agricultural land and water supply networks, further constraining access to safe drinking water and essential services.
  • In the Central Region (CR), flash floods across nine provinces resulted in two fatalities and six injuries. A total of 316 houses were affected, impacting 2,057 people – including 688 girls, 610 boys, 395 women and 364 men. Approximately 1.6 million square metres of agricultural land were destroyed, some 300 livestock were killed, and 17 schools sustained damage, further affecting livelihoods and access to basic services.
  • A separate flooding incident in Paktia province destroyed 11 houses and damaged agricultural land. A joint needs assessment team has been deployed to assess humanitarian needs, with distribution of assistance planned for 12 August.
  • The recent flash floods may also have displaced explosive ordnance (EO) or exposed previously buried hazards, increasing protection risks for affected communities and humanitarian personnel operating in flood-affected areas.

title: UNICEF South Asia Region Humanitarian Situation Report No.1 (Mid - Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Children and families across South Asia were affected by climate-related disasters, earthquakes, public health emergencies and conflict, resulting in significant humanitarian needs.
  • UNICEF provided life-saving health, nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), education and child protection services to 2.3 million crisis-affected people across India, Pakistan, Nepal and Sri Lanka, including 1.9 million children.
  • UNICEF strengthened national preparedness and anticipatory action capacities and promoted locally led, accountable and disability-inclusive humanitarian action.
  • By June 2026, UNICEF had received US$35.4 million against its regional Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal of US$71.4 million, limiting response, preparedness and anticipatory action efforts, including for emerging El Niño-related risks.

title: PHL: Cyclone - 08-2026 - Philippines Southwest Monsoon enhanced by Tropical Cyclones Maymay and Dolphin (2026-08-13)
content:
Description

At 8:00 PM on 4 August 2026, the Low-Pressure Area (LPA) located west of Bacnotan, La Union intensified into Tropical Depression MAYMAY, according to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA).

By 2:00 AM on 5 August 2026, Tropical Depression MAYMAY further intensified into Tropical Storm MAYMAY (international name: Kujira) while moving slowly near the western coast of Northern Luzon.

On 6 August 2026, Tropical Storm MAYMAY weakened into a Tropical Depression and made landfall over the Ilocos Sur–La Union area before traversing the mountainous terrain of Northern Luzon. As it moved inland, the system continued to weaken while crossing the rugged terrain and is forecast to emerge over the eastern coastal waters of Isabela or Cagayan. PAGASA indicated that the cyclone may further weaken into a remnant low by the afternoon or evening, although interaction with the mountainous terrain could result in an earlier weakening. The remnant low is then expected to move generally southeastward before merging with the larger circulation of Tropical Cyclone DOLPHIN.

Despite its weakening, MAYMAY, together with the enhanced Southwest Monsoon, continues to bring heavy rainfall, strong to gale-force winds, and hazardous sea conditions over affected areas. PAGASA also emphasized that localities outside the forecast track and confidence cone may still experience significant impacts, particularly heavy rainfall, strong winds, and rough to very rough seas.

title: Colombia: Flash Update 004 - Update on the Impact of the Earthquake in Colombia - August 12, 2026
content:
This Flash Update is produced by OCHA Colombia in collaboration with humanitarian partners, based on official reports (as of 12 August, 18:30 local time)

The emergency continues to escalate and has exceeded the local response capacity, with at least 49,214 people affected, 30,324 families impacted, 3,771 injured people, and 241 fatalities across 13 departments of the country. The damage to housing, social infrastructure, and essential services highlights a large-scale humanitarian crisis that requires a sustained and coordinated response.

Humanitarian needs are multisectoral, and significant response gaps remain, particularly in Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó, and Caldas. Damage to more than 54,900 homes (destroyed and damaged), educational institutions, health facilities, water supply systems, and roads is limiting access for thousands of people to basic services, protection, healthcare, safe water, and livelihoods.

The national and international response is underway and continues to expand to save lives and complement institutional capacity. While search and rescue operations, humanitarian assistance, and rapid needs assessments continue, the USD 5 million CERF allocation represents a critical boost to scale up the emergency response and support the populations most affected by the earthquake in Colombia.

title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #6 (August 12, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • On June 24, two earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 hit northern Venezuela in rapid succession, impacting at least seven states—including the capital city of Caracas and the neighboring city of La Guaira.
  • Official figures have so far confirmed 6,125 fatalities, 16,740 injuries and 24,477 people currently displaced.
  • Priority needs include healthcare services, clean water, food, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services, adequate sanitation and hygiene facilities, protection support and shelter.

Our Response

  • International Medical Corps has deployed three mobile medical units, which have provided 3,819 consultations since July 1.
  • On July 11, International Medical Corps opened an Emergency Medical Team (EMT) Type 1 Fixed facility to provide free medical services to impacted communities. To date, we have provided 3,263 consultations through the EMT.
  • Our teams have delivered 390,000 liters of safe water across displacement sites, benefitting an estimated 4,000 people.
  • Our teams have provided 759 MHPSS consultations.

title: Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 13, Data as of 09 August 2026
content:
Event description

The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo remains in a phase of intense and expanding transmission, with cumulative deaths crossing the grim milestone of 2,000 only 86 days after the outbreak was officially declared on 15 May 2026. Since External Situation Report #12, an additional 579 confirmed cases and 304 confirmed deaths have been reported, bringing the cumulative total to 4,381 confirmed cases and 2,011 confirmed deaths as of 9 August 2026, corresponding to a case fatality ratio of 45.9%. Ituri remains the epicentre, accounting for 85.8% of cumulative cases and 80.6% of cumulative deaths.

title: WFP Colombia: Earthquake Emergency Situation Report #1, 12 August 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• A 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia on 10 August, prompting the Government to declare a National Disaster Situation and activate a national response through the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) and the Unified Command Post (PMU).

• OCHA reports impacts across 16 departments and 357 municipalities, including areas already affected by conflict, displacement and recurrent climaterelated shocks, raising concerns over increased humanitarian needs and access constraints.

• The USGS estimates that approximately 2 million people experienced strong shaking and indicates a one-in-three probability that fatalities could exceed 1,000 people, highlighting the potential severity of the event.

• WFP currently operates emergency response activities in Chocó, Valle del Cauca and Risaralda, reaching approximately 100,000 people, and maintains field offices in Quibdó and Cali, providing an operational platform for assessments and response planning.

• All WFP personnel have been accounted for. WFP offices in Quibdó and Cali reported infrastructure damage and business continuity measures have been activated.

Situation Update

• At 07:34 local time on 10 August 2026, a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, with its epicenter near San José del Palmar, Chocó Department, at a depth of approximately 96 km. The earthquake was felt across the country, triggering evacuations and emergency response activations in multiple departments and major urban centers. Several aftershocks have been reported following the main event.

• The departments of Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Caldas and Quindío are among the most affected. Following an emergency meeting convened at UNGRD, the President declared a National Disaster Situation and established a centralized PMU to coordinate response efforts and consolidate official information.

• According to the latest official government balance, as of 7:00am COT - 11 August 2026, the earthquake has resulted in 176 confirmed fatalities and 2,503 injured people. Authorities also reported 7,436 damaged houses, 1,136 destroyed houses, and 48 collapsed buildings. Damage to essential infrastructure includes 377 health facilities, 791 educational facilities and 377 community centers, while 69 roads have been affected.

• According to Colombia´s Civil Aviation Authority six airports remain affected and suspended for commercial operations, pending safety and infrastructure assessments, and one additional airport has reported damage to its runway.

• Search and rescue operations remain ongoing in the most severely affected areas and casualty figures are expected to evolve as assessments continue.

• According to the USGS modelling, approximately 2 million people experienced strong shaking across western and central Colombia. USGS impact modelling also estimates a 33 percent probability that fatalities could eventually exceed 1,000 people, reflecting the severity of ground shaking and the concentration of exposed populations in affected urban areas. These figures are predictive estimates and remain subject to confirmation through ongoing government-led assessments.

• National and local authorities have mobilized Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams, emergency services, and technical assessment teams to support affected communities and restore critical services. The Government has indicated that updated information will be released regularly through the PMU as new reports are received from departmental and municipal authorities.

• The earthquake has affected several areas already facing humanitarian challenges linked to conflict, displacement, poverty and food insecurity. Damage to transport infrastructure, public services and local markets may further increase humanitarian needs and constrain access to food and basic services for vulnerable populations. WFP is monitoring the evolving situation and coordinating with government authorities, UN agencies and humanitarian partners to assess food security implications and potential response requirements.

• According to the National Route Institute (INVÍAS), the earthquake affected at least 13 locations across the national road network. The most significant access constraints include the total closure of the Cali-Loboguerrero corridor in Dagua (Valle del Cauca), the Cartago-Alcalá corridor, the Manizales-Fresno corridor in Caldas, and the Santa Cecilia-Asia corridor in Pueblo Rico (Risaralda). Multiple landslides have also affected strategic transport routes in Quindío, including the Calarcá-Cajamarca and Armenia-Montenegro-Alcalá corridors.

• Access assessments remain ongoing, particularly in earthquake-affected areas of Chocó, where access limitations continue to constrain damage assessments and the identification of humanitarian needs. Official estimates of the total number of affected people are not yet available.

title: Situation Report No.9: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), 12 August 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Seven weeks after the two earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026, the response continues to sustain emergency operations while transitioning toward early recovery. Current efforts are focused on maintaining essential health services, rehabilitating affected facilities, supporting transitional camps, and delivering health services through a comprehensive approach, while mitigating public health risks and ensuring a continuous, needs-based supply of medicines and essential equipment.

• Health service recovery and critical care capacity are advancing, with rehabilitation planning progressing in priority facilities and intensive care and maternity capacity being restored at Hospital Dr. José Gregorio Hernández, while assessments in Caracas and Miranda continue to identify critical gaps in equipment and human resources.

• Public health surveillance and immunization systems are being reinforced, with expanded epidemiological analysis and digital reporting, enhanced laboratory diagnostic capacity, and more than 31,000 vaccine doses administered; national vaccine supply security was further supported through a USD 18 million Revolving Fund credit line.

• Efforts advanced toward the provision of comprehensive care, focusing on mental health, sexual and reproductive health, noncommunicable diseases, and rehabilitation. This included dissemination of the national mental health protocol, training of transitional camp focal points, continuity of oncology care through three designated centers, and attention to emerging needs such as assessing rehabilitation center capacities and training on amputee management and wound care.

• PAHO/WHO continued supporting the response with critical medicines and equipment, most recently delivering targeted emergency medical supplies – including specialized kits, medicines, and high-complexity surgical instruments – to the Maternal and Child Hospital Leopoldo Aguerrevere in Petare, Sucre.

• PAHO/WHO continues to support the health response through its Regional Response Team, covering key areas such as emergency coordination, logistics, information management, epidemiology, laboratory services, WASH, immunization, risk communication, and Emergency Medical Teams (EMT) coordination. Additional experts in entomology and infection prevention and control are being deployed.

title: Ukraine war situation update | 25 – 31 July 2026
content:
Ukraine Conflict Monitor Update

Ukraine continued its campaign on energy infrastructure in occupied territories, while its strikes on oil tankers briefly suspended work at the CPC terminal.

Number of events and change compared to last week (per target):

Education: 21 events31% increase

Energy: 39 events7% decrease

Residential: 209 events3% increase

  • In July, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (SBS) launched a middle-strike drone campaign on energy infrastructure in the occupied territories, and particularly in Crimea. Over 170 energy infrastructure sites were struck, leading to water shortages in the occupied territories and a sharp decrease in both electricity consumption and production in the Crimean peninsula in July. The SBS’ Operation Crimean Switch Off — alongside the Ukrainian Security Service’s (SBU) campaign targeting military logistics on and around the R-280 road — aims to undermine the economic basis of the Russian occupation in Crimea and southern occupied territories. These continuous strikes are worsening living conditions for the Ukrainian civilians remaining in these territories, prompting Kyiv to issue instructions on how to deal with potential power outages, food shortages, and military actions. As Russia has shown little ability to contain the strikes, the SBS can be expected to continue the campaign well into August.
  • In Russia, the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) suspended its supplies of Kazakh oil for the third time in a month, after Ukrainian drones reportedly attacked two oil tankers near its mooring facilities used for loading. Although Chevron reported resuming oil flows and tanker loading through the CPC on 31 July, anxieties remain about Kazakhstan’s main route for 80-90% of its oil exports, and Chevron has resumed diplomatic efforts in Washington to persuade Kyiv to stop its CPC targeting. Meanwhile, the Kazakh president publicly asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to freeze the war, and the Astana government denounced the strikes without naming Kyiv. Kazakhstan also told the International Maritime Organization that it may seek compensation for damages inflicted by the strikes. Meanwhile, the United States recently issued another objection to the Ukrainian strikes on the CPC. Other staunch Ukraine allies may follow suit, albeit likely behind closed doors, as they suffer from high oil prices amid the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Nevertheless, the strikes on a terminal that provides 1-2% of global oil supplies are likely to continue in August.

title: Nigeria: Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe (BAY) states - Quarter 2 Situation Report, April - June 2026
content:
This report is produced by OCHA Nigeria in collaboration with humanitarian partners. It covers the April-June 2026 period. The next report will be issued in October 2026.

Highlights

  • Lean season takes hold with 6.4 million people food insecure across Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states
  • Record Nigeria Humanitarian Fund (NHF) allocation gets underway in northeast, northwest and northcentral Nigeria.
  • As cholera cases rise across Borno, humanitarian partners scale-up life-saving responses
  • Borno State progresses with plans to close IDP camps
  • Escalating insecurity disrupts lives and humanitarian operations across the northeast
  • Nigeria on its way to locally- led and financed humanitarian coordination

Situation overview

Lean season hits northeast communities, driving rising food insecurity.

More than 6.4 million people in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe (BAY) states are projected to face crisis-level hunger or worse during the June–August 2026 lean season, marking the worst acute food insecurity peak recorded in northeast Nigeria in more than a decade.

According to the latest Cadre Harmonisé (CH) food security analysis, conducted jointly by the Government and humanitarian partners, nearly 4 in every 10 people in the BAY states - about 36 per cent of the population - are expected to experience acute food insecurity during the season. The latest projection represents a 10 per cent increase from previously estimates made in October 2025, highlighting the rapid deterioration of food security conditions across the region.

The situation is particularly alarming for the most vulnerable households. More than 1.1 million people are projected to face Emergency (Phase 4) levels of food insecurity, characterized by severe food consumption gaps and heightened risks of acute malnutrition. At the same time, about 10,300 people could fall into Catastrophe (Phase 5), the most extreme level of food insecurity, by August 2026 if urgent action is not taken.

The CH warns that a combination of conflict, economic hardship and climate-related shocks is driving the crisis. Persistent insecurity continues to limit access to farmland and markets, undermining livelihoods and reducing food production. Renewed attacks in parts of Borno State, including Askira/Uba, Chibok, Gwoza and Kaga local government areas, have further restricted agricultural activities and access to essential services.

At the same time, families are grappling with soaring food prices, elevated fuel costs and expensive agricultural inputs as a result of the conflict in the Middle East. Inflation, currency depreciation and rising transportation costs have reduced household purchasing power, making it increasingly difficult for vulnerable communities to meet their basic food needs.

Climate risks are complicating the food security landscape. Early warning information points to the likelihood of localized El Niño-related impacts, including both dry spells and flooding during the current agricultural season. Such shocks could destroy crops, disrupt farming activities and further erode household food stocks and incomes, particularly among already vulnerable rural communities.

Humanitarian agencies say assistance remains a critical lifeline, but current resources are insufficient to match rising needs. As of May 2026, approximately 700,000 people targeted for food assistance under the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan had not received support, while 830,000 people missed out on planned emergency agricultural assistance because of funding shortfalls.

The Food Security Sector needs US$224.4 million in 2026 to provide food assistance to 1.5 million people and emergency agricultural support to 900,000 people. However, funding remains critically low. As of mid-year, the sector had received only US$76 million, representing only a third of requirements, leaving a funding gap of approximately 66 per cent (US$148.4 million). The shortfall is particularly concerning for agricultural interventions which are critical to helping vulnerable households produce food, protect livelihoods, and reduce dependence on humanitarian assistance.

Without urgent action during the lean season, aid agencies warn that worsening food insecurity could lead to increased displacement, deeper poverty, heightened malnutrition and greater instability across north-east Nigeria. Every day of delay increases the risk of irreversible harm for families already struggling to survive. Additional and rapid funding is urgently needed to expand lifesaving food assistance, support food production and reach the most vulnerable people before hunger escalates further across Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 80, as of 11 August 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Living conditions of internally displaced persons deteriorate in Gbazara, Ouham-Fafa Prefecture.
  • More than 1,000 medical consultations provided for displaced people in Am-Dafock.

GENERAL CONTEXT

Ouham-Fafa Prefecture – North-West

  • In Gbazara, living conditions for some 4,480 internally displaced persons (IDPs) continue to deteriorate. Since their arrival at the site on 22 April 2026, they have not received any food assistance, limiting their ability to meet essential needs. Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) needs remain high due to the lack of adequate latrines and shower facilities. Open defecation is increasing the risk of waterborne diseases. The rainy season could further exacerbate health risks at the site. Humanitarian partners continue to mobilize resources to address priority needs. The displaced families fled Béhilié in April 2026 following an armed attack that resulted in the village being burned down.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Multi-sector

Ouham-Fafa Prefecture – North-West

  • The Association des Femmes pour la Promotion et l’Entrepreneuriat (AFPE), with support from the Central African Republic Humanitarian Fund (CAR HF), provided cash assistance to 30 households caring for unaccompanied or separated children at the Batangafo displacement site. The assistance benefited 19 girls and 11 boys. Emergency food and clothing kits were also distributed to help meet the households’ immediate needs. Six gender-based violence (GBV) survivors were referred to the Gbazara health facility for appropriate care and support.

Health

Vakaga Prefecture – North-East

  • From 3 to 8 August, International Medical Corps (IMC) provided health services through a mobile clinic at the Am-Dafock gathering site. A total of 1,046 consultations were conducted, including 303 malaria cases, 195 acute respiratory infection cases and 89 diarrhoea cases. IMC continues to provide health services through a fixed clinic at the IDP site.

title: UNHCR Egypt - Monthly Operational Update (July 2026)
content:
LATEST DEVELOPMENTS – HIGHLIGHTS

• On 15 July, UNHCR engaged with Egypt's Permanent Committee for Refugee Affairs to advance preparations for the implementation of the country's new asylum system. Discussions focused on a proposed capacity-development package, including technical training, institutional strengthening, a strategic retreat, a learning management system, and a study visit to support the Committee's operational readiness. UNHCR and the Permanent Committee agreed to co-design the programme ahead of its planned implementation in September 2026, while UNHCR reiterated its appeal for sustained donor support to facilitate the transition towards a fully State-owned asylum system in Egypt.

• On 22 July, UNHCR briefed a visiting European Parliament Subcommittee on Human Rights (DROI) delegation on Egypt’s evolving displacement context, including the continued arrivals of refugees fleeing the conflict in Sudan, developments related to Egypt’s Asylum Law and Executive Regulations, registration and documentation challenges, and the impact of severe funding shortfalls. Discussions also covered refugees’ and asylum-seekers’ access to asylum, healthcare and education, as well as their livelihoods and self-reliance. The engagement helped raise awareness among European policymakers of the protection needs of refugees and the operational pressures facing Egypt and UNHCR.

title: WFP Tajikistan Country Brief, August 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Tajikistan is a landlocked, mountainous country with a population of 10.27 million, growing at 2 percent yearly, the highest rate in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. Half of the population is under 25 years, and a quarter resides in cities (TAJSTAT, 2020).

• Nutrition outcomes have improved substantially since 2023: stunting among children under five declined from 26 percent in 2012 to 14 percent in 2023, while wasting dropped from 10 percent in 2012 to 6 percent by 2017 and remained at 6 percent in 2023 (TDHS, 2023).

• Tajikistan’s economy remains strong, with Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growing above 8 percent in 2024 and early 2025, supported by remittances, services, and industrial activity, while inflation remains low. However, the economy remains highly exposed to external shocks, as remittances account for nearly half of GDP and export performance continues to be weak.

• Poverty declined from 20.4 percent in 2023 to 19.8 percent in 2024, driven by economic growth and remittances. However, rural households remain vulnerable due to limited employment opportunities and exposure to climate and economic shocks.

title: Syrian Arab Republic — Emergency Mobility Tracking and Cross Border Monitoring Situation Update — Round 19 (10 August 2026)
content:
OVERVIEW

Cross-border movements from Lebanon into the Syrian Arab Republic (hereafter referred to as Syria) have declined following the ceasefire in Lebanon announced on 17 April 2026. After reaching a peak of 153,087 arrivals on 27 April, DTM estimates that around 29,467 Syrian and Lebanese nationals have since returned to Lebanon. This trend suggests cross-border mobility is increasingly characterised by more gradual and stabilised patterns.

From 2 March to 10 August, DTM identified 123,620 arrivals across 1,163 locations in all 14 governorates. Syrian nationals continued to account for the overwhelming majority of arrivals, with Lebanese nationals representing less than 1 per cent. Flow monitoring at four assessed Syrian-Lebanese border crossings recorded 655,720 movements into Syria over the same period, of which approximately 98 per cent were Syrian nationals and 2 per cent Lebanese nationals. In addition, 3,375 Lebanese nationals were recorded transiting through Syria towards Jordan, highlighting the continued use of Syria as a route for onward regional movement.

The Arida border crossing was temporarily closed from 6 August, with closure expected to continue until 22 August due to technical works on the Lebanese side. Consequently, Arida movement figures are available only through 5 August and are substantially lower than in previous reporting periods. The closure has also created additional access constraints for travellers, with key informants (KIs) reporting that those previously using Arida have had to rely on alternative crossings located further from Tartous Governorate, increasing both travel times and associated costs.

title: Attacks on Health Care Bi-Monthly News Brief, 22 July - 04 August 2026
content:
Attacks on Health Care
in the occupied Palestinian territory

Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) identified 190 incidents of violence against or obstruction of health care across the West Bank and East Jerusalem in 2025. Health workers were arrested, threatened, or injured; health facilities were damaged, violently raided, or surrounded; and ambulances and emergency medical teams were repeatedly delayed, blocked, or searched amid Israeli military incursions and increasingly restrictive movement and access constraints imposed across the West Bank.

Most incidents were attributed to IDF troops armed with guns. Some incidents also involved the use of explosive weapons, including drone-fired missiles and controlled demolitions, which in several cases killed health workers and damaged nearby health facilities, including a hospital in Jenin.

Attacks on health care linked to Israeli settlers, typically armed with guns or rocks, more than doubled in 2025, compared to 2024, rising from around 2% to 9% of total reported attacks. Most Israeli settler attacks targeted ambulances and first responders, including blocking their access to those needing care. In one case, paramedics in Tubas governorate were reported assaulted by Israeli settlers under the protection of the IDF. Settler violence also impacted a health facility when around 17 Israeli settlers attacked and destroyed a clinic in Hebron governorate.

title: Lebanon: Flash Update #49 - Escalation of hostilities in Lebanon (as of 10 August 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • At least 4,335 deaths and 12,277 injuries recorded due to hostilities since 2 March, with 355 people killed and 276 injured since the 19 June ceasefire announcement, according to the Ministry of Public Health.
  • 352,793 people remain displaced within Lebanon as of 6 August, while 834,651 people have reported returning to their areas of origin. As of 10 August, 22,800 Internally Displaced Persons (>53% women and girls) remain in 232 collective shelters.
  • On 5 August, a new displacement order was issued for Mansouri in Tyre District (South Governorate), the first displacement order since 11 July. At least 130 families were newly displaced from Mansouri to Tyre following the displacement order.
  • 5 August demolition of a well and 7 August fires at Chaqra and Wadi Saluki water stations in Nabatieh Governorate, underscoring the continued destruction of infrastructure that limits civilian access to basic services.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

The humanitarian situation in Lebanon remains critical, as ongoing military activities, unstable returns, and prolonged displacement continue to drive humanitarian needs and exacerbate protection concerns. Displacement remains significant across the country, with access to adequate shelter, essential services, and livelihood opportunities posing persistent challenges for displaced populations. Returnees, particularly in conflict-affected areas of South and Nabatieh governorates, continue to face insecurity, recurring military activity, and widespread destruction of infrastructure and basic services. These conditions are hindering safe returns while amplifying protection risks and humanitarian needs among affected communities.

An increase in military activities was reported during the period covered across South and Nabatieh Governorates, with the first new displacement order in nearly a month issued on 5 August, for Mansouri, a village in Tyre District (South Governorate). Prior to the displacement order, approximately 130 families were present in Mansouri – all families were displaced to Tyre after the order, with 50 families now hosted in existing collective shelters, and the remaining 80 hosted by family members in Tyre city. Humanitarian partners supported the Tyre Union of Municipalities in providing emergency assistance, including non-food item kits, to the newly displaced families. Both ahead of and following the displacement order, artillery shelling on Mansouri village occurred daily from 3 August through 10 August, with airstrikes occurring on 5-7 and 9-10 August.

A total of 133 conflict incidents involving shelling, airstrikes, detonations and demolitions were reported between 4 and 10 August, compared with 97 incidents reported during 28 July-3 August and 130 incidents during 21-27 July. This increase was driven primarily by a surge in reports of artillery shelling (some 83 incidents), of which half were reported as targeting Mansouri as well as Ali el Taher and Haddatha (both Nabatieh Governorate). Airstrikes, shelling, demolitions and other security incidents were also reported in locations across Bint Jbeil, Marjaayoun, Hasbaya and Nabatieh districts in Nabatieh Governorate, as well as Tyre district in South Governorate.

The 5 August displacement order for Mansouri was only the second such order issued since the latest ceasefire announcement on 19 June. The first, on 11 July, involved leaflets dropped over the same municipality declaring it a "threatened area" and urging civilians to evacuate. Continued insecurity, destruction of civilian infrastructure, and recurring displacement are further exacerbating humanitarian and protection concerns by prolonging and triggering displacement, hindering safe returns, and increasing risks to civilian safety.

Ongoing destruction of critical infrastructure, agricultural land, and residential buildings continues to reduce access to services and exacerbate protection concerns. New incidents affecting water infrastructure were reported, including a fire at the Chaqra water station in Bint Jbeil District on 7 August and demolition activities affecting a water well at Wadi Saluki in Marjaayoun District on 5 August, followed by fires affecting the Wadi Saluki water station on 7 August. The incidents affecting the two water facilities further impacted access to water for the villages of Bint Jbeil and Chaqra in Bint Jbeil district and Mais al-Jabal in Marjaayoun district (Nabatieh Governorate). With water access already severely constrained by widespread damage to water infrastructure, continued attacks on civilian assets are further disrupting access to safe water for affected communities. In addition, reported incendiary strikes caused extensive fires in forested and mountainous areas of western Bekaa Governorate, resulting in further damage to agricultural land and environmental resources.

Conflict-related damage continues to pose threats to civilians. On 5 August, a building previously damaged by an airstrike collapsed in Haret Hreik, Baabda district (Mount Lebanon). While no casualties were reported, the incident underscores the ongoing dangers associated with conflict-damaged structures and highlights the need for timely debris removal, structural assessments, and rehabilitation of damaged infrastructure to reduce risks to affected populations.

The Ministry of Public Health reported 4,335 people killed (including 392 women and 253 children) and 12,250 injured (1,452 women and 1,037 children) as of 10 August. Since the latest ceasefire announcement on 19 June, 355 people have been killed and 276 injured. Since 2 March, 135 health care professionals have been killed while on duty and 410 injured, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Displacement levels remain significant nationwide. As of 6 August, 352,793 people remain displaced across Lebanon, according to the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), representing a 2 per cent decrease compared with 30 July. 61 per cent of the displaced are from three districts in Nabatieh Governorate – Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil, and Marjaayoun, and 20 per cent are from Tyre, South Governorate. While overall displacement continued to decline across most districts, increases in the number of displaced people were recorded in several districts, including Tyre (increase of 1,551), Nabatieh (increase of 1,217) and Bint Jbeil (increase of 60). Beirut (Beirut Governorate), Saida (South), Chouf (Mount Lebanon) and Tyre (South) host the largest caseload of IDPs, with 106,800 in Beirut and 63,800 in Saida. For displaced households outside collective shelters, where there is continued strain on local households and municipal systems, access to health care and medication, rental support, restoration of services, access to protection services, and emergency livelihoods interventions remain critical to support households' basic needs and safety.

Collective shelters continue to host displaced people from communities facing barriers to return. 22,800 remain hosted across 232 collective shelters in Lebanon as of 10 August (DRM). Most remaining shelters are in Mount Lebanon Governorate (96) and Beirut Governorate (50), with 7,600 and 7,000 people respectively hosted in each. In South Governorate, 42 shelters remain, hosting 6,100 people. IDPs in collective shelters continue to face challenges in accessing basic services. Limited fuel availability is affecting the continuity of electricity and water services, heightening health, hygiene and safety risks. Displaced households continue to identify cash assistance as a critical need to help cover essential living costs.

Persistent barriers to return contribute to slower return rates and ongoing humanitarian and protection needs. 834,651 people had begun the return to their areas of origin as of 6 August, representing a 2 per cent increase from the previous week (30 July). Notably, an additional 12,240 people returned to Nabatieh district (Nabatieh Governorate), 1,210 to Tyre district (South) and 929 to Bint Jbeil (Nabatieh). Returnees continue to face significant humanitarian needs and protection concerns, particularly for those returning to areas of South and Nabatieh governorates where continued military activities continue to pose risks to civilians, trigger new displacement, and impact service access. Returnees have expressed key priorities for housing, restoration of basic services, cash assistance, and livelihoods support to enable safe and sustainable returns. Protection needs also remain high as access to healthcare, mental health and psychosocial support, GBV and child protection services, Housing Land and Property (HLP) assistance, and mine clearance remain critical gaps.

Funding shortfalls continue to pose barriers to sustained humanitarian assistance as the end of the six-month Flash Appeal approaches. The 2026 Lebanon Flash Appeal has received less than half of the $639.9 million required as of 3 August, or $307.6 million (48.1 per cent).

title: Attacks on Health Care in Sudan, 22 July - 04 August 2026
content:
Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) identified 134 incidents of violence against or obstruction of health care in Sudan in 2025.

Drone strikes impacting health care surged in 2025, increasing from three incidents in 2024 to 24 in 2025. Over 75% of armed drone strikes that impacted health care were linked to the RSF, with high incident numbers reported in North Darfur and North Kordofan states.

Several other incidents were recorded of air strikes and shelling near or in the vicinity of hospitals, killing and injuring civilians in the area, and often forcing health care providers to suspend medical services. In turn, this impeded patients’ access to health care. Explosive weapons were most often used indiscriminately, with their wide-area effects causing widespread deaths, injuries or damage in populated areas.
