title: Colombia: Flash Update 003- Actualización afectaciones por terremoto en 13 departamentos de Colombia - 11 agosto de 2026 [ES/EN]
content:
SP

Este Flash update es producido por OCHA Colombia en colaboración con los socios humanitarios y reportes oficiales. Corte a 11 agosto (17:30 horas)

La magnitud e impacto de la emergencia supera lo esperado. El terremoto de magnitud 7,4 registrado el 10 de agosto en San José del Palmar (Chocó), junto con 29 réplicas significativas, ha generado una emergencia humanitaria de gran escala en Colombia. Hasta el momento, 13 departamentos y 357 municipios reportan afectaciones, con un saldo preliminar de 224 personas fallecidas, 2.595 heridas y severos daños en viviendas e infraestructura esencial, siendo Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó y Caldas los departamentos más impactados.

La respuesta se implementa y coordinada a pesar de desafíos operacionales. El Gobierno Nacional, a través del Sistema Nacional de Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres (SNGRD), lidera las operaciones de respuesta, rescate y asistencia inicial, con el apoyo complementario de Naciones Unidas y socios humanitarios nacionales e internacionales. No obstante, la continuidad de las afectaciones a servicios esenciales, incluyendo electricidad, agua, salud y conectividad, así como las restricciones de acceso derivadas de daños en al menos 73 vías, representan desafíos críticos para la asistencia y recuperación temprana de las comunidades afectadas.

Persisten necesidades humanitarias y brechas de información. Las necesidades prioritarias identificadas incluyen búsqueda y rescate, alojamiento temporal, atención en salud, seguridad alimentaria, educación y protección. Sin embargo, persisten importantes vacíos de información sobre el número total de personas damnificadas, la ubicación y condiciones de los albergues, así como sobre las necesidades específicas a nivel municipal, limitando una respuesta plenamente focalizada y basada en evidencias.

ENG

This Flash Update is produced by OCHA Colombia in collaboration with humanitarian partners and based on official reports. Reporting cut-off: 11 August (5:30 p.m.).

The scale and impact of the emergency exceed initial expectations. The 7.4-magnitude earthquake recorded on 10 August in San José del Palmar, Chocó Department, together with 29 significant aftershocks, has triggered a large-scale humanitarian emergency in Colombia. To date, 13 departments and 357 municipalities have reported impacts, with a preliminary toll of 224 fatalities and 2,595 injuries, as well as extensive damage to housing and critical infrastructure. Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó and Caldas are the most affected departments.

Response efforts are being implemented and coordinated despite operational challenges. The National Government, through the National System for Disaster Risk Management (SNGRD), is leading response operations, including search and rescue efforts and the provision of initial assistance, with complementary support from the United Nations and national and international humanitarian partners. However, continued disruptions to essential services, including electricity, water, health care and telecommunications, together with access constraints resulting from damage to at least 73 roads, pose critical challenges to humanitarian assistance and early recovery efforts in affected communities.

Humanitarian needs and information gaps persist. Priority needs identified to date include search and rescue, temporary shelter, health care, food security, education and protection. However, significant information gaps remain regarding the total number of affected people, the location and conditions of shelters, and specific needs at the municipal level, limiting a fully targeted and evidence-based response.

title: Afghanistan Flash Floods - Flash Update (20-30 July 2026)
content:
Since 20 July 2026, heavy rainfall and flash floods have affected Laghman, Nangarhar, Nuristan, Logar, Kapisa, Parwan, Ghazni, Paktia, and Paktika provinces, resulting in deaths and injuries, displacement, and widespread damage to homes, livelihoods, and public infrastructure.

Flooding has severely constrained access to essential health and protection services, affecting an estimated 1,994 women and girls of reproductive age. Pregnant women, adolescent girls, older women, and women-headed households face heightened protection and reproductive health risks as a result of disrupted services and limited access to care.

UNFPA continues to scale up its response by providing emergency sexual and reproductive health services and psychosocial support. As of 30 July, UNFPA’s mobile sexual and reproductive health and psychosocial support team had reached more than 1,400 people, providing antenatal and postnatal care, reproductive health and family planning services, general health consultations, and psychosocial support. In addition, 227 dignity kits and 50 mama and baby kits have been distributed to flood-affected women.

UNFPA is conducting joint needs assessments to identify emerging priority needs in sexual and reproductive health, gender-based violence, and psychosocial support among affected populations, alongside dedicated community feedback mechanisms. The findings continue to inform the scale, targeting, and prioritization of UNFPA’s response, in close coordination with humanitarian partners.

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Earthquakes in Venezuela (24 June – 7 August 2026)
content:
Venezuela continues to face significant humanitarian needs following the earthquakes of 24 June 2026. The most urgent needs among affected populations include healthcare, including sexual and reproductive health (SRH); food and safe water; mental health and psychosocial support; shelter; sanitation and hygiene; and specialized protection services, particularly for gender-based violence (GBV).

The loss of livelihoods, disruptions to health and protection services, and precarious living conditions—particularly for people residing in temporary shelters—are increasing the risk of GBV and harmful coping strategies. Currently, 24,477 people are residing in 107 transitional shelters, where overcrowding, limited privacy in sleeping and bathroom facilities, and inadequate lighting are heightening protection risks, particularly for women, girls, and adolescents.

Numerous health facilities in affected areas have sustained structural damage, while others are facing shortages of medicines, equipment, and health personnel, placing additional strain on an already overstretched health system. UNFPA is supporting the continuity of life-saving maternal, newborn, and obstetric care through its support to maternity wards in 16 hospitals across La Guaira, Caracas, and Miranda. UNFPA is also providing on-the-job training for health personnel and delivering critical medical equipment and supplies, including 62 Inter-Agency Reproductive Health Kits, which will support the needs of approximately 2,250 people.

UNFPA and its implementing partners are also delivering SRH and GBV services across four transitional shelters. To date, 4,327 people have received prenatal care, family planning services, psychosocial support, GBV case management, and dignity kits. In addition, 4,186 people have been reached through SRH and GBV awareness-raising and information sessions.

UNFPA is appealing for US$10 million to support the emergency response to the earthquakes in Venezuela. To date, US$4 million has been mobilized, leaving a 60 per cent funding gap. Additional support is urgently needed to sustain the delivery of life-saving SRH and GBV services to affected populations.

title: UNICEF Haiti Humanitarian Situation Report No. 2 (Mid - Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights:

  • A total of 1.5 million people, including 751,000 children are displaced. Some 5.8 million people, or about half of the Haitian population, faced high levels of acute food insecurity. 442 suspected cholera cases were reported, and 9 confirmed cases, including two deaths. Additionally, 11,550 children were forcibly returned to Haiti during the reporting period.
  • UNICEF and its partners continued to provide critical life-saving assistance, treating 21,500 children for severe wasting, enabling healthcare access to 198,800 people and providing safe water to 336,400 people. Protection Cluster partners supported the reintegration of 118 children formerly associated with armed groups. UNICEF's IDP response in sites, including Health/Nutrition, WASH and Protection interventions, covered the needs of about 103,000 IDPs.
  • With the 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children appeal only 21 per cent funded, urgent support is needed to sustain critical life-saving support.

title: DRC Eastern DR Congo Ebola Situational Report #4 (5 August 2026)
content:
Contextual updates

The Ebola outbreak continues to evolve in a highly complex operational environment, with more than 3,000 confirmed cases to date. Community transmission remains a major concern, with approximately 63% of reported deaths from 14-20 July occurring in the community, indicating that many patients continue to die at home rather than accessing timely treatment. This highlights persistent challenges related to risk communication, community engagement, trust in the response, and timely care-seeking. In addition, the Cash Working Group has monitored an increase of 35% in the minimum expenditure basket value between May and June 2026 in Bunia, showing the impact of Ebola outbreak on local markets and inflation.

The geographical scope of the outbreak also remains under close monitoring. Two additional provinces recently reported affected cases, including Tshopo and Haut-Uele Provinces (bordering the Central African Republic). Crossborder transmission continues to pose a significant regional concern.

title: WFP Ghana Country Brief, June 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Ghana continues to face widening regional and socioeconomic disparities, with northern and rural communities bearing the greatest vulnerability. In the north, where most households rely on climate‑sensitive agriculture, families remain highly exposed to erratic rainfall, rising temperatures, low farm‑gate prices and limited infrastructure. As a food‑deficit country, Ghana is also vulnerable to global price shocks, which continue to drive up the cost of staple foods.

• According to recent Cadre Harmonisé analysis, an estimated 1.5 million people (IPC Phase 3–5) are projected to face crisis‑level food insecurity between June and August 2026. Although severe food insecurity declined slightly, data from the Ghana Statistical Service and WFP’s Mobile Vulnerability Analysis and Mapping (mVAM) show that the number of people facing overlapping risks, food insecurity, multidimensional poverty and unemployment, continues to rise. Rural women are disproportionately affected, with severe food insecurity among female‑headed rural households reaching 8.1 percent.

• These trends risk undermining progress toward national development and the SDGs, particularly Zero Hunger. Through its 2024–2028 Country Strategic Plan, WFP Ghana supports the Government in building resilient, scalable systems and strengthening national capacity for effective emergency preparedness, response and recovery.

title: WFP Liberia Country Brief, August 2026
content:
SITUATIONAL OVERVIEW

• Liberia continues to face overlapping economic, climate and public health shocks. The country is responding to ongoing Mpox, Lassa fever and measles outbreaks, while declining external assistance and funding constraints continue to affect national response capacities.

• According to the 2025 Comprehensive Food Security and Nutrition Survey (CFSNS), 22.2 percent of households are food insecure, while 26.3 percent of children under five are stunted and 7.4 percent suffer from acute malnutrition. Food insecurity and poor nutrition remain significant challenges, particularly in rural areas.

• The Government of Liberia's ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development (2025–2029)— Agriculture, Roads, Rule of Law, Education, Sanitation and Tourism, provides the national framework for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals.

• WFP’s Liberia new Country Strategic Plan (CSP) 2026-20230 was approved during WFP’s Executive Board June session. The Government of Liberia expressed strong support for the new CSP and reaffirmed its commitment to continued collaboration with WFP to advance national development priorities, strengthen human capital, and address food security and nutrition challenges. WFP has operated in Liberia since 1968.

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #21 (7 to 10 August 2026)
content:
Situation Report No. 21 provides an update on IOM's response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 7 to 10 August 2026.

Highlights

  • On 10 August, IOM launched the distribution of non-food items in Mare II and Algarín following household registration and verification activities in Mare Abajo II and surrounding communities.
  • IOM and its partner Ven Da Tu Mano maintained mobile health and mental health services in temporary accommodation sites. Cumulative services reached 3,267 consultations at the José María Vargas Sports Complex and 2,864 consultations in César Nieves, while surveillance of diarrhoeal diseases was reinforced.
  • From 17 July to 7 August, NFI distributions supported by IOM and Fundación Vivienda Popular reached a cumulative total of 2,244 kits in La Guaira, Miranda, Capital District and Carabobo. The Playa Grande temporary accommodation site closed on 10 August.

IOM activities

IOM maintained the management of five temporary accommodation sites during the reporting period, including three sites co-managed with the Norwegian Refugee Council. Activities included service coordination, population registration, household verification and needs monitoring. At the José María Vargas Sports Complex, essential services were maintained for 751 people from 202 households, while population movements in Campo de Golf were monitored.

Household verification in Mare Abajo II supported the launch of NFI distributions in Mare II and Algarín on 10 August. IOM and Fundación Vivienda Popular also supported the provision of NFIs in sites and communities managed by the authorities. On 7 August, 70 kits were distributed at the Colegio Olivia Andrade temporary accommodation site in La Guaira.

IOM and Ven Da Tu Mano continued providing mobile health and mental health services, including care for chronic conditions and mental health needs associated with the emergency. In César Nieves, health teams responded to an incident affecting approximately 20 adults and 12 children, providing medical care, monitoring hydration status and strengthening surveillance of diarrhoeal diseases.

IOM expanded household verification in Mare Abajo II and surrounding communities and continued updating population records in César Nieves and José María Vargas. Needs assessments in community settlements and formal accommodation sites also continued in La Guaira, Miranda and Carabobo.

Protection activities included coordination of access to case management, health, legal assistance and specialized services. At José María Vargas, 40 women participated in information sessions on violence against women and girls and safeguarding. IOM also facilitated inter-agency coordination to update service coverage and schedules, strengthen referral mechanisms and monitor population movements.

IOM planned response

IOM will:

  • Complete NFI distributions in prioritized communities surrounding Mare Abajo II.
  • Address identified infrastructure gaps in Mare Abajo II, particularly drainage for newly installed showers and adjustments to tent anchoring systems.
  • Continue health surveillance and medical follow-up for diarrhoeal diseases and support continuity of treatment for hypertension, diabetes and other chronic conditions.
  • Strengthen referral pathways for mental health, legal assistance and specialized protection services.
  • Complete household verification in prioritized communities and expand needs assessments and population movement monitoring in Carabobo and other affected locations.
  • Maintain updated information on available services, operating schedules and referral mechanisms in temporary accommodation sites.
  • Strengthen accessible community information and feedback mechanisms.

title: WFP DRC Country Brief July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • In June 2026, WFP reached 1,433,057 people in the DRC, the highest monthly reach so far this year. In the four conflict-affected eastern provinces, life-saving assistance was delivered to some 898,608 people.
  • WFP also rolled out a verification system for in-kind distributions through its SCOPE platform to improve the efficiency of its operations, specifically using digital tools for supply chain optimization and predictive analysis, which help reduce response times and reach vulnerable populations more quickly.
  • UNHAS transported 3,570 passengers and 57 mt of cargo for 100 organizations across through 463 flights. Following the DRC Government’s reopening of Bunia airport under strict hygiene protocols, UNHAS resumed operations to facilitate critical humanitarian access for the response. As a result, UNHAS deployed two additional aircraft to support humanitarian and Ebola response operations in Bunia.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• The security and humanitarian situation in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo remains worrying. The provinces of North Kivu, South Kivu, and Ituri continue to grapple with armed conflicts and repeated violence, leading to massive population displacements.

• According to OCHA, more than 74,000 people have newly been displaced in the DRC, bringing the total to about 6.47 million internally displaced people (IDPs). Insecurity persisted with escalated fighting advancing frontlines into the Fizi highlands in South Kivu forcing thousands of people to move further south to Tanganyika.

• The 17th outbreak in the DRC declared in May continues to spread in DRC worsening an already fragile humanitarian situation. As of 31 July, there were 3,674 confirmed cases, 1, 621 deaths, and 666 recoveries across 48 health zones in three provinces. Uganda officially declared the end of the outbreak on July 28, after 42 days without a new confirmed case. However, the Ugandan authorities maintain high alert at the borders, as the disease is still active in the DRC.

• The affected areas overlap with regions facing food crises (2.6 million people in phase 3 or worse levels of food insecurity). Movement restrictions and the impact of the outbreak threaten access to food and risk worsening the food security situation and humanitarian situations further.

title: Colombia Earthquake: Situation Report #1 (August 10, 2026)
content:
Key Updates

• Project HOPE is assessing health facilities and deploying an additional team to identify needs in Pereira, Cali, and other affected communities in Colombia following today’s 7.4-magnitude earthquake.

• Early reporting indicates over 60 buildings collapsed, 1,500 homes damaged, 111 people killed, and 87 injured, with those numbers expected to rise in the coming days.

• Just hours after the earthquake, Project HOPE staff began assessments at Hospital Universitario del Valle Evaristo García in Cali, Colombia, which has partially collapsed.

• Public officials declared a “red alert” for hospitals in Cali and health facilities are setting up tents outside to treat injured survivors. • Displaced families are setting up temporary shelters outside homes that have been damaged and destroyed.

title: Occupied Palestinian Territory (oPt) Situation Analysis: [27/7/2026--2/8/2026]
content:
Executive Summary

The Occupied Palestinian Territories face a catastrophic humanitarian crisis marked by severe food insecurity, mass displacement, and the near-collapse of essential services. In Gaza, the majority of the population relies entirely on humanitarian assistance, with widespread destruction of housing, health facilities, water infrastructure, and educational institutions compounding the challenges faced by displaced families. Harsh winter conditions, repeated evacuation orders, and constrained humanitarian access continue to threaten the safety and well-being of civilians, with children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups bearing a disproportionate burden.

In the West Bank, escalating military operations, settler violence, and movement restrictions have driven significant displacement and disrupted access to livelihoods, healthcare, and education. Economic contraction and rising unemployment have eroded household resilience, while demolitions and settlement expansion threaten further territorial fragmentation. Across both territories, humanitarian organizations are working to scale up food assistance, shelter support, health services, and protection programming, yet persistent access barriers, funding shortfalls, and ongoing hostilities continue to outpace the response, leaving Palestinians in urgent need of sustained international support and durable solutions.

title: Quarterly Complaint and Feedback Mechanism Snapshot | Q3 & Q4 | July–December 2025
content: This snapshot provides an overview of how UNHCR listens and responds to Rohingya refugees’ questions, concerns, and feedback in Bangladesh between July and December 2025. It focuses on the Complaints and Feedback Mechanism (CFM), which allows refugees to share issues, seek information, and report problems through multiple safe and accessible channels, including helpdesks and a toll-free helpline. In Bangladesh, the CFM operates through the Centralized Automated, Information Processing Platform (CAIPP), which helps ensure automated referral of the issues, the provision of information provided by the service provider, supported by a FAQs messages library for reliable information, and access to needed services supporting UNHCR’s commitment to transparency, accountability to affected populations (AAP) and responsive humanitarian action.

title: Quarterly Complaint and Feedback Mechanism Snapshot | Q1 | January–March 2026
content:
KeyHighlights

• UNHCR strengthened remote engagement channels and reinforced the Helpline with additional staff during the four-day public holiday for Bangladesh national elections (11-14 February), mitigating impact of reduced in-person humanitarian presence. On 11 February, 11 staff (responded to over 500 calls, including election-related inquiries,

• UNHCR, the Protection Sector and AAP Technical Working Group delivered election-related safety messages through broadcast calls and the helpline IVR system, reaching approximately 7,000 refugee households and supporting access to critical information during the election period.

• Staff of partner CODEC were onboarded and trained to support 14 CFM desks across 11 camps.

• UNHCR helped facilitate a CAIPP orientation session for WFP–UNHCR Coordinated Help Desk (CHD) focal covering case intake, ticket submission and dashboard use.

title: WFP India Country Brief, August 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• To promote climate resilience approaches and strengthen community capacities, in collaboration with the Assam Agriculture University, over 60 plant clinics have been organised at the Climate Adaptation Information Centre. Under the ENACT-Assam project, the clinics connect smallholder farmers with experts to help protect diversified livelihoods.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Despite decades of gains in food production and nutrition, India continues to face significant food and nutrition insecurity. It ranks 102nd out of 123 countries on the 2025 Global Hunger Index, with malnutrition indicators remaining above acceptable thresholds: 35 percent of children under five are stunted, 19 percent are underweight, and anaemia affects 57 percent of women of reproductive age and 67 percent of children aged 6–59 months. The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World, released in July 2026, demonstrated India’s significant improvements in the prevalence of undernourishment and the affordability of a healthy diet.

• India operates some of the world’s largest food-based safety nets, reaching nearly 800 million people every month. WFP has partnered with the Government of India for over 60 years, providing technical assistance and capacity strengthening to enhance efficiency, nutrition quality, digital innovation, and climate resilience across the food system.

title: UNHCR India Factsheet, March - April 2026
content:
Operational Context

India continues to be a generous host to refugees and asylum-seekers from across the region and beyond. UNHCR works in close coordination with the Government of India and other UN agencies in fulfilling its mandate of ensuring access to protection, solutions, and humanitarian assistance to persons forced to flee.

Civil society organizations, working in partnership with UNHCR, are at the forefront of the refugee response ensuring that assistance reaches the most vulnerable within the overall objective of “leaving no one behind”.
Partnership agreements are in place with five national NGOs.

UNHCR works closely with the Government of India and the UN Country Team to ensure that refugees and asylum‑seekers are included in national efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals, in line with the principle of leaving no one behind

title: WFP Ebola Response Situation Report, Democratic Republic of Congo, 31 July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• The Ebola outbreak is spreading rapidly and geographically across eastern DRC with compounding effects across food security and nutrition to worsen an already dire humanitarian crisis. WFP requires USD 75.5 million for the Ebola response in DRC.

• Good governance & Efficient Delivery: In coordination with the Government, WHO and other partners, WFP is providing key support to the response through delivery of food and nutrition assistance, logistics and UNHAS support ensuring that assistance is provided where it is most needed.

• Humanitarian Solutions: WFP is implementing simultaneous delivery of hot meals in Ebola treatment facilities and food assistance to affected communities as a response strategy to protect ongoing assistance while responding to Ebola-specific needs.

Situation Overview

• The 17th Ebola outbreak (Bundibugyo strain) declared on 14 May 2026 continued to spread in eastern DRC. The outbreak has spread rapidly with 3,674 confirmed cases, 1,621 deaths and 666 recovered cases across 48 health zones in five provinces in eastern DRC as of 31 July.

• Transmission has been recorded in the Tshopo and Haut-Uele health zones, indicating continued geographic expansion of the outbreak. WHO has described it as the thirdlargest Ebola outbreak on record and the fastest-spreading to date.

• The outbreak has deepened humanitarian needs in DRC, increasing the number of people in need from 14.9 million to 18.6 million (including 8 million directly affected by EVD), according to the amended Humanitarian Needs Response Plan. Food security remains one of the most critical needs for affected people.

• Acting Executive Director for WFP Mr. Carl Skau and Emergency Coordinator for Ebola response Ms. Hsiao-Wei Lee visited DRC between 28 and 30 July, meeting with Authorities and key partners and staff in Kinshasa, followed by field visit to Bunia to witness WFP operations at the frontlines of the Ebola response in Ituri.

title: UNICEF State of Palestine Humanitarian Situation Report No. 48 (Mid - Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • The ceasefire has not brought safety for Gaza’s children. Since 10 October 2025, 277 children have been reported killed, while nearly nine in ten children consulted said they need psychosocial support.
  • Despite severe access restrictions and critical supply shortages, UNICEF provided safe water to 1 million people in Gaza, including 470,000 children, while sustaining essential health, nutrition, education and protection services.
  • UNICEF reached over 265,000 children through 173 Learning Centres across Gaza, supporting learning, psychosocial wellbeing and referrals to specialized services for children with disabilities.
  • In the West Bank, escalating violence, demolitions and movement restrictions continued to displace families and strain essential public services. UNICEF’s Rapid Response Mechanism reached 1,620 people, including 844 children. UNICEF and partners admitted 19,425 children (6-59 months) for treatment of acute malnutrition, including severe and moderate wasting.

title: WFP Venezuela Earthquakes Response Situation Report #08, 10 August 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

One month after the earthquakes in Venezuela, access to food remains one of the top concerns for families across the affected areas.

WFP has reached more than 120,000 people with food assistance through four modalities, since no two families are living through this period the same way. Assistance include hot meals in shelters, ready-to-eat rations for those still on the move, food baskets for households that can still cook and in communities who lost their sources of income, and prepaid electronic vouchers in areas where markets are functioning, giving families the power to prioritize their own needs.

The agency is also serving as the logistics backbone of the humanitarian response, moving relief supplies into hard-to-reach communities. WFP's logistics services have supported NGOs and UN agencies with the transport and storage of supplies spanning shelter, health, protection, and WASH.

To date, WFP has secured one third of the USD 80 million required to sustain and scale the response. Efforts continue to close the gap and safeguard the support for 500,000 people in 3 months.

Situation Update

  • A month after two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela, the World Food Programme (WFP) continues to provide food assistance to communities impacted by the devastation. This unprecedented response, tailored to different needs in each affected area, has already reached more than 120,000 people and, with proper funding, hopes to reach a total of half a million over the next two months.
  • Following needs assessments, WFP has expanded the scope of its assistance from assistance in temporary shelters, community kitchens and communities in the most populated cities, to remote communities in La Guaira, where residents have retained cooking capacities, but whose livelihoods have been severely affected.
  • WFP's response extends well beyond La Guaira. The operation plan spans seven states, considering both families directly displaced or affected in their homes, and those whose livelihoods were disrupted by the earthquake — people whose sources of income collapsed overnight.

title: TKM: Heat Wave - 07-2026 - Heat Wave (2026-08-10)
content:
Description

Turkmenistan is experiencing a severe heatwave combined with hydrological drought conditions, affecting vulnerable communities across several regions of the country. The situation is part of a wider regional climate crisis impacting Central Asia, characterized by exceptionally high temperatures, prolonged dry conditions, and increasing pressure on water resources.

According to national hydrometeorological observations and regional climate monitoring data:

  • Daytime temperatures have consistently reached 40-45°C, with localized temperatures exceeding 48°C in desert and remote communities.
  • Night-time temperatures have remained between 32-36°C, limiting physiological recovery from prolonged heat exposure.
  • Rainfall deficits during the spring recharge season, combined with exceptionally high summer evaporation, have resulted in reduced groundwater recharge and declining water availability.
  • Water levels in boreholes have fallen significantly, irrigation channel flows have decreased, and water availability for domestic and agricultural use has become increasingly limited.
  • The combined impacts of extreme heat and water scarcity are placing significant pressure on public health services, water supply systems, energy infrastructure, and agricultural livelihoods.

The most affected areas are located in:

  • Mary Velayat: Uchajy and Serhetabat districts
  • Lebap Velayat: Repetek and Koytendag districts
  • Balkan Velayat: Etrek and Esenguly districts

These areas are characterized by arid climatic conditions, remote settlements, limited access to treated drinking water, and increased vulnerability to drought and heat-related health risks.

Severity and Duration

The heatwave has persisted for several consecutive weeks, with sustained temperatures above seasonal norms and little overnight cooling. The prolonged exposure to extreme temperatures, combined with deteriorating water availability, has significantly increased humanitarian risks.

Key indicators include:

  • Sustained daytime temperatures of 40-45°C;
  • Night-time temperatures above 32°C;
  • Reduced access to safe drinking water due to declining groundwater and surface water availability;
  • Significant crop losses resulting from reduced irrigation water;
  • Reduced pasture productivity leading to decreased livestock production and household income;
  • Increased risk of dehydration, heat exhaustion, heat stroke, and exacerbation of chronic illnesses among vulnerable populations.

The situation continues to worsen as water resources become increasingly strained and vulnerable households exhaust their coping mechanisms.

Trigger for DREF Request

The proposed trigger date is the onset of sustained extreme heat conditions starting from April 2026 and associated drought impacts in the targeted districts, marked by:

  • Consecutive days of temperatures exceeding nationally recognized heatwave thresholds;
  • Reports of significant water shortages in affected communities;
  • Evidence of heat-related health risks among vulnerable populations;
  • Documented reductions in water availability from boreholes and irrigation systems.

The Turkmen Red Crescent Society will ensure that the DREF submission complies with the IFRC requirement that drought-related DREF requests are submitted within 21 days of the agreed trigger date.

title: COL: Earthquake - 08-2026 - 2026 Colombia Earthquake (2026-08-10)
content:
Description

According to information from the Colombian Geological Service (SGC), an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.4 was recorded on Monday, August 10, 2026, in the morning, with its epicenter in the town of San José del Palmar, in the department of Chocó, located on the Colombian Pacific coast, at a depth of 82 kilometers.

Although the epicenter was in the department of Chocó, direct impacts were also felt in the departments of Caldas, Risaralda, and Valle del Cauca. Preliminary reports from media outlets and municipal governments indicate damage in the capitals and other municipalities of these departments: in Valle de Cauca, 3 people were injured in El Cairo and 2 died in El Zarzal, in addition to the collapse of 20 buildings and minor structural damage to 2 hospitals; in Risaralda, 18 people died; and in Chocó, 10 people were injured and 3 are missing. The number of people affected in the area continues to rise, and the President of the Republic has established a Unified Command Post.

title: Eastern Chad: Sudan Situation - Flash Updates #56
content:
UPDATE ON SITUATION IN SUDAN

Context

The security situation in Chad remains generally stable, although some border areas with Sudan, particularly in the Wadi Fira and Sila provinces, continue to be closely monitored. Security incidents reported between 3 and 4 August 2026 in Birséliba and surrounding localities near the Sudanese border reportedly had a severe impact on civilian populations, causing loss of life, injuries, and new population displacements. As a result, several families were forced to flee to the Chadian localities of Korabo and Birak in search of protection and safety.

A joint mission by UNHCR, the National Commission for the Reception and Reintegration of Refugees and Returnees (CNARR), and the Chadian Red Cross (CRT) was deployed to the border area to better understand the evolving situation and assess humanitarian needs. The mission observed the arrival of new households from Sudan and initiated preregistration activities while maintaining regular monitoring of population movements. Authorities and humanitarian partners continue to monitor the area closely to guide any necessary assistance based on identified needs.

In eastern Chad, the security situation in refugee-hosting areas remains relatively calm. The ongoing disarmament operation in Sila Province continues to contribute to a secure environment, although the partial withdrawal of security forces from Goz Beïda calls for continued vigilance. Protection concerns nevertheless persist in Wadi Fira, where a refugee family relocated for security reasons continues to face threats.

In addition, several incidents of crime and delinquency, including burglaries and assaults involving minors, were reported in some refugee sites. Tensions were also observed in Métché between refugees and host communities, as well as in Adré and Goudrane, where demonstrations by local youth linked to access to land and economic opportunities were reported.

The rainy season currently represents one of the main threats to both affected populations and humanitarian actors. Flooding and rising seasonal rivers (wadis) have caused several deaths, material damage, and disruptions along major road networks, complicating access to refugee sites and the delivery of humanitarian assistance.

title: UNHCR Weekly Relocation Update - Eastern Chad (31 July 2026)
content:
Weekly Highlights

• From 27 - 31 July, 2,387 refugees (679 households) were relocated from border areas to the inland sites of Arkoum (Ouaddaï Province) under the accelerated relocation programme.

• Since 15 April 2026, a cumulative 31,059 individuals (8,519 households) have been relocated under the accelerated relocation programme, bringing the total number relocated since January 2026 to 47,902 refugees (15,910 households).

• Since April 2023, UNHCR and its partners have relocated 648,797 individuals (173,847 households) from border areas to safer sites, representing 69% of the 940,612 Sudanese refugees who have arrived in Chad since April 2023.

• Relocations have taken place to Ennedi Est (79,516 individuals), Sila (81,304), Wadi Fira (198,479), and Ouaddaï (289,498). • Since 15 April 2026, a total of 50,508 refugees has been biometrically registered and 11,293 others have been preregistered, making a total of 61,801 individuals under OCHA-US funding.

• Since 15 April, a total of 23,605 refugee documentation (households and individuals) has been delivered to refugees in Eastern Chad. • Since April 2026, a total of 10,542 emergency shelters constructed across selected sites in the Ouaddai, Sila and Wadi Fira, improving living conditions for newly relocated refugee families.

title: Yemen - Rapid Displacement Tracking Update (2 - 8 August 2026)
content:
IOM Yemen DTM’s Rapid Displacement Tracking (RDT) tool collects data on estimated numbers of households forced to flee on a daily basis from their locations of origin or displacement, allowing for regular reporting of new displacements in terms of estimated numbers, geography, and needs. It also tracks returnees who returned to their location of origin.

From 1 January to 8 August 2026, IOM Yemen DTM tracked 1,742 households (HH) (10,452 Individuals) who experienced displacement at least once.

Between 2 and 8 August 2026, IOM Yemen DTM tracked 50 households (300 individuals) displaced at least once. The majority of people moved into/within the following governorates and districts:

  • Ma’rib (20 HHs) – Ma’rib City (14 HHs), Harib (3 HHs), Ma’rib (3 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate originated from Ibb and Sanaa.
  • Tai’z (14 HHs) – Maqbanah (6 HHs), Jabal Habashi (6 HHs), Al Makha (2 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate were internal.
  • Lahj (8 HHs) – Al Musaymir (6 HHs), Al Hawtah (2 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate originated from Lahj and Tai’z.

The majority of people moved from the following governorates and districts:

  • Ta’iz (16 HHs) – Jabal Habashi (7 HHs), Maqbanah (6 HHs), Dimnat Khadir (3 HHs) districts.
  • Al Hodeidah (8 HHs) – Alluhayah (3 HHs), Al Jarrahi (3 HHs), Al Marawiah (1 HH) districts.
  • Shabwah (7 HHs) – Ayn (7 HHs) district.

IOM identified 28 additional households displaced in the previous reporting period, which covered 26 July - 01 August 2026, in the governorates of Ta’iz (16 HHs), M’arib (7 HHs), and Lahj (5 HHs). These figures have been added to the cumulative displacement total recorded since the beginning of the year.

title: UNHCR Romania Ukraine Refugee Situation Weekly Update #208 - 10 August 2026
content:
Key figures

215,532 refugees obtained temporary protection and refugee status in Romania (as of end June 2026).
1,949 refugees supported with community-based protection activities in 2026.
5,492 refugees provided with protection counselling services and legal support in 2026.
1,628 refugees supported with livelihood and employment services in 2026.

Highlight

On 30 July 2026, the EU Council adopted Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/1912, extending temporary protection for people displaced from Ukraine until 4 March 2028. The Decision, published in the Official Journal of the European Union, applies from 5 March 2027. It also introduces a requirement for people newly seeking temporary protection to provide, where applicable, proof of having fulfilled their military obligations in Ukraine, with this provision applying from 31 July 2026. The requirement does not apply to people who held temporary protection in a Member State on or before 30 July 2026 and continuously retained that status. UNHCR and its partner, the Romanian National Council for Refugees (CNRR), monitored the situation at UNHCR’s Community Centre for refugees at RomExpo, in Bucharest, and other locations. UNHCR is consulting with the General Inspectorate for Immigration (GII) to clarify the eligibility criteria and documentation they require to demonstrate compliance. UNHCR and CNRR noted an increase in the number of enquiries from Ukrainian men and procedural changes related to the renewal or updating of temporary protection permits.

title: Situation Report 6 - Extreme Weather Events in India - Assam, Odisha and Kerala (Date: 8th August 2026)
content:
A. Situation Overview : ( 2-8th Aug 2026)

Assam, Odisha and Kerala continue to face significant monsoon-related flooding with widespread humanitarian impacts. Assam reports 1.55 lakh people affected across 13 districts; Odisha faces one of its largest flood emergencies in recent years with 8.64 lakh people affected across 22 districts; Kerala’s situation remains dynamic with multiple districts reporting camp evacuations, road cuts, and rising river levels, as per media and SEOC updates.

1. Assam Flood - Severe Flooding Across 13 Districts

Impact on Humans

Floods continue to affect large parts of Assam, with 13 districts and 33 revenue circles impacted. A total of 464 villages remain inundated, affecting 1,55,849 people across multiple districts. While human casualties remain low, one confirmed death was reported from Charaideo. Relief camp populations have risen, with 10,326 people currently sheltered and 6,881 non-camp beneficiaries receiving assistance through distribution centres.

Animal Husbandry Loss

The floods have severely impacted livestock, with 47,879 animals affected, including 22,846 big animals, 18,083 small animals, and 6,950 poultry. No major incidents of animals washed away were reported, but widespread distress is evident across Golaghat, Lakhimpur, Darrang, and Nagaon. Livestock feed distribution has begun in several districts.

Structural and Property Damages

Structural damages are concentrated in Sivasagar, Dhemaji, and Darrang. A total of 126 houses have been fully/severely damaged and 344 houses partially damaged. Additional damages include 213 cattle sheds, multiple government buildings, schools, and water supply pipelines. Embankment breaches were reported in Biswanath and Karbi Anglong, posing continued risk.

Irrigation and Water Supply

Flooding has disrupted water supply systems in multiple districts. Two PWSS systems—Sonajuli (Biswanath) and Uriagaon (Nagaon)—have suffered pipeline damage and inundation, affecting household water access. Irrigation channels and agricultural bunds have been submerged or eroded in several locations.

Road and Transport Infrastructure

Floodwaters have damaged 32 roads across districts, with major impacts in Golaghat, Sivasagar, Darrang, and Kamrup. Several PWD roads have been overtopped, eroded, or suffered slope failures. One bamboo footbridge was washed away in Darrang. Culvert approach roads have also been damaged in Udalguri.

Electricity and Power Supply

Power infrastructure has sustained moderate damage, with 7 transformers and 6 poles affected across Sivasagar and Sribhumi. Conductors spanning 1.03 km were damaged in Nilambazar due to heavy rainfall. Restoration work is ongoing by APDCL teams.

title: Vanuatu Dengue Outbreak Situation Report #9 (South-West Efate, Shefa Province)
content:
Key highlights:

  • Nine new laboratory-confirmed dengue cases were reported in EW32, bringing the cumulative total to 76 confirmed cases.
  • Weekly case counts have remained above the outbreak threshold since EW24, indicating ongoing community transmission.
  • A total of 12 dengue-related hospitalisations (16%) have been reported; all patients have recovered and been discharged.
  • No severe dengue cases or dengue-related deaths have been reported to date.
  • DENV-1 remains the confirmed circulating serotype.
