title: The Republic of Korea contributes USD 30 million to WFP’s humanitarian assistance through REACH Phase II | World Food Programme
content:
ROME – The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) welcomes a USD 30 million contribution from the Republic of Korea (ROK) to launch the second phase of the ROK-WFP REACH initiative (Responding with Emergency Assistance for Conflict-affected Households), providing emergency food and nutrition assistance to vulnerable populations affected by conflict, displacement, and economic shocks.

Building on the success of REACH Phase I (2025-2026), the renewed initiative will support WFP's emergency response in Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Palestine, Somalia, Sudan, and Syria over a 12-month period.

At a time of growing humanitarian needs, this contribution will help WFP deliver lifesaving assistance to families facing some of the world's most severe crises. The initiative demonstrates ROK's humanitarian leadership and commitment to global solidarity, playing a critical role in saving lives and bringing hope to vulnerable communities.

Under REACH Phase II, WFP will provide emergency food assistance and nutrition support, including for vulnerable children, with the aim of reaching more than 1.2 million food-insecure people. The initiative's strategic and flexible approach enables WFP to respond effectively to evolving needs and operational challenges across complex humanitarian settings.

REACH Phase I supported WFP's emergency response in Myanmar, Palestine, Sudan, and Syria, reaching nearly 1.9 million people with food and nutrition assistance. Building on these achievements, Phase II expands the initiative to three additional countries, further strengthening WFP's ability to respond to humanitarian needs across multiple regions.

In 2025, the Republic of Korea contributed over USD 200 million to WFP, becoming one of WFP's top five government donors. Having received assistance from WFP more than 60 years ago, ROK has transitioned into a leading donor – an inspiring testament to progress in the fight against hunger.

title: Public Health Situation Analysis (PHSA)
content:
Mozambique continues to face recurrent public health and humanitarian challenges, driven by overlapping crises. The country is regularly affected by epidemics and extreme weather events and is currently experiencing widespread flooding and a cholera outbreak.

Nearly nine years after armed conflicts erupted in Cabo Delgado, humanitarian needs remain severe. Around 1.1 million people across northern Mozambique require humanitarian assistance, including 919 000 people in the districts most affected by the conflict in Cabo Delgado. Despite ongoing relief efforts, less than half of those in need have been reached, while humanitarian funding remains critically insufficient. As a result, many vulnerable families continue to face limited access to health care, food, education and protection services.
In 2026, humanitarian access in northern Mozambique remained highly constrained, primarily due to localized attacks, armed clashes and interference along key routes, compounded by damaged infrastructure and the impact of the rainy season, which continued to disrupt and complicate operations.

More broadly, Mozambique is facing its most severe cholera outbreak in 25 years and is grappling with ongoing internal conflict that has resulted in a complex and multifaceted crisis with significant humanitarian implications, including high levels of internal displacement. Mozambique is classified as one of the countries in the world most affected by extreme weather events. In 2025, more than 724 000 people were affected by floods. At the peak of the emergency, over 100 000 people were hosted in approximately 100 accommodation centres.

title: Health Cluster Workshop Report: Harmonization of Health Cluster Reporting and Beneficiary Calculation
content:
I. Rationale
Now in the fifth year of the full-scale war, the humanitarian
health response in Ukraine has evolved considerably, and
so have the expectations around collective reporting,
accountability, and evidence-based coordination. The
2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP)
introduced an issue-based approach around four strategic
priorities, new geographic targeting, and a joint reporting
platform managed by UN OCHA. Health partners must
now report against these four priorities while maintaining
focus on the most severely affected areas (severity levels
4 and 5).
Over five years, variations in how partners collect data, count
beneficiaries, and calculate results have accumulated,
making it harder for the Cluster to reflect the response
accurately. This prompted the Health Cluster to convene
75 partner representatives and reporting and MEAL
specialists for a one-day hybrid workshop to strengthen
shared understanding of reporting expectations, logic, and
beneficiary calculation.
The aim was not to impose uniformity, but to build enough
common ground for the collective humanitarian health
response to be reported coherently and credibly - to the
humanitarian community, donors, and the people the
response seeks to serve. As of June 2026, the Health
Cluster counts 154 partners delivering health activities
across priority war-affected oblasts. The Cluster looks
forward to continuing to guide these partners toward
alignment as part of this process.
Objectives
General Objective: To strengthen the capacity of Health
Cluster partners to collect, calculate, and report data in
line with HNRP requirements and Health Cluster reporting
standards — improving the coordination and visibility of
health interventions in Ukraine.
Specific Objectives:
1. Explain the rationale for accurate reporting and
alignment with Cluster requirements, alongside
bilateral donor interests and the funding partners
receive.
2. Identify and discuss the challenges partners face in
the reporting process in Ukraine.
3. Guide partners through an organization-specific
reflection on designing a counting method that fits
their reporting needs across emergency response and
early recovery.
4. Raise awareness of data sensitivity and the responsible
management of health-related data.
5. Surface the tensions in reporting under the OCHA-led
framework — regional targets versus the four strategic
priorities of the response.
6. Build a clear understanding of how reporting quality
shapes the Cluster’s visibility to donors, the wider
humanitarian community, and decision-makers
through its external products.

title: Pakistan-Afghanistan - Returns Emergency Response #54 (as of 1 August 2026)
content:
Context

Large-scale returns of Afghans from Pakistan continue to add pressure on Afghanistan’s already fragile humanitarian and protection environment.

Nearly two years since the initial announcement of the Illegal Foreigners Repatriation Plan, the impact of these measures continues to be felt. In 2025 alone, 1 million Afghans returned in adverse circumstances or were deported from Pakistan. This trend has continued in 2026 with 654,100 returns so far despite border closures earlier this year.

These movements are unfolding amid escalating hostilities between Afghanistan and Pakistan, further compounding an already deteriorating humanitarian and human rights situation, particularly for women and girls. The Torkham border point – the largest crossing between Afghanistan and Pakistan, accounting for some 80% of all returns prior to the crisis – was partially re-opened on 31 March.

Ensuring that returns are safe, voluntary and dignified, while sustaining critical assistance for those arriving and host communities, remains essential.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 306: Week 1 – August 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Market Overview

Market conditions remained generally stable at the national level during the first week of August, though provincial-level disparities persisted, with some regions facing more pronounced price pressures than others. While week-on-week price movements were moderate across most monitored commodities, prices remained elevated, reflecting the sustained impact of trade disruptions and high transportation costs. Fuel prices remained high, driven by constrained regional supplies, particularly from Russia, and reduced imports from Central Asia and Iran. While elevated fuel prices continued to keep supply chain and delivery costs high, their pass-through to retail food prices remained moderate during the reporting week.

Food Items:

• National average food prices showed a mixed but generally stable trend during the first week of August, with several staple commodities recording slight week-on-week changes. Prices remained elevated compared to historical levels, suggesting that markets continue to be adequately supplied, albeit at higher transportation costs.

• Wheat and Wheat Flour: Wheat grain and wheat flour prices remained largely unchanged week-on-week but stayed significantly higher year-on-year, reflecting elevated production and transportation costs.

• Rice: Rice prices were largely stable during the week. Nevertheless, rice prices remained substantially above last year and the three-year average, particularly Sholae rice, which is 35% higher year-on-year.

• Other Staples: Prices of cooking oil, pulses, sugar, and salt showed mixed but generally modest week-on-week movements. Cooking oil increased by 0.9%, while pulses, sugar, and salt declined slightly. Compared to last year, cooking oil, sugar, and salt remained elevated by 12%, 10%, and 9%, respectively, while pulse prices were 13% lower, reflecting relatively favourable availability.

• Vegetables: Vegetable prices increased during the first week of August, led by onion and potato prices, which rose by 5.9% and 4.6%, respectively. Compared to last year, tomato and potato prices remained significantly higher, by 30% and 49%, respectively, while onion prices are 7% lower.
Non-Food Items:

• Exchange Rate: The Afghani exchange rate remained broadly stable at AFN 66.0/USD. Although the currency remained broadly unchanged from last week, it continued to outperform both last year (4% stronger) and the three-year average (11% stronger), helping to partially offset imported inflationary pressures.

• Fuel: Diesel prices eased slightly during the week but remained 13% above last year and 16% above the three-year average, reflecting continued regional supply constraints and elevated international fuel prices.

• Fertilizers: Fertilizer prices show a slight decline from last week, with DAP price falling by 1.1% and Urea by 2.0%. However, prices remained substantially above last year's levels, with DAP 17% and Urea 42% higher.

• Livestock: The price of a 1-year-old live female sheep remained stable with moderate week-on-week fluctuations. However, it stood 6% below last year and 2% below the three-year average, reflecting weak pastoralists' terms of trade (purchasing power of livestock keepers).

• Labour Market: Labour market conditions remained subdued, with labour availability averaging 2.1 days per week. Availability remained 14% below both last year and the three-year average, while the daily wage for unskilled labour remained unchanged.

title: LAO: Flood - 08-2026 - Flooding caused by Heavy rainfall #5 (2026-08-07)
content:
Description

According to the local government, heavy rainfall associated with a low-pressure system and the southwest monsoon has caused rising river levels, localized flooding, waterlogging, and infrastructure damage across several provinces in Lao PDR. The Department of Meteorology and Hydrology (DMH) issued a nationwide flood warning for 6–8 August 2026, with continued moderate to heavy rainfall forecast until 9 August, increasing the risk of flash floods, riverine flooding, landslides, and inundation in low-lying areas. Several rivers, including the Xe Bangfai, Nam San, and Nam Tha, are approaching warning levels. Localized flooding has been reported in Khammouane, Savannakhet, Luang Prabang, and Vientiane Capital, while Phongsaly, Xaysomboun, Bolikhamxay, Khammouane, Savannakhet, and Attapeu have been identified as high-risk provinces. In Khounkham District, Khammouane Province, continuous rainfall from 3–5 August caused flooding of roads, disruption to transport, and impacts on several villages.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: No

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by National Society

Summary

The Lao Red Cross (LRC), together with its provincial and district branches, is closely monitoring the flood situation and coordinating with government authorities and humanitarian partners. Current actions include monitoring weather forecasts and river levels, maintaining communication with local authorities to assess emerging needs, disseminating early warning and preparedness messages to at-risk communities, promoting household preparedness, assessing the readiness of volunteers and emergency response teams, and preparing for deployment should the situation deteriorate. LRC continues to closely monitor flood developments in Khammouane Province, particularly along the Xe Bangfai River Basin.

Actions taken by Federation

Summary

IFRC is closely monitoring the situation and coordinating with the Lao Red Cross, remaining on standby to provide support as needed.

Actions taken by others

The Government of Lao PDR, through the Department of Meteorology and Hydrology and provincial authorities, has strengthened preparedness and response measures by issuing nationwide flood and landslide warnings, continuously monitoring rainfall and river levels, disseminating early warning information, and coordinating with provincial, district, and village authorities. Communities living in flood-prone areas have been advised to remain vigilant, protect property, and prepare for evacuation if required. Authorities continue to monitor affected areas, particularly in Khammouane Province, and stand ready to implement additional emergency measures as conditions evolve.

title: Somalia - WFP Joint VAM-Supply Chain | Market Bulletin (July 2026)
content:
KEY FINDINGS

The national total food and non-food basket2costs US$215, up 8.6 percent year-on-year, and has held above $200 since October 2025. The surge in fuel and transport costs linked to the Middle East crisis partially passed through to food and water prices, peaking in May 2026.

Price pressure is most acute in the southern sorghum belt. Following the failed 2025 deyrand below-average gurains, FEWS NET expects the July–August sorghum harvest at least 50 percent below average [FEWSNET]. Sorghum is up 67 percent year-on-year in Hirshabelle, 49 percent in Banadir and 63 percent in Baidoa; month-on-month declines in Southwest (−13%) suggest temporary relief from early harvest arrivals.

Nationally, terms of trade show the clearest loss of purchasing power: goat prices are down 17.7 percent year-on-year and wages 19 percent while sorghum rose 7 percent; a goat now buys only 87 kg of sorghum, down from 113 kg (−23%), and a day’s wage 7.4 kg versus 9.6 kg (−24%). Erosion is deepest in Jubaland, Southwest and Puntland (goat prices down ~30 percent year-on-year on distress sales); July’s 10.8 percent monthly drop also reflects post-Eid normalization.
Meanwhile, diesel prices remain elevated at US$1.15 per litre, 18.2 percent higher than a year agoand 26 percent above pre-Middle East crisis levels, keeping transport and water-trucking costs high and reinforcing food inflation.

title: Ukraine Regional Humanitarian Crisis: Regional Situation Report (January - June 2026)
content:
The war in Ukraine has created a protracted humanitarian crisis marked by intensifying aerial bombardments, hostilities, and systemic attacks on critical energy and civilian infrastructure, which significantly worsened during a severe 2025–2026 winter. This instability has caused large-scale displacement, with 3.4 million people internally displaced and 5.8 million recorded as refugees globally, most of whom face socio-economic pressures in European host countries, including rising living costs and diminishing international aid. The conflict has profoundly impacted the most vulnerable, particularly regarding sexual and reproductive health (SRH) due to infrastructure damage, while also escalating protection risks such as gender-based violence (GBV), psychosocial distress, and limited access to essential services for marginalized groups.

During the first half of 2026, UNFPA accelerated a strategic pivot in its regional Ukraine crisis response, shifting from emergency service provision toward institutionalizing critical SRH and GBV services within national health and protection systems to ensure sustainability and localization. UNFPA prioritized national ownership by integrating SRH services into state health systems while transitioning safe spaces and other protection services into government-funded or civil society-operated centres. Additionally, UNFPA advanced specialized, survivor-centred GBV services, economic empowerment initiatives, and targeted youth resilience programmes.

Although UNFPA has nominally secured 90 per cent of its $61.5 million regional requirement for 2026, this figure obscures a significant funding gap, as budget targets were reduced at the end of 2025 to prioritize the most vulnerable rather than reflecting a decrease in actual needs. Current resources are insufficient to balance immediate life-saving care with the transition to long-term recovery, particularly given the deteriorating humanitarian context and upcoming winterization challenges. Because the current appeal fails to cover the full scope of GBV and SRH needs, it is imperative to secure 2027 funding early and transition from 12-month project cycles to sustained, multi-year support.

title: Dengue in the Pacific: Multicountry Situation (As of 7 August 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Since 1 January 2025, twelve dengue outbreaks have been reported across Pacific Island Countries and Areas (PICs).

• During 2025, dengue outbreaks were reported in American Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Naoero, Samoa, Tonga, and Tuvalu. A total of 21,258 confirmed cases and 21 deaths were recorded across the Pacific. Fatalities were reported in Fiji (n=8), Samoa (n=7), Tonga (n=3), Naoero (n=2), and Kiribati (n=1).

• Between 1 January 2026 and 2 July 2026, a total of 4 511 dengue confirmed cases, 173 hospitalisations and 3 deaths have been reported across the Pacific.

• The Pacific Syndromic Surveillance System (PSSS) has reported a total of 8 873 Dengue-like Illness (DLI) cases to date, a lower trend compared to the same period last year.

• In 2026 dengue outbreaks were officially declared in New Caledonia, Tonga and Shefa province Vanuatu.

• The most affected countries and areas in 2026 include: American Samoa, Cook Islands, Samoa, and New Caledonia. These account for 94% of confirmed cases.

• Dengue serotype-1 (DENV-1) and serotype-2 (DENV-2) are currently in circulation.

• The Cook Islands officially declared the end of its dengue outbreak on 25 May 2026.

• Tonga has officially declared the end of its dengue outbreak on 31 July 2026.

• As of 7 August 2026: o The dengue outbreak remains ongoing in Shefa Province, Vanuatu, with dengue virus serotype 1 (DENV-1) continuing to circulate. o Low levels of transmission are observed in American Samoa, Kiribati, New Caledonia, Samoa, Vanuatu and Wallis and Futuna.

title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #5 (August 6, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • On June 24, two earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 hit northern Venezuela consecutively, impacting at least seven states—including the capital city of Caracas and the neighboring city of La Guaira.
  • Official figures have confirmed 6,125 fatalities, 16,740 injuries and 17,907 people who have lost their homes.
  • The earthquakes have compounded pre-existing humanitarian vulnerabilities, leaving millions of people with limited access to healthcare services, clean water, food and other basic services.

Our Response

  • International Medical Corps has deployed three mobile medical units, which have provided 3,336 consultations since beginning operations on July 1.
  • On July 11, International Medical Corps opened an Emergency Medical Team (EMT) Type 1 Fixed facility to provide free medical services to affected communities. To date, we have provided 3,109 consultations through the EMT.
  • Our teams have delivered 290,000 liters of safe water across displacement sites, benefitting some 3,820 people.
  • Our teams have so far provided 463 mental health consultations.

Our team is continuing to provide services to about 130 patients per day at the EMT. As patient loads have grown, we have been able to keep up with the demand by training and hiring locally recruited staff who are now managing EMT operations as we rotate out international personnel. The integration of local staff has helped to ensure we have the human resources necessary to scale up our response in La Guaira as needs evolve, and to transition our response programming responsibly and sustainably.

International Medical Corps is also delivering medical and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services through three mobile medical units (MMUs) in La Guaira that have provided 3,336 patient consultations to date. As needs within affected communities evolve, International Medical Corps will continue to coordinate closely with national and international partners to ensure that services are targeted to areas where they will have the greatest impact.

title: Ebola Outbreak, DRC and Region, Situation Report #11, August 6, 2026
content:
FAST FACTS

  • On May 15, the DRC declared an outbreak of Ebola virus disease (EVD), later confirmed to be caused by the Bundibugyo strain.
  • As of August 5, 3,973 confirmed EVD cases and 1,801 confirmed EVD deaths had been reported in the DRC, with 20 confirmed cases and two confirmed deaths in Uganda.
  • In the DRC, the outbreak remains centered in Ituri province, but cases have also been confirmed in Haut-Uele, North Kivu, South Kivu and Tshopo provinces.
  • In Uganda, reported cases remain linked to transmission originating in the DRC.
  • No EVD cases have been confirmed in South Sudan, but risk of an outbreak remains high due to transient populations and porous borders with the DRC.

OUR RESPONSE

  • Across the region, our teams are providing case management, infection prevention and control, screening and triage, risk communication and community engagement, training and preparedness planning.
  • We are supporting 159 facilities in the screening, identification and treatment of EVD.
  • Our supported sites have conducted 305,504 EVD screenings and provided treatment to 988 patients, including 296 confirmed cases.
  • We have so far trained 2,680 people in the DRC on EVD case management, response and transmission prevention.

With the support of the US Department of State, DG ECHO and other donors, International Medical Corps teams are actively responding to the outbreak across the region and collaborating closely with ministries of health, key actors and response partners. International Medical Corps has used a hub-and-spoke model since the outbreak was declared to provide case-management support at designated treatment and transit facilities, strengthen IPC in referring health facilities, conduct screening and triage, support RCCE in surrounding communities and train health workers on EVD response protocols.

We currently are operating four Ebola Treatment Centers and four Ebola Transit Centers in the DRC, with a combined total of more than 200 beds. In Uganda, we are working with a local partner to provide screening, preparedness, risk communications and training services. In South Sudan, where the risk of cross-border transmission remains high, International Medical Corps continues to operate two infectious diseases units (IDUs) in Juba and Nimule to ensure that suspected cases are safely isolated, managed and supported while awaiting laboratory confirmation. We are providing extensive training, and are building a third IDU as well as four holding stations integrated within selected health facilities that will provide dedicated spaces for triage, temporary isolation and infection-prevention measures.

title: Islamic Relief Pakistan: Humanitarian Situation Report (Period: 26-June to 05-August 2026)
content:
Location: KP, AJK, GB, Punjab, Balochistan and Sindh

BACKGROUND

Pakistan continues to face severe and compounding risks from both economic fragility and climate-induced disasters. The country remains among the most disaster-prone globally, ranking 18th out of 191 countries in the INFORM Risk Index, reflecting high exposure to hazards, vulnerability, and limited coping capacity. Over the past decade, disaster related damages have exceeded USD 18 billion, significantly constraining economic growth and development progress. More recent climate assessments also indicate that Pakistan is among the top 10 most climate vulnerable countries globally, despite contributing less than 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

Pakistan's 2026 monsoon began on 26 June and is forecast by the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) to bring 22–26% more rainfall than the previous season, compounded by accelerated melt across the country's more than 7,000 glaciers. As of the latest NDMA daily sitrep, the cumulative death toll (147) remains far below the same point in the catastrophic 2022 and 2025 seasons — but the situation has escalated in last 6 days: NDMA and PDMA Punjab have moved from advisory to an active flood alert for the Chenab, Jhelum and Ravi rivers in August, with evacuations already being directed in low-lying and riverbank areas. Current figures should be read as a running total from an in-progress, intensifying season, not a final toll.

Recent cloudburst incidents in the upper northern regions of Pakistan have resulted in significant losses to lives, property, livelihoods, and public infrastructure. The most severely affected areas include Astore, Diamer, Ghanche, Chitral, Buner, Shangla, and parts of Swat, where heavy rainfall and flash flooding have caused widespread damage to roads, bridges, irrigation systems, and residential structures. Additionally, Neelum Valley in Azad Jammu and Kashmir has been among the hardest-hit areas, facing severe disruptions due to flooding and landslides.

In KP, District Peshawar has experienced significant urban flooding over the last five days following continuous monsoon rains. Water accumulation in low-lying areas, damage to urban infrastructure, disruption of transportation networks, and inundation of residential areas have increased the vulnerability of affected populations. The ongoing situation continues to pose challenges for local authorities and communities, particularly those residing in flood-prone locations.

title: Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 12, Data as of 02 August 2026
content:
Event description

The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to expand rapidly, with sustained transmission, persistently high mortality, and ongoing geographic spread. It is now the largest BVD outbreak ever recorded and the second largest Ebola disease outbreak in history after the 2013 – 2016 West Africa epidemic. Since its detection only a few months ago, the epidemic has grown at an exceptional rate, highlighting its intensity and the challenges facing response efforts. Although no new international spread has been detected, continued transmission indicates that the outbreak remains in an expansion phase and continues to pose a high risk of regional and international spread.

Democratic Republic of the Congo

Since the last update of 26 July 2026 (Weekly External Situation Report #11), the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported an additional 540 confirmed cases and 270 confirmed deaths, representing increases of 16.6% and 18.8%, respectively, in cumulative confirmed cases and deaths. Although the absolute numbers of newly reported cases and deaths remain substantial, the proportional increases are markedly lower than those reported during the previous reporting period, reflecting the absence of the large retrospective data reconciliation that contributed to last week's increase. Nevertheless, the reporting of more than 500 additional confirmed cases and more than 250 confirmed deaths within a single week indicates that transmission remains intense and that the outbreak continues to expand. The crude case fatality ratio (CFR) increased from 44.1% to 44.9%, reflecting persistently high mortality despite ongoing response efforts. During the reporting period, the cumulative number of affected health zones increased from 48 to 51, with Kabondo and Wanie-Rukula in Tshopo Province and Lubero in North Kivu Province becoming the latest affected health zones, further demonstrating the continued geographic expansion of the outbreak.

During the last 21 days, transmission remained highly concentrated geographically, with an additional 1,867 confirmed cases and 953 confirmed deaths reported nationally. Approximately 87.9% (n=1,641) of recently reported confirmed cases and 84.8% (n=808) of deaths occurred in Ituri Province, with the Bunia–Rwampara–Mongbwalu– Nizi corridor continuing to represent the principal transmission focus. North Kivu, Haut-Uélé, and Tshopo together accounted for 223 cases (11.9%) and 144 deaths (15.1%), while South Kivu reported no new confirmed cases. However, an imported confirmed death from Tshopo Province generated new contacts requiring follow-up in South Kivu. Of the 51 affected health zones, 42 reported at least one confirmed case during the preceding 21 days, whereas nine health zones (Gety, Kambala, Lubunga, Mangobo, Mabalako, Makiso-Kisangani, Miti-Murhesa, Rungu, and Vuhovi) have not reported a confirmed case for more than three weeks, suggesting that transmission may have been interrupted in these areas, provided surveillance remains sufficiently sensitive to detect any ongoing transmission.

The largest increases in confirmed cases over the previous 21 days were recorded in Bunia (312 cases), Nizi (285), Rwampara (216), Mongbwalu (207), Katwa (104), Lita (84), Nia-Nia (66), Mangala (63), Fataki (31), and Butembo (29). Together, these ten health zones accounted for approximately 84% of all additional confirmed cases reported nationally during the period. Bunia, Nizi, Mongbwalu, and Rwampara remained the principal transmission corridor, accounting for nearly 55% of all newly reported confirmed cases. Continued increases in Lita, Nia-Nia, Mangala, and Fataki indicate sustained transmission within the Ituri epicentre, while ongoing transmission in Katwa and Butembo confirms persistent transmission in North Kivu. Continued increases in Isiro and Wamba further indicate that the outbreak is becoming increasingly established in Haut-Uélé Province.

Mortality remained concentrated within the same transmission corridor driving the epidemic. More than half (55.4%) of all confirmed deaths continue to occur outside designated treatment facilities, indicating that many patients are still being detected only late in illness or after death. Delayed case detection and delayed access to specialised treatment therefore remain major contributors to mortality. Recent analyses indicate a median interval of eight days from symptom onset to death, with almost half of deaths occurring within the first week of illness, emphasizing the narrow window available for life-saving clinical intervention.

Children younger than five years continue to experience disproportionately high mortality. Although they account for fewer than one in ten confirmed cases nationally, they represent approximately 17% of all confirmed deaths, experience the highest case fatality ratios of any age group, and have the shortest interval between symptom onset and death. Conversely, adults aged 20 – 59 years continue to account for most transmission, representing nearly two-thirds of confirmed cases. These findings suggest that outbreak control should continue to prioritise interrupting transmission among working-age adults while simultaneously strengthening rapid identification and referral of young children to reduce mortality.

Surveillance performance remains suboptimal. As of 2 August 2026, 18,276 contacts were under follow-up nationally, of whom 14,466 (79.2%) were successfully seen during the previous 24 hours, remaining well below the operational target of 95%. Contact tracing capacity continues to lag behind the growing number of contacts to follow, particularly in Ituri and North Kivu, while persistently low follow-up rates and intermittent reporting in Haut-Uélé and Tshopo limit interpretation of recent trends.

Since the beginning of the outbreak, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported 3,802 confirmed cases, including 1,707 confirmed deaths, corresponding to a crude CFR of 44.9%. The outbreak now affects 51 health zones across five provinces. Ituri Province remains the epicentre, accounting for 3,317 confirmed cases (87.2%) and 1,382 confirmed deaths (81.0%) nationwide. The most affected health zones remain Bunia (914 cases, 270 deaths), Rwampara (655 cases, 263 deaths), Mongbwalu (552 cases, 263 deaths), Nizi (402 cases, 194 deaths), Lita (141 cases, 84 deaths), and Nyankunde (115 cases, 34 deaths) in Ituri Province, together with Katwa (186 cases, 122 deaths) and Butembo (87 cases, 69 deaths) in North Kivu Province. Collectively, these health zones account for the overwhelming majority of confirmed cases and deaths reported nationwide.

title: Occupied Palestinian Territories (oPt) Situation Analysis: [20/7/2026] - [26/7/2026]
content:
Executive Summary

The Occupied Palestinian Territories face a catastrophic humanitarian crisis marked by severe food insecurity, mass displacement, and the near-collapse of essential services. In Gaza, the majority of the population relies entirely on humanitarian assistance, with widespread destruction of housing, health facilities, water infrastructure, and educational institutions compounding the challenges faced by displaced families. Harsh winter conditions, repeated evacuation orders, and constrained humanitarian access continue to threaten the safety and well-being of civilians, with children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups bearing a disproportionate burden.

In the West Bank, escalating military operations, settler violence, and movement restrictions have driven significant displacement and disrupted access to livelihoods, healthcare, and education. Economic contraction and rising unemployment have eroded household resilience, while demolitions and settlement expansion threaten further territorial fragmentation. Across both territories, humanitarian organizations are working to scale up food assistance, shelter support, health services, and protection programming, yet persistent access barriers, funding shortfalls, and ongoing hostilities continue to outpace the response, leaving Palestinians in urgent need of sustained international support and durable solutions.

title: India: Assam Floods - DREF Operation no. MDRIN029
content:
What happened, where and when?

A. Overview of the Assam Flood 2026

The Assam floods began on 19 July 2026, triggered by exceptionally heavy monsoonal rainfall, which reached up to 490% above normal levels in parts of Upper Assam. Rising river levels and continuous rainfall caused floodwaters to spread rapidly across multiple districts, inundating villages, agricultural land, and critical infrastructure.
The situation worsened throughout the following week as flooding expanded, and the number of affected people increased steadily. The emergency reached its peak on 27-28 July, when more than 800 villages were inundated and flood impacts were at their highest.

Charaideo, Sivasagar, and Jorhat emerged as some of the worst-affected districts, experiencing widespread village inundation and damage to livelihoods and agriculture.
Since late July, receding river levels and improving weather conditions have led to a gradual improvement in the flood situation.

However, despite the overall decline in flood impacts, 1,144,733 people remain affected across eight districts, with floodwaters still impacting 437 villages. While the crisis has moved beyond its peak, significant humanitarian and recovery needs persist in the most affected areas.

The floods have severely impacted communities that rely primarily on agriculture, livestock and daily wage labour for their livelihoods.

Prolonged inundation has restricted access to essential services, damaged household assets, disrupted agricultural activities and increased public health concerns related to water-borne and vector-borne diseases. The disaster has also resulted in significant loss of livestock and agricultural production, further reducing the coping capacity of already vulnerable households.

title: Afghanistan Flash Floods - Monsoon Effect - DREF Operation (MDRAF022)
content:
Date of event

20-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

Heavy and continuous rainfall from 20 July 2026 triggered sudden-onset flash flooding across eastern Afghanistan, subsequently extending to the central, central highlands, north-eastern and south-eastern regions. The trigger date for this operation is 20 July 2026, when the first and most destructive flood wave struck Parun City at approximately 15:00 hrs (ARCS-Parun; Flash Update (FU)#1).

Continued heavy rainfall between 20 and 28 July progressively widened the event, extending flooding to the south-eastern region on 21 July and to further central and central-highland provinces through 28 July (FU# 1, 2 and 3). Low-lying settlements along rivers and seasonal watercourses were worst affected (ARCS-Parun; FU#1; FU#3).
The most severe impact occurred in Parun City, the provincial capital of Nuristan. Because the flood ran through the built-up area of the town rather than through farmland, damage fell overwhelmingly on housing, public infrastructure and the local commercial base. ARCS recorded 30 houses damaged in Parun, of which seven were completely destroyed and 23 partially damaged, together with the destruction of one mosque, the municipality building, seven municipal and privately owned markets, five hotels and commercial buildings, and a number of shops and market stalls; six vehicles, two concrete public bridges, approximately two kilometres of main paved road, 100 metres of retaining wall, two water diversion structures and three water supply networks were also damaged or destroyed, and more than 45 livestock were lost. Agricultural losses in Parun were limited to roughly two jeribs (ARCS-Parun). Interagency reporting for the same location records damage to the urban water-supply network and 500 metres of pipeline, the destruction of one of two feeder springs, and the interruption of safe drinking water for some 1,000 families (FU#1; FU#2).

title: Türkiye: Basic Needs Sector Mid-year Review 2026
content: The Basic Needs Sector conducted its 2026 Mid-Year Review to assess progress against planned targets and examine the current funding situation. The Sector consulted its member organizations to identify the most pressing needs expected during the remainder of the year, in light of the Mid-Year Review analysis. Urgent funding is needed to prevent widening gaps in essential assistance The findings show that progress remains significantly below planned levels across several core areas of assistance. By mid-year, partners had reached only 16 per cent of the target for shelter and WASH related support, 29 per cent of the target for multipurpose cash assistance, and 22 per cent of the target for Core Relief Items. Food assistance recorded the highest level of progress, reaching 40 per cent of the annual target, largely due to ongoing assistance in camps and at border locations. Progress under the resilience component remains particularly limited. Activities intended to strengthen municipalities and public institutions for inclusive basic service delivery are severely underfunded. Rising needs and declining purchasing power Economic conditions have affected purchasing power, with only 30 per cent of refugee households able to comfortably meet their basic requirements and spend around or above the Minimum Expenditure Basket, MEB. (TRC IVS Round 3) Türkiye’s annual Consumer Price Index reached 32.11 per cent in June 2026, continuing to erode household purchasing power and increase the cost of meeting essential needs. The February 2026 analysis of the Cash Based Interventions Technical Working Group, based on Community Pulse, estimated that the most vulnerable refugee households faced a 60 per cent monthly gap between available income and the cost of meeting basic needs. This means that even households receiving some form of income or assistance remain unable to cover a substantial share of essential expenditure. Multipurpose cash assistance remains a high need for single parent households, older persons, persons with disabilities, and families with members living with chronic conditions, groups that are not expected to transition easily to self-reliant lives. Households rely on borrowing money, 57 per cent, or buying food on credit from local shops, 48 per cent. Even for households receiving food assistance, transfer amounts are not adequate to meet their needs. Additionally, food assistance programmes are focused only on southeastern cities, while needs remain high in other parts of the country. Vulnerable refugee households are in debt primarily to buy food, followed by paying rent. Households are mostly indebted to local markets, followed by relatives, and most have limited resources for further borrowing. Housing conditions remain a significant concern among refugee households, 48 per cent reported living in inadequate housing conditions (IVS). Households already living in cities, as well as those transitioning out of camps, struggle financially, as rents are high and several neighbourhoods are not open for registration. Across the country, most families face insecurity and cannot exercise their rights as tenants. The inability to secure housing also has implications for children’s enrolment in schools.

title: WFP Madagascar Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • In June, WFP continued unconditional food assistance in the Grand Sud, reaching 531,000 people. This included 38,593 children aged 6–23 months and 32,159 pregnant and breastfeeding women and girls supported through acute malnutrition prevention. The distribution marked the sixth and final cycle of the 2025–2026 lean season response. WFP also delivered nutrition supplements to 9,800 children aged 6–23 months and 3,400 pregnant and breastfeeding women in communities affected by Cyclone Fytia in the north‑west and Cyclone Gezani in the east of Madagascar.
  • Recurrent shocks are exposing the limits of short‑term emergency response and reinforcing the need for sustained investment in human capital, climate‑resilient food systems, and shock‑responsive social protection. Immediate resource mobilization remains critical to ensure operational readiness for the upcoming lean season, with USD 37.7 million required for July–December 2026.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Madagascar remains a low-income country grappling with structural vulnerabilities and recurrent climate shocks, including droughts and cyclones. About 80 percent of the population lives below the international poverty line, according to the World Bank’s Macro Poverty Outlook (2025). With more than three quarters of households dependent on agriculture, limited market access and low productivity continue to trap families in poverty and heighten their exposure to climatic and economic shocks.

• The June nationwide Emergency Food Security Assessment (EFSA), covering 120 districts and over 10,000 households, found that 40 percent of households are food insecure nationally. Food insecurity is most severe in the Great South (70 percent), driven by drought and chronic vulnerabilities, while 35–50 percent of households in cyclone-affected areas are food insecure due to cumulative climatic and economic shocks. Even areas with lower prevalence (<30 percent) remain fragile and at risk of deterioration.

• Preliminary results from Madagascar’s first nationwide IPC Acute Food Insecurity and Acute Malnutrition Analyses (MayJune 2026) indicate stabilization in some cyclone‑affected areas thanks to recent responses, but also project seasonal deterioration during the lean season, with several districts expected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or Emergency (IPC Phase 4) levels of food insecurity. Final validated results will be published in July 2026 to guide response planning.

• WFP continues to promote an integrated approach that links humanitarian action, climate adaptation, and development investments. This includes school meals for vulnerable children and resilience support for smallholder households, underpinned by strengthened emergency preparedness and aligned with the WFP Madagascar Country Strategic Plan.

title: Nigeria : Cholera Outbreak - DREF Operation (MDRNG046)
content:
Description of the Event
Date when the trigger was met
15-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) and the Borno State Ministry of Health have been responding to the outbreak since the first cases were reported on 1 May 2026. The outbreak escalated rapidly from Epidemiological Weeks 21–22, with cases increasing significantly during the onset of the rainy season. By Epidemiological Week 29, national cumulative suspected cases had increased to 44,129, with Borno State remaining the epicentre of the outbreak with more than 97 per cent of all reported cases and more than 99 per cent of weekly reported cases. 20 LGAs affected out of 27 withing the state.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), the Borno State Ministry of Health and humanitarian actors like Nigeria Red Cross have been responding to this outbreak in Borno since May 2026, but significant response gaps remain in several affected communities due to limited funding and insufficient partner presence. With the trend of the outbreak just at the onset of the worst transmission period, there is an urge to scale-up interventions.

On 15 July 2026, acknowledging the support from NRCS in Maiduguri and Jere LGAs, the Borno State Primary Health Care Development Board formally requested the NRCS to sustain and expand its response to underserved cholera-affected LGAs through strengthened Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE), Oral Rehydration Point (ORP) services, active case finding, referral mechanisms, hygiene promotion and community-based surveillance. The outbreak remains ongoing, with NCDC reporting increasing trends in key hotspot LGAs, particularly Monguno and Kukawa.

Sustained and scaled-up interventions are therefore required to reduce transmission, improve early treatment- health seeking behaviour, prevent cholera-related morbidity and mortalities and support the government's efforts to contain the outbreak before the peak of the rainy season.

title: Iran | Complex Emergency - Operation Update #1 (MDRIR018)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS
Description of the crisis

Since the escalation of hostilities on 28 February 2026, the Islamic Republic of Iran has experienced a nationwide complex emergency with severe humanitarian, social and economic consequences. What began as an acute conflict emergency rapidly expanded across the country, with incidents reported across 30 of 31 provinces and 275 counties, and with 262 districts affected. Following 40 consecutive days of strikes, a ceasefire reduced the immediate intensity of hostilities; however, the situation remains fragile and humanitarian needs continue to deepen.

The direct impact of the crisis has been severe. By the end of May 2026, approximately 60 million people were considered affected, of whom 10 million are among the most vulnerable and targeted through the Emergency Appeal. Reported casualties include more than 3,465 deaths, including approximately 1,460 civilians, and more than 34,000 people injured. Around 3.2 million people are estimated to have been internally displaced, placing additional pressure on host communities, urban infrastructure, public services and local economies.

The crisis has also caused widespread damage to civilian and humanitarian infrastructure. More than 149,000 civilian units have been damaged, including over 123,000 residential units, more than 24,000 commercial or business units, over 350 health facilities, 993 schools and 32 universities or research institutions. IRCS assets were also directly affected, including Red Crescent centres, logistics assets, ambulances and helicopters. Damage to homes, health facilities, schools, water and electricity systems, and humanitarian infrastructure has disrupted access to essential services and increased exposure to health, protection and socioeconomic risks.

While active hostilities have decreased under the ceasefire, the crisis is increasingly defined by indirect socioeconomic impacts. Inflation, food price increases, currency depreciation, disruption of trade and supply chains, unemployment, reduced household purchasing power, and constrained access to medicines and medical equipment are eroding coping capacities. These pressures are particularly severe for displaced people, low-income households, informal workers, women-headed households, migrants and refugees, older people, youth, persons with disabilities and people living with chronic illness.

The operational environment remains highly constrained. Sanctions-related restrictions, financial and banking limitations, procurement delays, shipping constraints, supplier hesitancy, damaged infrastructure, communications disruptions and the fragile security situation continue to affect the timely delivery of assistance. At the same time, the risk of renewed escalation remains present, requiring IRCS and IFRC to maintain full emergency response readiness while progressively expanding recovery-oriented and community-based interventions where conditions allow.

title: MMR: Flood - 07-2026 - Monsoon Flood (2026-08-05)
content:
Description

Continuous heavy rainfall caused river water levels to rise, resulting in flooding across Laymyethna Township, Ayeyarwady Region on 31 July 2026. Floodwaters inundated residential areas, agricultural land, roads, and public infrastructure, affecting people's safety, livelihoods, and access to essential services.
In response, MRCS Ayeyarwady Region activated trained National Disaster Response Team (NDRT) members to conduct a Rapid Needs Assessment using available resources under the MRCS Emergency Management Fund (EMF).

A rapid assessment found approximately 20,317 people across 16 villages, were affected and causing widespread displacement and damage to homes and livelihoods. The flooding has forced many families to seek temporary shelter, while others remain in their communities or are staying with relatives as they continue to monitor the evolving flood situation.

A total of nine temporary relief camps have been established, currently accommodating 441 households (approximately 1,411 people). In addition, around 1,200 houses have been affected by the flooding, highlighting the significant impact on local communities. The assessment also reported six missing persons, underscoring the humanitarian concerns arising from the disaster.

The findings indicate an urgent need for continued humanitarian assistance, including emergency shelter, relief items, safe drinking water, sanitation, health services, and ongoing monitoring of the flood situation to support affected communities and facilitate timely response efforts.

United Nations agencies and humanitarian partners stand ready to support affected populations through coordinated emergency assistance, including food, safe drinking water, shelter, health care, and WASH (water, sanitation and hygiene) services, drawing on established flood-response mechanisms that have previously been activated in Bago and other flood-affected areas of Myanmar. Private donors, community-based organizations (CBOs), civil society organizations (CSOs), and local volunteer groups have supported flood-affected communities in Ayeyarwady Region by providing emergency food, clean drinking water, clothing, hygiene kits, and cash assistance, while also helping with evacuations, temporary shelter management, and the distribution of relief supplies to vulnerable households. These local actors have played an important role in reaching affected communities quickly, complementing government and humanitarian response efforts, and supporting early recovery activities in flood-impacted areas.
