title: Situation Report 4 - Extreme Weather Events in India - Assam, Odisha, Gujarat, Kerala and Maharashtra (Date: 2nd August 2026)
content:
A. Situation Overview :

India is facing multi-state monsoon emergencies across Assam, Odisha, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Kerala, with Assam and Odisha the worst-affected due to severe flooding, large-scale displacement, and extensive crop and livestock losses.

1. Assam Flood - Severe Flooding Across 5 Districts

Impact on Humans

Heavy monsoon rains and rising river levels have caused widespread flooding across Assam, affecting 7 districts, 20 revenue circles, and 349 villages. As per ASDMA’s DRIMS report, 1,78,837 people have been impacted, and 15,060 hectares of crop area remain submerged. Floodwaters from the Dikhou (Sivasagar) and Dhansiri (South), Numaligarh have inundated major population clusters in Golaghat, Sivasagar, Charaideo, Bajali, Dhemaji, Sonitpur and Jorhat. The affected population comprises 75,388 males, 76,104 females, and 27,345 children, with the highest caseloads in Charaideo (75,199), Sivasagar (58,824), Jorhat (28,846) and Golaghat (14,545). No human deaths or missing persons have been reported as of 1 August 2026.

title: Agrometeorological 10 days Bulletin for 1–10 August 2026 Across the Northern Tonle Sap Basin of the PEARL Project
content:
Flood Early Warning

With floods forecasted during the next 10 days, protect roots from standing water and secure the orchard. On low ground, raise soil mounds around young trees 30-50 cm (about knee height) but do not bury the graft union. Open diversion channels one hand wide and one palm deep to lead water to safe outlets; keep inlets free of trash. Move tools, fertilizers, and crates to higher shelves (about one palm above floor). Mulch 10-15 cm (about a palm to a palm-and-a- half) with dry rice straw or chopped prunings, keeping a hand-width gap at the trunk. Harvestable fruit in very low plots should be picked early and stored above floor level. After floods recede, remove (rogue) trees that do not recover and dispose of plant waste away from the orchard; wash tools with soapy water.

Pest & Disease Early Warning

No elevated pest or disease risk for the next 10 days. Keep the canopy airy by removing crossing branches and lower shoots that touch the ground; avoid wetting leaves late in the day. Collect and destroy fallen fruit daily to reduce fruit-fly breeding; solarize in sealed bags left in the sun for two to three days or deep-bury away from trees. During flowering, avoid overhead irrigation; harvest only when foliage is dry to reduce anthracnose. Keep mulch 10-15 cm (about a palm to a palm-and-a-half) under the canopy, with a hand-width gap at the trunk. Clean pruning tools with soapy water and sun- dry.

title: Yemen: Agrometeorological Early Warning Bulletin (01 - 10 August 2026) [EN/AR]
content:
Overview:

In early August 2026, Yemen will likely experience peak summer rains over the western highlands, while hot conditions continue across the interior desert and coastal areas.

Key Concerns:

Precipitation Conditions: During the first dekad of August 2026, rainfall is expected to concentrate over the Central Highlands and Southern Uplands, with moderate to locally heavy convective showers and thunderstorms. Cumulative totals may locally exceed 200 mm in parts of Ibb, Dhamar, and Sana’a, raising the risk of flash floods across major watersheds. The Siham and Zabid watersheds are at Alert level, while Mour, Sordod, Dnah, Tuban, and Banna remain at Minimal level (Fig. 1). In contrast, the Tihama coastal plain, southern areas, and eastern plateau are likely to see only light, isolated rainfall. The International Research Institute for Climate and Society (IRI) indicates roughly a 50% chance of below-average rainfall over the Tihama Plain, Northern Highlands, and eastern regions.

Temperature Conditions: From 1–10 August 2026, maximum temperatures are expected to exceed 42°C in northern and eastern desert areas, with 35–40°C likely across many western lowlands and central regions, increasing the risk of heat stress and heatwaves (Fig. 2). Highland areas should remain comparatively cooler at 25–35°C, though still slightly above climatological averages.

Implications on Agricultural Livelihoods

  • Positive Impacts
    • Improved soil moisture for rainfed sorghum, millet, maize, sesame, and coffee in the western and central highlands.
    • Better crop establishment, with enhanced germination and vegetative growth of recently planted crops.
    • Improved rangeland conditions and increased pasture availability for livestock.
    • Increased water availability, including recharge of small reservoirs, ponds, and shallow groundwater where rainfall is sufficient.
  • Potential Adverse Impacts
    • Localized flash floods may damage terraces, agricultural infrastructure, and crops, particularly in valleys (wadis) amid ongoing general water stress fir the majoiur agro-ecological areas of the country.
    • Soil erosion and nutrient losses may occur due to heavy runoff on sloping farmland.
    • Increased disease risks due to high humidity and intermittent rainfall, particularly fungal diseases and bacterial infections affecting vegetables, coffee, and fruit trees.
    • Heat stress will persist in coastal and desert regions, affecting crops and livestock while increasing irrigation requirements.

Adaptation and Coping Strategies:

Key measures FAO and partners can take to mitigate the anticipated meteorological impacts during the first dekad of August 2026 include:

  • Crop Production and Field Management
    • Complete planting of rainfed cereals in areas that have received sufficient rainfall.
    • Clear and maintain field drainage channels to reduce flooding and waterlogging.
    • Monitor crops for fungal diseases after extended wet periods and apply appropriate control measures where feasible.
  • Livestock Management
    • Protect livestock from heat stress by providing adequate shade and reliable water supplies, particularly in hot lowland areas.
  • Flood Risk Management
    • Avoid cultivation or grazing in active wadis during periods of intense rainfall due to the risk of flash floods.
    • Maintain and utilize rainwater-harvesting structures to capture runoff for later irrigation and water use.

title: WFP Senegal Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP and the Ministry of National Education signed a new partnership agreement supporting WFP’s 2025-2029 Country Strategic Plan, laying the foundation for the sustainable scale-up of school meals in Senegal.

• Through its Mastercard Foundation-funded youth employment and food systems project Salouma, WFP enrolled 24,329 young people across eight regions, over 81 percent of them women. Partner organizations began delivering training and agricultural and livestock kits.

• WFP supported the revision of Senegal’s rice fortification roadmap and the introduction of fortified rice in school meals, benefiting 6,188 children and strengthening efforts to improve nutrition and reduce micronutrient deficiencies.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Food security and nutrition remain fragile in Senegal as households enter the June-August lean season. An estimated 836,786 people are projected to face crisis-level food insecurity, representing a 66 percent increase compared to March 2026. According to the latest Fill the Nutrient Gap assessment, 60 percent of the population lacks access to a healthy diet, while 46 percent cannot afford a nutritious diet.

• The onset of the agricultural season coincides with increased pressure on household food stocks and purchasing power, particularly in vulnerable rural areas already affected by climate variability and limited livelihood opportunities.

• Against this backdrop, the Government of Senegal is advancing Sénégal 2050: Agenda National de Transformation (Jubbanti), which provides the national framework for human capital development, food sovereignty, youth employment, and climate resilience.

• WFP aligns its interventions with these priorities through its Country Strategic Plan (CSP) 20252029, built on four pillars: (i) crisis response through food and nutrition assistance; (ii) prevention and treatment of malnutrition and school meals to support human capital; (iii) climate-smart livelihoods and sustainable food systems with a focus on women and youth; and (iv) strengthening national systems through technical assistance and capacity development.

title: Mali | Riverine Floods: Early Action Protocol Annual Report(EAP №: EAP2023ML002, Operation №: MDRML021)
content:
In March 2025, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) Emergency Disaster Relief Fund (DREF) approved the Mali Red Cross (CRM) Early Action Protocol (EAP) to enable the implementation of anticipatory actions aimed at reducing the humanitarian impacts of riverine floods across Mali.
The Early Action Protocol (EAP) targets flood-prone areas and primarily aims to reduce loss of life, mitigate economic damage, and prevent waterborne diseases such as diarrhea and cholera. The protocol is designed to reach up to 4,000 households, approximately 24,000 people, with a total budget of CHF 493,567.
Activation of the EAP is triggered by hydrological and meteorological forecasts produced by the National Directorate of Hydraulics (DNH), indicating that thresholds corresponding to at least a five-year return period have been reached. Once these thresholds are met, the Mali Red Cross (CRM) has a lead time of 4 to 8 days to activate the planned early actions and deploy its teams in the field.

Planned interventions include the activation of regional crisis committees, strengthened inter-agency coordination, community-based vulnerability assessments, door-to-door and radio-based awareness campaigns, distribution of WASH and health items, provision of empty sandbags for dike reinforcement, construction of emergency shelters, protection of critical infrastructure, and continuous monitoring of the evolving situation.
These measures were defined through national dialogue platforms, community consultations, and simulation exercises (“dry tests”) conducted in 2019 and 2020, and were subsequently refined following the real activation of the EAP in September 2022. They were selected based on their effectiveness in reducing priority risks, their operational feasibility within short lead times, and their acceptance by at-risk communities.

The Mali Red Cross has strong institutional and operational capacity to implement the EAP, including a nationwide network of trained volunteers, experienced technical teams across sectors, pre-positioned stocks in multiple regions, framework agreements with local suppliers, and close collaboration with government technical services—particularly the General Directorate of Civil Protection (DGPC). These capacities ensure a timely, efficient, and well-coordinated response, even in hard-to-reach areas.

Beyond immediate response, the EAP contributes to strengthening long-term preparedness and community resilience to flooding, including in situations where anticipated events do not fully materialize. This is achieved through sustained awareness-raising, reinforcement of protective infrastructure, and improvements in early warning systems

title: Cape Verde | Drought - Simplified Early Action Protocol (sEAP2025CV01 | MDRCV006)
content:
RISK ANALYSIS AND EARLY ACTION SELECTION

Priority risks and their historical impact.

Cape Verde is exposed to several natural hazards, including, but not limited to, droughts, floods, landslides, tropical storms, heatwaves, epidemics, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, locust infestations, coastal erosion and sea-level rise (IFRC, 2025; World Bank Group, 2025; World Bank Group and GFDRR, 2020). According to the INFORMRISK database, in 2025, Cape Verde has a risk and exposure index (probability of physical exposure associated with various risks) of 0.8 on a scale of 0 to 10, with a vulnerability index of 3.3 and an adaptation capacity deficit index of 4.1. This suggests that, although the country has an overall low level of exposure to all hazards combined, its low adaptive capacity linked to institutional challenges (disaster risk management and governance) and to those arising from a lack of infrastructure and health services increases the vulnerability of the population to disaster risks. These risks are exacerbated by high rates of rural exodus, soil degradation, poor connectivity between the islands, persistent poverty and high levels of debt (World Bank Group, 2025).
According to the EM-DAT database, which provides information on major disasters, Cape Verde recorded 24 major events between 1900 and 2024, affecting a total of 234,264 people and causing 85,298 deaths (Table 1). These disasters include droughts, which account for 50 per cent of recorded events, epidemics (13 per cent), tropical storms (13 per cent), floods (8 per cent), locust swarms (8 per cent) and volcanic activity (8 per cent).

title: Aceh, North Sumatra and West Sumatra Provinces, Indonesia Flood 2025 - DREF Operational Update (MDRID028), 31/07/2026
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
26-11-2025
What happened, where and when?

Tropical Cyclone Senyar originated as Tropical Disturbance 95B over the Strait of Malacca on 21 November 2025. The system gradually intensified into a tropical depression by 25 November and was officially upgraded to a tropical cyclone by Indonesia’s Meteorological, Climatological, and Geophysical Agency (BMKG) on 26 November 2025.

Forming near the equator northwest of Aceh Province, the cyclone tracked across Sumatra, affecting Aceh, North Sumatra, and West Sumatra. It made landfall on 26 November 2025, bringing torrential rainfall, destructive winds, and severe storm surges to multiple provinces.

Heavy rainfall had already intensified from 23 November, but the cyclone’s landfall triggered widespread flash floods and landslides. A total of 35 districts and cities across three provinces were directly affected, while many neighbouring areas experienced severe access and logistical disruptions. Emergency response operations were rapidly activated as structural damage and humanitarian needs escalated.

Current Humanitarian Situation and Recovery Needs

As of the reporting date of 15 June 2026, affected communities have not yet fully recovered from the disaster. While humanitarian response activities from agencies have concluded, recovery needs remain significant. Although there are no longer people living in internally displaced person (IDP) centres, many affected families continue to live in temporary houses constructed by the government, stay with relatives, or remain in their own homes despite ongoing challenges related to damaged structures, poor sanitation conditions, and an uncomfortable living environment.

Large areas of agricultural land remain covered by hardened layers of mud and waste, which are costly and difficult for individual households to remove, preventing communities from restarting agricultural activities. Many households also lost their tools and equipment needed for their businesses and livelihoods. Most affected families expressed the need for capital support to restart their businesses and restore their livelihoods.

The current situation is perceived as more challenging by some affected communities, as assistance received during the two to four months of displacement has ceased, while households now need to cover food and other basic needs despite significantly reduced or lost income sources. Many affected people are seeking temporary employment as daily labourers or selling remaining crops from available trees to meet their immediate needs.

Some village public health clinics have also not yet resumed operations, as health equipment and supplies were damaged or swept away during the disaster.

Government Housing Recovery Assistance Specific government stimulus assistance has been provided to households affected by the floods in Sumatra that occurred in late November 2025. Housing assistance is provided based on the level of damage: IDR 15 million for houses with minor damage (0–30 per cent damage), IDR 30 million for houses with moderate damage (30–70 per cent damage), and IDR 60 million for houses with severe damage (more than 70 per cent damage) for reconstruction. Housing damage assessments refer to the regulations of the Minister of Public Works and the BNPB Implementation Guidelines.

For disaster-affected households whose homes are severely damaged and no longer habitable, and who choose not to stay in temporary housing (huntara), the government provides Dana Tunggu Hunian (DTH) or Housing Waiting Funds amounting to IDR 600,000 per family per month.

As of June 2026, according to Indonesia’s Disaster Geoportal Data Bencana Indonesia, government housing recovery support includes:

(1) Aceh: The government has built 18,738 temporary houses and 260 permanent houses, distributed stimulus assistance to 15,192 houses with minor damage and 11,069 houses with moderate damage, and distributed 13,704 DTH assistance.
(2) North Sumatra: The government has built 1,024 temporary houses and 548 permanent houses, distributed stimulus assistance to 2,332 houses with minor damage and 1,228 houses with moderate damage, and distributed 4,288 DTH assistance.
(3) West Sumatra: The government has built 830 temporary houses and 19 permanent houses, distributed stimulus assistance to 811 houses with minor damage and 375 houses with moderate damage, and distributed 2,992 DTH assistance.

title: MAR: Population Movement - 07-2026 - Massive population movement at Bab Sebta (2026-08-01)
content:
Description

1. Executive Summary

An exceptional population movement toward the Bab Sebta (Ceuta) border crossing has generated significant humanitarian needs on the Moroccan side of the border. The situation escalated rapidly between 30 and 31 July 2026, resulting in a major migration, humanitarian, and security crisis affecting both Morocco and the Spanish autonomous city of Ceuta.

According to reports from the Moroccan Red Crescent (MRC) on ground, local information and international media sources, tens of thousands of people have gathered in and around Fnideq and attempted to enter Ceuta by sea and land. Spanish authorities have deployed military reinforcements, while Moroccan security forces have strengthened border controls and crowd management measures. The humanitarian impact includes fatalities, injuries, food and water shortages, psychosocial distress, and protection concerns among vulnerable groups.

The Moroccan Red Crescent, as an auxiliary to the public authorities, is well positioned to support the response through health and first aid services, WASH, food assistance, protection, psychosocial support, restoring family links (RFL), community engagement and accountability (CEA), and logistics.

2. Background

Ceuta is a Spanish autonomous city located on the northern coast of Africa and bordering Morocco. Together with Melilla, it constitutes the European Union's only land border with Africa. The area has historically served as a migration route for individuals seeking entry into Europe.

Since late July 2026, a substantial increase in migration movements originating from northern Morocco, particularly the Fnideq area, has evolved into a major cross-border humanitarian emergency. Large numbers of migrants have attempted to enter Ceuta by swimming around border barriers or by approaching land crossing points.

3. Current Situation

The situation deteriorated significantly on 30 and 31 July 2026.

Spanish authorities deployed additional police and military personnel to Ceuta to restore order and manage the influx. Moroccan authorities simultaneously reinforced security deployments around Fnideq and key border crossing points. Crowd control measures, including water cannons and dispersal operations, have been reported near the border area.

Large crowds continue to gather around the border area, and migration attempts remain ongoing despite heightened security measures.

4. Population Movement Overview

Migration figures remain fluid and continue to evolve.

  • More than 25,000 individuals have reportedly already returned or been returned to Morocco. Numbers may increase.
  • Field observations by the Moroccan Red Crescent indicate that arrivals remain ongoing and that the exact number of affected persons cannot yet be fully determined due to the continuous influx.

5. Humanitarian Impact

Casualties

*International media have reported 41 confirmed fatalities, while field-based operational reporting indicates figures may be higher and remain under verification. Most fatalities are reportedly linked to drowning incidents or crowd-crush events near crossing areas.

Reported Injuries

Field teams report:

  • Open wounds and lacerations;
  • Fractures of upper and lower limbs;
  • Exhaustion and dehydration;
  • Injuries linked to swimming attempts and crowd movement.

The total number of injured persons remains under assessment.

6. Moroccan Red Crescent Field Observations

The Moroccan Red Crescent has reported:

  • Significant numbers of individuals presenting with cuts, fractures, and physical trauma related to attempted sea crossings.
  • Insufficient access to food among newly arrived populations.
  • Limited access to safe drinking water.
  • Continuous arrivals from other parts of Morocco, increasing pressure on local response capacity.
  • Elevated levels of stress and psychosocial distress among migrants and their families.
  • Presence of vulnerable groups including women, children, and unaccompanied minors.

7. Multi-Sectoral Needs Analysis

8. Security and Operational Outlook

The situation remains highly volatile and is characterized by:

  • Continued arrivals and attempted border crossings.
  • Large crowd concentrations around Fnideq and the Ceuta border area.
  • Significant military and police deployments on both sides of the border.
  • Traffic disruptions and localized movement restrictions.
  • Risks of stampedes, crowd incidents, and accidental exposure to security operations.
  • Potential deterioration should migration attempts continue at the current scale.

9. Target Population (Planning Scenario)

For the initial response phase, the Moroccan Red Crescent proposes a planning scenario targeting up to 8,000 people requiring immediate humanitarian assistance.

This figure should be adjusted following rapid assessments and verification of needs on the ground.

10. Proposed Operational Strategy

The proposed response includes:

  • Deployment of first aid and emergency health teams.
  • Establishment of medical and first aid points.
  • Distribution of safe drinking water.
  • Distribution of emergency food assistance.
  • Implementation of Protection, PGI, MHPSS, RFL, and CEA activities.
  • Conducting a Rapid Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (MSNA).
  • Strengthening logistics, volunteer management, and coordination mechanisms.
  • Supporting authorities and humanitarian partners through auxiliary action in line with Red Cross Red Crescent principles.

11. Main Operational Risks

  • Continued influx of migrants.
  • Evolving and incomplete population data.
  • Security and access constraints.
  • Limited operational resources.
  • Adverse weather and maritime conditions.
  • Increased pressure on local humanitarian and public services.

12. PMER

The response should include:

  • Daily situation reports.
  • Tracking of beneficiaries reached.
  • Regular review of assumptions and planning figures.
  • Monitoring of sectoral indicators.
  • Ongoing operational assessments and lessons learned documentation.

Actions taken by others

Government of Morocco Moroccan authorities have significantly reinforced security measures in and around Fnideq, Bab Sebta, and key border crossing points to prevent further irregular crossings into Ceuta. Security forces reportedly deployed crowd-control measures. Increased police and security deployments have been observed across the affected area, with efforts focused on controlling movement towards the border and maintaining public order. Government of Spain Spain deployed military personnel and additional police forces to Ceuta to reinforce border management, maintain public order, and support ongoing humanitarian and security operations. Spanish authorities launched accelerated return procedures for migrants who entered Ceuta irregularly. As of 31 July, more than 25,000 individuals had reportedly returned or been returned to Morocco. Senior government officials, including Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and the Minister of Interior, visited Ceuta to assess the situation and coordinate the response. United Nations and International Organizations Humanitarian agencies and protection actors are closely monitoring the situation. Coordination with humanitarian partners is expected to increase should population movements continue and humanitarian needs escalate on either side of the border. Red Cross Red Crescent Movement The Moroccan Red Crescent (MRC) has conducted field observations and preliminary assessments in the affected area to identify urgent humanitarian needs and response gaps. The Spanish Red Cross is supporting humanitarian efforts in Ceuta, including assistance to vulnerable migrants and support to local authorities responding to the influx. The IFRC and relevant regional structures are monitoring developments and maintaining communication with Movement partners regarding potential humanitarian implications and response options.

title: ESP: Population Movement - 07-2026 - Population Movement Ceuta (2026-08-01)
content:
Description

On July 30–31, 2026, the Spanish enclave of Ceuta experienced the largest mass migration breach in its history. An estimated 40,000–60,000 people crossed the border from Morocco in less than 48 hours, swimming around the Tarajal breakwater or surging through border gates. The scale and speed of the arrivals have placed significant pressure on local reception capacities and emergency response services. Reports indicate that the situation has resulted in numerous rescue operations, injuries and fatalities linked to attempted crossings.

Spain's response included deploying military units to reinforce the overwhelmed Civil Guard. By July 31, approximately 25,000–37,500 people had returned voluntarily to Morocco.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: No

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by National Society

General

First Aid

Health

Search & Rescue

Summary

Spanish Red Cross remains actively engaged in the response to the migration crisis in Ceuta, providing emergency healthcare, rescue support and humanitarian assistance to people arriving through the Tarajal area. In coordination with local authorities, emergency services and Maritime Rescue, Red Cross teams are delivering first aid, support to vulnerable individuals, assistance to unaccompanied minors, referrals to reception facilities and emergency medical interventions at arrival points. The operation remains ongoing amid significant pressure on local reception and response capacities.

title: Philippines Davao Earthquakes 2025 - DREF Final Report (MDRPH058)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event
10-10-2025
What happened, where and when?

On 10 October 2025, two powerful earthquakes struck off the coast of Manay, Davao Oriental. The first earthquake, with a magnitude of 7.4, occurred at 9:43 AM, approximately 48 kilometres northeast of the Municipality of Manay, Davao Oriental, at a depth of 23 kilometres. The earthquake was felt as far as Davao City, Davao de Oro, and parts of Northern Mindanao, with reported intensities ranging from IV to V.

Immediately after the first tremor, a Tsunami Warning was issued, prompting the evacuation of residents in several low-lying and coastal areas of Davao Oriental, Surigao del Sur, and parts of Caraga. The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) recorded a 30 cm tsunami wave along the coast of Tandag City, Surigao del Sur at approximately 10:20 AM and lifted the warning at 1:43 PM on the same day.

Less than 10 hours after the first earthquake, a second earthquake with a magnitude of 6.8 struck the same offshore area at 7:12 PM. The epicentre was located approximately 43 kilometres southeast of the Municipality of Manay, Davao Oriental, with an estimated depth of 37 kilometres. The second earthquake was felt in the same areas affected by the first event, heightening fear among communities and causing further structural damage. This event triggered another tsunami warning, which was later cancelled at 11:12 PM without any tsunami waves observed.

Both earthquakes were tectonic in origin and were generated by movement along the Philippine Trench. According to PHIVOLCS, the second earthquake was not considered an aftershock of the first earthquake, as it exceeded magnitude 6.4. Instead, the events were classified as a “doublet earthquake”, referring to two separate earthquakes that occurred close together in time and location.

Within the first 48 hours following the earthquakes, PHIVOLCS recorded more than 1,310 aftershocks, with the strongest measuring magnitude 5.8. Although seismic activity continued to be recorded for up to six months after the two main earthquakes, these aftershocks were generally of lower magnitude and did not result in significant additional damage or impacts on vulnerable populations.

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 31 July 2026
content:
Highlights

  • In Gaza, food insecurity has eased, but needs remain high, and declining aid coverage since February 2026 risks reversing gains, according to the latest Integrated Food Security Phase Classification analysis.
  • Gender-based violence is on the rise, with a 27 per cent increase in reported cases between January-March to April-June 2026, according to UNFPA.
  • Shortages of insulin, cardiac catheterization materials, hemodialysis supplies and critical diagnostic and monitoring equipment hinder the treatment of non-communicable diseases in Gaza.
  • In the West Bank, eight Palestinians, including one child, and two members of Israeli forces were killed in Nablus, Jenin and East Jerusalem; July was jointly with March 2026 the deadliest month for Palestinians in incidents involving settlers since October 2023.
  • In just one week, Israeli settler attacks displaced at least 20 Palestinian families and caused damage to homes, vehicles and livelihood assets; over 40 settler attacks resulted in casualties or property damage.
  • Israeli forces and officials entered the United Nations Kalandia Training Centre in East Jerusalem for the second time in less than a month, disrupting educational activities and breaching the inviolability of UN premises.

Overview

Heightened violence and Israeli military operations continue to drive civilian casualties, destruction of property, and displacement across the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT). Coupled with severe and tightening access restrictions, these practices are further hindering people’s ability to safely reach workplaces and essential services, while humanitarian needs remain acute. In the Gaza Strip, airstrikes, shelling and other attacks over the past week have reportedly resulted in civilian casualties, including young children. n the West Bank, a series of deadly incidents and an intensifying pattern of settler violence brought July to match March 2026 as the deadliest month for Palestinians in settler attacks since October 2023. Demolitions, settler violence and related access restrictions have displaced an average of 17 people, including eight children, per day in 2026 – double the daily average recorded over the preceding three years.

Gaza Strip

This section covers 20 to 26 July unless otherwise specified.

The humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire. Ongoing military operations near the so-called “Yellow Line,” coupled with strikes reported in other locations of the Strip, are increasingly disrupting civilian life, damaging shelters, driving renewed displacement and restricting access to life-saving services. At the same time, 67 per cent of the population continues to face high levels of acute food insecurity, and the fragile gains made since the October 2025 ceasefire announcement risk being rapidly reversed as aid coverage declines amid growing funding constraints.

Shortages of essential medical supplies continue to hamper non-communicable disease services, while infectious diseases remain widespread due to overcrowding in displacement sites and poor water, hygiene and sanitation conditions. Against this backdrop, protection risks are on the rise, with women, children and other vulnerable groups disproportionately affected; a marked increase has been noticed in reported gender-based violence. All the while, shortages of basic supplies such as cooking gas and solar lanterns further undermine people’s ability to meet even their most basic needs.

According to the Ministry of Health (MoH) in Gaza, which operates under the de facto authorities, 30 Palestinians were reported killed, including those who died of wounds and had their bodies retrieved from under the rubble, and 134 people were injured between 22 and 29 July. This brings the overall casualty toll reported by MoH since the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 to 1,209 fatalities and 3,943 injuries.

Civilians continue to face significant security risks across Gaza, with incidents during the reporting period affecting both communities and service delivery points. In areas of North Gaza governorate, including Beit Lahia and Jabalya, ongoing Israeli military operations continued to severely disrupt people’s lives. Military advances and withdrawals occurred on multiple occasions throughout the week, while nearby strikes and shelling damaged shelters and forced affected households to relocate temporarily within and around displacement sites.

On 25 July, 13 families were temporarily displaced from Al Atatra site in Beit Lahia while in Jabalya, 25 families at Misr 16 site relocated internally following damage to their shelters. At Rahmaa Baynahum site in central Jabalya Camp, approximately 137 families temporarily sought refuge with relatives and friends or in open areas. Additional incidents at Zaad Al Khair site and Sumud site in Gaza Port resulted in the temporary displacement of nine families within the sites. Across all locations, affected households generally returned to their displacement sites within two to three days after humanitarian partners provided them with replacement tents and shelter materials.

Throughout the Gaza Strip, children remain exposed to severe and compounding protection risks, including hostilities, stray gunfire, explosive remnants of war, unsafe shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) conditions, disease outbreaks, family separation, school dropout, child labour, early marriage, neglect, violence and heightened risks of gender-based violence and sexual exploitation and abuse for adolescent girls. Unsafe site conditions – including damaged shelters, poor lighting, open pits, sewage leakage, overcrowding and water shortages – continue to restrict safe access to services and increase protection risks.

Recent discussions that Site Management partners led with children in 24 displacement sites hosting more than 11,300 families (over 54,600 people) highlighted the impact of poor lighting on children. Participants said it undermines their safety when accessing sanitation facilities at night, limits their ability to study, and contributes to broader protection concerns within crowded displacement environments.

Between 19 and 25 July, according to the Health Cluster, acute respiratory infections remained the leading reported condition, amounting to 43.2 per cent of all communicable diseases, followed by acute watery diarrhea (22 per cent), underscoring persistent risks associated with overcrowding and inadequate WASH conditions. Skin diseases continued to represent a significant burden, with ectoparasitic infestations accounting for 18.9 per cent of cases, impetigo showing an upward trend (10.8 per cent), and chickenpox continuing to decline (4.9 per cent).

Meanwhile the humanitarian community’s ability to respond remains constrained by Israeli access restrictions into and within Gaza as well as funding shortfalls.

Attempts by the de facto authorities to inspect humanitarian warehouses for alleged smuggled items continue but at a slower pace compared with previous periods. Between 6 and 26 July, the UN recorded eight cases where individuals identifying themselves as agents of the de facto authorities searched humanitarian warehouses, causing disruptions to humanitarian operations and breaching the inviolability of United Nations premises. No alleged contraband was found.

Fragile Food Security Gains

On 23 July, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) released the findings of its latest Acute Food Insecurity and Acute Malnutrition Analysis for the Gaza Strip. The analysis indicates that the scale-up of humanitarian assistance, enabled by improved access and reduced conflict intensity following the October 2025 ceasefire announcement, has driven improvements in food security and nutrition conditions across Gaza. However, needs remain high and recent gains are highly fragile.

Between mid-April and 30 June 2026, over 1.2 million people (59 per cent of the population) continued to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse levels of food insecurity, including 212,000 people in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) and none in Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5).

Looking ahead, the IPC projects a renewed deterioration in food security conditions between July and December 2026, with the number of people facing Crisis or worse expected to rise to 1.4 million (67 per cent of the population). The analysis noted that aid coverage has already declined since February 2026, and further reductions are expected due to funding constraints, and uncertainty regarding the renewal of operational authorizations for 37 international non-governmental organizations. According to IPC, coupled with continuing population displacement in an increasingly confined area of Gaza as militarized zones expand, dire health, water, hygiene and sanitation conditions, and volatile access for both humanitarian and commercial supplies, all these concurrent factors could rapidly trigger a sharp deterioration in food security and nutrition conditions, as livelihoods have collapsed and people have exhausted their coping mechanisms.

On the nutrition front, while acute malnutrition – particularly among children – has declined significantly, driven by a marked scale-up of nutrition programmes, the IPC expects an estimated 74,200 children aged 6-59 months and 24,600 pregnant and breastfeeding women (PBW) to continue requiring treatment through April 2027.

According to the latest World Food Programme Palestine Market Monitor, food prices in Gaza continued to decrease throughout June and the first half of July, particularly for fresh fruits and vegetables, while wheat flour prices remained stable. Food intake continues to be significantly below the levels recorded before October 2023, especially for protein-rich foods as meat and eggs (consumed the equivalent of only once per week, on average), fruits (consumed the equivalent of half a day per week), and vegetables (consumed the equivalent of twice per week), WFP found.

WFP notes that, although the entry of commercial and humanitarian supplies continued to increase in June and July, compared with the low levels observed in March and April, during the regional escalation, market access slightly worsened in July, with 77 per cent of surveyed households reporting difficulties accessing markets mainly to due lack of cash and unaffordability of basic food items, compared to 67 per cent in May. Cooking gas supplies remain extremely limited, with approximately 73 per cent of households surveyed by WFP reporting that they relied on waste burning as an alternative to cooking gas in July.

Rising Gender-Based Violence

Women and girls in Gaza continue to face escalating and life-threatening risks of gender-based violence (GBV), with devastating consequences for their physical safety and mental wellbeing, including Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, depression and suicide – according to the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) that leads the GBV response under the Protection Cluster. In April-June 2026, reported GBV incidents increased by 27 per cent compared with January-March 2026.

According to UNFPA, this reflects both worsening protection risks and expanded reporting, attributed to awareness raising sessions provided by protection partners (see below, in the section on response to GBV). The denial of resources, opportunities and services remains the most prevalent form of GBV, while psychological violence, sexual violence and forced marriage are increasing, particularly among adolescent girls, UNFPA says.

Male survivors of conflict-related sexual violence continue to face significant barriers to accessing confidential, survivor-centred services due both to stigma and to the inadequate resources available to GBV partners, which prevent them from recruiting more frontline service providers able to provide specialized support, UNFPA reports.

At the same time, caseworkers specializing in addressing GBV are managing unsustainable caseloads while many face GBV risks themselves within their homes and communities, further straining an already overstretched response. Despite an increase in GBV service delivery points from 74 to 84 in recent weeks, access to life saving services remains critically inadequate, with 17 Women and Girls’ Safe Spaces (WGSSs) still closed due to lack of funding and two others forced to close following movements of the “Yellow Line”, leaving many survivors without safe, confidential support.

Incoming Supplies

According to data collected by the Logistics Cluster, Ashdod remained the primary route for humanitarian cargo entering Gaza during the reporting period, with 308 UN and humanitarian partner trucks offloaded. Through Egypt, the offloading rate stood at 69 per cent, while the remaining 31 per cent of manifested trucks were either rejected and returned by the Israeli authorities or cancelled due to operational issues. In most return and rejection cases, no reason was provided; where specified, reasons included pallet conditions, cargo type and inconsistencies in information submitted. Via Jordan, aid truck volumes returned to normal levels following the resolution of the scanner malfunction at the Sheikh Hussein Bridge-Jordan River. Presently, the King Hussein Bridge-Allenby Crossing operates twice weekly (Mondays and Wednesdays) with a maximum of 60 trucks per convoy, while the Sheikh Hussein Bridge-Jordan River crossing operates Sunday to Thursday with a capacity of 15 trucks per day. More than two months following the closure of the Zikim Crossing in northern Gaza on 24 May, Kerem Shalom remains the only operational crossing point into Gaza.

Items that the Israeli authorities classify as having “dual use” are more difficult to secure approval for and bring in. Even when cleared, offloading items classified as such at Kerem Shalom remains limited to one day per week, creating significant bottlenecks that delay humanitarian assistance, disrupt supply pipelines, and constrain preparedness for the upcoming winter season. (For examples of such items, see the Shelter section below.)

The UN is only able to confirm the entry of supplies tracked by UN 2720. For breakdowns of those, see the online UN 2720 Mechanism Dashboard.

For a detailed account of the latest humanitarian operations in Gaza, see Annex 1 below.

West Bank

This section covers 21 to 27 July unless otherwise specified.

The reporting period was marked by a series of deadly incidents that resulted in the killing of eight Palestinians and two members of Israeli forces, including a settlement security guard. These developments occurred amid an intensifying pattern of settler violence, with July matching March 2026 as the deadliest month for Palestinians in settler attacks since October 2023. Across the West Bank, lack-of-permit demolitions, settler violence and related access restrictions have displaced an average of 17 people, including eight children, per day in 2026 – double the daily average recorded over the preceding three years.

Concerns over access to education were heightened after Israeli forces and officials forcibly entered the United Nations Kalandia Training Centre (KTC) in East Jerusalem for the second time in less than a month, disrupting educational activities. At the time of the unauthorized entry, more than 100 students and staff were attending classes and sheltered in place while the operation was underway. In a statement issued on 28 July, the Humanitarian Country Team stated that the raid "breached the inviolability of United Nations premises" and "impeded joint efforts by UN agencies and NGOs to provide humanitarian assistance and critical services."

Despite funding and operational constraints, as well as movement restrictions, Education Cluster partners continued to deliver summer learning programmes providing catch-up and remedial classes, recreational activities and psychosocial support to help children prepare for the new school year. Child protection partners also continued to provide critical protection services, reaching 2,320 children with disabilities since the beginning of 2026, as part of a Disability-Inclusion Action Plan focused on advocacy, capacity building, strengthening disability-disaggregated data collection and analysis, and improving the accessibility and inclusiveness of child protection services.

During the fourth week of July, Shelter Cluster partners reached 528 people (119 households) through 23 interventions, primarily minor-to-moderate shelter repairs (73 per cent), alongside the provision of essential non-food items and cash assistance. Assistance focused on communities affected by displacement, demolitions and settler violence in Nablus, Ramallah and Hebron governorates, with these three governorates accounting for about 62 per cent of all people reached. Meanwhile, more than 33,000 Palestine refugees displaced from Jenin, Tulkarm and Nur Shams refugee camps since early 2025 continue to face significant shelter needs.

Casualties and Settler Violence

During the reporting period, four deadly incidents resulted in the killing of eight Palestinians and two members of Israeli forces, including a settlement security guard, in Nablus, Jenin and East Jerusalem. On 23 July, one Israeli settler was stabbed and injured by a Palestinian and two Palestinians were shot and killed by an Israeli settler near Beit Furik following a fire that reportedly triggered confrontations between Palestinians, Israeli settlers and Israeli forces. On 24 July, four Palestinians from the same family and two members of Israeli forces, including a settlement security guard, were killed in Tell village. Palestinian sources reported that Israeli settlers from Havat Gilad settlement entered and attacked the village and Israeli media reported that the group had been hiking in the area and entered Areas A and B without coordination with the Israeli military. During the incident, a Palestinian man seized a rifle from an Israeli settler and reportedly opened fire.

Separately, on 23 July, Israeli forces shot and killed a Palestinian man at Shu'fat Camp checkpoint in East Jerusalem. The Israeli police stated that officers had ordered the man, whom they described as “behaving suspiciously,” to stop, but he did not comply; no Israeli personnel were injured. His body was returned to the family on 25 July. Also on 23 July, Israeli forces shot and killed a Palestinian man after he stabbed and injured an Israeli soldier at a checkpoint east of Jenin city.

On 24 July, a Palestinian man was reportedly attacked, stabbed and injured by Israeli settlers while his vehicle was stranded on Road 449 between Jericho and Ramallah after his vehicle ran out of fuel. According to the affected man, the settlers also seized his vehicle and personal belongings. Due to movement restrictions imposed following the deadly incidents in Nablus governorate, he was initially unable to reach hospital and received first aid in Al 'Auja town before being transferred to Jericho hospital after road access partially reopened.

Since the beginning of 2026, 76 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers or died of wounds sustained earlier, and three Israelis, including the two members of Israeli forces mentioned above, have been killed by Palestinians in the West Bank. More than 1,600 Palestinians have also been injured, including 46 per cent by Israeli settlers and the remainder by Israeli forces, while 24 Israelis, including 20 settlers and two soldiers, have been injured.

These incidents occurred amid an intensifying pattern of settler-related violence affecting Palestinian communities across the West Bank. In Tell village, they followed repeated settler attacks, including an arson attack on 18 July that displaced a Palestinian family.

Following the deadly incident in Tell village, Israeli settlers carried out multiple attacks across Nablus, Qalqiliya, Jenin, Ramallah, Jerusalem, Jericho and Bethlehem governorates. During the reporting period, at least 40 incidents involving Israeli settlers that resulted in Palestinian casualties, property damage or both were documented, about half of which occurred in Ramallah and Nablus governorates. At least 16 Palestinians were injured, including in physical assaults, stabbings, stone-throwing incidents and attacks involving live ammunition. The attacks also resulted in extensive damage to Palestinian property and livelihoods, including the burning or damage of at least 10 homes, more than 20 vehicles, two livelihood caravans, a stone crusher facility, a quarry and associated equipment, guard rooms, offices, agricultural structures and infrastructure. Hundreds of olive trees were bulldozed or otherwise damaged, while Palestinian vehicles travelling between communities were repeatedly attacked, further undermining access to livelihoods and essential services in areas already affected by movement restrictions imposed by Israeli forces.

Since the beginning of 2026, more than 1,380 settler-related incidents have been documented, affecting over 250 Palestinian communities and averaging about 6.6 incidents per day. During the same period, about 900 Palestinians were injured in the context of settler attacks, accounting for more than half of all Palestinian injuries documented across the West Bank, while more than 2,300 Palestinians were displaced due to settler attacks and related access restrictions.

Following the deadly incident in Tell village on 24 July, Israeli forces intensified movement restrictions across Nablus governorate, deploying additional forces, conducting search-and-arrest operations, and carrying out raids in several communities, including Tell village and Nablus city. The main checkpoints surrounding Nablus were closed, multiple road gates were blocked, and additional roadblocks and flying checkpoints were established, severely disrupting access to workplaces, health care, education and other essential services until some restrictions were eased on 26 July.

Attacks on Health Care

Attacks on health care and impediments to medical access continued across the West Bank during the reporting period. While fewer incidents were documented in 2026 than during the same period in 2025, this largely reflects the large-scale operations by Israeli forces launched across the northern West Bank in early 2025, which resulted in a sharp increase in attacks affecting health care. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 53 attacks on health care were documented between January and June 2026, resulting in one fatality and 23 injuries, and affecting four health facilities and 44 ambulances. Under WHO's Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care (SSA), these incidents include obstruction of or interference with the delivery of health services. Most incidents involved obstruction of access (50), the use of force (39), detentions (17) and militarized searches (10). Nearly half of all documented incidents occurred in Nablus governorate (26), followed by Ramallah (9), Hebron (5) and Salfit (4), reflecting the concentration of operations by Israeli forces in the northern West Bank over the first half of 2026.

Developments during the reporting period reflected many of these recurring patterns, particularly in Nablus governorate following the deadly incident in Tell village on 24 July. Following the incident, Israeli forces imposed extensive movement restrictions across Nablus governorate, closing checkpoints, road gates and other access points, while deploying additional forces and conducting search-and-arrest operations. The restrictions significantly impeded access to health care and hampered humanitarian operations. Medical teams reported multiple incidents in which ambulances transporting injured patients were delayed while attempting to reach hospitals. According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, these restrictions also impeded access to emergency obstetric care. Israeli forces raided Nablus Specialized Hospital, where Palestinians injured during the Tell incident were reportedly arrested, disrupting access to care.

Recent developments in Sinjil village further illustrate the humanitarian impact of prolonged movement restrictions on access to emergency health care. Following a two-day search-and-arrest operation by Israeli forces on 15 and 16 July, the village's main northern entrance was closed and the road connecting Sinjil with nearby Jiljilya was blocked with an earth mound. Although residents later partially reopened the latter road, the main entrance remained closed as of the end of the reporting period, forcing residents to rely on lengthy detours or back-to-back ambulance transfers during medical emergencies. On 17 July, a Palestinian woman requiring urgent medical evacuation was delayed at the closed gate despite coordination efforts through the Palestinian District Coordination Office. According to medical sources, she died shortly after arriving at hospital. As of the end of the reporting period, the village's main entrance remained closed, constraining access to emergency health care and other essential services.

Movement restrictions also continued to affect access to specialized health care requiring permits to enter East Jerusalem or Israel. According to WHO, during the first half of 2026, 78 per cent of the 51,444 patient permit applications submitted to Israeli authorities were approved, while more than one fifth were either denied or delayed beyond the scheduled medical appointment. The 2026 approval rate is the highest rate since 2023, when 74 per cent of applications were approved. Adults aged 18 to 60 accounted for 77 per cent of applicants, and Al Makassed Hospital in East Jerusalem received 42 per cent of approved referrals.

Displacement

During the reporting period, Israeli authorities demolished 44 Palestinian-owned structures for lacking Israeli-issued building permits, which are nearly impossible for Palestinians to obtain. The demolished structures included 14 homes, two uninhabited residential structures, 22 WASH and agricultural structures, and six livelihood-related structures. As a result, 16 households comprising 86 people were displaced, including 76 people in Area C and 10 in East Jerusalem.

More than half of those displaced (47 people, including 20 children) occurred on 22 July in Nahhalin (Bethlehem governorate) and on 27 July in the North Beit Hanina Bedouin community (Jerusalem governorate), where the Israeli Civil Administration, accompanied by Israeli forces, demolished seven residential structures and associated livelihood assets. In both incidents, families were unable to remove many of their personal belongings before the demolitions.

Displacement also continued as a result of recurrent settler attacks, intimidation and the expansion of settlement outposts. In Jalud village, south of Nablus governorate, two Palestinian households comprising seven people, including three girls, were displaced after months of escalating settler intimidation, threats and isolation. The displacement followed the establishment of an Israeli settler outpost near their homes in April and the takeover of a nearby Palestinian house by Israeli settlers on 29 June. Since then, the families had faced repeated intimidation, damage to water and electricity infrastructure, and restricted access to the village centre and essential services. On the day of the displacement, settlers reportedly blocked humanitarian attempts to deliver food and medicine to the families, who left behind their homes and most of their household belongings.

Ten Palestinian Bedouin households were displaced on 23 July from Area B of Al Mazra'a ash Sharqiya (Ramallah governorate) for a second time. The families had previously been displaced from the fully depopulated Bedouin communities of Al Mu'arrajat Centre and Ras at Tin due to Israeli settler attacks and related access restrictions. Their latest displacement followed the establishment of a new settler outpost on 22 July, after months of recurrent settler intimidation and threats, including night-time incursions, prompting the families to relocate to other areas in Ramallah and Hebron governorates.

Between 23 and 24 July, at least 10 Palestinian families comprising 49 people were displaced in three settler-related incidents across Nablus governorate. Four families were displaced in Sarra after Israeli settlers set fire to at least six homes, while five additional families in Urif were temporarily displaced after four homes sustained fire damage. A Palestinian family of four was also displaced from the Al Mas'udiya area following years of settler harassment, intimidation, and restrictions on grazing and access to water. Following the violence in Tell village on 24 July, Israeli settlers reportedly established several caravans and began land-levelling works, raising concerns about the establishment of a new settlement outpost and increased pressure on nearby Palestinian communities.

These incidents reflect a broader pattern of recurrent displacement driven by demolitions, settler violence and the expansion of settlement outposts. Since January 2023, more than 6,200 Palestinians, including over 3,000 children, have been displaced, including more than 2,300 people since the beginning of 2026.

For key figures and additional breakdowns of casualties, displacement, and settler violence between January 2005 and June 2026, please refer to the OCHA West Bank June 2026 Snapshot. For key figures on the impact of settler attacks, please refer to the West Bank – The Impact of Settler Attacks, January 2023 – April 2026.

title: LTC Palestine - Gaza Strip Conflict Factsheet: July 2026
content:
Operation overview

Armed conflict between Palestinian militant groups and Israeli military forces began on 07 October 2023. The conflict has resulted in a severe humanitarian crisis and significant disruption to communications networks, impeding humanitarian operations. The WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC Telecoms) was activated on 31 October 2023 to meet the urgent need to support access to reliable shared communications services for humanitarian organizations operating in Gaza.

title: Health Cluster Sudan Bulletin (June 2026)
content:
Key achievements

  • Health Cluster partners continued delivering essential health services across Sudan through supported health facilities, hospitals, and mobile teams. Services included outpatient consultations, maternal and reproductive healthcare, immunization, nutrition support, mental health and psychosocial ser-vices, and referrals.
  • Partners strengthened outbreak preparedness and response efforts through cholera response activities, vaccination campaigns, infection prevention and control training, community awareness initiatives, rapid response team deployments, and enhanced dis-ease surveillance.
  • Access to healthcare services was expanded through support to health facilities, rehabilitation activities, distribution of medical supplies and essential medicines, deployment of mobile clinics, and capacity-building for health workers.
  • Integrated health, nutrition, sexual and reproductive health, and protection services continued to reach vulnerable populations in conflict-affected and dis-placement-affected areas.
  • Coordination mechanisms remained active at national and subnational levels, supporting prepared-ness planning, information management, partner co-ordination, and resource mobilization despite ongoing operational challenges.

title: Palestine - Conflict LTC Situation Report (Telecoms Area) #71 (Reporting Period: July 2026)
content:
The WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) was activated as the Emergency Telecommunications Cluster (ETC) on 31 October 2023 in response to the crisis in Gaza. This Situation Report provides a monthly update on LTC telecoms activities. All references to the LTC in this report relate specifically to the telecommunications area of the cluster1.

Summary Points

• LTC Telecoms continued coordinating with humanitarian, UN, and private-sector partners to address telecommunications equipment access constraints and support critical communications services for humanitarian operations in Gaza.

• The inter-agency Security Communications System (SCS) was further strengthened through progress on the Unified Radio Configuration Project, Very High Frequency (VHF) radio standardization, and security communications training.

• Telecommunications services remained severely constrained by infrastructure damage and restrictions on the entry of ICT equipment, spare parts, and consumables, limiting network expansion and affecting service continuity across Gaza.

title: UNICEF Afghanistan Flash Update #2 (Central, Eastern, and Northern Regions Flash Floods), 29 July 2026
content:
Highlights

  • On 20 July, heavy rainfall triggered flash floods across several provinces in central, northern and eastern Afghanistan.
  • In the eastern region (ER), Parun district, Nuristan Province, was the most impacted. Preliminary reports indicate 23 fatalities (26 per cent women and 74 per cent men) and 125 injuries (7 per cent women and 93 per cent men), with additional individuals still missing. The floods destroyed and damaged 92 houses, affected a health clinic and markets, disrupted livelihoods, and damaged critical infrastructure, including bridges, roads, flood protection walls, agricultural land and water supply networks, disrupting access to safe drinking water.
  • In the central region (CR), flash floods across nine provinces resulted in two deaths and four injuries. A total of 306 houses were affected, impacting 1,917 people (613 girls, 556 boys, 389 women, and 359 men). Approximately 1.6 million square meters of agricultural land were destroyed, around 300 livestock killed, and 11 schools sustained damage.
  • In the northern region (NR), flash floods were reported in Shughnan and Maimai districts of Badakhshan province during the same period. Floods caused damages to schools, 428,000 square meters of cultivated agricultural land, killing livestock, and damaging critical infrastructure, including bridges and water mills.
  • Recent flash floods may have displaced explosive ordnance (EO) or exposed previously

title: UNICEF Niger Humanitarian Situation Report No. 1 (Mid-Year), January–June 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Despite ongoing funding shortfalls, UNICEF reaffirmed its commitment to lead the Nutrition, WASH and Education clusters, and the Child Protection Area of Responsibility, ensuring continued coordination of the humanitarian response.
• As of June 2026, Niger had reported 10,232 measles cases across 47 health districts. ln response, UNICEF procured measles vaccines, enabling emergency vaccination campaigns in nine priority health districts and reaching 140,508 children aged 6 months to 14 years.
• ln the first half of 2026, 194,903 children under five were admitted to nutritional recovery canters for severe acute malnutrition (SAM), marking a 15.25% increase compared to the same period in 2025. Most cases are concentrated in the Maradi and Zinder ragions.
• To reduce learning disruptions, UNICEF reached 14,320 children (over half girls) with remediation activities to prevent school dropouts and supported 4,389 children with distance learning solutions in areas affected by insecurity and displacement.
• UNICEF's appeal for $82.9 million to deliver life-saving assistance faces an 85% funding gap, threatening the continuity of essential interventions. UNICEF continues to provide vital support through strengthened partnerships and coordination with government, UN agencies and NGOs ensuring coordinated delivery across health, nutrition, education, WASH, and child protection sectors.

title: Sri Lanka National Dengue Control Unit: Weekly Dengue Update, Week 30 (20th - 26th July 2026)

The Western Province accounted for 56.5% of total cases, with the Colombo Municipal Council (CMC) contributing 4.1%, the rest of Colombo District 20%, Gampaha District 25%, and Kalutara District 7.3%. title: South Sudan Health Cluster Bulletin, June 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS – MAY 2026

• Cholera remained active but declining: 107,779 cumulative cases and 1,706 deaths (CFR 1.6%) as of 30 June, rising to 108,414 cases and 1,713 deaths by 5 July, across 55 counties in 9 states and 3 administrative areas. An OCV mop-up campaign of 435,477 approved doses is planned for Rubkona, Mayom, and Leer.

• Insecurity increasingly targeted the health response directly: since late May, at least four attacks on health actors killed at least 9 health workers (20 people in total, including a 29 June ambush of a humanitarian convoy in Duk County) and injured 9 more – see the new Security Incidents section below.

• Renewed clashes in Akobo on 5 July drove fresh displacement, with Walgak alone hosting an estimated 30,000 IDPs; MSF’s Akobo Teaching Hospital continued to operate under severe pressure, with bed occupancy above 100% across all wards since reopening on 11 May.

• The EVD/BVD outbreak in the region continued to grow: DRC reported 1,502 confirmed cases and 473 deaths and Uganda 20 confirmed cases and 2 deaths as of 5 July, while South Sudan remained at zero confirmed cases with cumulative Point-of-Entry screening rising from 116,989 travelers (16 June) to 552,071 (9 July).

• A Health Cluster 4W preparedness mapping found that only 9 of the 15 Tier 1 priority counties are reporting EVD/BVD readiness activity, with 6 (Budi, Kapoeta South, Nzara, Tambura, Ibba and Maridi) reporting zero activities, and no partner reporting laboratory/specimen-referral or safe-and-dignified- burial capacity anywhere in the priority set.

• The Health Cluster response remained only 38.3% funded (US$43.7 million of the US$114 million required), a gap of US$69.9 million (61.7%); in June, partners submitted 45 supply requests through the HERMES pipeline from 16 organizations across 34 locations in 22 counties.

• A new cVDPV1 polio case was confirmed in Longochok even as Round 2 SNID campaign coverage reached 92% (809,994 of 877,943 target children), and 7.8 million people (55% of the population analyzed) faced acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3+).

title: WHO Situation Report No. 3: Flash Floods in Afghanistan (August 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

Heavy rainfall and flash floods impacted the eastern, southeastern, and central regions of Afghanistan, causing widespread humanitarian consequences across multiple provinces. The floods affected communities across eastern Afghanistan, including Nuristan, Nangarhar, and Laghman provinces; southeastern Afghanistan, including Paktika, Paktia, Khost, and Ghazni provinces; and the central region, including Kabul, Kapisa, Panjshir, Parwan, Logar, and Maidan Wardak provinces. The disaster resulted in loss of life, injuries, displacement of families, and extensive damage to homes, public facilities, and community infrastructure.

WHO, together with Health Cluster partners, has been closely coordinating with local health authorities to support rapid assessments, deploy emergency health supplies and ensure the continuity of essential health services, including trauma care and treatment for injured and flood-affected populations.

This will be WHO’s final situation report on the recent flash floods.

title: Afghanistan Nutrition Cluster Bulletin, Issue 6, Jan–Jun 2026
content:
Afghanistan Nutrition Cluster Bulletin (Issue 5, Jan–Mar 2026)

In 2026, the Nutrition Cluster prioritized nutrition response to 27 IPC Severity 3 and 4 provinces, covering 342 priority districts. During the first half of the year, partners reached 1,649,973 beneficiaries (29% of the annual target), including 533,434 children under five and 1,156,621 pregnant and breastfeeding women (PBW). Overall, 27% of the annual target in Severity 3 areas and 31% in Severity 4 areas had been achieved by the end of June 2026. Coverage remained well below planned levels due to prolonged therapeutic and supplementary nutrition commodity stock-outs, significant funding shortfalls, and reduced service availability following the closure of nutrition sites and Mobile Health and Nutrition Teams.

  • Outpatient Therapeutic Programme and High Risk MAM was provided through 3,184 (3,034 fixed and 150 Mobile Health Nutrition Teams MHNTs) sites across 309 districts, and 144 Stabilization Centres (SCs) across all 342 nutrition cluster targeted districts.
  • A total of 227,621 children under five with severe acute malnutrition (131,435 girls and 96,186 boys) were admitted to OTP sites, reaching 32% of the annual target. Additionally, 26,216 children under five (13,730 girls and 12,486 boys) with severe acute malnutrition and complications received treatment in Stabilization Centers (SC) reaching 33% of the annual target.
  • A total of 105,096 children with high risk moderate acute malnutrition (HRM) (60,924 girls and 44,172 boys) were treated representing 16% of annual target.
  • A total of 149,177 children under five with early moderate acute malnutrition (83,740 girls and 65,437 boys) were admitted to the TSFP, representing 8% of the annual target. Additionally, 123,464 malnourished PBW were reached through the TSFP, accounting for 16% of the annual target.
  • Meanwhile, 122,853 children under two years of age (62,376 girls and 60,477 boys) and 51,252 pregnant and breastfeeding women were enrolled in the Blanket Supplementary Feeding Program (BSFP), reaching 9% and 7% of their annual targets, respectively.
  • In addition, MIYCN counseling to improve breast feeding and complementary feeding practices for children aged 0-23 months was provided to 1,030,497 pregnant and lactating women and care givers, representing 45% of the annual target.

title: South Sudan Humanitarian Update (as of 31 July 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Joint assessment finds worsening food insecurity in Lafon County, Eastern Equatoria State.
  • An estimated 9,100 people displaced by fighting along the South Sudan–Uganda border in Central Equatoria State; an Ebola screening point disrupted.
  • Two aid workers abducted on the Yei–Kaya Road, highlighting growing risks facing humanitarian personnel.
  • Oral Cholera Vaccination campaign launched in hotspot counties of Unity State.
