title: Sudan WASH Cluster Mid-Year Report 2026 (July 2026)
content:
The Sudan WASH Cluster has published its 2026 Mid-Year Report, highlighting both the achievements and challenges of the humanitarian WASH response during the first half of 2026. Despite ongoing conflict, displacement, disease outbreaks, and access constraints, partners continued to deliver life-saving water, sanitation, and hygiene services to millions of vulnerable people across Sudan.

The report showcases key response achievements, progress in cholera preparedness and response, the operationalization of the Sudan WASH Core Pipeline, and a series of partner case studies demonstrating innovative approaches to improving water supply, water quality, sanitation, and public health outcomes across the country.

At the same time, the report highlights the scale of unmet needs and the urgent need for additional resources. With only US$70 million received against requirements of US$375.9 million, the sector faces a funding gap of more than US$306 million, threatening the continuity of essential WASH services and public health interventions.

title: Situation Report No.8: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), 30 July 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• More than a month after the two earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June 2026, the emergency response remains active while laying the groundwork for early recovery. Priorities now center on sustaining essential health services, strengthening referral pathways, and supporting temporary camps, while preventing public health risks and ensuring the continuous, needs-based supply of medicines and essential equipment.

• Integrated surveillance continues to strengthen early detection and public health risk monitoring across affected areas. Approximately 30,638 vaccine doses have been administered, while laboratory, environmental and event-based surveillance activities continue supporting timely verification and response.

• Transitional camps now shelter 24,477 people across 107 sites at 87% occupancy, with health, WASH, and protection needs extending beyond La Guaira toward Distrito Capital and Miranda as populations move, requiring coordinated action across multiple states.

• PAHO/WHO continued supporting the response with critical medicines and equipment, benefiting 29 actors through its supplies and donations to date, and facilitated logistical support for 11 accepted donor offers. The latest delivery equipped four health facilities in La Guaira—extending primary care to 40,000 people—and delivered WASH items ensuring safe water for 800 families and nearly 110,000 people per month.

• PAHO/WHO continues strengthening the Ministry of Popular Power for Health (MPPS) through its Regional Response Team across emergency coordination, logistics, information management, epidemiology, laboratory, WASH, immunization, risk communication, and EMT coordination, with additional experts arriving for entomology, infection prevention and control. It also supports the virtual CICOM and EMT mobilization, with ten teams now operational across La Guaira, Caracas, Miranda, while the EMT Network reinforces the Ministry's epidemiological surveillance and early detection in affected areas

title: Project 21 - Chad: Sudanese Emergency | Border Monitoring Key trends - July 2026
content: A comparative analysis of border monitoring results between June and July 2026 highlights notable changes in arrival dynamics, displacement profiles, and protection risks. While overall trends confirm the predominance of security-related factors, the data reveal a moderate redistribution of entry points, relative stability in displacement drivers, and a contrasting evolution of reported risks during displacement.

title: PAHO Regional Situation Report No.8: Measles in the Region of the Americas (31 July 2026)
content:
Situation Overview

Between epidemiological week (EW) 1 and EW 29 of 2026 (ending on 25 July 2026), the Region of the Americas reported 47,026 confirmed measles cases from 17 countries and territories, representing approximately a 5-fold increase compared to the same period in 2025. Guatemala (30,040), Mexico (12,233), the United States (2,318) and Canada (1,107) accounted for the majority (97%) of confirmed cases. Additionally, 48 deaths have been reported. The increase in the regional cumulative total compared with Situation Report No.7 is primarily attributable to Guatemala, which remains the major contributor of newly confirmed cases with 1395 added cases, followed by additional cases reported by Mexico with 119 added cases, Peru with 93 added cases, the United States with 77 added cases, Canada with 9 added cases, Bolivia with 3 added cases and Colombia with 1 added case.

During EW 27 and EW 28 of 2026, the Region of the Americas reported 1,697 new confirmed measles cases across seven countries and territories, representing a 6.7% decrease compared with the previous two-week period (EW 25-26; 1,818 new cases)2 (Figure 1). The decrease was driven mainly by fewer cases reported in Guatemala after the retrospective update was incorporated in the previous situation report.

Following the earthquakes, while the risk of measles introduction and spread in Venezuela remains a concern, there have been no confirmed cases reported in the country thus far.

title: Lebanon: Flash Update #47 - Escalation of hostilities in Lebanon (as of 31 July 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • At least 4,333 deaths and 12,236 injuries recorded due to hostilities since 2 March, with 353 fatalities and 235 injuries since the latest ceasefire announcement, according to the Ministry of Public Health.
  • 821,077 people reported returning to their areas of origin, while 360,132 people remain displaced (as of 29 July), including 27,200 Internally Displaced Persons (over 53 per cent women and girls) in 258 collective shelters as of 31 July.
  • On 27 and 28 July, the Humanitarian Coordinator visited conflict-affected villages in Nabatieh Governorate to speak with communities about humanitarian conditions and needs (Chaqra, Baraachit, Ain Ebel, Rmeich and Debel).

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Persistent humanitarian and protection challenges continue to affect communities across Lebanon. As displacement becomes increasingly prolonged and return conditions continue to be uneven, with high levels of destruction and insecurity in some areas, the coping capacities of displaced people, returnees and host communities continue to erode. Protection concerns remain across the country, including ongoing insecurity, inadequate shelter conditions, risks of eviction for displaced households and overstretched basic services. Reports of airstrikes, artillery shelling, demolitions and sonic grenades continued daily across South and Nabatieh governorates, including in Bint Jbeil, Marjayoun and Nabatieh districts in Nabatieh Governorate, and Tyre District in South Governorate. On 26 July, in Markaba, a village in Nabatieh Governorate, the reported destruction of a water pumping station has raised concerns over water security, access to water for surrounding communities, and ongoing targeting of critical civilian infrastructure. Continued hostilities and demolitions impede safe and sustainable returns, heighten risks for civilians and civilian infrastructure, and place additional strain on already limited services in conflict-affected areas of southern Lebanon.

The Ministry of Public Health reported that 4,333 people had been killed (including 392 women and 253 children) and 12,236 injured (including 1,451 women and 1,036 children) as of 30 July. Since the latest ceasefire announcement, 354 people have been killed and 232 injured. Two health-care personnel were injured following the ceasefire announcement. Since 2 March, a total of 135 health-care workers have been killed and 408 injured while on duty.

Despite continued returns, displacement levels remain significant, with 360,132 people remaining displaced across Lebanon as of 29 July, representing a 4 per cent decrease since 22 July. While displacement declined in major hosting districts, including Beirut (Beirut), Chouf and Aley (Mount Lebanon), and Saida (South), increases were recorded in Tyre (South) and in Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil and Marjayoun (Nabatieh) as some households moved closer to their areas of origin. However, insecurity, movement restrictions, limited access to services and livelihoods, and ongoing hostilities in some areas continue to impede safe and sustainable returns and drive humanitarian needs. Collective shelter populations also declined, with approximately 27,200 IDPs residing in 258 shelters, a 9 per cent decrease compared with the previous week. Despite this reduction in displacement levels, humanitarian needs remain considerable, with communities highlighting the need to rehabilitate shelters and address overcrowding, strengthen health and Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) services, and expand cash assistance to help households meet food, shelter, health, and hygiene needs while reducing reliance on debt and negative coping strategies.

Returns remain highly uneven, reflecting significant differences in conditions across areas of return. As of 29 July, 821,077 people had begun returning to their areas of origin. In southern Lebanon, the scale of damage to housing, infrastructure and basic services, combined with ongoing security incidents and movement restrictions, continues to constrain safe and sustainable returns.

Sustained access to essential services, health care, and livelihoods and recovery assistance remain key priorities for communities in conflict-affected areas. In the most heavily conflict-affected areas, priority needs include rehabilitation of water and electricity networks, restoration of health services, cash assistance to meet basic needs, and livelihood support. In areas less affected by destruction and insecurity, communities continue to identify access to health care, including essential medicines, mental health and psychosocial support, and women's health services, as a key concern, as well as support to restore livelihoods and agricultural production, and sustain water, electricity and other basic services essential for recovery.

Protection concerns persist among displaced people, returnees and host communities, with continued concerns related to security incidents, explosive ordnance contamination, inadequate housing, economic hardship, civil documentation issues, and psychosocial distress. Vulnerabilities are being exacerbated by prolonged displacement, rising living costs and limited livelihood opportunities, particularly for women, girls, children, older persons, persons with disabilities and other at-risk households. For those in collective shelters that are being decommissioned, communities report not having clear information about alternative shelter or housing arrangements, heightening the risk of resorting to unsafe accommodation and increasing vulnerability to exploitation, eviction, homelessness and other protection risks.

Financing gaps are straining services to communities. Communities in collective shelters report a reduction in both the scale and frequency of assistance compared with the 2024 response, underscoring the difficulties of maintaining large-scale support amid protracted displacement and growing humanitarian needs. Shortfalls for health sector response may threaten the continuity of services for affected communities, including primary and secondary health care services, essential medicines, ambulance and Emergency Medical Services operations, psychosocial support, physical rehabilitation, and assistive device provision. Continued reliance on reprogrammed resources may also limit partners' ability to sustain both emergency and routine health interventions over time.

On 27 July, United Nations Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator, Imran Riza, accompanied by UNICEF and OCHA representatives, visited the villages of Chaqra and Baraachit in Nabatieh Governorate, two areas in Bint Jbeil District outside the IDF-declared military area that are partially accessible to returning families. On 28 July, Imran Riza, accompanied by OCHA and the President of the Order of Malta, Marwan Sehnaoui, visited the border villages of Ain Ebel, Rmeich and Debel in Nabatieh Governorate to assess humanitarian situation and needs in communities whose residents remained in place throughout the conflict despite prolonged insecurity. During meetings with local authorities, returnees, displaced families, and community representatives, the delegations heard first-hand about the challenges people continue to face, including damaged infrastructure, lack of or limited access to basic services, particularly water, health and education, disrupted livelihoods, and other obstacles to safe return and recovery.

During the visit of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, to Lebanon on 27 July, he met with the Prime Minister, government, internally displaced people, and civil society organizations to discuss the ongoing impacts of the escalation of hostilities and broader human rights situation. In his visit briefing, the High Commissioner noted the ongoing work of an impartial, independent mission to collect evidence on alleged violations of international humanitarian law and highlighted the widespread impact on civilians during the 2026 conflict including attacks on civilians, destruction of civilian infrastructure, and attacks on health care workers.

Funding shortfalls remain a key obstacle to sustained humanitarian response. As of 31 July, the 2026 Lebanon Flash Appeal has received $289.3 million, or 45.2 per cent of the $639.9 million requested.

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #18 (28 to 30 July 2026)
content:
The eighteenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 28 to 30 July 2026.

Highlights

Between 28 and 30 July, IOM continued its multisectoral response in temporary accommodation sites and affected communities through interventions in shelter and camp coordination and management, health, protection, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), and information management.

To date, IOM and Fundación Vivienda Popular have provided 4,627 kitchen sets, 4,232 plastic tarpaulins, 3,148 solar lamps, 2,990 collapsible water containers, 2,345 buckets, 2,210 hygiene kits, 947 mosquito nets and 821 shelter kits to earthquake-affected families.

IOM-supported teams have delivered 7,374 medical consultations to 6,565 earthquake-affected people through health, mental health and psychological support services in temporary accommodation sites and affected communities.

IOM Activities

IOM continued co-managing five temporary accommodation sites in La Guaira: Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo II, José María Vargas Sports Complex, Playa Grande and César Nieves, supporting service delivery, population registration, community information services and operational coordination.

At Campo de Golf, progress continued on the centralized service hub, installation of solar lighting, establishment of a child-friendly space and infrastructure improvements. At Mare Abajo II, service mapping was updated and preparations advanced for coordinated distributions. In César Nieves and Playa Grande, IOM continued supporting service coordination, infrastructure monitoring and population movement follow-up.

During the reporting period, IOM and Fundación Vivienda Popular provided 491 plastic tarpaulins, 491 kitchen sets and 54 buckets to earthquake-affected families.

In WASH, IOM continued expanding access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services through water quality monitoring, drainage improvements, waste management and sanitation infrastructure support. To date, IOM has provided 2,990 collapsible water containers, 284 semi-collapsible 10-liter water containers and 2,210 hygiene kits.

IOM and its implementing partner Ven Da Tu Mano continued delivering health, mental health and psychological support services through mobile teams. During the reporting period, more than 160 health and mental health consultations were provided at José María Vargas Sports Complex.

IOM continued supporting registration and information updates through the unified Information Management System (IMS) across the five temporary accommodation sites and advanced information collection activities in community settlements in Zamora Municipality, Miranda State. Preparations also continued for informal settlement assessments and mobility monitoring through the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM).

In protection, IOM continued providing information services, legal assistance, case management, child protection activities, trafficking in persons prevention and community feedback mechanisms. Activities included strengthening referral pathways, community outreach and awareness activities conducted in connection with World Day Against Trafficking in Persons. To date, 207 individuals have received individualized protection assistance through IOM-supported services.

As co-lead of the Infrastructure and Temporary Accommodation Working Group together with UNHCR, IOM continued supporting operational coordination, service mapping, information management and joint planning across temporary accommodation sites.

IOM Planned Response

IOM will continue strengthening infrastructure, service delivery, WASH interventions, shelter support and camp coordination and management activities in temporary accommodation sites.

IOM will also continue delivering health, mental health, psychological support and protection services while strengthening referral pathways for specialized assistance.

In addition, IOM will maintain mobility monitoring, registration activities, information management, community settlement assessments and coordination with authorities and implementing organizations to support evidence-based response planning.

title: Global Price Watch June 2026 Prices (July 31, 2026)
content:
Key Messages

  • In West Africa, staple food prices showed mixed seasonal trends across the Sahel but broadly remained below last year and the five-year average, except in conflict-affected areas. Prices continued to increase seasonally in Nigeria but remained generally stable in other coastal countries. In southern Cameroon and the CAR, prices were above average due to high transportation costs and insecurity. Prices will likely remain high through the lean season before easing with new harvests around September (Page 3).
  • In East Africa the prices of staple foods remained elevated and uncharacteristically stable across the region despite increased market supply from ongoing long rains harvests, sales of carryover stocks and higher than expected cross-border inflows. Prices increased in Sudan, and localized areas of South Sudan due to lean season demand pressures, high and rising transport costs and market disruptions caused by continuous conflicts and insecurity. Livestock prices stabilized at above-average levels due to good body conditions and productivity, and the seasonally low market supply (Page 5).
  • In Southern Africa, maize and maize product prices were generally stable or declining in June, supported by improved supplies from favorable 2025/26 harvests and a strong regional maize supply balance. Prices remained below the previous year in most countries, although seasonal increases were recorded in Malawi, while conflict and market disruptions continued to drive volatility in parts of the DRC. Elevated transportation costs continued to exert upward pressure on consumer prices across the region (Page 7).
  • In Central America, white maize prices were stable compared to May but remained above average in El Salvador and Honduras. Red and black bean prices were below average in El Salvador and Guatemala and above average in Honduras due to tighter domestic supply and average imports. In Haiti, local food prices were stable or declined due to spring harvest availability. In Venezuela, food prices increased in VED due to currency depreciation. In Colombia, cereal prices remained stable compared to May due to local production and import availability (Page 9).
  • In the Middle East and Europe, staple food price trends remained mixed. In Syria, rice, wheat flour, vegetable oil, and cooking gas prices increased amid higher import costs and exchange-rate depreciation. In Lebanon, staple food prices remained stable, supported by adequate imports, while diesel and cooking gas prices declined. In Gaza, staple food prices eased despite lower food inflows, while prices in the West Bank remained stable despite market access issues. In Ukraine, seasonal supply provided price relief for eggs and vegetables, while conflict-related logistics constraints continued to affect frontline markets (Page 11).
  • Across Asia, staple food prices remained mixed. Staple food prices were generally stable in Sri Lanka and Nepal, supported by domestic harvests, adequate market supplies, and stable macroeconomic conditions. Staple food prices in Burma remained broadly stable nationally, but localized conflict-related supply disruptions and elevated logistics costs continued to exert upward pressure in conflict-affected areas. In Pakistan, wheat flour prices increased despite the ongoing harvest due to higher transport costs, supply constraints, and continued market speculation (Page 13).
  • International markets showed mixed trends in June. Maize prices declined on favorable U.S. crop prospects and Argentina's record harvest. Rice prices rose on tight Thai supplies and El Niño concerns, although global stocks remain ample. Wheat prices decreased from a near-two-year high amid harvest pressure and a stronger USD. Crude oil and fertilizer prices fell sharply after the Strait of Hormuz reopened in mid-June, with Brent at 85 USD/bbl and urea driving an overall fertilizer price decline (Page 2).

Recommended citation: FEWS NET. Global Price Watch July 31, 2026: July 2026 Price Watch, 2026.

title: Earthquakes in Venezuela: Situation Report #31 (31 July 2026, Time: 05:00 pm)
content:
Situation Report No. 31
Earthquakes in Venezuela
31 July 2026
Time: 5:00 pm

Highlights

  • More than 207,700 people affected by the earthquakes have received humanitarian assistance and essential services through a coordinated multi-sector response involving humanitarian organizations, United Nations agencies, communities, and national and local authorities.
  • As of 24 July, authorities reported 5,546 deaths and 16,740 injuries as a result of the earthquakes.
  • The United Nations system and its partner organizations continue scaling up the multisectoral response to the emergency. To address the needs of 1.3 million people affected by the earthquakes over the next six months.

Situation overview

Venezuela is facing a national emergency following two consecutive major earthquakes (magnitude 7.2 and 7.5) that struck the country's north-central region on 24 June (18:00 local time). The first earthquake, measuring 7.2, was centered along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán axis (Yaracuy/Carabobo). According to a recent update from the United States Geological Survey (USGS), the second earthquake, measuring 7.5, had its epicenter 17 kilometers west of Catia La Mar, off the coast of La Guaira State. As of 24 July, authorities reported 1,500 aftershocks.

As of 24 July, authorities reported 5,546 deaths and 16,740 injuries resulting from the earthquakes. They also reported that 17,907 people lost their homes, while 856 buildings were affected, including 190 that collapsed. A preliminary assessment by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) estimates direct damage to housing and infrastructure at approximately US$37 billion, while preliminary estimates from UNDP place direct physical damages at US$6.7 billion, equivalent to 6 per cent of GDP.

The government response continues to focus on assisting affected populations and managing temporary displacement sites. According to authorities, 107 temporary camps remain operational, with a capacity for 28,223 people and a current occupancy of 24,477 people. Of those accommodated, 12,752 people are in La Guaira, 9,092 in the Capital District, 1,958 in Miranda, and 675 in Aragua.

More than one month after the earthquakes, the humanitarian response continues to expand across the affected states. As of 30 July, more than 207,700 people had access to essential services and humanitarian assistance through the joint efforts of communities, humanitarian organizations, United Nations entities, donor partners, and national and local authorities.

Note

The report will be published on a weekly basis. We thank partner organizations, United Nations entities and donors for their valuable contributions, and encourage them to continue reporting their earthquake response activities through the 345W platform. For more information on reporting and the use of the tool, please refer to the presentation: 345W Preparedness and Response

title: Sudan Situation: UNHCR Monthly External Update #120 - June 2026
content:
Highlights

▪ Sudan: The security situation in Sudan was marked by airstrikes, and ground clashes across Kordofan, Darfur, Blue Nile, and White Nile States. Repeated drone attacks in El Obeid damaged civilian areas, fuel infrastructure, health facilities, and transport routes, including locations near schools and displacement sites, while intercommunal violence in South and Central Darfur caused further displacement.

▪ Central African Republic (CAR): In June, the security situation at the border with Sudan deteriorated sharply. A security escalation in Am-Dafock involving attacks by non-state armed groups from Sudan and airstrikes targeting Rapid Support Forces (RSF), positions triggered a new influx of Sudanese refugees into Manou toward the end of the month. While local authorities and NGOs registered 1,958 new arrivals, the total influx is estimated at between 7,000 and 8,000 people, with thousands yet to be registered due to security and access constraints.

▪ Chad: The Government of Chad's border closure, in place since February 2026 in response to security and protection concerns, remains in force, though humanitarian corridors continue to facilitate access to asylum for those fleeing the conflict. Security measures have been reinforced through increased deployment of Defence and Security Forces, tighter border controls, civilian disarmament initiatives, and community awareness campaigns.

▪ Egypt: From 23 to 25 June, the UN High Commissioner for Refugees conducted his first official visit to Egypt, meeting with senior government and religious leadership to reaffirm UNHCR's cooperation on refugee protection, host community support, responsibility-sharing, and the transition toward a nationally-led asylum system. The High Commissioner underscored the need for expanded complementary pathways, stronger development and private sector partnerships, and increased investment in refugee self-reliance in line with UNHCR's goal of reducing long-term displacement by 50 per cent over the next decade.

▪ Ethiopia: On 20 June, the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, together with donors, partners, and African Union officials, visited Ura Refugee Site as part of World Refugee Day commemorations, engaging directly with refugees, host communities and government counterparts. From 23 to 24 June, a joint mission by the Ministry of Labour and Skills and the European Union Delegation reviewed progress under the EU-funded Interregional Innovation Investments (I3) Instrument, covering skills development, employment, livelihoods, and implementation of the Right to Work.

▪ Libya: On 23 June, the Libyan Government issued Prime Minister's Decision No. 113 of 2026 banning the entry of nationals from Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Somalia into Libyan territory through all land, sea, and air border crossings, while exempting accredited diplomatic and consular personnel and certain education and healthcare professionals with the required approvals and valid work contracts. The decision has effectively restricted access through official border crossings for nationals of the affected countries. UNHCR continues to engage with the Libyan authorities and relevant stakeholders to advocate for access to territory, protection safeguards, and the preservation of asylum space for people in need of international protection.

▪ South Sudan: UNHCR handed over health and education facilities, including Nyamlel County Hospital and new classrooms and WASH facilities at Salvation Primary School in Aweil West County. Funded by the African Development Bank Group and the European Union, the investments will benefit refugees, returnees, and host communities, including over 35,000 Sudanese refugees hosted in the area since 2023.

▪ Uganda: Despite Ebola-related movement restrictions, Sudanese asylum-seekers continued to arrive in Uganda as insecurity and humanitarian conditions in Sudan continue to drive people to seek safety and protection outside the country.

title: Ukraine Health Cluster Bulletin #6 (June 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• June 2026 recorded the highest number of civilian casualties in Ukraine since April 2022, surpassing the previous peak set in May 2026. The UN HRMMU verified at least 293 civilians killed and 1,990 injured this month alone. In the first half of 2026, 1,396 were killed and 7,987 injured, a 37 percent increase compared to the same period last year.

• Long-range weapons remained the leading cause of civilian casualties, with large-scale attacks striking densely populated cities. On 2 June, strikes hit Kyiv, Dnipro, and Kharkiv; in Kyiv alone, attacks killed 27 people and injured at least 90. On 15 June, a large-scale attack further killed six people in Kharkiv, five of them rescue workers. Over the first six months of 2026, health partners, in support of national authorities, reached more than 900 people via their post-strike response and prepositioned medicines and consumables to health facilities to cover the treatment of 1,345 people.

• Attacks on civilians near the frontline reached their highest level of the full-scale war in June 2026, according to HRMMU. Short-range drones alone killed 89 people and injured 588, the worst month since February 2022. Amid daily attacks and disrupted access to essential services such as water and gas, evacuations from frontline areas rose significantly. In June, more than 15,000 people were registered at transit centers where health partners operate. In response, partners delivered 3,712 health consultations.

• Humanitarian access has become increasingly constrained for health partners. At least six health partners reported reduced or lost access in Donetska, Dnipropetrovska, Kharkivska,
Sumska, and Zaporizka oblasts owing to deteriorating security conditions, leaving gaps where vulnerable people still require medical services. The Health Cluster is supporting the roll-out of alternative modalities, including temporary relocation and remote service delivery where feasible.

• On 24 June, the Health Cluster convened a workshop on reporting and beneficiary calculation to strengthen partners’ capacity to collect, calculate, and report data in line with HNRP 2026 priorities and Health Cluster reporting standards, promoting coherent and credible reporting while enhancing the coordination and visibility of health interventions in Ukraine.

title: Health Cluster – End of HNRP Addendum 2026 (Floods)
content: Heavy rains beginning in late December 2025 and persisting through January 2026 caused widespread flooding across southern and central Mozambique. By mid‑January, nearly 600,000–700,000 people were affected, with projections rising to 1.1 million as rains persisted and controlled dam releases in South Africa worsened flooding. Health infrastructure was heavily affected: 229 facilities nationwide, including nearly 100 in Gaza. Of these, 20 were completely flooded, 26 temporarily closed, and five medical warehouses submerged, resulting in critical stock and equipment losses. The Health Cluster has responed with life-saving interventions in 18 different districts.To date, more than 150,000 interventions have been done by Health Cluster partners and an estimated 130,000 people have been reached through the health response across the affected areas, of which 105,000 are in Gaza Province.

title: Attacks on Health Care in the occupied Palestinian territory (08 - 21 July 2026)
content:
Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) identified 625 incidents of violence against or obstruction of health care in the occupied Palestinian territory (oPt) in 2025, compared to 1,463 in 2024 and 1,188 in 2023. Despite the two ceasefires, incidents continued in Gaza throughout 2025, often increasing in conjunction with IDF military movements and ground operations. On average, 2.8 attacks were reported each week during the January 2025 ceasefire, and 1.9 attacks per week from the start of the October ceasefire through December 31, 2025. During both ceasefires, four health workers were killed and two others injured, and the IDF shelled a clinic in Jabalia IDP camp, injuring multiple people, including a pregnant woman. The IDF repeatedly fired at and bombed ambulances responding to emergencies.

title: Cameroon: North-West and South-West Situation Report No.86, 1 April to 30 June 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Nearly 4,000 people displaced following armed attacks, intercommunal violence, and confrontations between armed actors between 13 April and 13 May 2026.
  • More than 9,000 children, including 7,564 girls reached with non-formal education services.
  • At least, 537 children identified with severe acute malnutrition received life-saving treatment in partner-supported treatment centres.
  • More than 1,200 protection incidents reported in the North-West and South-West regions.

SITUATION OVERVIEW / HUMANITARIAN ACCESS

Between April and June 2026, the humanitarian situation in the North-West and South-West (NWSW) regions remained dire, marked by attacks from parties to the crisis, kidnapping for ransom, arbitrary arrests, the multiplicity of illegal checkpoints and the demand for illegal payments, roadblocks, and worsening protection concerns. Clashes between state security forces (SSF) and non-state armed groups (NSAGs) persisted across several divisions. The unstable security context continued to erode livelihoods, disrupt access to essential services, and exacerbate humanitarian needs among affected populations.

Population displacement persisted, with new waves of forced displacement recorded in Momo and Mezam divisions in the North-West region and Manyu division in the South-West region. According to the Danish Refugee Council (DRC), nearly 4,000 people (787 households) were forced to leave their places of habitual residence following armed attacks, intercommunal violence, and confrontations between armed actors. Displaced populations sought refuge in neighbouring communities and forested areas, often under precarious conditions. Many faced limited access to adequate shelter, food, non-food items (NFIs), healthcare, and protection services. Ongoing insecurity continued to impede safe and voluntary returns, while repeated displacements further eroded household coping capacities and increased vulnerabilities among affected populations.

Humanitarian needs remained acute across the NWSW. These constraints adversely affected agricultural production, disrupted market functioning, weakened food security and other economic activities. Access to essential services, including education and healthcare, remained limited in several localities due to insecurity and the proximity of armed actors to civilian infrastructure.

Several NSAGs announced a coordinated three-day lockdown from 18 to 20 May with the aim of disrupting the 20 May National Unity Day celebrations. In addition, the weekly Tuesday lockdown in Widikum (Momo division) remained in effect. In April, some NSAGs declared temporary ceasefires during the Pope’s visit to Bamenda in the NW; however, implementation remained weak, with sporadic gunfire reported on 16 April in parts of Bamenda and surrounding areas. Insecurity and the presence of illegal checkpoints continued to limit the ability of humanitarian organizations to safely access some affected communities, especially along the Bamenda-Ndop-Kumbo axis.

The multisector needs assessment (MSNA) in the NWSW commenced in June, during an extended period of the national census. To mitigate the risk of confusion among communities and to clearly differentiate the two activities, humanitarian partners put in place several measures, including enhanced community sensitization and clear messaging about the purpose and scope of the assessment.

Overall, the operational environment in the NWSW remained highly challenging, with access constraints, limited presence of responders in some areas, and persistent funding gaps hindering response efforts. These challenges are expected to further reduce operational capacity and exacerbate humanitarian needs in the coming months.

title: South Sudan: BVD Outbreak Readiness - DREF Operational Update (MDRSS019)
content:
Date when the trigger was met

20-05-2026

What happened, where and when?

Regional Context: The regional outbreak remains primarily centered in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the epidemic has spread across 41 health zones in the provinces of Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Tshopo, and Haut-Uélé, with the latter two representing newly affected provinces with confirmed cases. In Uganda, the final official tally stands at 20 cumulative confirmed cases and 2 confirmed deaths, with 18 recoveries. According to the National Public Health Institute of South Sudan, as of 24 July, confirmed cases in the DRC continue to grow steadily, with confirmed deaths nearly doubling and suspected cases showing significant fluctuations. Given South Sudan’s geographic proximity to the DRC, this epidemiological trend presents a direct threat to national health security. South Sudan remains at high risk of BVD importation, driven by porous borders, active cross-border trade, humanitarian displacement, and major transit corridors along the western and southern border interfaces with both the DRC and Uganda.

To support the regional response across IFRC Secretariat coverage, the Emergency Appeal has mobilized approximately CHF 29.5 million as of 11 July 2026, representing 56.7% in hard pledges (including in-kind contributions) and 43.3% in soft pledges.

Country Context & Situational assessment: On 15 May 2026, the Ministry of Public Health, Hygiene and Social Welfare of the DRC and the Ministry of Health of Uganda formally declared an outbreak of Ebola Disease following the confirmation of Bundibugyo Virus Disease (BVD) in both nations. Consequently, on 16 May 2026, the WHO Director-General declared the outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern under International Health Regulations provisions, convening the first Emergency Committee meeting on 19 May 2026 to issue temporary recommendations to State Parties. As of 21 May, 746 suspected cases and 176 suspected deaths were reported in DRC, alongside 85 total confirmed cases (including two in Uganda) and ten confirmed deaths across both affected countries. On 20 May 2026, the South Sudan Ministry of Health and WHO, through the Health Cluster in which SSRC is a member, designated South Sudan as a high-risk country for BVD importation due to porous borders and intense cross-border population movement with DRC and Uganda. All health partners were called upon to initiate preparedness and readiness activities across core response pillars in priority border locations. This aligns with the IFRC BVD risk categorization, which places South Sudan as a Tier 1 country requiring direct preparedness actions.

Following further temporary recommendations issued by the IHR Emergency Committee on 22 May 2026 for land-bordering states, the Health Cluster continues to emphasize high operational alertness. Although South Sudan has recorded no confirmed cases to date, the risk of importation remains elevated due to porous borders, high population mobility, fragile health infrastructure, limited infection prevention and control capacity, and historical vulnerability to public health emergencies.

title: WFP Cameroon Country Brief, July 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Cameroon is facing a neglected humanitarian crisis marked by overlapping emergencies: armed clashes between non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and state security forces in the Northwest and the Southwest Regions; NSAG insurgency and climate shocks in the Far North Region; and an influx of Central African Republic refugees in the Adamawa, East and North Regions. These emergencies have resulted in over 2.2 million forcibly displaced people, including 412,520 refugees, one million internally displaced people (IDPs) and 790,840 returnees.

• GDP projected growth of 4.4 percent in 2025, but food and nutritional needs remain severe with 2.9 million people projected to face IPC3+ food insecurity between June and August 2026, including 250,000 people in IPC4. Stunting is affecting 29 percent of children under five with rates as high as 40 percent in some areas.
Furthermore, 1.5 million school age children require education support due to conflict.

• WFP delivers lifesaving food and nutrition assistance while strengthening resilience among refugees, IDPs, and host communities across six crisis-affected regions. WFP also supports capacity strengthening of national institutions to identify and address the root causes of food insecurity; and provides logistics and air transport services to humanitarian partners to reinforce national and regional stability.

title: Aid in Danger Bi-Monthly News Brief (08 - 21 July 2026)
content:
In the 26 months since the adoption of UN 2730 resolution, Insecurity Insight recorded 1,281 attacks and acts of violence against aid workers from the UN, humanitarian and civil society, resulting in 771 aid workers killed, 721 injured, 381 kidnapped and 580 arrested. These acts of violence underscore the urgent need for strengthened collective action and the promotion of collaborative security risk mitigation strategies to enhance aid worker safety and security and to provide crisis and post-incident support to affected individuals and their families.

In total, 381 aid workers were kidnapped in 158 incidents across 23 countries: 295 were national aid workers, representing 75% of total kidnappings, while 19 were international aid workers. These figures underscore how aid workers closest to affected communities - often working with the least protection and visibility - bear the greatest risk.

title: TUN: Fire - 07-2026 - Tunisia Wildfires 2026 (2026-07-30)
content:
Description

The wave of fires in the Republic of Tunisia began on 1 June 2026, but reached a sharp peak from 12 July 2026 onward, continuing to the time of writing, coinciding with an exceptional heatwave in which temperatures reached close to 50°C in several governorates — including Kairouan, Jendouba, Gabès, Tozeur and Béja — while temperatures in the south-west reached around 49°C due to the hot, dry "Chehili" desert winds, according to the National Institute of Meteorology. The heatwave has been accompanied by strong winds and severe drought, triggering a wide series of forest and agricultural land fires, particularly in the mountainous and forested areas of the north and north-west of the country.

According to the latest official update, the total forest and agricultural area damaged by fire since the outbreak began has risen to around 12,000 hectares — a marked increase compared to earlier estimates of only 4,400 hectares as of 23 July 2026 (compared to 2,705 hectares over the same period in 2025) — reflecting the continued spread and intensification of the fires alongside the ongoing heatwave. Civil Protection also reported more than 35 forest fires between 1 June and 25 July 2026, while statistics show that forest areas damaged by fire over the past ten years totalled around 70,000 hectares (an annual average of about 7,000 hectares), underscoring the severity of the current season compared to the historical average. The Director General of Forests, Mohamed Naoufel Ben Haha, confirmed that the fires mainly affected cork-oak and Aleppo pine forests of significant social and economic importance to local forest communities, and that the situation in Le Kef governorate still requires continuous field vigilance.

Among the most significant fires recorded, by way of illustration and not an exhaustive list: the Ghar El Melh and Rafraf fire in Bizerte governorate (around 300 hectares); the Cap Negro fire in the Nefza delegation of Béja governorate (around 300 hectares); the Saqiyat Sidi Youssef fire in Le Kef governorate, which burned around 2,000 hectares and whose effects are still being dealt with; a fire in the Zaghouan mountains (Jebel Chahma area) affecting around 1,300 hectares of forest and farmland; along with scattered fires in Jendouba (Ain Draham), Nabeul (Rafraf, Jebel Nadhour), Siliana, Sfax, Gafsa, Kebili, Mahdia, Tozeur, Kasserine, Sidi Bouzid, Manouba and Tunis. Given the continued evolution of the fires and their expanding geographic scope, a detailed, reliable breakdown of the areas damaged by governorate is no longer available at this stage; the adopted cumulative figure remains 12,000 hectares to date, and the detailed regional breakdown will be updated later in coordination with the Directorate General of Forests.

The fires have also destroyed large numbers of fruit trees and hundreds of species of medicinal, cosmetic and aromatic herbs that thousands of residents in and around forested areas rely on gathering and selling as a primary or supplementary source of income, directly harming the livelihoods of these groups and deepening their economic vulnerability.

Firefighting operations have also become more difficult due to the rugged, mountainous terrain in many of the affected areas, the highly flammable nature of certain tree species such as Aleppo pine, and the continuing drought combined with the hot, dry "Chehili" winds — factors that together complicate the work of firefighting teams and increase the risk of fires reigniting and spreading further.

In terms of intervention frequency, Civil Protection units recorded hundreds of interventions per day in recent days; within just 48 hours, close to 2,800 interventions were logged, covering around 600 fires (roughly one fire every 5 minutes), while 900 fires were recorded over 72 hours between 20 and 22 July, and 296 fires were recorded among 939 interventions within a single 24-hour period. The Directorate General of Forests, for its part, took part in 917 firefighting operations since the start of the season, compared to only 620 operations over the same period in 2025.

The fires led to emergency evacuations of the population in several threatened areas (particularly in Bizerte and Jendouba), precautionary evacuation of sheep and livestock in the Siliana and Ain Draham areas, and material damage affecting a number of homes, wooden cabins, restaurants and beachfront tourist facilities in Bizerte (specifically Ghar El Melh and Rafraf), with no human casualties reported in official data as of the preparation of this document,except cases of smoke inhalation or limited skin burning .Based on the field assessment carried out by the Tunisian Red Crescent, the number of families affected by the electricity and water cuts accompanying the heatwave is 1,183.

• Activation of the emergency watch and response cell at central level and in the affected regional branches (Bizerte, Jendouba, Le Kef, Siliana, Béja). • Deployment of field volunteers to participate in fire extinction and to support precautionary evacuation of the population and transport of vulnerable cases. • Distribution of initial relief assistance (drinking water, food items, first-aid supplies and hygiene items ,baby diapers ,and sanitary pads ,cleaning items) to temporarily displaced households. • Field coordination with Civil Protection, the Directorate General of Forests and regional authorities to direct assistance. Additional accompanying response for the heatwave and electricity/water cuts include: • Placing the Tunisian Red Crescent's ambulance and citizen-transport vehicle fleet at the disposal of emergency medicine, rescue and Civil Protection departments to strengthen national rescue capacity. • Transporting people suffering from heatstroke or respiratory distress to hospitals, or to temporary shelter centres equipped with electricity, to avoid the effects of power cuts in their homes. • Distributing electricity generators to some patients in their homes, particularly critical cases dependent on medical devices requiring a continuous power supply. • Distributing drinking water to hospitals and dialysis centres to ensure the continuity of life-sustaining treatments. • Distributing water to elderly-care homes, childcare centres, and animal-welfare associations, to mitigate the impact of water-supply disruptions. • Organising several awareness campaigns on the risks of the heatwave and ways to prevent heatstroke and dehydration, targeting the general public and vulnerable groups in particular. • Providing initial psychosocial support (PSS) to affected people and to volunteers working in the field. • Launching a Rapid Needs Assessment in the areas affected by the fires and in the areas most affected by the nationwide electricity and water cuts. • A team from Tunisian Red Crescent headquarters, in coordination with the local Red Crescent committee in Nebeur delegation, conducted a field visit to the Nebeur and Touiref and to sakiet delegations in Le Kef governorate , and to ain Drham and jaouydya in Jandouba governorate, and to kap nigrou , chitana , Doga in Beja governorate , and to Ghar el Mileh , rarfraf ,Menzel Bourguiba in Bizerte governorate,assess the scale of losses and the humanitarian situation of families affected by the forest fires.

content:

KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • WFP sustained essential food and nutrition assistance for 106,426 refugees in Nyarugusu Camp at 50 percent ration while maintaining full planned nutrition support for children under five and pregnant and breastfeeding women and girls.
  • WFP strengthened national preparedness and anticipatory action through emergency simulation exercises, climate information exchange and supply chain support to improve response readiness with the Prime Minister’s Office Disaster Management Department (PMO-DMD)
  • WFP advanced resilience and systems-strengthening work with government and partners, including clean cooking, financial education for young agripreneurs, climate-smart public works and school feeding learning exchanges.

title: UNHCR-IOM Pakistan Flash Update #104 on Arrest and Detention/Flow Monitoring, 15 Sep 2023 to 25 Jul 2026
content:
INTRODUCTION

In response to the Ministry of Interior's (MoI) decision of 26 September 2023 to enact an “Illegal Foreigners' Repatriation Plan”, UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency and IOM, the UN Migration Agency, have collated their data on the arrest, detention, and deportation of Proof of Registration (PoR) holders, Afghan Citizen Card (ACC) holders, and undocumented Afghan nationals as well as on the outflows of Afghan nationals at the Torkham, Ghulam Khan, Chaman, Badini and Bahramcha border crossing points, to better understand the protection environment and movements of Afghan nationals returning to Afghanistan from Pakistan. In 2025, the Government of Pakistan (GoP) issued several directives impacting Afghan nationals. In January, the GoP announced that Afghan nationals should relocate from Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) and Rawalpindi, or else face deportation. In April, further announcements indicated the implementation of the second phase of the “IFRP”, targeting ACC holders, in addition to undocumented Afghans. In July, the GoP issued a Statutory Regulation Order (SRO) directing the repatriation/deportation of PoR card holders following the expiry of PoR card validity on 30 June. The GoP later indicated a deadline of 1 September for PoR holders to leave Pakistan, before the start of the repatriation/deportation process. UNHCR issued a press briefing expressing concern regarding the decision and urging the GoP to exempt Afghans with international protection needs, as well as those with particular circumstances or vulnerabilities, from involuntary return.

title: Myanmar Health Cluster Bulletin July 2026
content:
Highlights

- Preliminary data collected from 34 health partners delivering life-saving health services in 227 townships in Myanmar, shows 740,968 people have been reached during the first 6 months of 2026. This excludes data submitted by partners using the new online ActivityInfo system before the extended deadline of 4 August 2026. In addition, the Health Cluster received reports from health partners operating in all 330 townships reaching 824,312 people in need of humanitarian health services.

- Between 1 January and 31 July 2026, 99 attacks on health care were reported by Insecurity Insight, as compared to 45 verified incidents by WHO’s Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care (SSA).

- Floods affecting over 100,000 people in Rakhine, and 20,000 in Hpakant, Kachin. In Rakhine severe shortages of medical supplies are reported. - Conflict displacing over 200,000 people in Magway. Thanks to prepositioning by UNICEF, lifesaving medical supplies were distributed to health partners delivering mobile health services to displaced population. WHO provided 100 First Aid Kits.

- Increase in requests for malaria and dengue supplies shows a surge in vector-borne diseases from various parts of the country, combined with a chronic shortage of malaria supplies, in particular Long-lasting Insecticide Treated Nets (LLIN), but also diagnostic tools and treatment. - Noncommunicable Diseases (NCDs) in Emergencies workshops conducted throughout Myanmar for almost 100 participants shows urgent need for further integration of NCDs in health services delivered to conflict-affected populations.

title: WFP Pakistan- Weekly Market Report (23 July 2026)
content:
• For the week ending on 23 July the national average prices of staple foods (wheat flour and edible oils) remained 9 percent higher compared to their prices on 26 February**,** pre-Middle East crisis.
  • Compared to the week ended on 16 July, wheat flour prices increased marginally, likely due to higher transport costs associated with increased fuel prices.
  • The cost of the basic food basket stands at PKR 16,513 per month (USD 59), equivalent to PKR 4,128 per week (USD 15) nationwide, excluding lower cost items such as vegetables or spices.
  • Fuel prices increased during the reporting period, with petrol increased slightly by 5 percent while HSD increased significantly by 16 percent. Fuel prices remain significantly higher compared to their pre-crisis levels with petrol 27 percent higher and HSD 36 percent higher.

title: Dengue Epidemiological Situation in the Region of the Americas - Epidemiological Week 26, 2026
content:
In the epidemiological week (EW) 26 of 2026, a total of 1,373,756 suspected cases of dengue were reported, resulting in a cumulative incidence of 133 cases por 100,000 population. This represents a decrease of 61% compared to the same period in 2025 and 67% compared to the average of the last 5 years. Figure 1 shows the trend of suspected dengue cases as of EW 26.

Out of the 1,373,756 reported dengue cases in the Region, 396,500 cases (28%) were laboratory-confirmed, and 2,578 (0.2%) were classified as severe dengue. A total of 388 deaths have been recorded, resulting in a case fatality rate (CFR) of 0.028%. 16 countries and territories within the region reported dengue cases in epidemiological week (EW) 26, accounting for 28,925 new suspected cases. Of these, 64 were classified as severe dengue (0.2%), and 15 deaths reported, yielding a case fatality rate of 0.052%. The distribution of cases by country is detailed in Table 1.

title: Escalation in the Middle East and Beyond — Mobility Report (14 July - 27 July)
content:
On 17 June 2026, the United States of America and the Islamic Republic of Iran reached an agreement on a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) concerning the cessation of hostilities. The escalation in the Middle East and beyond had triggered a humanitarian crisis affecting multiple regions in an already fragile context. A resurgence of hostilities in recent weeks are placing pressure on humanitarian access and threatens civilian and essential services. Mobility dynamics across the region and beyond due to renewed escalation remains uncertain. The situation continues to be highly fragile, requiring sustained monitoring and operational preparedness.

In the Islamic Republic of Iran, population movements remain localised, temporary, and economically driven, with no signs of mass displacement.

In Lebanon, displacement nationwide remains significant despite continuing returns. As of 22 July 2026, 375, 090 people remain internally displaced across 729 cadasters, a 9 per cent decrease compared to the previous reporting period (as of 15 July 2026). Of the total IDPs in Lebanon, 30,007 individuals remained displaced in 273 collective shelters. Returns have increased, with 753,024 returned IDPs reported as of 22 July 2026, marking a 2 per cent increase from the previous round (as of 15 July 2026). Meanwhile, cross-border flows into the Syrian Arab Republic are continuing, with a total of 603,615 movements recorded as of 27 July 2026.

IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) is on the ground, actively tracking displacement and cross border mobility while scaling operations in coordination with local authorities and partners to better understand how the crisis is impacting human mobility in the region.

title: UNICEF Europe and Central Asia Region Humanitarian Situation Report No.1 (Mid-Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Between January and June 2026, approximately 40,688 refugees and migrants1 arrived along the Mediterranean and Balkan routes. Countries displayed mixed trends: arrivals declined significantly compared to the same period in 2025 in Serbia (-46 per cent), Italy (-50 per cent), and Greece (-32 per cent), while Bosnia and Herzegovina recorded an increase (+59.5 per cent) and Bulgaria remained below the peak levels observed in 2023–2024.
  • Armenia's refugee response is shifting from emergency assistance toward addressing persistent needs within national systems, with more than 115,000 ethnic Armenian refugees, including 36,000 children residing in the country, joining 26,700 people displaced since the 2020 conflict.
  • Central Asia faced recurrent climate shocks: Tajikistan recorded 741 hazardous natural events, and Kyrgyzstan logged more than 240 mudflows. Kazakhstan is seeing early signs of a new measles outbreak with 3,012 cases in the first six weeks of 2026.
  • UNICEF strengthened child-centred emergency preparedness in partnership with national, regional and sub-regional governments, systems and communities, while scaling up responses to sudden- and slow-onset emergencies through direct service delivery and systems strengthening across health, nutrition, child protection, education, WASH and social protection.
  • As of June 2026, UNICEF had received US$5.9M million against its US$21.4 million funding requirement. This, in addition to US$6.6 million carry-over funds from 2025, resulted in an overall funding gap of 42 per cent. UNICEF is grateful to all donors for their continued, generous, and important contributions.

title: UNICEF Afghanistan Humanitarian Situation Report No. 6 (Mid-Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • More than 18.9 million people accessed essential health services through UNICEF-supported health facilities across all 34 provinces.
  • UNICEF screened 6.8 million children for wasting and provided treatment to 363,810 children with severe wasting and high-risk moderate wasting.
  • UNICEF supported 55,937 vulnerable children through community-based education and temporary learning spaces, including returnee and out-of-school children, 67 per cent of whom were girls.
  • UNICEF's Mother and Child Cash Transfer programme reached 65,162 households, benefiting 576,279 people, with evidence showing improvements in food security and maternal and child health outcomes.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 305: Week 4 - July 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Market Overview

Heavy rainfall, flash floods and landslides affected several provinces during the week, with Parun district of Nuristan among the hardest hit. Flooding damaged homes, shops and sections of the local market, temporarily disrupting economic activity. However, the rapid response of WFP and other humanitarian partners helped stabilize local markets and demand, preventing localized disruptions from translating into broader price increases. At the national level, market conditions remained generally stable despite continued pressure from elevated transportation costs. Fuel prices remained high, driven by constrained regional supplies, particularly from Russia and reduced imports from Central Asia and Iran. While high fuel prices kept supply chain and delivery costs elevated, their passthrough to retail food prices remained moderate during the reporting week.

Food Items:

• National average food prices showed a modest easing during the fourth week of July, with several staple commodities recording slight week-on-week declines. However, prices remained elevated compared to historical levels, suggesting that markets continue to be adequately supplied, albeit at higher transportation costs.

• Wheat and Wheat Flour: Wheat grain and wheat flour prices remained largely unchanged week-on-week but stayed significantly higher year-on-year, reflecting elevated production and transportation costs.

• Rice: Rice prices declined slightly during the week, reversing the slight increase observed during the previous week. Nevertheless, prices remained significantly above both last year and the three-year average levels.

• Other Staples: Prices of cooking oil, pulses, sugar, and salt remained broadly stable throughout the week. However, compared to last year, cooking oil, sugar, and salt prices continued to remain elevated, while pulse prices showed a decline, reflecting adequate market availability and domestic production.

• Vegetables: Seasonal supplies continued to improve vegetable markets. Tomato prices recorded the largest weekly decline (-14.4%), while onion and potato prices remained stable overall. Compared to last year, tomato and potato prices showed a significant increase, whereas onion prices showed a decline.

Non-Food Items:

• Exchange Rate: The Afghani exchange rate remained broadly stable at AFN 66.0/USD. Although the currency remained broadly unchanged from last week, it continued to outperform both last year (4% stronger) and the three-year average (12% stronger), helping to partially offset imported inflationary pressures.

• Fuel: Diesel prices eased slightly during the fourth week of July following the sharp increases observed earlier in the month. Diesel prices remained 18% above last year, 20% above the three-year average, reflecting continued regional supply constraints and elevated international fuel prices.

• Fertilizers: Fertilizer prices declined during the week, with DAP falling by 1.6% and Urea by 3.4%. However, prices remained substantially above last year's levels, with DAP 17% and Urea 45% higher.

• Livestock: The price of a 1-year-old live female sheep remained stable with moderate week-on-week fluctuations. However, it stood 6% below last year and 3% below three-year average, reflecting weak pastoralists' terms of trade.

• Labour Market: Labour market conditions remained subdued, with labour availability averaging 2.0 days per week. Availability remained 14% below both last year and the three-year average, while the daily wage for unskilled labour remained unchanged.

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Crisis in Yemen, April - June 2026
content:
Yemen continues to face one of the world's largest and most severe humanitarian crises. More than 22 million people – nearly half of the population – are in need of humanitarian assistance and protection services. Women and girls are disproportionately affected, with 10.95 million across the country requiring urgent support.

Recent military escalations and political tensions in the country and across the region risk undermining Yemen’s fragile stability. These developments exacerbate an already dire humanitarian situation, marked by acute food insecurity, cuts to humanitarian funding, and collapsing health and protection services.

Since January 2026, UNFPA has provided life-saving reproductive health, protection services, information and emergency relief to nearly 400,000 people. This has been achieved through support to 26 health facilities, 15 safe spaces, three shelters, seven youth spaces and six specialized mental health centres.

In 2026, UNFPA is appealing for US $71.9 million to maintain its critical support for women and girls, in alignment with the Yemen Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan. To date, only US $12.8 million has been received, leaving a funding gap of US $59.1 million (82 per cent).

title: WFP Nigeria Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• About 36.3 million people across the country are acutely food insecure at crisis or worse levels. The key driver of food security in Nigeria is insecurity compounded by economic challenges and extreme climate events.

• The Nigeria Hydrological Service Agency (NIHSA) projects medium flood risk for 13 states in Nigeria including Borno and Adamawa.

• In June, WFP provided nutrition and resilience integrated food assistance to 847,346 beneficiaries in Borno, Adamawa, Yobe and Katsina states.

• Monitoring reports show improved food security outcomes for beneficiaries and participants of WFP’s programme activities. About half of the households surveyed reported acceptable food consumption levels.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Food insecurity remains a major challenge in Nigeria. As the lean season period enters its peak, more households are experiencing severe food consumption gaps.

• The situation is particularly dire for internally displaced people and other vulnerable households living in conflict-affected areas with 12.8 million people, (i.e. 31 percent of the population) across Borno, Adamawa, Yobe, Katsina, Sokoto and Zamfara facing acute hunger.

• WFP is supporting the Government of Nigeria since 2016 to provide emergency food and nutrition assistance in Northern Nigeria. Currently, WFP is implementing a five-year Country Strategic Plan (2023-2027) that aims to deliver emergency food assistance and support recovery and resilience-strengthening efforts for vulnerable people and communities. WFP’s strategy for lasting solutions is aligned with national priorities while enhancing the domestic capacity for Government-led solutions.

• WFP Nigeria also manages critical humanitarian enabling services that support the broader response architecture, including the United Nations Humanitarian Air Service (UNHAS), Emergency Telecommunications Sector (ETS), and the Logistics Sector. • WFP urgently requires USD 99.4 million to sustain food assistance over the next six months (August 2026 – January 2027.

title: Update on cash-based interventions
content:
Cash-Based Interventions for Burundian Returnees January - June 2026

As part of the implementation of the Tripartite Agreement between the Governments of Burundi and the United Republic of Tanzania and UNHCR, efforts to promote the voluntary return and sustainable reintegration of Burundian refugees continued throughout the first half of 2026. To support this process, UNHCR strengthened the use of Cash-Based Interventions (CBIs) as a key assistance modality to help returnees meet their immediate needs and facilitate their reintegration into their communities of return. This document provides an overview of cash assistance returnees between January and June 2026, highlighting key achievements, protection outcomes, and remaining challenges. It also underscores the importance of sustained reintegration support to promote self-reliance and ensure durable solutions for returning populations.

title: WFP Syria Monthly Market Price Bulletin, June 2026 - Issue 138
content:
• The cost of living in June 2026, as measured by the Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB), remained stable at New SYP 26,551 compared to the previous month. However, it was 33 percent higher than in June 2025 (year-on-year).
  • The Syrian pound (SYP) depreciated in the official market, with the exchange rate increasing from New SYP 113.00 per USD to New SYP 122.00 per USD in June 2026.also in the parallel market depreciated to New SYP 140.76 from 136.21 New SYP per USD.
  • The Syrian Grain Corporation announced that it had procured 1.1 million metric tons of wheat from farmers as of 27 June, covering approximately 44 percent of Syria's annual wheat requirement. Wheat procurement is expected to reach 2.5 million metric tons by the end of July, which would strengthen domestic wheat availability, support farmers' incomes, and reduce reliance on imports.
