The measure aims to protect local producers and encourage investment in the poultry sector. Its impact on poultry meat and egg prices will depend on the domestic sector's ability to meet market demand.

title: Flash Update #54 New Sudanese Refugee Influx into Chad
content:
UPDATE ON SITUATION IN SUDAN

Context

The security situation in Eastern Chad remains generally stable but fragile. Following clashes in the Kulbus region of Sudan, new arrivals were reported in Koulbous and Birak (Chad), where an assessment mission identified approximately 3,000 people in need of assistance. To respond to the situation, UNHCR and its partners plan to launch an asylumseeker pre-registration operation from 27 July 2026 to strengthen identification, facilitate relocation to Marasabré, and improve humanitarian assistance planning. Despite challenges related to the rainy season, logistical and operational preparations are underway for the start of the exercise. In refugee-hosting areas, several security incidents were also reported this week, including assaults against refugee women near the Metché site, an armed robbery in the same area, and a road accident involving a humanitarian partner in Aboutengué. These incidents highlight the continued need for protection and security efforts in operational areas.

title: Flash Update #55 New Sudanese Refugee Influx into Chad
content:
Context

The security situation in Chad remains generally stable but continues to be marked by persistent risks along the Sudanese border, particularly in Wadi Fira Province. On 21 July 2026, drone-related incidents were reported near the border town of Tiné, Chad. In Indour, approximately 22 km from the border, a water point was hit, resulting in unconfirmed casualties and significant livestock losses. Later the same day, another incident was reported in Bamina, located 35 km from Tiné, where an administrative vehicle was damaged. These events occurred amid intensified fighting in Darfur near the Chadian border, heightening concerns over possible spillover effects of the conflict. However, no impact on humanitarian personnel or operations was reported.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 78, as of 28 July, 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Suspension of movements along road corridors around Kabo
  • Markounda: The host community receives one month of food assistance

GENERAL CONTEXT

Vakaga Prefecture – North-East

  • On 22 July, a team from an NGO was robbed by armed men approximately 35 km from Birao, along the road to Tiringoulou. After departing Birao in the morning, the team was intercepted, taken into the bush and subjected to physical violence. The vehicle was subsequently searched and personal belongings were stolen. The assailants left the area before the team was able to resume its journey to the village of Delembé, located about 50 km from Birao. The NGO implements a food security program in the area aimed at strengthening community resilience. Birao remains the second most affected location by incidents impacting humanitarian actors, after Zemio.

Ouham-Fafa Prefecture – Center

  • Local authorities have suspended, until further notice, movements along the main road corridors around Kabo, including for humanitarian actors, to mitigate risks to civilians during ongoing security operations. On 27 July, reports of a possible attack on Kabo, as well as the alleged presence of armed elements in surrounding localities, triggered precautionary population movements, including arrivals from neighbouring villages. In response, the Central African Armed Forces (FACA) conducted security operations and increased patrols in and around Kabo. Movement restrictions are limiting humanitarian access to communities outside Kabo, preventing or delaying field missions, assessments, the delivery of humanitarian assistance and the provision of essential services until road access is restored.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Multi-sector

Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

  • A humanitarian coordination mission was conducted from 20 to 23 July in the localities of Dembia and Rafaï. Discussions with affected communities indicated that approximately 450 displaced households from Guinikoumba (located about 15 km from Dembia, across the Ouara River in Haut-Mbomou Prefecture) intend to remain in Dembia, while continuing to monitor the security situation in their areas of origin for a possible return. Humanitarian needs remain significant across multiple sectors, including emergency shelter, essential household items, food assistance, health services, and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH). ACTED conducted a follow-up multisectoral assessment on 21 July to assess potential assistance. On 22 July, World Vision started collecting supplementary household data to facilitate the provision of essential household items and shelter assistance. In addition, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) plans to provide shelter assistance to address any remaining unmet needs.

Nutrition

Ouham Prefecture – North-West

  • On 24 July, the WFP distributed 1.164 tons of ready-to-use supplementary food to eight health facilities in Bossangoa. This assistance will support the nutritional treatment of more than 1,600 children aged 6 to 59 months suffering from moderate acute malnutrition (MAM). The intervention aims to improve the nutritional status of affected children, reduce the risk of malnutrition-related complications, and strengthen access to nutrition services in supported health facilities.

title: Syrian Arab Republic - Emergency Mobility Tracking and Cross Border Monitoring Situation Update - Round 18 (27 July 2026)
content:
Following the ceasefire in Lebanon announced on 17 April 2026, cross-border movements from Lebanon into the Syrian Arab Republic (hereafter referred to as Syria) have declined, reflecting a sustained reduction in displacement across the border. Since arrivals peaked on 27 April 2026 (153,087 individuals), DTM estimates that approximately 30,050 Syrian and Lebanese nationals have subsequently returned to Lebanon. This trend suggests that large-scale emergency movements have largely subsided, with cross-border mobility increasingly characterised by more gradual and stabilised patterns. In response to these developments, DTM transitioned its Emergency Mobility Tracking data collection from a weekly to a bi-weekly (every two weeks) cycle as of Round 17. The revised frequency better reflects the evolving operational context while allowing for more in-depth analysis of population movements.

Between 2 March and 27 July, DTM identified 123,037 arrivals across 1,163 locations covering all 14 governorates of Syria. Syrian nationals represented the vast majority of recorded arrivals, while Lebanese nationals accounted for fewer than 1 per cent.

Flow monitoring conducted at four assessed Syrian-Lebanese border crossings recorded a cumulative 603,615 movements into Syria between 2 March and 27 July. Of these, approximately 98 per cent involved Syrian nationals and the remaining 2 per cent involved Lebanese nationals. During the same period, DTM also recorded 3,184 Lebanese nationals transiting through Syria towards Jordan, highlighting the continued use of Syria as a transit route for onward regional movement.

The situation remains fluid, and DTM continues to monitor developments.

title: Bosnia & Herzegovina - Migrant Mobility Situation Report (June 2026)
content: This report provides insights into the profiles, experiences, needs, routes travelled and intentions of migrants transiting through Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH).1 Data were collected from 1 to 30 June 2026. IOM carried out a route observation exercise in the Republika Srpska, Sarajevo Canton, Posavina Canton, Tuzla Canton, Bosnian-Podrinje Canton and Una Sana Canton to monitor trends in entries and exits as well as transit modalities within BiH. IOM also surveyed 83 migrants in active transit locations such as bus stops or at key entry and exit locations throughout the country as well as 351 migrants in two transit reception centres (TRCs) in BiH (Blažuj, and Lipa).

title: WHO Weekly Situation Update on Ongoing Health Emergency Events in South Sudan - Week #30, Date: 20–26 Jul 2026
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

South Sudan remains in EVD/BVD preparedness and readiness mode with no confirmed cases; national-level readiness is 65% (subnational readiness remains much lower and needs support), while DR Congo has now reported 3,200 cases and 1,405 deaths (CFR 43.9%, 47 health zones) and Uganda declared the end of its 2026 Ebola outbreak on 28 July leaving DRC as the only country with active regional transmission. Cholera rose sharply to 210 new cases, with zero deaths (▲1.5% w/w), while OCV mop-up continues in Mayom, Leer & Rubkona. Polio detected two new isolates (a cVDPV1 in Nasir and a cVDPV2 in Tonj South), measles stayed localized (4 new cases), and malaria fell to 57,303 cases, 32.3% below 2025. The Jonglei & Akobo situation remains critical, GAM at 22.3%, IPC Phase 5 in several counties, and a fresh clash in Uror on 26 July.

? PRIORITY ACTIONS

▸ Sustain the ongoing OCV mop-up in Mayom, Leer & Rubkona with a multi-sectoral WASH/case-management response, and strengthen RDT testing in Rubkona (highest caseload, lowest testing).

▸ Restore routine immunization in Akobo (0%), Nyirol (25%) & Uror (55%), support solar-powered vaccine refrigerators and catch-up campaigns to avert a measles outbreak.

▸ Investigate the new polio isolates (Nasir cVDPV1, Tonj South cVDPV2) and advance IPV intensification and SNID preparations (25–28 August).

▸ Drive EVD/BVD readiness below the national level; the 65% score is national, while state, county and PoE readiness lags well behind; operationalize capacities beyond Juba.

▸ Conduct the planned IRNA assessments in Walgak & Waat (first week of August) and scale up the Jonglei nutrition response (GAM 22.3%, IPC Phase 5).

title: UNICEF Syrian Arab Republic Humanitarian Situation Report No. 2 (Mid -Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Since November 2024, approximately 3.7 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) and Syrian refugees have returned to their areas of origin or other locations in the Syrian Arab Republic, half of whom are children.
  • Returns are taking place amid significant humanitarian needs, limited access to basic services, economic hardship, and ongoing protection risks.
  • Localized conflict and population movements, including the arrival of more than 336,000 people from Lebanon since 2 March 2026, are placing additional pressure on services.
  • Children continue to bear the brunt of the threat posed by explosive ordnance (EO), which has reportedly killed 219 children and injured 601 since December 2024.
  • During the reporting period, UNICEF reached 3.1 million people, including 1.9 million children (1 million girls), with life-saving and life-sustaining interventions.
  • UNICEF's 2026 HAC appeal is only 27 per cent funded, constraining the scale and continuity of essential services.

title: South Sudan Nutrition Cluster - Quarterly Bulletin | Q3 2026
content:
NUTRITION RESPONSE SUMMARY

January–June 2026 (Q2 2026) Update

The second quarter of 2026 was characterised by a significant deterioration in both the operational landscape and the funding environment, posing considerable challenges to the nutrition response. Nevertheless, Nutrition Cluster partners continued to provide essential life-saving services across the country. By the end of June 2026, a total of 758,784 beneficiaries were admitted into Community-based Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) programmes during the reporting period. These admissions comprised 195,476 children with Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) enrolled in Outpatient Therapeutic Programmes (OTP), 341,047 children with Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM) treated through Supplementary Feeding Programmes (SFP), 7,123 admissions to Stabilisation Centres (SCs), and 222,261 Pregnant and Breastfeeding Women (PBW) receiving nutritional support. In the Blanket Supplementary Feeding Program (BSFP), 180,371 children 6 - 23 months and 135,546 PBW have been supported.

Despite increasing humanitarian needs and operational constraints, the response has demonstrated notable progress toward achieving the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP) targets. By the end of June 2026, partners had reached 36% of the annual SAM target, 51% of the MAM target, and 41% of the target for Pregnant and Breastfeeding Women. These achievements represent an improvement compared with the same reporting period in 2025, when coverage stood at 27% for SAM, 42% for MAM, and 35% for PBW. 39% of children 6 - 23 months and 23% of PBW have been reached by Blanket Supplementary Feeding Programmes (BSFPs). The improved performance reflects the sustained commitment of implementing partners to maintain service delivery despite severe funding shortages, worsening insecurity, and persistent supply chain disruptions affecting many hard-to-reach locations. However, unless additional financial resources are mobilised urgently, there is a high likelihood that programme coverage will decline during the third and fourth quarters of 2026, when the seasonal burden of acute malnutrition is expected to peak.

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Chad Humanitarian Response (1 - 30 June 2026)
content:
In June 2026, the humanitarian crisis in Chad worsened as the country hosted 2.26 million forcibly displaced people, including over 934,000 Sudanese refugees, while food insecurity during the lean season threatened 3 million individuals, exacerbating protection risks like gender-based violence (GBV) and child marriage. Military activity in Lac Province caused the fresh displacement of approximately 60,300 people, and a critical GBV crisis emerged in the Fouli and Kaya departments due to women having to travel over two kilometres for water, which exposed them to high risks of physical and sexual violence. Additionally, a new cholera outbreak declared on 18 June in the Karal District threatened to limit the delivery of essential sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services and confidential GBV responses.

UNFPA responded by deploying 127 midwives across the country, with 97 of them stationed in humanitarian areas to support health facilities in the east, south, and Lac Province. These midwives were instrumental in providing comprehensive SRH care, including assisting 2,518 safe births, conducting 9,452 antenatal consultations, and reaching 4,509 women with family planning services. UNFPA also addressed GBV through case management in multiple provinces, operating 11 safe spaces that supported 933 women and girls, conducting awareness sessions for 4,959 people, and providing capacity-building training on cash transfers for survivors to 19 staff members.

As of the end of June 2026, UNFPA has secured US $2.5 million toward its $18.7 million requirement, leaving a staggering funding gap of 87%. UNFPA is urgently appealing for critical funding for Chad to address the scale and urgency of the humanitarian needs, particularly for women and girls who require life-saving SRH and protection services.

title: Bangladesh WASH Cluster Newsletter, June 2026 Edition
content: The Bangladesh WASH Cluster, led by the Department of Public Health Engineering (DPHE) and co-led by UNICEF, brings together government, UN agencies, NGOs, and partners to coordinate effective WASH responses during emergencies. It ensures timely, equitable, and accountable delivery of services for vulnerable populations affected by floods, cyclones, and other disasters. The Cluster also promotes the Humanitarian-Development Nexus (HDN), strengthens Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP), and advances climate change (CC) adaptation by supporting climate-resilient, inclusive, and sustainable WASH solutions across Bangladesh.

title: Cameroon Cholera Outbreak: Situation Report #1 (July 29, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • An outbreak of cholera involving at least 24 people has been reported in Minawao Refugee Camp, which hosts more than 81,000 refugees and is operating at approximately 325% of intended capacity.
  • The wider cholera outbreak in the Far North region had reported 754 cases and 25 deaths across nine health districts as of July 26.
  • Multiple transmission chains are suspected within the camp, increasing the risk of rapid spread among vulnerable populations.

OUR RESPONSE

  • International Medical Corps is coordinating with the Ministry of Public Health, UN agencies and humanitarian partners to support a coordinated cholera response.
  • We are preparing a three-month emergency intervention focused on outbreak containment, case management and community protection.
  • Efforts include expanding treatment capacity through additional staff, essential medicines and pre-positioned cholera response supplies.
  • To support early detection and treatment, we are strengthening surveillance, community alert systems and risk communication.
  • We are scaling up emergency sanitation, hygiene promotion and infection prevention activities in high-risk areas.

Following the detection of suspected and RDT-positive cholera cases in Minawao Refugee Camp, International Medical Corps prepared an emergency response targeting some 14,600 people to help contain the outbreak and reduce morbidity and mortality among refugee and host populations.

To strengthen case management, we are recruiting additional technical staff and procuring essential medical supplies and consumables. We also are supporting enhanced disease surveillance, community-alert systems and risk-communication activities to improve early detection, timely referral and healthcare-seeking behavior.

Given the heightened transmission risks associated with overcrowding and inadequate sanitation conditions, International Medical Corps is prioritizing emergency WASH interventions, including hygiene promotion, targeted disinfection of high-risk locations, strengthened IPC measures, and pre-positioning cholera treatment and prevention supplies.

As always, we are working closely with national authorities and humanitarian partners while addressing priority operational gaps identified through ongoing coordination efforts.

title: OCHA Haiti : Nationwide Humanitarian Response (1-30 June 2026)
content: According to IOM’s Round 13 DTM report published in May, the number of internally displaced persons (IDPs) reached 1.47 million, including more than 300,000 people in the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area alone, representing a 1 per cent increase compared to Round 12. Following the clashes in Cité Soleil in May, which displaced more than 18,000 people, a new wave of violence between 13 and 19 June forced over 5,000 additional people from Cité Soleil to flee their homes. This persistent insecurity also had a direct impact on access to essential services. In June, Doctors Without Borders (MSF) was compelled to suspend activities at the Isaïe Jeanty maternity hospital in Cité Soleil following intense armed clashes, during which more than 100 people sought refuge at the facility amid crossfire, leaving thousands without access to healthcare services.

title: Global Weather Hazards Summary, July 30, 2026 – Aug 05, 2026
content:
Global Overview: El Niño is present. Flood risk across Africa, northern and eastern Central Asia, eastern and southern Central America, and northern South America.

Africa Weather Hazards

Persistent dryness continues across East Africa, while flood alerts stay active in coastal West Africa due to heavy rains.

1) Inundation continues in the Sudd wetlands of South Sudan.

2) Severe rainfall deficits across large parts of East Africa over the past 90 days have resulted in abnormal dryness. Due to this persistent dryness, conditions have been upgraded to “Drought” across the equatorial provinces of South Sudan as well as eastern, central, and north-central Ethiopia.

3) Southern Mali, and central and eastern Liberia continue to experience abnormal dryness due to sustained below-average rainfall.

4) Persistent and forecasted localized heavy rainfall maintains an elevated risk of flooding across coastal areas of Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia, southeastern Nigeria, and western Cameroon.

5) A recent 40°C+ heatwave across Mediterranean coastal areas resulted in wildfires in Algeria that spread to Morocco and Tunisia. In the coming week, abnormal heat will shrink to northeastern Algeria and Morocco, while separate areas of abnormal heat are expected across southeastern South Sudan, southwestern and eastern Ethiopia, and parts of southeastern Eritrea.

6) As heavy rainfall migrates slightly northward, the high alert for flash flooding is shifting north across western Ethiopia.

7) Heavy rainfall (up to 100 mm) on July 27–28 triggered coastal flooding, road disruptions, and damage near KuGompo along South Africa's southeastern coast; although the alert level is downgraded, the area remains under elevated risk.

title: Amel Situation Report #3 : Supporting all populations affected by the crisis - March, April & May 2026
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

SITUATION IN LEBANON

Three months into the renewed conflict in Lebanon, nearly 1.3 million people remain displaced and the humanitarian situation continues to deteriorate, with critical infrastructure damage restricting access to food, healthcare, and assistance across South Lebanon. Amel Association International's emergency response reached 148,107 people across 207 sites in all eight governorates between March and May 2026, delivering 6,267 activities in health, protection, education, and distribution. Health teams provided 85,139 services through 15 active Primary Health Care Centres and 11 Mobile Medical Units, while protection programming reached 23,941 people through integrated General Protection, GBV, Child Protection, and MHPSS support. Education activities reached 27,282 children, and 15,091 relief items were distributed to the most vulnerable, including older people and persons with disabilities. Eight Amel centres sustained damage during the reporting period, underscoring the operational risks faced while sustaining life-saving services amid a critically underfunded Lebanon Flash Appeal.

title: Amel Situation Report #4 : Supporting all populations affected by the crisis - March, April, May & June 2026
content: Nearly four months into the renewed conflict in Lebanon, at least 4,247 people have been killed and 12,195 injured since hostilities resumed on 2 March 2026, though displacement figures show early signs of stabilization, with over 523,000 people beginning to return despite continued insecurity and destruction. Amel Association International scaled up its response to reach 194,266 people across 218 sites between March and June 2026, delivering 8,482 activities. Health services expanded to 120,455 consultations and interventions through 18 active health centres and 11 Mobile Medical Units, with Primary Support Units redeployed to match population returns. Protection programming reached 27,035 people, and education activities reached 34,077 children. Amel distributed 18,604 relief items and mourns the loss of two staff members killed in the line of duty. With the Flash Appeal only 32% funded and pipeline breaks expected from July, sustained donor support remains critical to maintaining life-saving operations.

title: Sudan Situation: UNHCR Monthly External Update #119 - May 2026
content:
Highlights

▪ Sudan: The security situation deteriorated further, marked by increased use of airstrikes targeting transport routes, airports, and critical infrastructure across Khartoum, Darfur, Kordofan, and Blue Nile States. Intercommunal violence in Darfur and Kordofan States resulted in civilian casualties and triggered further displacements. In Khartoum, large-scale returns continued to strain basic services and livelihoods, compounded by fuel shortages, and rising prices. International and domestic flight operations were suspended for approximately two weeks during the reporting period due to security incidents, further disrupting humanitarian access and supply chains. Despite these challenges, UN agencies have gradually re-established their offices in the city.

▪ Central African Republic (CAR): The security situation in Birao remains calm but fragile, with persistent volatility along road axes and in surrounding villages, where security incidents and intercommunal tensions have been reported across Vakaga prefecture in northern CAR, where the majority of Sudanese refugees are hosted.

▪ Chad: From 25 to 27 May, UNHCR, together with Action Against Hunger (AAH) and with support from WFP, hosted a high-level British parliamentary delegation in Adré, Ouaddaï province, eastern Chad, to assess the border situation and the response to displacement from Sudan. The delegation observed new arrivals and reception arrangements including the pre-registration process and engaged directly with refugees in Metché. A visit to a UNHCR-supported 11-hectare farming site highlighted the positive impact of livelihood interventions. Discussions focused on durable shelter, resilience, and evolving refugee flows. The delegation commended the quality of the response, while emphasising the importance of sustained international support and durable solutions.

▪ Egypt: On 20 May, UNHCR welcomed a high-level visit from the European Union (EU) delegation.
The UNHCR Representative expressed gratitude for EU’s continued support and underscored the need for sustained funding in the current context. The delegation was briefed on the refugee response in Egypt and then visited the Reception and Registration Centre on 6 th October City. The delegation commended UNHCR’s work and ongoing efforts to respond to the increasing needs of refugees and asylum-seekers in Egypt.

▪ Ethiopia: In the Benishangul-Gumuz region, the security conditions were generally calm despite tensions along the Ethiopia–Sudan border, with no new asylum movements or relocations reported.
High-level missions from the World Bank and Government of Ireland reaffirmed support for refugee inclusion, while highlighting persistent gaps in food security, infrastructure, and basic services amid continued funding constraints.

▪ Libya: On 3 May, the UNHCR Chief of Mission met with the Foreign Minister of the eastern-based government during a mission to Benghazi to discuss the situation of Sudanese refugees and strengthen coordination on refugee protection, humanitarian assistance, and solutions for those seeking safety in Libya.

▪ South Sudan: The operation hosted the Crisis Response Coordinator from the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (SIDA) for an official visit to Juba and Aweil, including Wedweil and Barniwinyi refugee settlements. The mission reaffirmed UNHCR as a key SIDA partner and highlighted the donor’s strong interest in area-based coordination, refugee-led and community-based organizations, as well as more sustainable and self-reliance-oriented responses. SIDA reiterated its flexibility and trust in UNHCR and the potential for continued partnership in 2026, including interest on “Solutions from the Start.”

▪ Uganda: UNHCR, the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM), and relevant authorities continued to monitor and assess the drivers of inter- and intra-community tensions in refugee settlements, including possible spillover effects from the security developments in South Sudan.

title: World Health Organization - Middle East Escalation of Conflict, Global Situation report #10 - 22 July 2026
content:
This is the tenth global public WHO situation report on the escalation in the Middle East. It covers the health situation and WHO operational updates from affected countries in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean and European regions, as well as WHO's global response activities and priorities.

On 17 June 2026, the United States of America and the Islamic Republic of Iran signed an agreement on a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) concerning the cessation of hostilities. Since the announcement of the MoU and subsequent ceasefire, there has been a decline in the overall intensity of hostilities. However, military activities continue, impacting civilian infrastructure and access to care.

On 8 July 2026, media reports circulated that the MoU has been rendered ineffective, and a further intensification of hostilities has continued, with airstrikes reported daily. In Lebanon, the security situation remains fragile despite reduced hostilities following a ceasefire announcement, with daily localized military activity reported. Acute health threats include trauma and mass casualty risks, communicable disease risks linked to displacement and overcrowded shelters, rising measles and leishmaniasis in Syria, measles transmission in Jordan, and persistent fuel, power and supply-chain constraints affecting continuity of essential health services.

title: Islamic Relief Pakistan: Humanitarian Situation Report (Period: 26-June to 28-July 2026)
content:
Location KP, AJK, GB, Punjab, Balochistan and Sindh

BACKGROUND

Pakistan continues to face severe and compounding risks from both economic fragility and climate-induced disasters. The country remains among the most disaster-prone globally, ranking 18th out of 191 countries in the INFORM Risk Index, reflecting high exposure to hazards, vulnerability, and limited coping capacity. Over the past decade, disasterrelated damages have exceeded USD 18 billion, significantly constraining economic growth and development progress. More recent climate assessments also indicate that Pakistan is among the top 10 most climatevulnerable countries globally, despite contributing less than 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

Pakistan's 2026 monsoon began on 26 June and is forecast by the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) to bring 22–26% more rainfall than the previous season, compounded by accelerated melt across the country's more than 7,000 glaciers. As of the latest NDMA daily sitrep, the cumulative death toll (109) remains far below the same point in the catastrophic 2022 and 2025 seasons — but the situation has escalated in last 7 days: NDMA and PDMA Punjab have moved from advisory to an active flood alert for the Chenab, Jhelum and Ravi rivers from 29 July–05 August, with evacuations already being directed in low-lying and riverbank areas. Current figures should be read as a running total from an inprogress, intensifying season, not a final toll.

According to the State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA), a cloudburst in Neelum Valley caused significant damage to infrastructure, including houses, shops, government schools, and bridges. Losses of livestock were also reported in the affected areas. The Azad Jammu and Kashmir State Disaster Management Authority (AJK SDMA) is closely monitoring the situation and has initiated coordination, response, and relief efforts in collaboration with relevant departments and local authorities to support affected communities.

As of 28 July 2026, a total of 109 deaths and 360 injuries have been reported nationwide. The majority of casualties resulted from house collapses and flash floods triggered by heavy rainfall. Additionally, 796 houses have been damaged, either fully or partially, while 379 livestock have perished. These numbers are expected to increase as ongoing rainfall and forecasted precipitation continue to impact affected areas. More Monsoon Rains predicted in the country from 29th July to 05th August.

title: Lebanon: What's New? LRP Update July 2026
content:
This Flash Update reports that the humanitarian situation in Lebanon remains critical despite continued returns, with significant humanitarian and protection needs persisting among displaced populations, returnees, and host communities. Ongoing hostilities in or near the IDF-declared military area continue to expose civilians to significant protection risks.

As of 23 July, the Ministry of Public Health reports at least 4,329 people were killed and 12,233 were injured. Moreover, 753,024 people reported returning to their areas of origin, while 375,090 people remain displaced, including 29,500 displaced inside 271 collective shelters. The Flash Appeal stands at 44.8 per cent funded, making it challenging to sustain humanitarian assistance.

Humanitarian partners continue to prioritize the delivery of a coordinated, multi-sector response across Lebanon while prioritizing de-escalation and cessation of hostilities, as well as the protection of civilians.

title: UNHCR Tunisia Monthly Operational Update (June 2026)
content:
UNHCR operates in Tunisia in support of refugees and asylum-seekers, including individuals with specific needs. The country hosts a population of registered refugees and asylum-seekers from Su-dan, Syria, Somalia, and various West, Central and East African countries, the majority of whom have fled conflict, persecution, and other protection risks. Among them are particularly vulnerable individuals, including victims of torture, survivors of gender-based violence, people with serious medical or psychosocial needs, and unaccompanied children.

In recent years, the operational environment has changed significantly: access to protection and to some essential services has become increasingly limited, heightening the vulnerability of forcibly dis-placed population. In line with its humanitarian mandate, UNHCR provides life-saving protection and assistance to registered refugees and asylum-seekers, working with national partners including the Tunisian Scouts, the Arab Institute for Human Rights (IADH), and the Tunisian Association for Man-agement and Social Stability (TAMSS)

title: Afghanistan: Flash Update #3: Flooding in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Afghanistan (as of 28 July 2026)
content:
HIGHIGHTS

  • Heavy rainfall, flash floods and related natural hazards continued to affect communities in central, eastern, northeastern and southeastern regions of Afghanistan.
  • Significant impacts were reported in Ghazni, Kapisa, Laghman, Logar, Nangarhar, Paktia, Paktika and Parwan, among other provinces. In Laghman, three people were killed and four others were injured, with 187 families affected. A total of 183 houses were damaged or destroyed, while approximately 800 acres of seasonal crops and around 310 livestock were also reportedly lost or damaged.
  • Nuristan Province remains the most severely affected area. The completed inter-agency needs assessment in Parun district identified 120 families eligible for humanitarian assistance, while humanitarian assistance has already been provided to the first 92 identified families.
  • Joint needs assessments have now been completed in Logar, Kabul, Kapisa and Parwan. Humanitarian assistance is scheduled for 79 families in Logar, 28 families in Kabul, 65 families in Kapisa, and 45 families in Parwan. Assessments in Maidan Wardak and Panjshir are expected to commence shortly.
  • Humanitarian partners continue to scale up the response through shelter, health, WASH, protection and education interventions. Water network rehabilitation is underway in Parun, emergency health services continue to be provided, and cluster partners are expanding protection, psychosocial support and education responses.
  • Recent flooding and landslides may have displaced or exposed explosive ordnance (EO), increasing risks for affected communities and humanitarian personnel.

title: Burundi | Flood - Early Action Protocol Summary, July 2026 (EAP2025BI02 | MDRBI027)
content:
SUMMARY OF THE EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL

The IFRC Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) has approved a total of CHF 778,786 CHF for the implementation of the BURUNDI NATIONAL SOCIETY FLOODS EAP. The approved amount consists of an allocation of CHF 85,100 for readiness, CHF 371,227 for 2 rounds of prepositioning and CHF 322,459 allocated to implement 2 rounds of early actions once the defined triggers are met.

Allocations are made from the Anticipatory Pillar of the DREF, under the DREF appeal code MDR00001. Unearmarked contributions to the DREF are encouraged to guarantee enough funding is available for the Early Action Protocols being developed.

Summary

Over the past decade, Burundi has suffered shocks that have caused enormous human and material damage at an increasingly frequent frequency. The most threatening risks are above all meteorological, climatic, epidemic and geomorphological phenomena. The severity resulting from the combination of the probability of occurrence and the impact of natural shocks often exceeds the capacity for preparation and anticipation to mitigate the impacts of the latter.

Climate and weather events such as floods, landslides, landslides and ravines have resulted in loss of life and other damage. The El Nino phenomenon of 2023-2024 has caused floods and landslides that have affected more than 237,000 people and led to more than 42,000 displaced, 29 deaths and 175 injured people since September 2023 to April 26, 20241. Another example is 20192 where more than 13,000 people were affected and 45 deaths were reported, in addition to the losses to crops and public and private infrastructure as a result of the floods.

The Early Action Protocol (EAP) is a tool that allows for the effective and timely implementation of early actions based on specific weather or climate forecasts of extreme events that, if they materialize and no appropriate action is taken, will most likely generate a humanitarian crisis. This crisis can be avoided or mitigated by joint and rapid action by the government, at-risk communities, stakeholders and the National Red Cross Society.

This EAP will be implemented by the Burundi Red cross in coordination with several partners, namely the Government of Burundi through the National Platform for Risk Prevention and Disaster Management, the Geographical Institute of Burundi (IGEBU), United Nations agencies and other actors working in disaster risk reduction. This document is expected to form an essential part of the national and local emergency plans of the Burundian government and the Burundi Red Cross Society.

This Early Action Protocol targets areas at risk of flooding, more specifically the area exposed to the periodic rise of the waters of Lake Tanganyika. The EAP explains the reasons for prioritizing early actions and gives detailed explanations for the selected actions that should be activated when the triggers are reached in a specific order.

title: Zimbabwe Flood 2026 - DREF Operational Update (MDRZW027), 28 July 2026
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

24-01-2026

What happened, where and when?

Zimbabwe faced a severe and evolving flood emergency during the 2025/26 rainfall season that lasted until March with persistent heavy rains and storm events across the country. Especially from January to February. Between 13 and 24 January 2026, intense rainfall caused dam spillages, riverine overflow, and flash flooding in multiple areas, and the situation, which began in early January, worsened further in late January. This escalation led the Department of Civil Protection to request support from the Zimbabwe Red Cross Society to deliver lifesaving assistance to affected families. For all February 2026, Hydrological conditions remained extremely concerning. According to the Zimbabwe National Water Authority (ZINWA), several major dams were full or over-spilling, including Tugwi Mukosi, Manjirenji, Manyuchi, and Bubi-Lupane dams, significantly increasing downstream flood risk. Controlled and uncontrolled spillages have already resulted in river flooding, marooning of communities, damage to agricultural land, and destruction of bridges and irrigation infrastructure.

At least 109 people were confirmed dead due to rainfall-related incidents, including drowning, people being swept away by floodwaters, and lightning strikes, while 61 people were injured. Nationwide, an estimated 8,295 households (41,475 people) were affected, with many families displaced and in urgent need of shelter and basic assistance. Several communities were cut off as damaged infrastructure led to marooning incidents where floodwaters severed access routes. (Data as of 25 Jan. 2026)

For weeks, the conditions isolated communities, restrict humanitarian access, and further disrupt access to social services, particularly for learners who cross rivers or travel long distances to reach schools. With that situation prolonged to march, the access and limited assistance available make the need for displaced communities still persistent. ZRCS DREF operation bridging that gap.

title: Cameroon Multi-Country Office (MCO) - Quarterly Operational Update April-June 2026
content: UNHCR supports governments in Cameroon, the Republic of Congo (RoC), Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and São Tomé and Príncipe to protect and assist forcibly displaced and stateless populations, expand access to asylum and essential services, and strengthen national protection systems, advocating for national inclusion, self-reliance and promoting durable solutions. Cameroon hosts the largest displaced population, while the RoC hosts over 70,800 refugees and asylum-seekers.

title: Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda | France - Weekly External Situation Report 11, Data as of 26 July 2026
content:
Event description
The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continued to intensify during the reporting period, with sustained transmission, increasing mortality, and ongoing geographic expansion within the country. The cumulative number of reported cases has exceeded the two previously documented Bundibugyo virus disease outbreaks, making this the largest outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus to date. Although no new cases have been reported outside the Democratic Republic of the Congo, persistent transmission in areas connected by major national and cross-border mobility corridors continues to sustain a high risk of regional spread. These epidemiological trends underscore the need for strengthened surveillance, cross-border collaboration, and preparedness to rapidly detect and contain any international spread.

title: Central African Republic: Am Dafock Mass Displacement Crisis - Situation Report #1, July 28, 2026
content:
FAST FACTS

  • Am Dafock, in Vakaga prefecture, is experiencing a mass displacement crisis triggered by armed attacks in and around the city since the beginning of June.
  • More than 19,000 internally displaced people have sought refuge at the MINUSCA base in Am Dafock.
  • The local health system has collapsed—the health facility at the base has been looted and medical personnel have fled for their safety.
  • Am Dafock remains inaccessible via road, limiting the supplies and assistance that can reach the area.

OUR FOOTPRINT

  • International Medical Corps has worked in the Central African Republic since 2007, delivering lifesaving services such as primary and secondary healthcare, surveillance and response to infectious diseases, health system strengthening, nutrition and food security, prevention and response to violence against women and girls, and water, sanitation and hygiene.

OUR RESPONSE

  • International Medical Corps has deployed an emergency response team, as well as lifesaving health and nutrition supplies, in the affected area.
  • We have delivered 1,294 kilograms of medical supplies, essential medicines and ready-to-use therapeutic foods, as well as infection-prevention and control supplies.
  • We have provided 1,778 curative consultations and 290 antenatal consultations, and registered 26 home deliveries, providing connections to further health services at the clinic.

Despite the challenges, International Medical Corps is committed to scaling up lifesaving interventions. Additional staff—including one mental health nurse, one nutrition nurse and one case manager providing services to survivors of violence against women and girls—will be deployed soon, which will enhance the mobile clinic's capacity to deliver integrated health, nutrition and protection services. Additional nutrition supplies, dignity kits and IPC materials are being prepared for deployment.

Though the response continues to face significant operational challenges that are delaying the deployment of additional humanitarian assistance and critical supplies, continued and increased funding support is essential to address growing health, nutrition, protection, food security and livelihood, and water, sanitation and hygiene needs.

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #17 (24 to 27 July 2026)
content:
The seventeenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 24 to 27 July.

Highlights

Between 24 and 27 July, IOM continued its multisectoral response in transitional sites and affected communities through interventions in shelter and site coordination, health, protection, WASH, and information management.

During the reporting period, IOM and its partner Fundación Vivienda Popular distributed 343 tarpaulins, 343 kitchen sets, 343 solar lamps, 618 jerry cans, 275 ropes, 275 blankets, 35 mosquito nets, and 33 buckets, contributing to improved shelter conditions and access to essential items.

To date, IOM continues supporting the management of five transitional sites in La Guaira, where 4,538 people remain hosted, through the provision of multisectoral services, coordination, and needs monitoring.

IOM Activities

IOM continued the co-management of five transitional sites in La Guaira, strengthening coordination mechanisms, registration, community participation, and inter-agency coordination. In Campo de Golf, registration of 102 families was completed and spatial reorganization advanced for the future installation of 100 tents with IsraAID. In Mare Abajo II, Playa Grande, and César Nieves, infrastructure improvements, registration updates, and transition planning processes continued.

Under WASH, coordination advanced for the installation of a 20,000-litre-per-day water storage and treatment system in Campo de Golf, alongside sanitation improvements, waste management, and sanitary infrastructure enhancements in other sites. To date, 2,170 collapsible jerry cans, 1,091 hygiene kits, and 93 water storage containers have been distributed.

IOM and its partner Ven Da Tu Mano continued providing primary health care and psychological first aid (PFA) through mobile teams, conducting more than 500 consultations during the reporting period, including follow-up and referrals for specialized care. IOM also continued co-leading the PFA Technical Working Group with PAHO/WHO to strengthen referral pathways.

Under information management, IOM completed the DTM Household Survey in transitional sites. Preliminary findings show that 12% of households reached their current location through progressive movements, 55% reported loss of income during the last month, and 55% indicated they do not feel safe when leaving their accommodation.

Under protection, IOM continued providing guidance, legal assistance, documentation support, referrals, and actions to prevent violence against women, trafficking in persons, and sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA). HIAS joined as an IOM implementing partner to expand protection service coverage, including psychological support, legal counselling, child protection, and safe spaces.

Planned IOM Response

IOM will continue strengthening infrastructure and essential services in transitional sites, as well as coordination mechanisms, information management, and community participation.

IOM will also maintain mobile health and psychological support services, strengthen referral pathways, and expand specialized protection services, while continuing site monitoring, needs assessments, and coordination with authorities and humanitarian partners.

title: AKFP Pakistan: Monsoon Flood 2026 - Situation Report 01 (28 July, 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

Alkhidmat Foundation Pakistan is closely monitoring the ongoing monsoon situation across the country, with particular focus on Azad Jammu & Kashmir (AJK), Gilgit-Baltistan (GB), and Central Punjab. Heavy monsoon rains have triggered flash floods, riverine flooding, urban flooding, and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs), affecting vulnerable communities and damaging homes, roads, bridges, and other critical infrastructure in several areas.

Alkhidmat's Disaster Management teams, volunteers, and response centers remain on high alert, coordinating with relevant authorities while continuously monitoring weather forecasts and river conditions. Rescue resources and emergency relief stocks have been pre-positioned to ensure a swift and effective response. Alkhidmat Foundation Pakistan remains committed to delivering timely rescue, relief, and humanitarian assistance to affected families throughout the ongoing monsoon emergency.

title: UNFPA Cameroon Situation Report: Humanitarian Crisis (1 - 30 June 2026)
content:
Cameroon continued to face a highly volatile and complex humanitarian environment in June 2026, driven by persistent conflict and compounding crises across the Far North, North-West, and South-West regions. In the North-West and South-West, the security situation remained unstable, characterized by ongoing localized insecurity, a fire incident, and the strict enforcement of "ghost towns", characterized by night-time curfews and enforced socio-economic lockdowns, as well as general movement restrictions; these issues heightened protection risks for women and girls. Concurrently, the Far North region remained heavily impacted by a cholera outbreak alongside ongoing attacks by non-state armed groups, particularly within hard-to-reach areas already experiencing significant humanitarian pressure. Beyond these immediate security and health threats, humanitarian needs and vulnerabilities remained high across the Far North region, with almost 1,000 displaced individuals across divisions facing severe protection risks and limited access to sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services.

In June, UNFPA provided extensive support across 22 health facilities, deploying 33 midwives to assist 1,330 deliveries — including 157 emergency Caesarean sections — and conduct thousands of SRH consultations, such as treatments for sexually transmitted infections and family planning services. Simultaneously, the organization reached 4,649 individuals through gender-based violence prevention and mitigation efforts, which provided psychosocial support, case management, and the distribution of 225 dignity kits to strengthen resilience in displacement settings.

For 2026, UNFPA requires US $4,013,060 to implement critical reproductive health and protection services in Cameroon. As of June, UNFPA has secured US $2.4 million thanks to the generous support of the European Union, German Agency for International Cooperation, and the UNFPA Emergency Fund.

title: Nigeria Situation Report - June 2026
content:
In June 2026, Nigeria faced a multifaceted humanitarian crisis characterized by protracted conflict, macroeconomic inflation, and disease outbreaks, leaving an estimated 36.3 million people food insecure. The north-east epicenter is suffering from non-state armed violence, severe malnutrition, and a massive cholera outbreak, while the forced closure of internally displaced person camps in Borno State has triggered mass displacement and relocation. Simultaneously, banditry and intercommunal violence have destabilized the north-west and north-central regions, exemplified by a mid-June attack in Zamfara State that caused numerous casualties and widespread displacement. These compounding factors, along with early seasonal flooding, have severely disrupted health infrastructure and heightened protection risks for women and girls, including increased exposure to gender-based violence (GBV) and limited access to essential sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services.

UNFPA's humanitarian response in Nigeria focused on delivering integrated SRH, GBV, and youth empowerment services through a network of health facilities, safe spaces, youth spaces, and one-stop centres. SRH interventions provided critical care, including 359 managed deliveries, antenatal and postnatal services for thousands of women, contraception access for nearly 3,000 individuals, and comprehensive medical treatment for survivors of sexual violence. GBV response efforts reached over 12,600 people with mental health and psychosocial support, referral linkages, and specialized protection services, while youth programming engaged over 7,300 young people through life-skills training, vocational programmes, and civic engagement initiatives.

To deliver the required SRH and GBV humanitarian response, a total of US $11,900,000 is required. As of June 2026, UNFPA’s appeal was 11.6% funded, leaving a significant gap in support for essential SRH and GBV services.

title: Eastern Afghanistan Flash Floods - Flash Update (20 - 21 July 2026)
content:
Heavy rainfall and flash flooding have affected communities across Nangarhar, Nuristan and Laghman provinces in eastern Afghanistan, causing deaths, injuries, displacement risks, damage to homes and livelihoods, and disruption to essential services. In Nangarhar, flooding affected the Torkham border area, disrupting returnee movement at the border crossing. In Nuristan, the impact has been severe, with reported deaths, injuries and more than 100 people missing, alongside extensive damage to homes, markets, roads, bridges, agricultural land and water systems. Around 1,000 families reportedly face disrupted access to safe drinking water. In Laghman, flooding damaged agricultural land and crops, threatening livelihoods and household food security.

UNFPA is working with partners to monitor the situation and to identify emerging needs, particularly for women and girls, including pregnant women, adolescent girls and women-headed households. Ensuring continued access to essential sexual and reproductive health and gender-based violence services, dignity supplies, safe referrals, and protection support will be critical as assessments continue.

title: UNFPA Central African Republic Situation Report - June 2026
content:
In June 2026, the Central African Republic (CAR) faced a convergence of health and security crises, beginning with the government’s validation of an Ebola contingency plan to prevent the virus's introduction and the subsequent declaration of a cholera outbreak in Bimbo and Mbaïki that resulted in hundreds of suspected cases and dozens of deaths. The humanitarian landscape was further destabilized by armed attacks in the Vakaga prefecture, which forced thousands to flee and left the town of Am-Dafock deserted, and by rising security incidents in Haut-Mbomou that targeted humanitarian actors and forced a temporary suspension of UNFPA and other operations in the south-east. These crises severely restricted humanitarian access, increased protection risks such as conflict-related sexual violence and child mortality, and exacerbated existing vulnerabilities across the region.

In response, UNFPA provided critical sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and gender-based violence (GBV) support to vulnerable populations, particularly women and girls, across crisis-affected areas. By deploying an integrated approach that combined mobile clinics with support for reference health facilities, UNFPA achieved significant results, including hundreds of assisted births, antenatal and postnatal care visits, and emergency Caesarean sections, alongside extensive family planning and gynaecological services. UNFPA also prioritized protection through targeted GBV awareness sessions, support to safe spaces, and the distribution of dignity kits, while actively working to increase SRH awareness and improve clinical outcomes for sexual assault survivors through comprehensive medical care and community outreach.

In 2026, UNFPA requires US $13.2 million to deliver essential SRH and protection services in the CAR. As of the end of June 2026, UNFPA has mobilized US $2.2 million of funding. A significant 83% funding gap remains, which is hindering UNFPA’s ability to provide life-saving services to women and girls in need.

title: UNFPA Regional Situation Report - Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak (1 - 30 June 2026)
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda
content:
As of June 2026, the ongoing Ebola outbreak, driven by the Bundibugyo virus, has escalated into a severe public health crisis, with 406 confirmed cases and 438 deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Conversely, Uganda has achieved strong containment of a smaller cluster of 20 confirmed cases, with the majority of cases now recovered. UNFPA is supporting containment and preparedness efforts in the DRC and Uganda, as well as preparedness activities in high-risk neighbouring countries. Collaborating with the World Health Organization and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention through the continental Incident Management Support Team, UNFPA directly supports infection prevention and control, continuity of essential services, and risk communication and community engagement.

To address the regional Ebola crisis, UNFPA has activated its highest level of emergency response (Level 3) for the DRC and Uganda. UNFPA has been supporting 182 health facilities across the two countries, providing vital reproductive health supplies, personal protection equipment (PPE) and infection prevention materials, as well as delivering training for health staff on Ebola prevention and health facility safety. During June, UNFPA also reached 58,887 people with sexual and reproductive health services, 81,582 with gender-based violence prevention and response in the DRC and Uganda. In neighbouring at-risk countries, UNFPA is proactively procuring and strategically prepositioning life-saving supplies, including PPE, specialized isolation tents for pregnant women, and Inter-Agency Reproductive Health kits. UNFPA is also training healthcare and community-based workers on specialized infection protocols, mobilizing to deploy midwives and gender-based violence caseworkers to protect vital maternal health and protection systems from disruption should an Ebola outbreak occur.

As the outbreak continues to escalate in the DRC, and other countries remain at high risk, urgent funding is required to sustain critical sexual and reproductive health and gender-based violence services and implement prevention and preparedness activities. UNFPA requires US $20.8 million to ensure continued access to vital care for affected communities and prevent further loss of life.

title: Somalia | Desert Locusts - Simplified Early Action Protocol (sEAP2026SO03 | MDRSO027)
content:
RISK ANALYSIS AND EARLY ACTION SELECTION

Prioritized hazard and its historical impact.

The desert locust (Schistocerca gregaria) is considered the world's most destructive migratory pest. A single swarm can contain billions of individuals, travel vast distances, and consume an amount of food equivalent to tens of thousands of people daily. Somalia, along with other East African nations, has experienced severe locust upsurges, with the 2019 outbreak being one of the worst in decades. In 2019-2020, Somalia faced one of the worst desert locust infestations in decades, triggered by heavy rains linked to the Indian Ocean Dipole. The locusts spread rapidly across the Horn of Africa, severely impacting Somalia’s fragile food security by destroying farmland, pastures, and rangelands. The government declared a national emergency as locusts threatened the livelihoods of millions dependent on agriculture and livestock. Despite efforts from the FAO and international partners, response efforts were hampered by security issues, rapid locust reproduction, and limited resources. The peak of the upsurge occurred at the end of 2020 and the beginning of 2021, when large swarms gathered in significant numbers. Around 7,500 locust activities were recorded, with an average swarm radius of 0.5 km, and these activities mainly emerged in the north districts (EU Delegation, Somalia 2021). The most affected areas, particularly in the northeast and northwest regions—such as Bossaso, Burco, and Hargeisa—suffered substantial damage with nearly 13.4 thousand hectares of shrubland damaged in Burco.

Desert locust invasions pose a significant and recurring threat to Somalia's agricultural sector and food security, with impacts ranging from crop destruction to the destabilization of livelihoods and regional economies. The swarms, considered the world's most destructive migratory pest, devastate agricultural production and pastoral lands, threatening food security and compounding pre-existing vulnerabilities caused by recurrent droughts and floods. The country's geographical location and climatic conditions make it particularly vulnerable to these outbreaks. The primary impact of desert locust invasions in Somalia is the devastation of crops and rangelands (ICPAC IGAD, 2021). Swarms consume vast quantities of vegetation, including staple crops like maize and sorghum, as well as pastureland essential for livestock. This destruction directly threatens the livelihoods of farming and pastoral communities, many of whom rely solely on agriculture for their income and sustenance. For instance, in the coastal regions, planting of main season (Deyr) maize and sorghum crops faces a high risk of impact and thus is particularly vulnerable. The loss of crops exacerbates existing food insecurity, especially in regions already prone to humanitarian crises and conflict.

Beyond immediate food shortages, locust invasions have profound economic and social consequences. Agriculture forms the backbone of Somalia's economy, and widespread crop destruction can destabilize the national economy. Farmers who lose their entire harvest face significant financial losses, leading to increased debt and reduced purchasing power. This can force families to neglect basic needs such as nutrition, healthcare, and education, particularly affecting children (World Bank Group, 2021). Past locust plagues have shown a notable decrease in school enrolment and evidence of stunting in infants and children in affected areas (Somalia Safety Net for Locust Response Project, 2021). The combination of locust outbreaks with other challenges, such as conflict, drought, floods and disease outbreaks, further undermines the resilience of vulnerable populations.

Several factors contribute to the severity and recurrence of desert locust invasions in Somalia, namely:

● Favorable Climatic Conditions: Desert locusts thrive in wet weather, which allows for rapid maturation and breeding in the coastal areas of Somaliland and Puntland (Northern Somalia). Unusually heavy rainfall creates ideal breeding grounds and abundant vegetation for locust populations to explode (Salih, A.A.M. et al, 2020). The stage for the recent plague was set in 2018 with two tropical cyclones over the Arabian Peninsula in May and October 2018, supporting initial development of populations, which the heavy seasonal rainfall associated with the extreme positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) event of late 2019 acted to amplify. Whilst desert locust outbreaks are part of the long-term historical ecology of the region, climate change increases the frequency of outbreaks through increasing the frequency of extreme positive IOD events and associated rainfall (Cai et al, 2014; MacLeod et al, 2023).

● Geographical Location: Somalia's position in the Horn of Africa makes it a key breeding ground and transit point for locust swarms.

● Fragility, Conflict, and Violence (FCV): Ongoing conflict and instability in parts of Somalia can hinder effective monitoring and control operations, making it difficult for the Ministry of Agriculture´s (MoA) Desert Locust Centre and SRCS to access affected areas and implement timely interventions such as EWI dissemination, advisory services/awareness-raising on how to take protective measures, such as harvesting crops early, pre-positioning fodder, preparing for potential biological spraying operations, digging trenches around fields to trap the flightless “hoppers”, as well as moving livestock to safer areas.

● Limited Resources: Localized, preventative locust response efforts led by the MoA Desert Locust Centre are often possible; however, some regions may lack the necessary equipment, pesticides, or trained personnel to effectively manage large-scale invasions due to financial resource constraints. Once an outbreak has occurred, traditional methods, such as making noise or throwing stones, are often insufficient against massive swarms

title: Attacks on Health Care in Sudan, 08 - 21 July 2026
content:
Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) identified 134 incidents of violence against or obstruction of health care in Sudan in 2025, compared to 274 in 2024 and 280 in 2023. Among incidents reported in 2025, health facilities were damaged or destroyed 40 times, while 54 health workers were killed and 47 arrested. Over three-quarters of the reported incidents affected local health care providers working for national health care structures.

Incidents more than quadrupled in North, South, and West Kordofan states and persisted in the Darfur region – all areas where fighting between conflict parties was intense. Reported cases decreased in Gezira state in 2025 after the SAF recaptured the state capital, Wad Madani, and surrounding areas in January, pushing RSF forces out. More than 80% of reported incidents were attributed to the RSF. Other named conflict parties linked to attacks on health care in 2025 included Darfur communal militia, JFASM, SAF, SLM, and SPLM/ A-North fighters. In some incidents, the responsible conflict party remained unidentified.

Documented incidents

08-21 July 2026

The publicly reported incidents below are not a complete nor a representative list of all incidents that affected the provision of health care between 08-21 July 2026. The incidents below have not been verified through ground investigations. There is a delay in reporting incidents due to our open source verification protocol.

As reported 14 July 2026: In Kurmuk town, Blue Nile state, a hospital was reportedly damaged by the RSF during a raid. Kurmak had been taken-over by SAF on 08 July, though RSF claimed they had since taken it back. Sources: Al Jazeera and Centre for Information Resilience

As reported 15 July 2026: In Khazan Orshi area, Ambro administrative unit, North Darfur state, Urshi General Hospital was reportedly damaged when joint forces allied with the SAF took over the area. Source: Al Jazeera

title: Attacks on Health Care in Myanmar: 08 - 21 July 2026
content:
Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) identified 259 incidents of violence against or obstruction of health care in Myanmar in 2025, compared to 317 in 2024, 420 in 2023, 290 in 2022 and 490 in 2021. Health care facilities were damaged or destroyed at least 110 times, while 34 health workers were killed and 33 arrested. Most incidents affected health care providers working for a de facto government authority, either health structures set up by the National Unity Government, ethnic health organizations or the General Administration Department of the State Administration Council (SAC).

The proportion of incidents attributed to Myanmar Armed Forces (MAF) soldiers in 2025 increased from around 64% of incidents in 2024 to 75% in 2025, measured against an overall reduction in the total number of incidents attributed to the MAF. Multiple other conflict parties were also implicated in adverse effects on health care in 2025, including the AA, KIA, KNLA, LDFs, MNDAA, PDF and TNLA, but proportionally much less than the MAF.

Throughout 2025, parties to the conflict in Myanmar increasingly restricted access to medicines and essential medical supplies, particularly in areas perceived to support opposition groups or outside SAC control. Military and opposition checkpoints blocked or confiscated medicines, anti-retroviral treatment, anti-venom and other critical supplies, while transport routes into Chin, Kachin, Rakhine, Sagaing and northern Shan were repeatedly restricted. In Bago and Kayah, civilians were limited to “personal-use” quantities of medicines, worsening shortages of essential and chronic disease treatments. At the same time, authorities intensified punitive measures targeting health care providers and access to care, especially in Kachin, Rakhine, Sagaing, Shan, and Tanintharyi. Private hospitals and pharmacies were shut down over alleged links to the CDM or opposition groups, while health workers and medical students faced blacklisting, arrest, and intimidation. Patients were blocked from crossing checkpoints to seek treatment, humanitarian organizations were denied access to some earthquake-affected areas, and communities in conflict zones were prevented from traveling to nearby towns for medical care.

Documented incidents

The publicly reported incidents below are not a complete nor a representative list of all incidents that affected the provision of health care in Myanmar between 08-21 July 2026. The incidents have not been verified through ground investigations. There is a delay in reporting incidents due to our open-source verification protocol.

13 July 2026: In Ngar Tin Gyi village and village tract, Khin-U township, Shwebo district, Sagaing region, a rural health centre, a public school, and at least six houses were damaged by bombs and cannon fire used by two Myanmar military fighter jets. Two buildings of the health centre, including medicines and equipment, were damaged. At least six people, including a 25-year-old female nurse, were injured. At the time of the attack, the health centre was operating with the support of donors. Sources: Democratic Voice of Burma, Khit Thit Media, and Voice of Myanmar

As reported on 17 July 2026: In Htantlang town, Htantlang township, Hakha district, Chin state, a township hospital was found severely damaged and bunkers were found in the hospital after the town had been reseized by the Myanmar military on 16 July 2026. After the 2021 military coup, the town was taken over by Chin ethnic armed groups twice and reseized by the Myanmar military twice. Sources: Mandalay Free Press and Telegram

20 July 2026: In Sittwe town, Sittwe township, Sittwe district, Rakhine state, an X-ray technician, a fire brigade officer, and a general administrative office staff member were arrested by the Myanmar military, on accusations of having connections with the Arakan Army. The X-ray technician was not affiliated with the civil disobedience movement. Sources: Narinjara and Paletwa Times

title: Myanmar Monthly Food Price Report – May Thet Htar, Bart Minten, and Ian Masias (June 2026)
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • Rice prices rose modestly in June 2026, up 5.2 percent year-on-year and 1.8 percent month-on-month. While national price movements were limited, substantial regional price disparities persisted, reflecting differences in production conditions, market access, and transport costs.
  • Most export crop prices showed limited month-on-month movements. Pulses prices remained broadly stable, while maize prices increased modestly, supported by continued export demand. In contrast, green gram prices declined as concerns over pesticide residues and grain quality reportedly led some Chinese buyers to reject shipments.
  • Vegetable prices showed mixed trends. Onion and chili prices increased, supported by stronger export demand, while garlic and potato prices declined as increased market supplies, including higher inflows of Chinese garlic and potatoes, placed downward pressure on prices.
  • Most animal-sourced food prices remained substantially above year-earlier levels, led by mutton, fish, and beef. Month-on-month price movements were generally modest, although mutton prices remained at record highs due to constrained goat supply, while fish prices continued to be supported by seasonal fishing restrictions through the end of June.
  • The conflict in Iran and partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz — through which more than a quarter of the world's oil and 20–30 percent of global fertilizer exports transit — continue to keep fuel and fertilizer prices in Myanmar well above year-earlier levels. Some farmers report cultivating smaller areas or reducing plowing in response. With paddy prices largely flat, thinner margins are likely to translate into lower fertilizer application rates and, ultimately, reduced monsoon-season production.
  • Flood warnings have been issued in recent weeks for parts of the country. Moreover, a new El Niño phase is expected to develop within the coming weeks, increasing the risks of drought in the country.

title: Saarathi Alert - Assam Floods 2026 (27 July 2026)
content:
CURRENT SITUATION

  • LOCAL has verified 26,400 families in urgent need (21,000 families in Sivasagar, 2,400 families in Jorhat and 3,000 families across Golaghat and Charaideo districts)
  • The death toll has risen to 68. Over 5.24 lakh people remain affected across Charaideo, Golaghat, Jorhat, Nagaon and Sivasagar. Sivasagar is now the worstaffected district with nearly 1.9 lakh people impacted. 354 relief camps and distribution centres are operational across four districts, sheltering 37,724 people.
  • Floodwaters are gradually receding across Upper Assam. The focus has shifted to relief distribution, power restoration and medical deployment, with air-drops continuing in inaccessible areas. However, breached embankments and shallow waters are hampering both boat and vehicle access in several villages.
  • As waters recede, a public health crisis is emerging in areas like Dergaon, with stagnant water, waste, snake infestations and disease risk. Residents are urgently calling for disinfectants, bleaching powder and health camps.
