title: Kyrgyzstan Pluvial/Flash Flood 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRKG022)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
13-07-2026
What happened, where and when?

On 13 July 2026, at approximately 19:30 local time, intense short-duration rainfall over the mountainous catchment areas of Nooken district triggered mudflows along two separate channels. The Besh-Korgon channel overflowed and inundated the lower streets of Kochkor-Ata city, destroying 3 electricity poles in the Besh-Korgon settlement. Simultaneously, the Kara-Bulak channel overflowed into Ergesh Aliev village, while separate mudflows descending from higher elevations submerged the villages of Kurulush, Boston, and Kop- Tam in the Mombekov village area. The event occurred in Nooken district, Jalal-Abad oblast, Kyrgyzstan, affecting Kochkor-Ata city and the villages of Ergesh Aliev, Kurulush, Boston, and Kop-Tam.

The mudflows struck the evening of 13 July 2026 (19:30 local time). District civil protection authorities were mobilized the same evening, and clearance and mud-pumping operations were still ongoing as of 02:00 on 14 July 2026. A state of emergency has been declared in the district, and the situation is being monitored by RCSK in coordination with local civil protection authorities.

title: Tajikistan Flood 2026: DREF Operation (MDRTJ038)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
11-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 11 July 2026, at approximately 15:40 local time, following intense rainfall, flash floods and mudflows affected the villages of Darg and Kazdon in Shamtuch Jamoat, Ayni District, Sughd Region. The disaster caused significant damage to residential houses, auxiliary structures, agricultural land, drinking water supply and irrigation systems, electricity infrastructure, internal village roads, and private property. The affected population experienced disruptions to essential services and livelihoods.

On 15 July 2026, the Red Crescent Society of Tajikistan (RCST) received an official request from the Executive Authority of Ayni District seeking humanitarian assistance for the population affected by the disaster. The local authorities requested RCST to provide support to the most affected households. According to the official assessment, 672 households in the villages of Darg and Kazdon were affected by the flash floods and mudflows. Further assessments are ongoing to determine the full extent of the damage, humanitarian needs, and priority areas for response.

title: Yemen | Floods - Simplified Early Action Protocol - Final Report, May 2026 (sEAP №: sEAP2023YE01, Operation №: MDRYE015)
content:
SUMMARY - SIMPLIFIED EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL

The IFRC Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) has allocated CHF 220,000 for the (Yemen Red Crescent
Society) to implement early actions to reduce and mitigate the impact of Floods in Yemen. The early actions conducted have been pre-agreed with the National Society and are described in the Early Action Protocol.
https://www.ifrc.org/appeals?date_from=&date_to=&location%5B%5D=6325&search_terms=&search_terms=&
appeal_code=&search_terms=&text=

Below is a summary of key achievements focusing only on the key results against the planned activities under this sEAP including early actions, readiness and pre-positioning activities. Further details are provided under each sector/strategic priority and enablers.

Early Actions:

• Activated sEAP on 21st Aug 2025
• Distributed 100 emergency shelter and repair kits to highly vulnerable households living in degraded shelters, enabling timely reinforcement and repairs prior to anticipated flooding.
• Successfully cleaned drainage systems within and around targeted IDP sites following trigger activation, improving water flow, reducing water stagnation, and minimizing flood risks in coordination with CCCM, Shelter/NFI partners, and community committees.
• Implemented flood mitigation measures in Bani Al-Mashṭā’ and Al-Mithaq IDP sites through strategic placement of sandbags, construction of stone gabions, and earthen embankments to redirect floodwater and protect shelters and infrastructure.
• Delivered anticipatory Multi-Purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA) to 700 HHs 2–3 days before forecasted flooding, enabling vulnerable households to reinforce shelters, relocate temporarily, protect household assets, and meet urgent needs such as food, hygiene items, and rental support.
• Distributed 30 first aid kits and stretchers to community committees, local authorities, and civil defense actors, strengthening frontline emergency response and evacuation capacity prior to flooding.
• Installed 6 flood risk signposts in high-risk locations within and around targeted IDP sites to improve community awareness of flood hazards, mitigation measures, and safe movement routes.
• Distributed IEC materials containing early warning messages and practical guidance on shelter safety, flood preparedness, lightning safety, and hygiene promotion, enhancing community preparedness and risk awareness.
• Distributed 10 megaphones to community committees to strengthen community-based early warning dissemination and ensure timely communication of alerts and preparedness messages.

• Conducted community-based awareness campaigns and dissemination of early warning messages through YRCS volunteers, community committees, and local authorities using megaphones, community meetings, and door-to-door outreach.
• Activated PMER mechanisms to ensure real-time monitoring, quality assurance, accountability, and compliance with targeting and operational standards throughout implementation.
• Established accessible complaints and feedback mechanisms, including help desks and feedback boxes, to strengthen Community Engagement and Accountability (CEA/AAP), transparency, and beneficiary trust.
• Conducted a comprehensive Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM) survey covering 249 households (1,876 individuals) to assess the effectiveness, accountability, and impact of anticipatory cash assistance interventions.

Readiness activities:

• Coordinated with community committees, local authorities, CCCM actors, and Shelter/NFIs partners to finalize cleaning kits and flood mitigation requirements for targeted IDP sites.
• Conducted assessments and prepared BOQs for flood mitigation works, while identifying and engaging local suppliers for sandbags and other mitigation materials under framework arrangements.
• Finalized pre-identified beneficiary lists for Cash-for-Work activities and emergency shelter repair kits in consultation with community committees prior to sEAP activation.
• Completed orientation sessions for pre-selected Financial Service Providers (FSPs) on cash distribution methodologies, Red Cross principles, code of conduct, beneficiary dignity, and data protection.
• Reviewed and validated targeting criteria for Cash and Voucher Assistance (CVA) through coordination between YRCS HQ, branch teams, staff, and volunteers.
• Conducted a one-week CVA training for 10 YRCS Hajjah branch staff and volunteers (5 male and 5 female) on beneficiary registration, cash distribution processes, CVA tools, key messaging, and code of conduct.
• Oriented community committees and camp management teams in the targeted sites on sEAP activities, vulnerability-based targeting, and beneficiary selection processes for MPCA and shelter assistance.
• Finalized the initial registration and selection of vulnerable households eligible for MPCA and emergency shelter assistance in the targeted sites.
• Coordinated with IFRC and YRCS health teams to finalize specifications and contents of first aid kits and stretchers for emergency preparedness activities.
• Trained 60 participants from community committees, camp management, and civil defense on disaster preparedness, emergency response, anticipatory actions, and basic first aid through two six-day training sessions.
• Developed and finalized early warning, mitigation, and prevention messages in coordination with Civil Defense, YRCS DM, and communication teams, including translation and adaptation for local contexts.
• Reviewed, updated, and finalized IEC materials, including posters and brochures on flood preparedness, shelter safety, mitigation measures, and hygiene promotion.
• Finalized Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM) tools and guidelines for cash assistance activities to support accountability and monitoring processes.
• Conducted orientation and planning sessions for YRCS HQ and Hajjah branch staff and volunteers on anticipatory action approaches, planned sEAP activities, and operational readiness, with participation of more than 20 personnel.
• Successfully designed and conducted a simulation exercise in collaboration with IFRC, YRCS, and Civil Defense to test the feasibility and operational readiness of the sEAP prior to activation, generating valuable lessons learned for the actual response phase.

Pre-Positioning Activities:

• Finalized the Bill of Quantities (BOQ) for emergency shelter repair kits in coordination with the Shelter/NFIs Cluster and successfully procured and pre-positioned 250 emergency shelter kits prior to sEAP activation.
• Coordinated with community committees, CCCM actors, and Shelter/NFIs partners to finalize the contents of cleaning kits and successfully procured and pre-positioned 6 cleaning kits/tools (3 per targeted site).
• Finalized specifications and contents of first aid kits and stretchers and successfully procured and prepositioned 30 first aid kits and stretchers to support emergency preparedness and response activities.
• Coordinated with YRCS DM and IFRC logistics teams to finalize specifications and complete procurement of 10 megaphones for early warning and community alert dissemination prior to sEAP activation.
• Finalized and printed IEC materials, including posters and brochures containing early warning messages and practical guidance on flood risk reduction, shelter reinforcement, safety during thunderstorms and lightning, and hygiene practices during flooding.

title: AFG: Flood - 07-2026 - Afghanistan Flash Flood 2026 #2 (2026-07-25)
content:
Description

Following heavy and sustained rainfall, flash floods occurred in July 2026 across the country, affecting communities in Nuristan,Laghman, Parwan, Logar, Kabul, Kapisa, Panjsher,Nangarhar,Ghazni,Khost,Maidan Wardak,Paktika and Paktia provinces. Low-lying areas and settlements located along riverbeds were particularly impacted. The floods resulted in loss of life, injuries, and widespread damage to shelters, livelihoods and agricultural land, reflecting the broader pattern of seasonal flooding currently affecting several parts of the country.

According to preliminary information compiled by the Afghan Red Crescent Society (ARCS), more than 910 families were affected. The floods caused 31 deaths and 11 injuries, with 77 cases of missing persons reported. Shelter damage was significant, with 910 houses completely and partially damaged, particularly in several provinces of Nuristan,Laghman, Parwan, Logar, Kabul, Kapisa, Panjsher,Nangarhar,Ghazni,Khost,Maidan Wardak,Paktika and Paktia provinces. In addition, the floods had a severe impact on livelihoods, resulting in the loss of 330 livestock and damage to approximately 5240 jeribs of agricultural land, further increasing vulnerabilities among farming and pastoral households.

As part of ongoing support of ARCS, distributed 600 Parcel hot meal in Laghman Province ,NFI for one affected HHs in Maidan wardak province to the families who have been affected severely by floods.

ARCS, through its provincial branches and volunteers, is monitoring the evolving situation and conducting initial assessments in coordination with local authorities and Movement partners. Priority humanitarian needs identified include emergency shelter and essential household items for families whose homes were destroyed or damaged, food assistance and multipurpose cash support, as well as livelihood and agricultural recovery assistance, including livestock support. With possibility of further rainfall, affected communities remain at risk of additional flooding, underscoring the need for timely humanitarian support.

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 23 July 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Fatalities linked to settler attacks in 2026 have already surpassed the total recorded during all of 2025, with 18 Palestinians killed as of 20 July compared with 17 throughout 2025.
  • About 90 Palestinians were displaced by demolitions and settler attacks during the reporting period, most following a large-scale demolition carried out by Israeli authorities in a Bedouin community in Qalqiliya governorate.
  • Demolitions and settler attacks continued to affect Palestinian homes, water systems, schools and livelihood assets, further undermining access to essential services and community resilience.
  • In Gaza, deteriorating sexual and reproductive health conditions are placing pregnant women at growing risk: in the first half of 2026, nearly 4,000 miscarriage cases were recorded, severe maternal morbidity reached 82 cases per 1,000 deliveries, and more than 57 per cent of pregnant women were anemic.
  • Nearly 630,000 tonnes of debris have been cleared from roads and essential service facilities to date across the Gaza Strip, but this remains only a fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes generated since October 2023, much of which remains inaccessible.

Overview

Across the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT), humanitarian needs continue to deepen as insecurity, access restrictions, repeated displacement and the erosion of essential services affect Palestinians in both the Gaza Strip and the West Bank. In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, Israeli forces' operations, demolitions, settler violence and settlement expansion continued to drive displacement, casualties and property damage, with Bedouin and herding communities in Area C among the most affected. During the reporting period, demolitions and settler attacks displaced about 90 Palestinians and damaged homes, water and sanitation infrastructure and livelihood assets. Meanwhile, the number of fatalities linked to settler attacks in 2026 has already surpassed the total recorded during all of 2025.

In the Gaza Strip, civilians continued to face severe protection risks amid ongoing military operations, repeated displacement and widespread insecurity, while access constraints, shortages of essential supplies and funding gaps continued to hamper the humanitarian response. Deteriorating sexual and reproductive health indicators point to growing risks for women and girls, including high levels of pregnancy loss, maternal complications and anaemia. At the same time, overcrowded displacement sites, limited shelter capacity, damaged water and sanitation infrastructure, and the massive accumulation of debris continue to undermine safe living conditions and access to basic services, despite ongoing efforts to clear roads, restore critical infrastructure and facilitate the delivery of humanitarian assistance.

West Bank

The reporting period for this section is 14 to 20 July unless otherwise specified.

Across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, Israeli forces' operations, demolitions, settlement expansion, settler violence and movement restrictions continued to drive displacement, heighten protection risks, and undermine Palestinians' access to housing, livelihoods and essential services.

During the third week of July, Shelter Cluster partners reached approximately 1,180 people (228 households) through about 224 interventions, primarily minor-to-moderate shelter repairs, alongside essential non-food items, protection kits and, where feasible, cash assistance. Response prioritized communities affected by displacement, demolitions and settler violence, particularly in Nablus, Ramallah and Hebron governorates. Meanwhile, the prolonged displacement of more than 33,000 Palestine refugees from Tulkarm and Nur Shams refugee camps continued to generate significant shelter needs, but funding shortfalls continue to limit partners' capacity to scale up assistance.

Since the beginning of 2026, Child Protection partners have provided case management and referrals to specialized services for 758 children and caregivers affected by settler violence, Israeli forces' operations, movement restrictions, displacement and deteriorating socioeconomic conditions. Partners also provided cash-for-protection, in-kind assistance and clothing kits to 1,331 children and 211 caregivers.

Health Cluster partners continued to deliver life-saving services through a network of 870 health service points, including 230 mobile clinic locations. During the third week of July, mobile teams reached 232 of the 249 communities requiring these services (approximately 205,800 people), while about 10 Barrier-isolated communities in the Seam Zone remained inaccessible. Ongoing military operations, movement restrictions, settler violence, shortages of essential medicines and funding shortfalls continued to constrain humanitarian health operations.

Casualties

Between 14 and 20 July, Israeli forces shot and killed two Palestinian men and injured two others during a settler attack in Deir Jarir village, east of Ramallah, after dozens of settlers, some armed and accompanied by Israeli forces, raided the village while attempting to seize sheep. Separately, on 18 July, a 17-year-old Palestinian boy succumbed to wounds sustained six days earlier after Israeli settlers, accompanied by Israeli forces, attacked a Palestinian home in Al Mughayyir village, also in Ramallah governorate.

These incidents reflect a broader rise in fatalities linked to settler attacks. As of 20 July, 18 Palestinians had been killed in such incidents in 2026, including 12 by Israeli settlers, three by Israeli forces, and three where it remains disputed whether Israeli settlers or Israeli forces were responsible. This already exceeds the 17 fatalities recorded in all of 2025. More than half of those killed in settler attacks this year (10 of 18) were in Ramallah governorate.

Overall, during the reporting period, about 36 Palestinians, including two children and eight women, were injured by Israeli forces or settlers. More than 90 per cent were injured in the context of settler attacks, while the remainder were injured mainly during Israeli forces' raids and other operations. Nearly 30 Palestinians were injured by Israeli settlers, including nine during a single attack targeting Palestinian herders, among them five women, in Isfey al Fauqa community in Firing Zone 918, Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron governorate, where armed settlers assaulted residents while attempting to seize livestock.

Since the beginning of 2026, about 880 Palestinians have been injured in the context of settler attacks, including 720 by Israeli settlers and the remainder by Israeli forces, accounting for 56 per cent of all Palestinian injuries in the West Bank. The number of injuries by Israeli settlers linked to settler attacks has risen sharply, increasing from an average of one injury every three days in 2020 to two injuries per day in 2025 and more than three per day so far in 2026.

Settler Attacks and Property Damage

During the reporting period, at least 50 settler attacks that resulted in casualties, property damage, or both were documented, of which nearly 60 per cent were in Ramallah and Nablus governorates. Since the beginning of 2026, more than 1,330 such incidents have been recorded across 250 Palestinian communities, averaging more than six incidents per day.

During the reporting period, five settler attacks targeting Palestinian homes and community infrastructure were documented in Burqa (Ramallah), Khalet al Luza (Bethlehem) and At Tuwani in Masafer Yatta (Hebron). The predominantly night-time attacks involved arson, vandalism, stone throwing and attempted break-ins, damaging at least five homes, a mosque, a community dairy factory and other civilian property, including water infrastructure, a livelihood vehicle and a residential solar water heating system. At least 570 Palestinians were directly affected, including about 560 residents of At Tuwani, among them 58 farmers who rely on the village dairy factory for their livelihoods. Beyond the physical damage, the attacks disrupted livelihoods and community services and heightened protection concerns, particularly following repeated night-time raids on residential areas.

Similar protection concerns were reported in Jalud village, south of Nablus governorate, where Israeli settlers have continued to occupy an under-construction Palestinian house since 29 June. As of the end of the reporting period, the takeover had effectively isolated three neighbouring households comprising nine people from the village centre and essential services. Since early July, settlers have repeatedly vandalized nearby homes and infrastructure, including water pipelines, water tanks and electricity cables, while preventing residents from carrying out repairs. As of the end of the reporting period, the affected households had been without electricity for more than four days after coordination through the Palestinian District Coordination Liaison (DCL) to facilitate repairs was unsuccessful. The families remain increasingly isolated, with limited access to water, electricity, and essential services.

Access to Water

According to the Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) Cluster, access to water and sanitation services across the West Bank remains constrained by damage to infrastructure resulting from demolitions and settler attacks. Settler attacks affecting WASH structures have been concentrated in Ramallah and Tubas governorates, while demolitions have primarily affected Jerusalem, Hebron and Bethlehem governorates. Nablus and Jericho governorates have been significantly affected by both types of incidents. The loss of water infrastructure increases reliance on emergency water trucking and undermines access to sufficient water for domestic use and livestock, particularly in Bedouin and herding communities where alternative sources are limited.

The demolition of WASH infrastructure has increased significantly in recent years. In 2025 and during the first seven months of 2026, Israeli authorities demolished an average of about 14 WASH structures per month in Area C – more than three times the monthly average recorded between 2009 and 2024 (see graph).

At the same time, settler attacks continue to affect water infrastructure. Since the beginning of 2026, water tanks have accounted for more than half of the approximately 160 WASH structures damaged, destroyed or seized in settler attacks across the West Bank, followed by water networks, household connections and other water infrastructure. Recent attacks have increasingly targeted shared water infrastructure serving entire communities. In June alone, water networks were vandalized in at least six communities, disrupting water supply to all or large parts of those communities.

This pattern was reflected in several incidents during the reporting period. On 19 July, Israeli settlers from surrounding settlement outposts attacked Nkheila, one of 18 Bedouin communities located within the area designated for the planned expansion of the E1 settlement plan, in Jerusalem governorate. Settlers damaged water pipelines serving approximately 200 residents, restricted access to grazing areas, and took over the nearby Ein Rawabi spring, a key water source for the community's livestock. According to residents, repeated attacks and harassment have prevented repairs to the damaged pipelines, leaving the community dependent on inadequate alternative water sources for domestic and livestock use.

Similarly, on 21 July, Israeli settlers from a newly established settlement outpost took over a Palestinian-owned water cistern in Khallet al Hums, in Masafer Yatta, Hebron governorate, by installing an electric pump. According to local sources, the takeover has prevented at least 90 people from accessing three water cisterns used for domestic purposes and livestock, exacerbating water shortages in the community.

To mitigate these challenges, WASH partners continue to implement emergency and resilience-focused interventions across the West Bank, including water trucking, the distribution of hygiene kits, mobile latrines and water storage solutions. Since the beginning of 2026, partners have provided water trucking support to approximately 60 communities and locations hosting displaced families. Most assistance has focused on Bedouin and herding communities in Masafer Yatta and the northern Jordan Valley, where recurrent settler violence, demolitions and restrictions on access to water sources have heightened humanitarian needs. Partners have also provided support to highly vulnerable communities in Ramallah and Jerusalem governorates affected by demolitions, settler violence and acute water shortages, as well as to locations hosting displaced families in Hebron, Nablus, Salfit, Jericho, Jenin and Tulkarm governorates.

Access to Education

On 21 July, the Khallet al Miyah Municipality, in coordination with a legal aid organization, secured a temporary injunction suspending the execution of a demolition order against Ar Rifa'iyya Mixed Basic School, east of Yatta in Hebron governorate. The school, which serves 175 students from kindergarten to Grade 7 and employs 14 staff, had faced imminent demolition after an Israeli court rejected the community's appeal on 8 July (see previous Sitrep).

While the injunction temporarily delays the demolition, it comes amid growing concerns over the impact of settler violence, displacement and demolition threats on access to education. According to the Education Cluster, 20 of the 84 Palestinian schools currently subject to demolition or related orders are assessed to be at high risk of abandonment due to settler violence, demolitions and related displacement risks, placing about 1,600 students at heightened risk of educational disruption. Since 2023, the displacement of Bedouin and herding communities has led to the abandonment of 10 schools that previously served more than 460 students. Seven of these schools have since been vandalized and three demolished, including two by Israeli settlers. Although Education Cluster partners have facilitated school transfers and temporary learning arrangements, many children continue to face longer journeys to school, overcrowded classrooms, transportation challenges and an increased risk of dropping out.

Throughout 2026, Education Cluster partners reached more than 60,000 students through remedial and catch-up learning programmes, rehabilitated 30 schools, provided transportation assistance and other protective measures to more than 2,600 students and education personnel in high-risk areas, and delivered education-specific cash assistance, psychosocial support and legal aid. However, chronic underfunding continues to constrain the response. As of mid-2026, less than 10 per cent of the Education Cluster's Flash Appeal requirements had been funded, limiting the cluster's capacity to sustain emergency interventions and support longer-term learning recovery and resilience.

Displacement

During the reporting period, Israeli authorities demolished 61 Palestinian-owned structures for lacking Israeli-issued building permits, which are nearly impossible for Palestinians to obtain. These included 56 structures in Area C, displacing 15 households comprising 79 people, three structures in Area B, and two structures, including one home, in East Jerusalem, displacing five people. Overall, the demolished structures comprised 18 homes, four uninhabited residential structures, 32 WASH and agricultural structures, and seven livelihood-related structures.

Most of the displacement in Area C occurred in the Arab al Jahalin/Wadi Mu'nes Bedouin community, near Immatin village in Qalqiliya governorate, where Israeli authorities demolished 37 structures, including 19 donor-funded structures. As a result, 13 Bedouin households comprising 64 people, including 34 children, were displaced. The demolitions included 15 residential shelters, 13 latrines, nine livestock shelters and multiple water tanks, severely affecting shelter conditions, access to WASH services and livestock-based livelihoods. Many of the demolished structures had been provided as humanitarian assistance in 2021 and 2022. Humanitarian partners subsequently delivered emergency assistance, including food parcels, bedding, kitchen and hygiene kits, a one-off multipurpose cash payment, mental health and psycho-social support (MHPSS) services, WASH support, emergency tents and assistance to restore livestock shelters.

Separately, one Palestinian family was displaced after about 40 masked Israeli settlers, believed to be from Gilad settlement, raided the western side of Tell village, south of Nablus governorate, on 18 July and set fire to a Palestinian home. The family fled minutes before the house was completely destroyed, resulting in the displacement of five people. During the same incident, settlers also set fire to nearby Palestinian agricultural land before withdrawing.

The incident in Tell village reflects a broader pattern of recurrent settler attacks and related access restrictions that has intensified across the West Bank since January 2023, particularly in Bedouin and herding communities in Area C. Between January 2023 and 6 July 2026, 123 Palestinian communities experienced full or partial displacement, including 47 that were fully displaced. More than 6,200 Palestinians, including over 3,000 children, were displaced during this period, including more than 2,300 people in 2026 alone. Repeated displacement, attacks on homes and infrastructure, and restrictions on access to land and essential services continue to increase humanitarian needs and undermine community resilience.

For key figures and additional breakdowns of casualties, displacement, and settler violence between January 2005 and May 2026, please refer to the OCHA West Bank May 2026 Snapshot. For key figures on the impact of settler attacks, please refer to the West Bank – The Impact of Settler Attacks, January 2023 – April 2026

Gaza Strip

This section covers 13 to 19 July unless otherwise specified.

The humanitarian situation across the Gaza Strip remains critical, with ongoing military operations, insecurity and repeated displacement continuing to drive humanitarian needs, heighten protection risks and disrupt access to essential services. Civilians, including children and frontline service providers, continue to face serious safety risks, while sexual and reproductive health indicators are deteriorating amid the cumulative effects of displacement, food insecurity, and the degradation of health services.

At the same time, severe funding constraints, access restrictions, shortages of supplies and operational challenges are limiting partners' ability to sustain and expand assistance, including in displacement sites where living conditions remain dire. Although some progress has been made in debris clearance and the entry of supplies, needs continue to outpace available resources, leaving many vulnerable people unable to access the support and services they require.

According to the Ministry of Health (MoH) in Gaza, which operates under the de facto authorities, 59 Palestinians were reported killed, including those who died of wounds and had their bodies retrieved from under the rubble, and over 190 people were injured between 15 and 22 July. This brings the overall reported casualty toll since the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 to 1,180 fatalities and 3,810 injuries.

Against this backdrop, civilians, including children, and service providers continued to face significant security risks across Gaza, with incidents affecting both communities and service delivery points. On 14 July, a child was reportedly killed by stray gunfire in Al Mawasi area, in Rafah. The following day, on 15 July, a female teacher was injured after reportedly being shot by a bullet fired by Israeli forces while she was working inside a temporary learning space (TLS) west of Khan Younis, approximately 3.3 kilometres from the “Yellow Line”. Separately, on 13 July, a bullet landed in the yard of another TLS in Rafah, forcing the suspension of all activities and its interim closure. Several additional cases of children being killed or injured were also reported during the reporting period, underscoring the urgent need for enhanced protection measures and safe access to services.

Sexual and Reproductive Health Indicators Continue to Deteriorate Across Gaza

Sexual and reproductive health indicators continued to deteriorate across the Gaza Strip during the first half of 2026, reflecting the cumulative effects of crisis, displacement, food insecurity, and the degradation of essential health services. Between January and June 2026, over 3,950 miscarriage cases were recorded in the Bayan Dashboard, the MoH’s reproductive health information platform, which consolidates data from partners providing reproductive health services across the Strip. The miscarriage rate reached 208.5 per 1,000 live births, a 3.3-fold increase compared with the second half of 2025 and peaked at 377.3 per 1,000 live births in April 2026. Nearly 74 per cent of pregnancy losses occurred during the first trimester, while 57.1 per cent of pregnant women were anaemic, highlighting the worsening health and nutritional status of women across the Gaza Strip.

The number of deliveries declined by 3.2 per cent in the first six months of 2026 compared with the first half of 2025, with sharper monthly decreases observed since April. Alongside the increase in miscarriages, severe maternal morbidity reached 82 cases per 1,000 deliveries, while caesarean sections accounted for 49.2 per cent of all deliveries, largely driven by emergency procedures among women arriving in critical condition. Haemorrhages, hypertension, and infections accounted for 92 per cent of severe maternal complications, underscoring the increasing severity of maternal health risks.

To better understand the drivers of these adverse outcomes, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), in collaboration with humanitarian partners, is commissioning a comprehensive study to identify risk factors, service gaps and barriers to care, and to inform an evidence-based response to strengthen maternal and newborn health services. Meanwhile, UNFPA continues to distribute reproductive health supplies, dispatching medicines, contraceptives, midwifery supplies and equipment sufficient to support approximately 1,950 women and girls between 13 and 19 July. These supplies were provided to the Al Helou, Al Awda and Nasser hospitals, as well as to medical points operated by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF). Additionally, over 3,700 postpartum kits were distributed to 15 maternity hospitals, based on recent delivery figures from the Bayan Dashboard.

Debris Management Supports Access and Early Recovery Amid Major Constraints.

The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)’s debris management efforts continue to play a critical role in restoring humanitarian access and improving access to essential services, markets and neighbourhoods across the Gaza Strip. Despite highly constrained operating conditions, significant progress has been achieved in clearing conflict-generated debris and supporting early recovery interventions.

To date, nearly 630,000 tonnes of debris have been cleared in a risk-managed manner from roads and essential service facilities. In parallel, 231,334 tonnes of concrete debris have been crushed across five dedicated debris-crushing sites, generating materials that are being reused to support local recovery efforts. This includes 184,191 tonnes of crushed concrete used to pave 264,873 square metres of roads and provide foundations for shelters and essential service facilities, helping to improve mobility and service delivery in affected areas.

However, debris management operations continue to face substantial challenges. Volatile security conditions, access constraints, restrictions on the entry of critical machinery and spare parts, and severe shortages of fuel and engine oil continue to limit the pace and scale of activities.

The scale of needs also remains overwhelming. The volume of debris cleared to date represents only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris generated, much of which remains inaccessible. This underscores the magnitude of the recovery effort required and the need for sustained access, equipment and resources to expand debris management operations across the Gaza Strip.

Dire Conditions in Displacement Sites Heighten Health and Protection Risks

Living conditions in displacement sites across the Gaza Strip remain extremely concerning, particularly in collective centres where access constraints and limited site management capacity continue to hinder the identification of urgent needs and timely response. During the reporting period, the Site Management Cluster analysed 181 non-UNRWA collective centres hosting approximately 28,000 households (138,258 people). Many of these sites lack active site management support for routine monitoring, community engagement, care and maintenance, and the referral of priority needs. Although 93 per cent of assessed sites reported having site management committees, only 42 per cent of these committees had received training on site management approaches, humanitarian principles, protection principles, and codes of conduct, leaving many sites reliant on overstretched community structures to address daily challenges.

Recent site monitoring findings highlight severe risks to health, safety, and dignity. Sixty-nine per cent of assessed sites reported visible sewage within the compound, largely due to damaged or blocked sewage systems, increasing the risk of contamination and disease transmission. Inadequate sanitation facilities have forced some families to improvise toilets inside their shelters or use buckets and plastic bags, while rodent infestations have been reported in several sites. In addition, 80 per cent of sites lack functional lighting, limiting safe movement at night and heightening protection risks, particularly for women, girls, older people, and people with specific needs. Existing Women and Girls’ Safe Spaces cover less than half of the 537 sites with active Site Management Cluster presence according to the latest joint service mapping by the Site Management and Protection cluster. This is equivalent to roughly 270 sites, or only about 17 per cent of the approximately 1,600 displacement sites mapped across the Gaza Strip, leaving many women and girls without access to essential support services. Some school buildings currently hosting displaced families also show structural damage from previous military operations, raising concerns about potential building collapse.

Site Management Cluster partners continue to support collective centres where possible, including through care and maintenance activities implemented via Cash for Work initiatives, which have reached 42 per cent of the assessed sites. However, needs continue to far exceed available capacity, underscoring the urgent need for additional support to improve living conditions and address critical infrastructure, protection, and public health risks in displacement sites across the Gaza Strip.

Incoming Supplies

Ashdod remained the primary upstream route for humanitarian cargo entering Gaza during the reporting period, with 334 UN and humanitarian partner trucks offloaded, marking a continued improvement following the scanner breakdown between 16 June and 2 July, which had disrupted cargo flow and contributed to a backlog. This represents a 21 per cent increase compared with the previous week, when 276 trucks were offloaded, and an 81 per cent increase compared with two weeks earlier, when 185 trucks were offloaded.

Despite this improvement, access and logistical constraints continued to affect the predictability and volume of incoming supplies. On 19 July, a scanner malfunction at the Sheikh Hussein Bridge-Jordan River Crossing prevented 14 trucks carrying water, sanitation and shelter items for two partners from crossing. Although the scanner was subsequently repaired and operations resumed, the delay meant that no cargo carrying items designated as “dual-use” from Jordan was offloaded during the reporting period. Such items, once cleared by the Israeli authorities, are currently authorized to offload at Kerem Shalom only once per week; as a result, the delayed cargo missed the available offloading window. Humanitarian partners continue to advocate for the authorization to have two weekly offloading days for “dual-use” items, particularly to reduce the backlog from Jordan.

The closure of the Zikim Crossing on 24 May has further reduced aid throughput and removed direct cargo access to northern Gaza, with approved cargo now channelled through the only available crossing, Kerem Shalom, in the south. Following the October 2025 ceasefire announcement, when Zikim and Kerem Shalom were both operational and Kissufim was used intermittently, UN and partners’ aid throughput averaged 749 trucks per week. After Zikim was temporarily closed following the 28 February regional escalation and later reopened for six weeks from 12 April to 22 May, weekly throughput averaged 639 trucks. Since the final closure of Zikim on 24 May, average weekly throughput has fallen to 517 trucks, representing a 31 per cent decrease compared with the period when Zikim and Kerem Shalom were both operational, and a 19 per cent decrease compared with the six-week period when Zikim temporarily reopened.

On the commercial front, data from the Gaza Chamber of Commerce, shared with the Cash Working Group (CWG), indicate that the private sector collected 828 truckloads into Gaza between 13 and 19 July. Of these, 419 truckloads (50 per cent) contained food items, 21 (2.5 per cent) cooking gas, 46 (5.5 per cent) hygiene products, and 88 (11 per cent) shelter materials. Smaller quantities included baby care items, insecticide, stationary supplies and solid fuel. In addition, 238 truckloads (28 per cent) contained non-essential goods, in line with the pattern observed in previous weeks.

According to the Gaza Chamber of Commerce, prices remained relatively stable, with only minor differences (+/- 5 per cent) for fresh products, compared to the preceding week. However, prices of baby diapers and infant formula increased by 12 and 8 per cent, respectively, likely due to reduced supply and continued demand. Overall inflation moderated slightly in July, averaging 187 per cent compared with 194 per cent in June. The combination of inflation and limited income-generating opportunities continue to undermine purchasing power and increase reliance on humanitarian assistance.

The UN is only able to confirm the entry of supplies tracked by UN 2720. For breakdowns of those, see the online UN 2720 Mechanism Dashboard.

For a detailed account of the latest humanitarian operations in Gaza, see Annex 1 below.

title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #04 (Reporting period: 15 - 23 July 2026)
content:
This Situation Report provides an overview of the twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026 (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.

Summary Points

• LTC Telecoms in Venezuela is working with government authorities, mobile network operators, internet service providers (ISPs), the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), and other partners to restore critical communications, and prioritize support in the most affected areas.

• LTC Telecoms is strengthening power continuity across response sites through real-time monitoring of battery systems linked to solar-powered internet connectivity. This provides timely visibility on energy gaps, allowing teams to monitor and take corrective action to keep critical internet connectivity services operational for over 1,400 humanitarian responders and affected communities.

• Grupo Telefónica has provided a charging kiosk at each of Polideportivo and César Nieves, supporting 48 power-strip connections, enabling affected people to charge mobile phones and other Information Communication Technology (ICT) devices to maintain access to communication, information and basic services. The kiosks will be returned to Grupo Telefónica once the emergency transitions fully into recovery.

title: Dengue in the Pacific: Multicountry Situation (As of 27 July 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Since 1 January 2025, twelve dengue outbreaks have been reported across Pacific Island Countries and Areas (PICs).

• During 2025, dengue outbreaks were reported in American Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Nauru, Samoa, Tonga, and Tuvalu. A total of 21,258 confirmed cases and 21 deaths were recorded across the Pacific. Fatalities were reported in Fiji (n=8), Samoa (n=7), Tonga (n=3), Nauru (n=2), and Kiribati (n=1).

• Between 1 January 2026 and 2 July 2026, a total of 4 466 dengue confirmed cases, 173 hospitalisations and 3 deaths have been reported across the Pacific.

• The Pacific Syndromic Surveillance System (PSSS) has reported a total of 8 723 Dengue-like Illness (DLI) cases to date, a lower trend compared to the same period last year. • In 2026 dengue outbreaks were officially declared in New Caledonia, Tonga and Shefa province Vanuatu.

• The most affected countries and areas in 2026 include: Cook Islands, French Polynesia, Samoa, and New Caledonia. These account for 94% of confirmed cases.

• Dengue serotype-1 (DENV-1) and serotype-2 (DENV-2) are currently in circulation. • The Cook Islands officially declared the end of its dengue outbreak on 25 May 2026.

• As of 27 July 2026:

o The dengue outbreak remains ongoing in Shefa Province, Vanuatu, with dengue virus serotype 1 (DENV-1) continuing to circulate.

o Low levels of transmission are observed in American Samoa, Kiribati, New Caledonia, Samoa, and Tonga.

o Wallis and Futuna is under monitoring, following recent reports of community transmission in both Wallis and Futuna.

title: Yemen Agrometeorological Early Warning Information Bulletin, July-September 2026 (EN/AR)
content:
Executive Summary

Analysis of the July–September (Kharif) 2026 seasonal rainfall forecast, vegetation conditions, and agricultural stress indicators suggest a high probability of widespread drought across Yemen's rainfed agricultural areas.

The forecasted rainfall anomalies are broadly consistent with climatic patterns typically associated with El Niño episodes. While direct attribution cannot be made at this stage, the expected below-average rainfall may be influenced by evolving large-scale climate conditions linked to El Niño, alongside other regional and local climatic drivers.

Key Projections:

  • Large parts of Yemen are expected to receive below-normal rainfall during JAS (July-August-September) 2026, with deficits exceeding 40% below the Long-Term Average (LTA) in many agricultural areas.
  • Widespread vegetation stress is anticipated, with the Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) projected to decline to severe and extreme drought levels in several key agricultural governorates.
  • An estimated 53% of the population in Yemen are projected to face IPC Phase 3+ (Crisis or worse) acute food insecurity situation during 2026.

This anticipated climatic shock coincides with a deteriorating food security situation driven by contracted humanitarian assistance, regional conflict, and economic instability. Together, these factors are expected to intensify pressure on agricultural livelihoods and household food security, underscoring the urgent need for timely preparedness and anticipatory action.

title: Lebanon Health Emergency Situation Update #30 (23 July 2026)
content:
Situation overview

Impact of ongoing airstrikes

• Since 2 July 2026, the security situation in Lebanon has remained fragile, with ongoing security incidents in southern Lebanon continuing to impede safe and sustainable returns, exacerbate protection risks, and disrupt service delivery and infrastructure rehabilitation.

• Daily reports of airstrikes, artillery shelling, demolitions and sonic booms have continued across South and Nabatieh governorates, particularly in Bint Jbeil, Marjayoun, Nabatieh and Tyre districts.

• These incidents, together with extensive infrastructure damage and the presence of unexploded ordnance (UXO), continue to limit safe movement and delay the return of displaced populations.

• According to the Disaster Risk Management (DRM) Unit, a total of 27,668 hostilities had been recorded since 2 March 2026 as of 14 July, including 1,885 incidents reported between 1 and 14 July 2026.

Casualties and injury overview

• MoPH reported a cumulative number of casualties since 2nd March has reached 16,560 including 4,328 deaths (including 253 children and 392 women) and 12,232 injuries as of 6:00pm on July 22, 2026., Fig.1 Causality Distribution by day since March 2, 2026.

• Out of the total injuries, 6,307 (51%) were treated at Emergency rooms as outpatient, 4,966 (41%) admitted to regular wards and 959 (8%) admitted to ICU.

• For total casualties since March 2,2026, the majority of fatalities and injuries occurred in Nabatiyeh (7,075 casualties), followed by the South (6,951 casualties), and Mount Lebanon (1,202 casualties), Additional cases were reported across other governorates. Fig 2.

• Of the total casualties, 14,286 (86%) were male and 2,274 (14%) females.

• 8% of the total casualties are children, 253 children are dead, and 1,036 children are injured. Fig 3. Shows age distribution of casualties.

• Nationality data shows that 15,632 casualties (94%) were Lebanese, 536 casualties (3%) were Syrian, 234 casualties (2%) were Palestinian, and 158 casualties (1%) from other nationalities, Fig 4.

• Between 17 April and 22 July 2026 (ceasefire period), MoPH reported a cumulative number of casualties of 6,137, including 1,822 deaths and 4,315 injured. Fig.5. Casualty Distribution by Day since April 17, 2026.

• Out of a total of 6,137 post-ceasefire casualties, 5,383 were male (88%) and 754 were female (12%), while children accounted for 6% of the total.

• The majority of cases were reported from South (3,065) and Nabatiyeh (2,795). The toll also included 1,822 deaths. Among the injured, 1,818 were admitted to regular wards, 2,094 were treated in emergency rooms, and 403 required admissions to intensive care units

title: UNICEF South Sudan Humanitarian Situation Report No. 4, 01-31 May 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Between January and May, over 420,800 people were newly displaced due to conflict, with Jonglei State accounting for the majority. Recurrent displacement, insecurity and continued population movements are overwhelming already fragile services, widening gaps in health, education, WASH and protection, particularly in conflict-affected areas.
  • Public health emergencies continue to strain South Sudan’s fragile health system. Cholera remains the primary concern, with more than 104,648 suspected cases and 1,678 deaths reported as of 31 May 2026. The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in neighbouring DRC and Uganda has heightened preparedness measures due to cross-border transmission risks. Concurrent measles outbreaks and circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV) in Upper Nile and Central Equatoria highlight persistent immunization and surveillance gaps. Rising access constraints further hinder assistance delivery..
  • The 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal remains only 43 per cent funded, with critical shortfalls in WASH and education limiting life-saving response efforts amid escalating needs.

title: Yemen Market and Trade Bulletin June 2026 - Issued on 25th July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

SHORT-TERM OUTLOOK AND IMPLICATIONS ON FOOD SECURITY: Yemen faces a critical surge in acute food insecurity, with over 53% of the population projected in IPC Phase 3+ (Crisis or worse) and the world's highest burden of IPC Phase 4 (Emergency) conditions. This baseline vulnerability—where over 50% of rural households depend on agriculture for survival—is compounded by severe macro-economic shocks, including critical funding gaps (~14% funded as of June), currency depreciation, poor purchasing power, and trade disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea. The crisis is now intensified by an impending El Niño climate shock that actively suppresses the Yemeni Kharif monsoon through July–September 2026. Meteorological models project a >70% probability of below-normal rainfall nationwide, with southern, central, and western agricultural zones experiencing >80% rainfall deficits and extreme heat stress. This drought threatens primary Kharif cereal and vegetable crops, accelerates livestock pasture degradation, and threatens to push the share of agricultural households requiring emergency assistance from 36% to 55%—underscoring an urgent requirement before mid-August to prevent further significant deterioration across key priority governorates (Al Hudaydah, Taizz, Ibb, Dhamar, Al Mahwit).

title: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak Situation Report No. 10
content:
According to the World Health Organization, as of 15 July, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 2,124 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus (BVD), including 828 deaths. In Uganda, no new cases had been reported since 21 June, and the country began the 42-day period of enhanced disease surveillance required before the end of the outbreak can be declared, following the discharge of the most recent case from treatment after two negative tests. Continued surveillance and preparedness measures remain essential to prevent resurgence and mitigate the risk of cross-border transmission while transmission persists in neighboring DRC. key highlights include :

  • In total 8.6 million health screenings have been conducted at points of entry and points of control across affected and at-risk countries since the start of the response.
  • During the reporting period alone, IOM supported more than 1.68 million screenings in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, generating 74 alerts and facilitating the verification and referral of suspected cases.
  • 6.6 million people have been reached through risk communication and community engagement activities, helping communities access timely information and reduce transmission risks.
  • IOM is currently supporting 215 points of entry and points of control across the region, strengthening surveillance, screening, infection prevention and cross-border preparedness efforts.
  • Preparedness and response activities continued in priority countries, including DRC, Uganda, Burundi, Rwanda and South Sudan, while readiness measures were reinforced across other at-risk countries in the region.
  • IOM’s mobility tracking and population mobility mapping work continues to support governments in identifying high-risk mobility corridors and strengthening cross-border surveillance and coordination

The outbreak continues to unfold in a complex operational environment marked by insecurity, displacement and population mobility. As transmission persists in eastern DRC, sustained investment in surveillance, border health measures, community engagement, and support to displaced and mobile populations remains critical to containing the outbreak and preventing cross-border spread. title: Lebanon: Flash Update #46 - Escalation of hostilities in Lebanon (as of 23 July 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • At least 4,329 deaths and 12,233 injuries recorded due to hostilities since 2 March, with 349 fatalities and 229 injuries since the latest ceasefire announcement, according to the Ministry of Public Health.
  • Two attacks on health care workers were reported, with an explosive device injuring two paramedics on 21 July and an airstrike injuring two paramedics on 23 July (WHO, MoPH)
  • 753,024 people reported returning to their areas of origin, while 375,090 people remain displaced, including 29,500 Internally Displaced Persons (over 53 per cent women and girls) in 271 collective shelters as of 23 July.
  • Humanitarian and protection needs remain acute, driven by the destruction of homes and services, prolonged displacement, explosive ordnance risks, protection concerns, and declining coping capacities.

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #16 (22 to 23 July 2026)
content:
The sixteenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 22 to 23 July.

Highlights

Between 22 and 23 July, IOM continued its multisectoral response in transitory camps and affected communities through interventions in shelter and site coordination, health, protection, WASH and information management.

To date, IOM has reached 8,676 unique individuals through 16,265 instances of assistance and services, mainly in shelter and transitory camp coordination, health, WASH and protection.

IOM and its partner Fundación Vivienda Popular have distributed 3,175 kitchen sets, 3,617 tarpaulins, 2,115 buckets, 1,759 solar lamps and 819 shelter kits to affected households.

IOM activities

IOM continued managing and coordinating five transitory camps in La Guaira and advanced the operational transition of three of them to the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC).

At Tanaguarena Golf Course, IOM continued preparations to expand accommodation and service provision capacity, while in Mare Abajo II accommodation capacity was updated with 206 bunk beds and 635 mattresses recorded.

In WASH, IOM continued expanding access to safe water storage and hygiene items. To date, 1,552 collapsible water containers, 1,091 hygiene kits and 93 water containers have been distributed.

IOM and its partner Ven Da Tu Mano have provided 6,194 health assistance and services, including primary healthcare, mental health and psychosocial support. Mobile health and MHPSS teams remained operational at José María Vargas Sports Complex and César Nieves Stadium.

IOM finalized the Household Survey in Transitory Camps and the analysis of mobility flows during the first 15 days of July, while advancing preparations for the assessment of 107 transitory camps.

In protection, IOM continued providing guidance, legal assistance, documentation support and referrals to specialized services, with 218 protection assistance and services recorded to date.

IOM planned response

IOM will continue the operational transition of three camps to NRC, infrastructure improvements and service delivery activities, while strengthening WASH, health, mental health and protection services.

It will also strengthen camp and mobility monitoring, advance assessments of transitory camps and affected populations, and continue coordination with authorities and humanitarian partners.

title: Situation Report No.7: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), 23 July 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• More than three weeks after the two earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June 2026, affecting at least seven states, the emergency response remains active. While the most acute phase of rescue, trauma care and immediate postdisaster surgery has eased, priorities are now focused on sustaining essential health services, strengthening referral pathways, supporting temporary camps and preventing public health risks.

• The health response continues transitioning from emergency care to early recovery, prioritizing restoration of integrated health service networks, continuity of specialized care, and implementation of the Ministry of Health’s National Mental Health Response Plan.

• Integrated epidemiological surveillance continues to reinforce early detection, laboratory verification and environmental risk monitoring. PAHO/WHO supported the roll-out of a real-time surveillance dashboard and the delivery of 1.15 million vaccine doses donated by Brazil to strengthen national preparedness.

• PAHO/WHO continues supporting the Ministry of Popular Power for Health (MPPS) through the deployment of its Regional Response Team, covering health emergency coordination, logistics, information management, epidemiology, laboratory, WASH, immunization, risk communication and community engagement, and EMT coordination. In coordination with the MPPS, PAHO/WHO is also supporting the virtual CICOM and EMT mobilization, with fourteen EMTs now operational across La Guaira, Caracas, Miranda, and Aragua, increasing clinical capacity in the affected areas.

• PAHO/WHO continued supporting the response through the delivery of computers to strengthen on-site epidemiological surveillance and body bags for the dignified management of the deceased, and through the coordination of in-kind donations from seven partners, most recently from Direct Relief: water purification tablets covering 20 days of chlorinated supply, medicines, and hygiene kits. A second distribution of TESK and IEHK kits to 18 health facilities and 36 transitional camps is planned.

title: Guatemala: Earthquake - DREF Final Report (MDRGT026)
content:
Description of the Event

What happened, where and when?

On 8 July 2025, the central region of Guatemala was shaken by a series of earthquakes with epicenters located in the departments of Sacatepéquez and Escuintla. These seismic events aected several localities in those departments, as well as municipalities within the department of Guatemala.

According to ocial reports, the rst earthquake occurred at 3:11 p.m. with a magnitude of 5.2, triggering a seismic sequence that reached its peak at 3:41 p.m. with a second tremor measuring magnitude 5.6. Both events had their epicenter in Santa María de Jesús, located in the department of Sacatepéquez.

Information from the National Institute of Seismology, Volcanology, Meteorology and Hydrology (INSIVUMEH) indicates that by 15 July— exactly one week after the initial event—a total of 1,062 earthquakes had been recorded, 36 of which were reported as felt by the population. The seismic activity was concentrated primarily along the border area between Sacatepéquez, Escuintla, and Guatemala departments.

INSIVUMEH further reported that the focal mechanism analysis of the seismic sequence was conducted using FMNEAR software, conrming that the earthquakes were related to ruptures in normal and strike-slip fault systems. The solutions obtained were considered high quality, with condence levels above 70%, providing a high degree of precision to the applied seismic model and allowing for an accurate understanding of the magnitude and characteristics of the events.

On the same day, 8 July, the National Coordinator for Disaster Reduction (CONRED) announced the declaration of a nationwide Institutional Orange Alert. This measure was taken in response to the recent seismic activity as well as the presence of multiple concurrent threats posing risks to the population. As part of the alert, response plans were activated at local, municipal, and departmental levels, and the public was urged to follow the authorities' guidance and act responsibly.

On 9 July 2025, the Ministry of Public Health and Social Assistance (MSPAS) issued a statement announcing the activation of an Institutional Red Alert for the health service networks in the departments of Sacatepéquez, Escuintla, and Guatemala. This decision was made within the framework of the "Institutional Operational Protocol for Geological Threats" with the goal of anticipating potential impacts on health infrastructure and ensuring the continuity of essential health services, even in the event of aftershocks or additional seismic events.

On 12 July, the Municipal Coordinator for Disaster Reduction (COMRED) declared a Municipal Institutional Red Alert in the municipality of Santa María de Jesús due to the emergency caused by seismic activity.

Following this declaration, the emergency response became the responsibility of CONRED at the departmental level in Sacatepéquez. In the departments of Escuintla and Guatemala, the response was coordinated by CONRED at the national level.

By the end of 2025, seismic activity associated with the July earthquake sequence had decreased compared with the initial emergency period. However, seismic monitoring continued throughout the year, as Guatemala remained exposed to recurrent seismic activity due to its geological conditions.

According to INSIVUMEH, a total of 11,811 seismic events were recorded nationwide in 2025, of which 397 were reported as felt by the population. The highest levels of seismic activity were recorded in July and August, with 2,533 and 2,246 seismic events respectively. July also reported the highest number of felt earthquakes, with 145 events, followed by August with 75.

Although seismic events continued to be monitored until the end of the year, no additional major humanitarian impacts directly linked to the July earthquake sequence were identied in the available information by the end of the operation.

title: WFP Sudan Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • In June, WFP reached 3.7 million people, the highest monthly number in 2026, driven by WFP’s strong logistical and procurement capacity, ability to access hard-to-reach areas, close coordination with partners and government counterparts, and the scale-up of both in-kind food assistance and cash-based transfers (CBT).
  • Of all the people reached, 1 million received assistance in areas classified as at Risk of Famine (RoF).
  • WFP reached 1.4 million people through CBT in June, also the highest monthly reach achieved since the onset of the conflict.
  • WFP is facing severe funding constraints. Without additional resources, WFP's food stocks are expected to be exhausted by September, while funding for lifesaving CBT assistance is projected to run out in August, leaving millions of vulnerable people without support.

title: WFP Zambia Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • WFP and partners supported livelihood interventions that reached 1,000 refugee households and 200 host-community households in the Mantapala Refugee Settlement, strengthening climate-smart agriculture, irrigation, and seed systems to support long-term resilience and recovery.
  • Preparations commenced for a South-South learning exchange with Namibia to share Zambia’s experience in school feeding programme design, procurement systems, and coordination mechanisms, strengthening regional collaboration and positioning Zambia as a leader in Home-Grown School Meals programming.
  • WFP’s Vulnerability Analysis and Mapping (VAM) monitoring indicated a favourable food security outlook in June, supported by the strong 2025/26 harvest, improved food availability, declining inflation, and a reduction in the national cost of the basic food basket.

title: WFP Ethiopia Country Brief July 2026
content:
• WFP reached 1.8 million food insecure people with 10,700 metric tons of food and USD 4.5 million in cash assistance across all activities.
  • WFP continued to provide fuel to partners through On-Demand Services (ODS) to mitigate fuel supply constraints and address earlier delays.
  • WFP will provide food assistance to new South Sudan arrivals in the Gambella Region.
  • WFP supported 40,500 households across seven regions through resilience and livelihood activities, including climate-smart agriculture, irrigation, market systems and nutrition-sensitive livelihoods.

title: WFP Venezuela Earthquakes Response Situation Report, 23 July 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

One month after the earthquakes in Venezuela, access to food remains one of the top concerns for families across the affected areas.

WFP has reached more than 120,000 people with food assistance through four modalities, since no two families are living through this period the same way. Assistance include hot meals in shelters, ready-to-eat rations for those still on the move, food baskets for households that can still cook and in communities who lost their sources of income, and prepaid electronic vouchers in areas where markets are functioning, giving families the power to prioritize their own needs.

The agency is also serving as the logistics backbone of the humanitarian response, moving relief supplies into hard-to-reach communities. WFP's logistics services have supported NGOs and UN agencies with the transport and storage of supplies spanning shelter, health, protection, and WASH.

To date, WFP has secured one third of the USD 80 million required to sustain and scale the response. Efforts continue to close the gap and safeguard the support for 500,000 people in 3 months.

title: WFP Palestine Emergency Response External Situation Report #93, 24 July 2026 (Reporting period: 1-15 July 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Funding shortfalls are impacting WFP’s ability to meet significant humanitarian needs. From July, WFP will provide monthly cash assistance to 100,000 households through a revised, vulnerability-based approach, maintaining full transfers to the most vulnerable households and reduced transfers for others, which will help extend available cash assistance through late November.
  • Additional funding is urgently needed to prevent further reductions in food assistance. Without new contributions, in-kind assistance, which is already being provided at a 75 percent ration, will be reduced from October, with fewer people receiving reduced rations.
  • Newly released IPC analysis shows improvements in food security and child nutrition across Gaza, however progress remains fragile, with the improvements driven largely by expanded humanitarian food, nutrition and health interventions rather than a recovery of livelihoods, local food systems or essential services.

title: Ukraine Situation: Moldova - Operational Update (June 2026)
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT

As of June 2026, 141,528 refugees from Ukraine are in the Republic of Moldova, many of whom continue to face challenges in meeting basic needs and achieving self-reliance. While the Temporary Protection (TP) holders retain access to primary healthcare services and family doctors, access to specialized health care and essential medicines has deteriorated. The latest Participatory Assessment found that 20 per cent of refugee households identify healthcare as an urgent need, while 31 per cent require more information on available medical services. These challenges are largely driven by the closure or scale-down of humanitarian health and cash assistance programmes and the lack of corresponding government funding to absorb these services into national systems, leaving many vulnerable refugees to cover consultation, treatment and medication costs out of pocket.

Economic inclusion remains a significant challenge. Participatory Assessment findings show that only 20 per cent of surveyed refugees are employed and 1 per cent are self-employed, despite a strong willingness to work. Language barriers, skills mismatch, caregiving responsibilities and limited access to suitable jobs continue to constrain labour market participation, particularly among women, older people, and persons with disabilities, highlighting the need for targeted employment support measures.

title: WFP Sao Tome and Principe Country Brief, July 2026

title: Ivory Coast Cholera - DREF Final Report (MDRCI018)
content:
Description of the Event
Date when the trigger was met
01-08-2025
What happened, where and when?

On 5 June 2025, health authorities confirmed a cholera outbreak in the village of Vridi Ako (also referred to in some early alerts as Ako Brakré), located in the Port-Bouët Vridi health district of Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire. The area, home to approximately 19,800 inhabitants—mainly fishing communities and migrants—has long been vulnerable to waterborne diseases due to poor sanitation, limited access to safe drinking water, and recurrent flooding.

While the first confirmed cases were reported in early June in Vridi Ako, retrospective epidemiological investigations indicated that alertsignals and suspected cases had already emerged in late May, explaining the discrepancy in reported start dates across different reportsand surveillance updates.

Following confirmation of the outbreak in Vridi Ako, the situation evolved rapidly from a localized outbreak into a multi-district epidemic. Within days, additional cases were reported beyond the initial epicentre, first spreading to nearby peri-urban and coastal areas, and subsequently extending to five additional health districts: Yopougon Est, Jacqueville, Sassandra, Fresco, and San Pedro. This marked a clear transition from a concentrated outbreak in Port-Bouët Vridi to a wider geographic spread affecting both urban and coastal periurban settings.

The epidemiological curve showed two distinct phases of transmission intensity. The first peak occurred in June, concentrated in Vridi Ako, reflecting rapid local transmission driven by environmental contamination and high population mobility. A second and more geographically dispersed peak followed in July, associated with the emergence of new transmission hotspots in Yopougon Est and Sassandra, indicating secondary spread and establishment of additional foci outside the initial epicentre. A particularly high-risk cluster was also identified in a detention centre in Abidjan, where overcrowding and inadequate sanitation conditions accelerated transmission dynamics.

This escalation from a single-community outbreak to a multi-district epidemic required a corresponding scale-up of the response. As an auxiliary to public authorities, the Red Cross Society of Côte d’Ivoire initially supported rapid needs and situation assessments during the first alerts in late May and early June, leveraging pre-positioned volunteers in Vridi Ako. As the outbreak expanded geographically and intensified during the July peak, the National Society scaled up operations across affected districts, reinforcing its WASH activities, health interventions, and risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) to address both containment in the original hotspot and prevention of further spread in newly affected areas.

Despite continued transmission over several months, the outbreak gradually declined after the second peak. On 1 December 2025, the Ministry of Health and Public Hygiene officially declared the end of the outbreak across all six affected health districts. In total, 556 cases and 24 deaths were reported over the course of the epidemic.

By the end of the operation, no new cholera cases were being reported, and the Ministry of Health and Public Hygiene officially declared the end of the outbreak on 1 December 2025. Transmission had been interrupted across all six affected health districts.

However, important vulnerabilities remained in the affected communities, which continue to face overcrowding, recurrent flooding, inadequate sanitation, and limited access to safe water. Communities also expressed continued socio-economic needs and requested sustained support beyond the emergency phase.

While health facilities resumed normal operations, many still faced shortages of medical supplies and equipment. To support preparedness, first-contact health centres in all affected districts were provided by CRCI with essential medical and hygiene supplies, including chlorine and soap during this operation to ensure sustainability of interventions beyond the outbreak.

As part of the exit strategy, trained teams in the Abidjan detention centre remained operational and continued implementing disinfection activities using equipment provided by CRCI and the ICRC.

In addition, recognizing the socio-economic impact of the epidemic, CRCI mobilized complementary funding to provide cash assistance to vulnerable households in Vridi Ako in February 2026, ahead of the Lent and Ramadan periods.
